https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Michigan High School Athletic Association Representative Council meeting held in East Lansing on May 3, 2021, distributed to member districts with the instruction that changes take effect Aug. 1, 2021 unless otherwise indicated. The Council adopted rule changes across regulations, officiating, and individual sports, including a move of all fall high school practice starts to Monday, Aug. 9, 2021, permanent authorization of multi-school district cooperative programs in nine sports, adoption of girls wrestling as an individual division, and a CPR certification attestation for head coaches. It also approved the 2021-22 budget, which forecasts an addition in cash of $818,301.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Meeting**
MHSAA Representative Council, East Lansing, May 3, 2021. Mark Uyl served as recorder. Eighteen Council members were present (including Eric Albright of Midland, Nicole Carter of Novi, Karen Leinaar of Bear Lake, Vic Michaels of Detroit, and Alex Tiseo of Marquette); Jay Alexander of Detroit was absent. Scott Eldridge and Bill Zaagman of Lansing also attended. Minutes of the March 26, 2021 Council meeting and the March 25 and April 21, 2021 Executive Committee meetings were approved on a motion by Kris Isom, supported by Chris Miller.

**Administration report**

| Measure | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| High school members, 2020-21 (as of April 1, 2021) | 747 |
| Junior high/middle school members (as of April 1, 2021) | 751 |
| Comparable figures as of April 1, 2019 | 753 and 819 |
| Elementary schools with 6th-grade participation | 69 |
| High school cooperative agreements / teams (as of April 4, 2019) | 355 / 640 |
| Junior high-middle school cooperative agreements / teams | 86 / 330 |
| Eligibility advancement applications, 2020-21 | 0 (lowest since 1987-88; high was 94 in 1991-92) |
| Educational Transfer Forms, 2020-21 through April 5, 2021 | 110 (213 in 2019-20; 266 in 2015-16) |
| Out-of-State Practice travel forms, 2020-21 | 6 (72 prior year) |
| Athletic Director In-Service/Update registrants | more than 732 |
| Coaches Advancement Program participants, 2021-22 | more than 2,000, with over 1,200 in CAP 1 |

Public-to-public transfers were the most common category (67) and the divorce exception (#8) the most frequent reason (40). More than 33,000 CAP levels will have been completed since the start of 2004-05. Officials' registrations continued a decade-long decline.

**Ongoing business**
A task force was formed to meet three times over spring and summer on out-of-season contact days. The waiver of the previous academic record regulation (Regulation I, Section 7) was extended for fall 2021 sports. All fall high school practices move to Monday, Aug. 9, 2021, and thereafter to the 16th Monday before Thanksgiving. Multi-school district cooperative programs in baseball, bowling, girls competitive cheer, cross country, golf, soccer, girls softball, tennis, and wrestling were made permanent notwithstanding the 3,500-student enrollment maximum.

**Regulations**
The Council voted not to print the 2021-22 Handbook, providing a password-protected online version instead. It amended Regulation I, Section 4, Interpretation 24 on 8th/9th grade classwork; Regulation I, Section 12(C) on all-star events, requiring written notice at least 30 calendar days prior; and Regulation II, Section 3(B) requiring CPR certification attestation for head coaches, with the non-varsity requirement effective Aug. 1, 2022.

**Sports and officials actions**
Adopted: Phantom bowling oil pattern; competitive cheer choreography study and two technical changes; sideline officials switching sides at halftime; iWanamaker golf scoring; a black quarter-zip option for gymnastics officials; a softball suspended-game policy mirroring baseball's 2020 policy; a 117-game daily tennis limit and revised seed-withdrawal handling; girls wrestling as an individual division (D1, D2, D3, D4, Girls); and a late arrival skin check. Not approved: expansion of the football 5-quarter rule, playoff region seeding by playoff points, and a tennis opt-up letter requirement. The officials rating system replaces the 1-5 scale with four categories, and baseball Quarterfinal assignments move to four umpires, increasing umpires selected at that level by 16.

**Budget and future meetings**
Two budget deficits in excess of $670,000 occurred in two of the past four years. The 2021-22 budget forecasts an addition in cash of $818,301 and a profit of $318,301 after repayment of the line-of-credit loan; salaries remain frozen. Next meetings: Dec. 3, 2021; Friday, March 25, 2022; and May 1-2, 2022, the latter to be held at Treetops Resort in Gaylord.

Accounts of Meetings. Motion by Kris Isom, supported by Chris Miller, to approve the minutes of the Representative Council meeting of March 26, 2021, and the Executive Committee meeting minutes of March 25 and April 21, 2021. Adopted.

Administration report. MHSAA membership during 2020-21 was 747 high schools and 751 junior high/middle schools as of April 1, 2021, compared with 753 and 819 respectively as of April 1, 2019. There were also 69 elementary schools with 6th-grader participation. As of April 4, 2019 there were 355 cooperative program agreements for high schools covering 640 teams, an increase of 16 programs and 33 teams over the previous year, and 86 cooperative program agreements covering 330 teams for junior high/middle schools, an increase of 1 program and 5 teams. The most frequent high school cooperative sports, in order, are ice hockey, boys and girls swimming and diving, girls softball, and boys lacrosse; at the junior high/middle school level they are boys and girls track and field, boys and girls cross country, and wrestling. No eligibility advancement applications were received during 2020-21, the lowest number since the provision began in 1987-88, compared with 3 during 2019-20, 3 during 2018-19, 6 during 2017-18, 5 during 2016-17, 5 during 2015-16, 4 during 2014-15, 14 during 2013-14, 15 during 2012-13, 9 during 2011-12, 15 during 2010-11, 2009-10 and 2008-09, and 7 during 2007-08; the highest was 94 during 1991-92. There were 110 Educational Transfer Forms processed for 2020-21 through April 5, 2021, a figure the report says cannot be compared to prior years because of the pandemic and because all spring sports transfers were eligible in 2020-21; prior-year counts were 213 for 2019-20, 215 for 2018-19, 219 for 2017-18, 237 for 2016-17, and 266 for 2015-16. Public-to-public school transfers remain the most common at 67, and the divorce exception (#8) remains the most frequent reason at 40. Six Travel Forms for Out-of-State Practice were filed during 2020-21 compared to 72 the year before; the highest number filed was 113 during 2007-08 and the lowest 40 during 2003-04, with the requirement beginning in 1994-95. A listing of violations by schools and officials between April 9, 2020 and April 8, 2021 showed a total much lower than previous years because of cancelled contests and seasons. Virtual Athletic Director In-Service and Update Meeting programs attracted more than 732 registrants in 2020-21; for the 11th year, two in-service programs for athletic department administrative assistants are planned for September. The Coaches Advancement Program has already involved more than 2,000 participants in 2021-22 with over 1,200 registrations in CAP 1, and by the end of the year individuals will have completed more than 33,000 CAP levels since the start of 2004-05. The decade-long decline in officials' registrations continued through 2020-21, with the pandemic complicating recruiting and retention. Officials Reports for spring 2020, fall 2020, and winter 2020-21 were provided, broken down by sport and by level (varsity, junior varsity, and sometimes 9th, 8th, and 7th grade); sportsmanship problems were described as statistically rare. From the National Federation of State High School Associations, the Reaching Higher event in girls volleyball will not be held in summer 2021, with final decisions on basketball summer plans due by May 15.

Legislation and litigation. Bill Zaagman reported that the State Legislature's current focus is the budget process and that he will continue monitoring bills affecting the association. Scott Eldridge reported the MHSAA is not involved in public, legislative, or judicial challenges, and provided an update on recent COVID-19 legal activity involving MDHHS and local health departments.

Ongoing business. On the COVID-19 update, the Council discussed the financial impact of the pandemic and the formation of a task force to meet three times during spring and summer to discuss out-of-season contact days and develop concrete proposals for school discussion and input during fall 2021. Staff will send a summer guidance document reminding schools that the traditional summer dead period regulation remains in place. Motion by Vic Michaels, supported by John Thompson, to extend the waiver of the previous academic record regulation (Regulation I, Section 7) for sports played in fall 2021. Adopted. On the common fall practice date, motion by Chris Miller, supported by Eric Albright, to move the start of all fall high school sports practices to Monday, Aug. 9, 2021; beginning in fall 2021 all high school fall sports may begin practice on the 16th Monday before Thanksgiving, the same as football. Adopted. Staff provided a volleyball scheduling update on input from administrators and coaches regarding the MHSAA Finals and the length of the season, noting the issue also involves the start date of winter sports. On multi-school district cooperative programs, the Council recalled that in May 2016 it approved a two-year experiment, extended for two additional school years through 2020-21, allowing two or more schools of the same public school district with the same governing board to apply for cooperative programs in nine sports regardless of the 3,500-student enrollment maximum: baseball, bowling, girls competitive cheer, cross country, golf, soccer, girls softball, tennis, and wrestling, subject to a demonstrated history of inadequate participant numbers and not approvable on financial grounds. Motion by Vic Michaels, supported by Karen Leinaar, to approve these programs on a permanent basis with the same requirements as all other programs, including the two-year renewal process with league approval. Adopted. Fall Tour planning anticipates a normal Update tour with remote alternatives, covering lessons of the pandemic in remote learning and instruction, potential use of school transportation in the summer, classification and cooperative program limits, out-of-season regulations, basketball contest limitations, and the length of the girls volleyball and basketball seasons.

Regulations. Regulations I through V of the MHSAA Handbook and their interpretations were submitted for review. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Jason Mensing, to not print the MHSAA Handbook for the 2021-22 school year only and to provide an online password-protected version for administrators, with a printed and emailed supplement of changes and calendars for 2021-22 and beyond also placed online and provided to schools. Adopted. Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Steve Newkirk, to approve the consent package of miscellaneous changes for organization, clarity, or updating and to incorporate previously adopted changes or interpretations. Adopted. Regulation I, Section 4, Interpretation 24: motion by John Thompson, supported by Jason Mensing, addressing students whose classwork is divided between the 8th and 9th grades, who are considered enrolled in the grade where they take the major part of their work in that term, with ties resolved to the 8th grade; a student who has completed the 7th grade at any school may be considered an 8th grader if the student does not exceed the enrollment threshold of Interpretation 46, namely enrollment in 3 high school classes of 4 taken in the 8th grade, 4 or 5 of 6, 5 of 7, or 6 of 8; this 66% allowance applies only to a student enrolled for the first time in the 8th grade and not to a student repeating the 8th grade, and a student not in the 9th grade or higher is ineligible for senior high athletics except as provided in Regulation I, Section 1(D) and Regulation III, Section 2(B). Adopted. Regulation I, Section 12(C): motion by Chris Riker, supported by Chris Miller, allowing a student who has completed a 12th-grade season in a sport to participate without loss of eligibility for other sports in one high school all-star event in that sport held after the MHSAA Final, provided the student is eligible under all MHSAA regulations including academic eligibility and amateur status, the event requires or receives no financial support from an MHSAA member school or school-related organization, and participation is approved by the principal or athletic director with written notice to the MHSAA at least 30 calendar days prior to the event. Adopted. Regulation II, Section 3(B): motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Kris Isom, requiring high schools to attest by each season's established deadline that all head coaches of each high school team (varsity, JV, or 9th grade) hold valid current CPR certification, with the requirement for non-varsity head coaches taking effect Aug. 1, 2022; the deadline is the latest date set for completion of the MHSAA rules meeting for the sport, a person who is head coach for more than one sport must meet the deadline for the first, and schools are expected to impose the penalty of Section 8(B) on varsity head coaches who do not comply, extended effective Aug. 1, 2022 to JV and 9th-grade coaches. Adopted. The Council also discussed extending the requirement to middle schools and was updated on a fall discussion item allowing school transportation for out-of-season summer activities.

Classification, athletic equity, and officials. The Summary of MHSAA Tournament Classification for 2021-22 was provided, with future committee topics to include a possible fifth division in sports where 600 or more schools sponsor the sport. Motion by Chris Miller, supported by Chris Riker, to approve the Athletic Equity Committee recommendation to publish a statement encouraging local review of nicknames and logos considered offensive or hurtful to minority groups, stating that the MHSAA recognizes the importance of equity in high school sports, that schools and mascots are rich in tradition and unique to each community, and that the MHSAA encourages member schools and communities to evaluate and reconsider names and mascots that may be offensive. Adopted; schools will be encouraged to review the information at fall Update and Athletic Director In-Service sessions, and the Council discussed a possible sanction of barring such schools from hosting tournaments. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Jason Mensing, to adjust the officials rating system for 2021-22 to encourage more ratings from schools with a simpler format, eliminating the 1-5 rating in favor of four categories: judgement, presence and demeanor, attitude and effort, and administration and communication. Adopted. Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Chris Miller, to change baseball umpire assignments at the Quarterfinal round from three umpires officiating three games with two umpires each to four umpires officiating the two Regional Final games with two umpires and the Quarterfinal game with all four, increasing the number of umpires selected at this level by 16 and matching softball practice. Adopted.

Sports Medicine and committees. The Sports Medicine Advisory Committee reported ongoing discussion of providing the Pre-participation Physical Exam on a two-year cycle with an interim Health Questionnaire in intervening years, noting that health history is the most important part of the exam and that the Health Questionnaire was established with good results in 2020-21. Council members were supplied with committee descriptions, appointment procedures, candidate lists, and a list of schools unrepresented for five years, and were encouraged to nominate superintendents, principals, small schools, females, minorities, and unrepresented schools. Committee members for 2021-22 will be published in benchmarks, and staff suggested all committee meetings remain virtual for 2021-22.

Sports activities. Bowling: motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Don Gustafson, to adopt the Phantom oil pattern for the 2021-22 bowling season. Adopted. Girls competitive cheer: motion by Kris Isom, supported by Vic Michaels, to continue studying a new choreography chart awarding points based on team tumble, OLEs, vertical twist/360s, and release skills. Adopted. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Nicole Carter, to allow a connected tumbling skill to count as a new variety point for Round 3 and to allow four difficulty points for a one-leg flair at the elevator level for middle schools. Adopted. Football: motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Eric Albright, to not approve expanding the 5-quarter rule to exempt special teams play. Adopted (no change). Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Kris Isom, requiring sideline officials (linesman and line judge) to change sidelines at halftime for all varsity contests, optional at subvarsity. Adopted. Motion by Don Gustafson, supported by Chris Miller, to not approve seeding Playoff Regions based on playoff points. Adopted (no change). Golf: motion by John Thompson, supported by Karen Leinaar, requiring use of the iWanamaker scoring program and app during the regular season beginning in 2021-22. Adopted. Girls gymnastics: motion by John Thompson, supported by Karen Leinaar, adding an option for officials to wear a specified black quarter-zip with the MHSAA logo. Adopted. Boys lacrosse: a committee recommendation on voluntary coach/player contact days was referred to the task force created under the COVID-19 update for review prior to August 2021. Softball: motion by Don Gustafson, supported by John Thompson, adding a suspended game policy under which a game is suspended if called before reaching regulation or if called with the score tied, mirroring the baseball policy approved in 2020. Adopted. Tennis: motion by Vic Michaels, supported by Kris Isom, limiting a player to no more than 117 games in a given day. Adopted. Motion by Chris Riker, supported by Don Gustafson, on adjusting seeds when a seeded player withdraws on the day of the tournament. Adopted. Motion by John Thompson, supported by Karen Leinaar, to not approve requiring a letter when a school opts up in tennis. Adopted (no change). Wrestling: motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Kris Isom, adding girls wrestling as an individual division rather than a new sport (D1, D2, D3, D4, Girls) using a sectionals concept with a qualifying event before the Finals, with girls still allowed to wrestle on boys teams during the team postseason. Adopted. Motion by John Thompson, supported by Don Gustafson, approving a late arrival skin check for multiple dual meets in the regular season. Adopted.

Operations. Motion by Chris Miller, supported by Jason Mensing, to approve the Quick Reference Calendars for 2021-22 and 2022-23 and the seven-year calendar of MHSAA events. Adopted. Council members were invited to vote for up to two Allen W. Bush Award candidates from the five presented, with winners notified in May, honored during fall 2021 or early 2022, and featured in the fall issue of benchmarks. The next Representative Council meeting is Dec. 3, 2021 at the MHSAA office in East Lansing; the March meeting will be the morning of Friday, March 25, 2022 in East Lansing; and the May meeting will be Sunday and Monday, May 1 and 2, 2022. Motion by Sean Jacques, supported by Karen Leinaar, to hold the May 2022 meeting at Treetops Resort in Gaylord. Adopted.

Budget. The report states that since COVID hit in March 2020 the association has managed unprecedented times with severe reductions in tournament revenue, aided by the sacrifices of member schools and tournament hosts in 2020-21. While two installments of the federal Payroll Protection program have been helpful, the reality of two budget deficits in excess of $670,000 in two of the past four years still exists. The 2021-22 budget proposes a modest increase in most ticket prices beyond the entry level of the tournament, allowing prompt repayment of a line-of-credit loan and rebuilding of reserves. The MHSAA anticipates a break-even 2020-21 fiscal year with an average spring tournament season. Staff salaries will remain frozen for 2021-22, including the hiring of three new staff members following the retirements of Nate Hampton and Peggy Montpas and the departure of Faye Verellen. The 2021-22 budget forecasts an addition in cash of $818,301 and a profit of $318,301 after repayment of the line-of-credit loan from last spring and fall. Motion by Karen Leinaar, supported by Kris Isom, to approve the 2021-22 budget. Adopted.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Summary of the Michigan High School Athletic Association's Athletes and Officials Accident Medical and Concussion Care insurance programs distributed to high schools and junior high/middle schools for 2020-21. The accident medical policy, provided at no cost since the 1970-71 school year, pays up to $1,000,000 in medical expenses per claim after a $25,000 deductible in paid medical expenses has been met. A separate concussion care program in place since 2015-16 carries a policy limit of $25,000 for each accident and reimburses deductibles and co-pays left unpaid by other coverage.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Program overview**
Since the 1970-71 school year the MHSAA has provided participants at each member school and all registered officials with insurance intended to help pay excess accident medical bills for injuries sustained in athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. The MHSAA is the policyholder and pays the premium; coverage is provided at no cost to eligible athletes of member schools and to registered officials. The document states it is not intended to be a complete description of coverage and exclusions.

**Who and what is covered**
Coverage applies to grades 6-12 for students accidentally injured while engaged in interscholastic athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction, namely baseball, basketball (boys and girls), bowling (boys and girls), cross country (boys and girls), football, golf (boys and girls), gymnastics (girls), competitive cheer (girls), ice hockey, lacrosse (boys and girls), soccer (boys and girls), softball (girls), alpine skiing (boys and girls), swimming and diving (boys and girls), tennis (boys and girls), track and field (boys and girls), volleyball (girls), and wrestling. Students are covered in sports ending with an MHSAA tournament provided their principal attests in writing and the MHSAA agrees they were eligible under all MHSAA regulations at the time of injury. Coverage extends to travel directly to and from a scheduled event in school-sponsored transportation and to in-season participation in an allowed activity under the direct supervision of a full-time school employee or designated coach.

**Exclusions and edge cases**
Student-athletes ineligible under MHSAA regulations are not covered. Students ineligible under local school rules but eligible under MHSAA rules are covered if allowed to practice with the team, as are students suspended from contests under Regulation V, Section 3 who continue practicing. Officials must be on the premises of the contest worked. Sideline cheerleaders are covered while traveling in school-sponsored transportation and while cheering under supervision of a designated school employee, provided their activity does not exceed the safety norms of MHSAA Girls Competitive Cheer. The insurance does not cover any out-of-season activities or activities occurring beyond the mileage limits of Regulation II, Section 6, Interpretation 193, even if not expressly prohibited.

**Accident medical benefits**

| Benefit | Amount / condition |
| --- | --- |
| Medical expense limit | up to $1,000,000 per claim |
| Deductible | $25,000 in paid medical expenses per claim |
| Paralysis or coma cash benefit | up to $50,000, if occurring within 180 days after the accident |
| Certification waiting period | physician certifies permanence after a 16-month waiting period |
| First medical expense | must be incurred within 90 days after the accident |
| Accidental death or dismemberment | $10,000 if the event occurs within 365 days |

The MHSAA-arranged program pays medical expenses above the $25,000 deductible left unpaid by parents' or officials' insurance or other sources such as school-purchased insurance.

**Concussion care insurance**
Provided since the 2015-16 school year to athletic participants at each MHSAA member junior high/middle school and high school, paying accident medical expense benefits resulting from concussion sustained while participating in an MHSAA in-season covered activity (in-season practice or competition). Policy limit is $25,000 for each accident, with covered students, sports, and situations following the accident medical insurance. The program is intended to assure that all eligible student-athletes in grades 6 through 12, male and female, in all levels of all sports under MHSAA jurisdiction receive prompt professional attention for head injury events even if uninsured or under-insured.

**Claims administrators**
Accident medical: Mr. Bryan Cronen, FIRST AGENCY, INC., 5071 West H Avenue, Kalamazoo, MI 49009-8501, phone 269.381.6630, fax 269.381.3055, bcronen@1stagency.com. Concussion care: Ms. Terri Bruner, K & K Insurance Group, 1712 Magnavox Way, Fort Wayne, IN 46801, phone 800-237-2917, fax 312-381-9077, Terri.Bruner@kandkinsurance.com. Districts are advised to make sure all high schools and junior high/middle schools are designated by their board of education as MHSAA member schools so athletes at both levels are covered by the MHSAA-purchased plan.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Informational summary titled "Athletes and Officials Accident Medical & Concussion Insurance," issued by the Michigan High School Athletic Association to high schools and junior high/middle schools for the 2020-21 school year. The document carries the caveat that it is not intended to be a complete description of coverage and exclusions.

History and purpose. Since the 1970-71 school year the MHSAA has provided participants at each member school and all registered officials with insurance intended to help pay excess accident medical bills to administer to injuries sustained in athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. The MHSAA is the policyholder and pays the premium for this layer of accident medical coverage, and the coverage is provided at no cost to the eligible athletes of MHSAA member schools and to registered officials.

Scope of covered activity. Coverage is provided for grades 6-12 for all students accidentally injured while engaged in interscholastic athletic activities under MHSAA jurisdiction. The enumerated sports are baseball; basketball (boys and girls); bowling (boys and girls); cross country (boys and girls); football; golf (boys and girls); gymnastics (girls); competitive cheer (girls); ice hockey; lacrosse (boys and girls); soccer (boys and girls); softball (girls); alpine skiing (boys and girls); swimming and diving (boys and girls); tennis (boys and girls); track and field (boys and girls); volleyball (girls); and wrestling.

Eligibility conditions. All eligible students who participate in interscholastic athletic activities at an MHSAA member school in sports which end with an MHSAA tournament are covered provided their school principal attests in writing and the MHSAA agrees that they were eligible under all MHSAA regulations at the time of the injury. Eligible student athletes are covered while traveling directly to and from a scheduled event as a representative of the school in transportation sponsored by the school, and while participating in season in an allowed activity under the direct supervision of a full-time school employee or a coach designated by the school acting within the scope of his or her coaching duties, in those sports for which the MHSAA provides a tournament series.

Ineligibility and special cases. Student-athletes ineligible under MHSAA regulations are not covered. Students who are ineligible under local school rules but would be eligible under MHSAA rules are covered if they were allowed to practice with their school team. Students who are otherwise eligible but suspended from contests under Regulation V, Section 3 (contest disqualifications) are covered if they continue practicing with the school team. Officials must be on the premises of the contest worked to be covered under the policy. Sideline cheerleaders are covered while traveling directly to and from interscholastic athletic events as a representative of the school in school-sponsored transportation, and while cheering at interscholastic athletic events under the direct supervision of a school employee designated by the school; to be covered by MHSAA-purchased insurance, the activity of sideline cheerleaders at interscholastic athletic events must not exceed the safety norms of MHSAA Girls Competitive Cheer, meaning the height of mounts, flips, stunts, and similar elements. The document states in emphasized text that MHSAA Accident Medical Insurance does not cover any out-of-season activities or any activities occurring beyond the mileage limits of Regulation II, Section 6, Interpretation 193, even if those activities are not expressly prohibited by the MHSAA.

Accident medical benefit structure. The policy will pay up to $1,000,000 in medical expenses after a deductible of $25,000 in paid medical expenses per claim has been met. The MHSAA-arranged program then pays medical expenses above the $25,000 deductible left unpaid by the parents' or official's insurance or any other sources such as school-purchased insurance. A cash benefit payment of up to $50,000 will be made if a covered person is paralyzed or in a coma within 180 days after the accident; payment will not be made until a physician certifies that, after a 16-month waiting period, the injury is permanent and irreversible, and this payment must result in disability and is in addition to payments already covered for medical expenses. The first medical expense must be incurred within 90 days after the date of the accident. An accidental death or dismemberment benefit of $10,000 is paid if either event occurs within 365 days of the date.

Accident medical claims administration. The claims administrator is Mr. Bryan Cronen, FIRST AGENCY, INC., 5071 West H Avenue, Kalamazoo, MI 49009-8501, phone 269.381.6630, fax 269.381.3055, email bcronen@1stagency.com.

District action item. The document instructs in emphasized text that districts make sure all high schools and junior high/middle schools in the district are designated by their board of education as MHSAA member schools so athletes on both levels are covered by the MHSAA-purchased plan.

Concussion care insurance. Since the 2015-16 school year the MHSAA has provided athletic participants at each MHSAA member junior high/middle school and high school with insurance intended to pay accident medical expense benefits resulting from concussion. The suspected concussion must be sustained while the athlete is participating in an MHSAA in-season covered activity, defined as in-season practice or competition. The policy limit is $25,000 for each accident. Covered students, sports, and situations follow those of the accident medical insurance described above. The program intends to assure that all eligible student-athletes in MHSAA member schools in grades 6 through 12, male and female, in all levels of all sports under MHSAA jurisdiction receive prompt and professional attention for head injury events even if the child is uninsured or under-insured, and accident medical deductibles and co-pays left unpaid by other policies are reimbursed under this program.

Concussion claims administration. The claims administrator is Ms. Terri Bruner, K & K Insurance Group, 1712 Magnavox Way, Fort Wayne, IN 46801, phone 800-237-2917, fax 312-381-9077, email Terri.Bruner@kandkinsurance.com.

The district served 12,723 students in 20 schools and closed the year with a governmental-activities net position deficit of $(201,057,958), reflecting a net pension liability of $308,094,061 and a net OPEB liability of $48,088,931 under MPSERS. The most consequential operating result was in the General Fund, where fund balance increased $6.7 million to $32,734,102, a sixth consecutive year of growth, leaving the available (unassigned) balance at 19.88 percent of 2021 general operating expenditures.

**Statement of activities**
Total expenses were $203,874,829: instruction $120,915,752, support services $67,702,339, community services $6,324,376, interest $4,533,849, food services $2,416,697, athletics $1,700,708, and other debt costs $281,108. Charges for services totaled $1,802,535 and operating grants and contributions $52,855,894, leaving net expense of $(149,216,400). General revenue of $144,318,096 included property taxes of $39,308,501 for general purposes, $17,345,162 for debt service, and $4,152,751 for capital projects, plus $81,687,900 of unrestricted state aid. Change in net position was $(4,898,304).

**Fund results**
Governmental funds ended with a combined fund balance of $57,844,378, a decrease of $6.2 million. Special revenue fund balance rose from $2.8 million to $3.1 million; debt service funds fell $1.2 million; capital project funds fell $12.1 million. Sinking fund millage collections were $4.1 million.

**Budget**
The final General Fund budget was amended in June 2021, raising budgeted revenue $21.7 million. Bonds outstanding were $130,280,000 plus $7,678,963 of unamortized premium. The district issued $40,425,000 of refunding bonds and advance refunded $37,860,000 of 2012 and 2014 bonds, reducing debt service over seven years by approximately $4,064,000 for an economic gain of about $2,559,000. Standard & Poor's affirmed the AA/Stable rating in May 2021.

**Pension and OPEB**
Pension contributions were $27,611,786 (including $11,658,202 of state UAAL stabilization funding) and OPEB contributions $6,980,805. Pension expense was $47,852,726; OPEB recovery was $860,940.

**Item:** 8.C. Bond Resolution (SBQLP) - Troy 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds, document 44944687.1, before the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, at a regular meeting held in the School District on November 18, 2025 at 7:00 p.m. local time. The certification page carries the signature block of Emina Alic, Secretary, Board of Education, with an Open Meetings Act (Act 267, Public Acts of 1976) compliance certificate. The adoption blanks for PRESENT, ABSENT, the offering and supporting members, and the AYES/NAYS tallies are unfilled in this draft.

**Authorization background**

- At the General School Election of November 8, 2022, electors approved bonds in one or more series not to exceed $555,000,000 for remodeling and re-equipping school buildings, athletic fields and playgrounds; erecting a replacement middle school and classroom additions; instructional technology infrastructure; site acquisition and improvement; and the purchase of school buses.
- Tax levies are without limitation as to rate or amount under Article IX, Sections 6 and 16 of the Michigan Constitution of 1963.
- The first series, the 2023 School Building and Site Bonds dated March 7, 2023, was issued in the original principal amount of $171,370,000 with net original issue premium of $18,629,212.85, which counts against the $555,000,000 authorization.

**Sale parameters**

| Parameter | Limit |
| --- | --- |
| Aggregate principal amount | not to exceed $220,000,000 |
| New money (Projects) portion | not to exceed $193,000,000 |
| True interest cost | not to exceed 5.50% per annum |
| Underwriter's discount | not to exceed 0.75% of principal |
| Net present value refunding savings threshold | at least 3.00% |
| Final maturity | not later than 30 years from date of issue |
| Denomination | $5,000 or integral multiples |

If the Authorized Officer, on the Municipal Advisor's advice, determines the net present value savings on the refunding falls below 3.00%, the district may instead issue up to $193,000,000 of new money only, redesignated 2026 School Building and Site Bonds.

**Professionals and structure**

**Funds created:** 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Debt Retirement Fund, Capital Projects Fund, Cost of Issuance Fund, and an Escrow Fund held by an Escrow Agent under an Escrow Agreement to pay the Refunded Bonds.

**Other provisions:** unlimited tax levy duty commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2026; Treasury qualification under the School Bond Qualification, Approval, and Loan Act, Act 92, Public Acts of Michigan, 2005; reimbursement declarations under Treas. Reg. Section 1.150-2 with maximum debt for the Projects stated as $193,000,000; and a continuing disclosure undertaking under SEC Rule 15c2-12 with first filing for the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Resolution of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, authorizing the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), presented as agenda item 8.C. and identified as document 44944687.1. It is offered at a regular meeting held in the School District on November 18, 2025, at 7:00 p.m., local time; the lines for PRESENT and ABSENT members, for the offering and supporting members, and for the AYES and NAYS tallies remain blank in the version presented. The closing certification, signed by Emina Alic, Secretary, Board of Education, attests that the copy is true and complete and that notice was given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of 1976, as amended.

RECITALS. At the General School Election held in the School District on November 8, 2022, qualified electors approved the issuance of bonds, in one or more series, in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000 (the 2022 Bond Proposal), for remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields and playgrounds; erecting, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; acquiring and improving sites; and the purchase of school buses (the Projects). Under Section 6, Article IX and Section 16, Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, the tax levies for those bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount. The School District previously issued its 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated March 7, 2023, in the original principal amount of $171,370,000 as the first series under the 2022 Bond Proposal; because of prevailing market conditions those bonds were issued with net original issue premium of $18,629,212.85, which counts against the $555,000,000 authorization. The Board now desires to authorize a second series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $193,000,000 to pay Project costs and a portion of issuance costs. Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, permits refunding of funded indebtedness; the School District previously issued its 2016 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated December 28, 2016 (the Prior Bonds), and the Board determines it is in the district's best interest to currently refund all or a portion of the Prior Bonds maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032, inclusive (the Refunded Bonds). Because the source of payment is the same and to reduce issuance and administration cost, the Board combines the new money and refunding issues into a single series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000 while maintaining a separate capital projects fund for the Projects. If market interest rates rise so that the refunding becomes noneconomic or inefficient, the Board retains the option of authorizing only the $193,000,000 new money issue.

ISSUANCE AND PARAMETERS. The Bonds may be issued in one or more series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000, or such lesser amount as the Authorized Officer determines upon sale, to finance a portion of the Projects, refund the Refunded Bonds, and pay costs of issuance. The Projects portion shall not exceed $193,000,000. If the Authorized Officer, on the advice of the Municipal Advisor, determines that net present value savings from the refinancing are not at least 3.00% of the principal of the Refunded Bonds, the district may issue Bonds of not more than $193,000,000 for the Projects and associated issuance costs only, in which case the Bonds are redesignated 2026 School Building and Site Bonds.

BOND DETAILS. Bonds are registered as to principal and interest in denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of the date of delivery or another date set by the Authorized Officer, and numbered as determined by the Transfer Agent. Maturities fall on May 1 and/or November 1 in years and amounts fixed at sale, with final maturity not later than thirty (30) years from the date of issue. Interest is set at negotiated sale at a rate or rates not exceeding a true interest cost of 5.50% per annum, payable semi-annually on May 1 and November 1. The underwriter's discount shall not exceed 0.75% of principal. Interest is payable by check mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month preceding each payment date. The Bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company in New York, New York, and may be serial or term bonds subject to optional or mandatory redemption. Bonds are signed by manual or facsimile signatures of the President and Secretary of the Board and are not valid until authenticated by the Transfer Agent.

FUNDS. Unless a Common Debt Retirement Fund is established, the Treasurer opens a special depositary account designated the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Debt Retirement Fund, into which all tax proceeds levied for principal, interest and redemption price are deposited, together with any accrued interest received on delivery. A special depository account designated the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Projects Fund (the Capital Projects Fund) receives the amounts specified at sale from net proceeds and net original issue premium, to be used solely for Project costs and, as needed, to rebate arbitrage earnings to the United States Department of Treasury under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended. Costs of issuance are deposited into a separate 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Cost of Issuance Fund; residual balances there are allocated between the Capital Projects Fund and the Debt Retirement Fund on the advice of Bond Counsel. Money remaining in the Capital Projects Fund after completion may be used first for any purpose permitted by the 2022 Bond Proposal and second for any other lawful purpose; net original issue premium attributable to the new money portion counts against the 2022 Bond Proposal authorization. The Escrow Fund holds the balance of proceeds plus moneys transferred from the Prior Bonds debt retirement funds, invested in obligations of or guaranteed by the United States of America sufficient without reinvestment to pay the Refunded Bonds; the Escrow Agent acts under an Escrow Agreement irrevocably directing the call for redemption of the specified Prior Bonds.

TAX LEVY, SALE METHOD AND PROFESSIONALS. Commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2026, the School District must levy annually a tax sufficient to pay principal and interest as due, without limitation as to rate or amount. Having compared competitive and negotiated sale under Act 34 and on the Municipal Advisor's advice, the Board determines that a negotiated sale provides greater flexibility in structuring maturities and timing. Huntington Securities, Inc. is appointed senior managing underwriter, with the Authorized Officer permitted to appoint co-managing underwriters if the Municipal Advisor recommends. The Authorized Officer, defined as the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually, may negotiate, award, execute and deliver the bond purchase agreement without further Board approval provided the true interest cost does not exceed 5.50% per annum, net present value savings are not less than 3.00% of projected debt service on the Refunded Bonds under Treasury guidelines, and the underwriter's discount does not exceed 0.75% of principal. The Authorized Officer may execute a sale order evidencing final terms, apply for bond ratings, and purchase municipal bond insurance if deemed appropriate. Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. is appointed Bond Counsel, approved notwithstanding Miller Canfield's periodic representation in unrelated matters of Huntington Securities, Inc. PFM Financial Advisors LLC is appointed financial advisor (Municipal Advisor). The Authorized Officer may apply to the Michigan Department of Treasury for prior approval or file a qualifying statement, request waivers including rating waivers, file a Security Report under Act 34, and seek qualification under the School Bond Qualification, Approval, and Loan Act, Act 92, Public Acts of Michigan, 2005, as amended; the Secretary of the Board is directed to submit the completed Application for Final Qualification.

TAX AND REIMBURSEMENT MATTERS. The district covenants to maintain the exclusion of interest from adjusted gross income for federal income tax purposes under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. Reimbursement declarations under Treas. Reg. Section 1.150-2 state that the district expects to reimburse itself from bond proceeds for Project expenditures paid subsequent to sixty (60) days prior to the resolution date; that the maximum principal amount of debt expected for the Projects, including issuance costs, is $193,000,000; and that reimbursement allocation will occur not later than 18 months after the later of payment or placed-in-service, and in no event more than three (3) years after the original expenditure. All conflicting resolutions and parts of resolutions are rescinded.

EXHIBITS. Exhibit A is the bond form, showing Registered Owner Cede & Co., interest computed on a 360-day year of twelve 30-day months, issuance under Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended, and Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, pursuant to the resolution adopted November 18, 2025 as the second series authorized by the November 8, 2022 election; redemption notice at least 30 days and not more than 60 days before the redemption date; calls in multiples of $5,000; full faith and credit irrevocably pledged; Certificate of Authentication dated 2026. Exhibit B is the form of Continuing Disclosure Undertaking under SEC Rule 15c2-12, requiring filing with the MSRB through EMMA on or before the last day of the sixth month after fiscal year end, commencing with the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, of Audited Financial Statements and tables covering Historical Enrollment, State Aid Payments, Property Valuations, Major Taxpayers, School District Tax Rates per $1,000 of valuation, Tax Levies and Collections, Contribution to MPSERS, Debt Statement Direct Debt, the School Loan Revolving Fund (SLRF) Program, and the current-year General Fund Budget Summary in Appendix C; it also lists material event notices due within ten business days, including payment delinquencies, defeasances, rating changes, bankruptcy, and incurrence of a Financial Obligation. Exhibit C is the form of Application for Final Qualification of Bonds.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Packet of Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) resolutions distributed for the December 9, 2025 Troy School District Board meeting in advance of the January 9, 2026 OCSBA resolution vote, containing two proposed new resolutions plus the association's continuing resolutions. Under OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, a resolution approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts becomes the official position of the association. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Board meeting:** Troy School District, December 9, 2025.

**Document:** Five-page OCSBA resolutions packet headed "Proposed New Resolutions for January 2026" / "Proposed Amendments for January 2026." OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5 states that resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors.

**Proposed new resolution #1 - Non-partisan school board elections**

OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections. The rationale responds to HB 4588, then moving through the state House (legislature.mi.gov, ObjectName 2025-HB-4588). Partisan elections are argued to decrease the number of willing candidates; increase campaign costs, since members would have to win both a primary and the November election; align local education decisions with party interests rather than student needs; and exclude thousands of current or potential board members, including federal employees legally prohibited from running in partisan races.

**Proposed new resolution #2 - Early On Michigan**

OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or at risk for delays due to certain health conditions. The rationale notes that the Michigan Mandatory Special Education law (MMSE) requires services for eligible children from birth through age 25; IDEA Part B covers ages 3 through 21 and IDEA Part C covers birth through age 2, which Michigan calls Early On; services for ages 22 through 25 fall under MMSE. Early On is coordinated by the Michigan Department of Education, funded to communities through their local Intermediate School District, and guided locally by an interagency coordinating council and memoranda of understanding among education, mental health, public health and social services.

| Early On funding | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Estimated annual cost of high-quality services | $230M |
| Recommended state appropriation (60% of estimated cost) | at least $138M |
| Section 54d, FY26 School Aid Act state funding | $48M |

The rationale also notes 50 years of advocacy for IDEA funding and the congressional promise to fund 40% of the cost of special education, applying to both Part B and Part C.

**Continuing resolutions** (adoption/amendment dates as printed): Accountability and Transparency (adopted 9/24/2019, amended 6/5/2025); Broadband Access and Devices (9/11/2021, amended 6/5/2025); Early Childhood (9/24/2019, amended 6/5/2025); Evidence-Based Decision Making (9/24/2019); Lame Duck (9/24/2019); Local Control (9/24/2019); Mental Health (9/24/2019, amended 6/5/2025); School Aid (9/24/2019, amended 6/5/2025); School Finance Research Collaborative (9/24/2019, amended 9/11/2021, 3/3/2023, 6/5/2025); School Nutrition (3/3/2023, amended 6/5/2025); School Safety (3/3/2023); Special Education (9/24/2019); Teacher Shortages (9/11/2021, amended 6/5/2025); Unfunded Mandates (9/24/2019). Each cites MASB resolution numbers, and the packet closes by endorsing the legislative agendas of NSBA, MASB, the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) and COSSBA when aligned with OCSBA priorities, with links to masb.org/resolutions.aspx, nsba.org/Advocacy and cossba.org/advocacy.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on December 9, 2025.

Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) resolutions packet, five pages, prepared for the association's January 2026 resolution process and circulated to member boards including Troy School District. The header cites OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, Resolution Adoption: resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors. The packet contains two proposed new resolutions followed by the full set of continuing resolutions previously adopted by the membership, each carrying its adoption and amendment dates.

PROPOSED NEW RESOLUTION #1: OCSBA supports non-partisan school board elections. The stated rationale is that the proposal responds to House Bill 4588, then moving through the state House, with the bill link given as https://legislature.mi.gov/Bills/Bill?ObjectName=2025-HB-4588. The packet argues that partisan school board elections will decrease the number of willing candidates; increase campaign costs, because school board members would have to be successful in two elections, a primary election as well as the November election; align local education decisions with party interests rather than student needs; and exclude thousands of current or potential board members, including federal employees, who are legally prohibited from running in partisan races.

PROPOSED NEW RESOLUTION #2: OCSBA supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or who are at risk for delays due to certain health conditions. The rationale states that the resolution is proposed to shine a light on the importance of early intervention programs such as Early On Michigan and on the need for additional state funding to adequately serve families of children already identified as eligible and to serve all children who should be identified as eligible. It explains that the Michigan Mandatory Special Education law (MMSE) requires special education services for eligible children and students from birth through age 25, and that federal law also mandates early intervention programs. Part B of the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) refers to special education services for students ages 3 through 21; Part C of IDEA refers to early intervention services for eligible infants and toddlers from birth through age 2, and in Michigan Part C is called Early On; special education supports and services for students age 22 through 25 are part of MMSE. The packet states that OCSBA has always supported early childhood education and that the earlier the intervention begins, the greater the impact. Early On is described as Michigan's statewide, comprehensive, coordinated interagency system of early intervention services for infants and toddlers, birth to age three years, with disabilities and their families; it is coordinated by the Michigan Department of Education and provides services under Part C of IDEA. Local communities receive funding through their local Intermediate School District (ISD) to implement Early On. Each local ISD jurisdiction has an interagency coordinating council, comprised of individuals from human service agencies, parents, educators and other agency personnel who serve families, that guides implementation locally, and implementation is also guided through local memoranda of understanding between education, mental health, public health and social services.

The funding argument states that for 50 years the association has advocated for IDEA funding for students, and that the congressional promise to fund 40% of the cost of providing special education services applies to Part B, children age 3 to 21, and to Part C, early intervention services for infants and toddlers through age 2. Three figures are given for Early On: the estimated annual cost is $230M to provide high-quality early intervention services; the state should appropriate at least $138M, described as 60% of the estimated annual cost; and Section 54d of the FY26 School Aid Act provides state funding of $48M. A reference link is given to the Early On Foundation case for funding document at earlyonfoundation.org.

CONTINUING RESOLUTIONS. ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY (OCSBA adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): supports holding every school that receives public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act, covering local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities; cites MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f). BROADBAND ACCESS AND DEVICES (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025): broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; supports additional federal and state funding to expand affordable and reliable broadband access; supports federal and state programs for the purchase of internet capable devices and software; supports dedicated resources for cybersecurity; cites MASB Resolution A-10.30, 2021 amendment. EARLY CHILDHOOD (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): supports additional new dollars to fund universal, public preschool for all four year old children, and mandatory kindergarten for all five-year-old children; cites MASB Resolution A 6.15 (c). EVIDENCE-BASED DECISION MAKING (adopted 9/24/2019): supports evidence-based education policy that will maximize opportunities for the highest achievement of each student; cites MASB Resolution G 11.01. LAME DUCK (adopted 9/24/2019): supports lame duck parameters addressing introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election. LOCAL CONTROL (adopted 9/24/2019): supports local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards; cites MASB Resolutions A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70. MENTAL HEALTH (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025): supports increased mental health services and professionals in schools and, at a minimum, annual inflation adjusted state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe; help staff identify potential mental health issues for students; encourage MDE to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response; cites MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50.

SCHOOL AID (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025), four parts: (A) specify that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and oppose any attempts to create private school vouchers or tax credit programs, citing MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (a) and A 10.05; (B) support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students, citing MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (g) and (j) and A 10.55; (C) protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes, citing MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (c) and A 10.55; (D) support enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts have factual information to meet their constitutional and statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30, citing MASB Resolution A 10.25 (h). SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC) (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 9/11/2021, 3/3/2023, 6/5/2025): supports implementation of the SFRC recommendations while holding higher funded districts harmless; cites MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25, 2021 amendment. SCHOOL NUTRITION (adopted 3/3/2023; amended 6/5/2025): supports codification of free universal meals. SCHOOL SAFETY (adopted 3/3/2023): supports adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe. SPECIAL EDUCATION (adopted 9/24/2019): supports full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, noting that although federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities, appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local districts to make up the difference; cites MASB Resolution A 5.01 and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA. TEACHER SHORTAGES (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025): supports statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, including incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states; cites MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority. UNFUNDED MANDATES (adopted 9/24/2019): opposes any state or federal legislation that results in increased costs for school districts without full funding, and encourages the Michigan Legislature to oppose federal laws or programs that are not fully funded and thus cost the state valuable resources; cites MASB Resolution A 10.20.

The packet closes with a statement that, when aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda, the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda, the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda, and the Consortium of State School Board Associations (COSSBA) Legislative Agenda (adopted 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025), with links to MASB Resolutions at masb.org/resolutions.aspx, NSBA Advocacy at nsba.org/Advocacy, and COSSBA Advocacy at cossba.org/advocacy.

TEACHER SHORTAGES (adopted 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025): supports statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, including incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states; cites MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Presentation slide deck on AP Spanish and AP French resource adoption, prepared for the 12/9/25 Board Workshop and carried to the December 16, 2025 Troy School District Board meeting. Troy's current AP world language texts, Abriendo Paso (2014) for Spanish and T'es Branche (2014) for French, are described as outdated and lacking interpersonal speaking practice and AP test preparation, and the resources adopted in 2017 do not represent current culture. After a selection process guided by Oakland Schools consultant Jen Howe, Vista Higher Learning is recommended over Wayside and Klett, with seven-year licenses beginning in August.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Title:** AP Spanish and AP French Resource Adoption, 12/9/25 Board Workshop, Troy School District.

**Context and rationale.** World Language levels run Level 1 through Level 5 AP; the AP exams are written at the intermediate high / advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision states that learners can communicate in an ever-expanding global community, experience the heritage of another culture, become resilient risk-takers, improve memory and problem-solving skills, enhance college applications and professional marketability, and open themselves to world travel. AP World Language and Culture is equivalent to an intermediate level college course, with students applying interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication across themes of family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The exam assesses both language and culture, but the resources adopted in 2017 do not have current culture represented.

**Current state.** World Languages operates on a 7 year adoption cycle. With the PLC structure, Troy AP World Language teachers desire a common resource to build cohesion among programs. Current resources: Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, with outdated readings, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources. Teachers are pulling resources from a wide variety of sources, some at their own cost.

**Selection process.** Facilitated with Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. AP resources timeline: 24-25 school year, exploration of resources; 8/11 leadership planning; 8/20 department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7 rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20 pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18 PLC check-ins; 12/2 pilot feedback and synthesis.

**Vendors considered**

| Vendor | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Wayside | French and Spanish: relatable content with a variety of authentic resources, but does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment and is only a textbook without assessment practice |
| Klett | French: no AP resource. Spanish: many authentic resources and AP practice, but does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment, has fewer resources than Vista, and less user-friendly technology |
| Vista Higher Learning | French and Spanish: matches the rigor of the AP exam, culturally relevant resources and a large resource bank; because of its rigor resources may need scaffolding at the start of the year |

**Vista specifics.** The authors of Vista are also College Board trainers, and Vista has 80% of the AP World Languages market share. The 26-27 AP Exam will be updated, and Vista has agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year; when it updates its textbooks it will provide updated electronic and physical resources free of cost, and the district will bank its professional learning credit to support the change in August.

**Features shown.** AP French culturally relevant resources, with and without student supports; AP Spanish cultural comparison, in which students compare the country they are studying with the United States, illustrated by Maya sharing how the role of grandparents differs in the United States versus El Salvador; AP Spanish simulated conversations; and an example of interpersonal communication supporting the Free Response AP tasks, which are 50% of the exam.

**Stakeholder support.** Student quotations praise the online textbook for more listening and speaking resources, faster navigation, and portability on an iPad, and credit the ebook with building confidence for the heavily weighted speaking sections of the AP test. Student Survey and Caretaker Survey slides follow, along with a Financial Request slide whose amounts are not captured in the extracted text.

**Timeline moving forward.** December: order placed. January: physical materials inventoried; pilot licenses extended into June. August: 7 year licenses begin and are rostered; PD from Vista with College Board changes.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Slide presentation titled AP Spanish and AP French Resource Adoption, delivered at the 12/9/25 Board Workshop of the Troy School District and appearing on the December 16, 2025 Board of Education agenda. The deck moves through context and rationale, current state, the process of resource selection, vendor comparison, features of the recommended texts, additional stakeholder support, a financial request, and an anticipated timeline.

CONTEXT AND RATIONALE. The World Language sequence is presented as Level 1, Level 2, Level 3, Level 4 and Level 5 AP, with the note that the AP exams are written at the intermediate high and advanced levels. The TSD World Languages vision statement holds that World Language learners can communicate in an ever-expanding global community; discover and experience the rich heritage of another culture; become resilient risk-takers with a greater capacity to adapt to new environments; improve their memory and problem-solving skills for better overall academic performance; enhance their college applications and increase their professional marketability; and open themselves up to opportunities for world travel. The AP overview states that AP World Language and Culture is equivalent to an intermediate level college course, in which students cultivate their understanding of language and culture by applying interpersonal, interpretive and presentational modes of communication in real life situations while exploring concepts related to family and communities, personal and public identities, beauty and aesthetics, science and technology, contemporary life, and global challenges. The deck notes that the exam assesses both language and culture, but that the resources adopted in 2017 do not have current culture represented.

CURRENT STATE. World Languages follows a 7 year adoption cycle. With the PLC structure in place, Troy AP World Language teachers desire a common resource to help build cohesion among programs. The current resources are Abriendo Paso (2014) for AP Spanish, described as having outdated readings that have not been updated, no interpersonal speaking practice and no AP test prep; and T'es Branche (2014) for AP French, described as a Level 4 textbook with outdated readings and listening resources that have not been updated. The current reality slide states that teachers are doing their best to pull resources from a wide variety of sources, some even at their own costs.

PROCESS OF RESOURCE SELECTION. The process was supported by Jen Howe, Oakland Schools Heritage and World Language Consultant. The AP resources timeline lists: the 24-25 school year for exploration of resources; 8/11 leadership planning; 8/20 department kickoff and visioning; 10/2 and 10/7 rubric creation and vendor presentations; 10/20 pilot planning; 11/11 and 11/18 PLC planning and check-ins; and 12/2 pilot feedback and synthesis.

AP VENDORS CONSIDERED, PROS AND CONS. Wayside, for French and Spanish: while the resource has relatable content for students with a variety of authentic resources, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment, and it is only a textbook without assessment practice. Klett, for French: no AP resource. Klett, for Spanish: while the resource has a lot of authentic resources and AP practice, it does not represent the rigor of the AP assessment, it does not have the number of resources that Vista has, and the technology was less user friendly. Vista Higher Learning, for French and Spanish: the resource matches the rigor of the AP exam and provides meaningful resources that are culturally relevant as well as a large resource bank, and because of its rigor resources may need to be scaffolded at the start of the year. Additional Vista points: the authors of Vista are also College Board trainers; Vista has 80% of the AP World Languages market share; the 26-27 AP Exam will be updated and Vista has agreed to provide an updated crosswalk for launching the 26-27 school year; when Vista updates its textbooks it will provide the district updated electronic and physical resources free of cost; and the district will bank its professional learning credit to support this change in August.

FEATURES OF RECOMMENDED TEXTS. Sample slides cover AP French culturally relevant resources and AP French culturally relevant resources with student supports. An AP Spanish cultural comparison slide explains that on the AP test students must compare the country they are studying with the United States, illustrated by a segment in which Maya shares how the role of grandparents is different in the United States versus El Salvador. A further slide shows AP Spanish simulated conversations, described as a free response task on the AP exam, and another gives an example of interpersonal communication that fosters student confidence and practice for the Free Response AP tasks, which the deck states are 50% of the exam.

ADDITIONAL STAKEHOLDER SUPPORT. Two student comments are quoted. The first: the student likes an online textbook because it has more resources such as listening and speaking, allows better and faster navigation of pages, and makes it easier to have the textbook on an iPad. The second: the student has used the ebook many times in class and found the variety of resources really helpful, notes that the hardest part of learning Spanish at this high a level is being able to speak their thoughts about everything, and reports that the ebook provided speaking practice that has already increased confidence in speaking ability, adding that the speaking sections of the AP test are huge, very important for the overall score, and heavily weighted, so having these resources builds confidence in trying to earn a good score. The deck then includes a Student Survey slide and a Caretaker Survey slide, whose underlying results are not captured in the extracted text.

FINANCIAL REQUEST AND TIMELINE. A Financial Request section appears in the deck; no dollar figures for the request are present in the extracted text. The anticipated timeline moving forward is given in three columns: December, order placed; January, physical materials inventoried and pilot licenses extended into June; August, 7 year licenses begin and are rostered, with professional development from Vista covering the College Board changes. The deck ends with a Questions slide.
