https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A 37-slide staff presentation to the Troy School District Board of Education, dated to the June 14, 2022 meeting, reporting mid-year progress on the Project 2026 Blueprint accountability plan and its four World Class for All pillars: Early Childhood to Career (Green), Equity and Well-Being (Red), Deep Learning (Blue), and Building Capacity (Gold). Each pillar is presented with objectives, key results, January-June 2022 celebrations, challenges, and recommendations. Among the reported results, Career and Technical Education program growth provided almost triple the funding from year 20/21 to 21/22, and a 1.0 social worker was placed at every elementary school.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
## Overview
Project 2026 Blueprint, District / School / Troy - a Troy School District Board of Education presentation of the accountability plan tied to the 2026 Troy School District Blueprint. The deck moves through an Introduction, Key Themes and Next Steps, the four pillars, and a Summary across 37 slides (slides 23-30 and 37 carry no extracted text).

## Framework
Mission and Vision (Re) Fresh restates the Troy School District mission as Ensuring learning for all, centering the ONETROY community, with four pillars: Early Childhood to Career (expands on research with access through career); Equity and Well-Being (ensures safety, belonging, and connection); Deep Learning (ensures learning for all throughout the system); Building Capacity (expands to include students, staff, and community as learners). Core values named are Collaboration, Deep Learning and Focus. The Accountability Plan holds the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results.

## Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career
Objectives: continue investing in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three and four-year-olds; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students through high-quality career and technical education, expanded computer science access, connections for underrepresented students to in-demand careers, and partnerships with higher education and employers for work-based learning, credentials and college credit.

| Key result | Target |
|---|---|
| Additional GSRP slots requested from the state of Michigan in 2021-22 | 16-32 |
| Additional PreK classrooms opened in 2021-22 | 2-3 (40-60 students) |
| Meetings/site visits with local legislators on free preschool for all | 2 during 2021-22 |
| Building leader reports back from Career Readiness meetings | 2 times during 2021-22 |
| Career Readiness meetings devoted to Portrait of a Graduate research | 2 |

Celebrations (January-June 2022): record-high early childhood enrollment with waitlists for PreK, GSRP, tuition and before/after school programs; CTE growth providing almost triple the funding from year 20/21 to 21/22; k-5 Career Readiness engagement partnered with Media Specialists and Maker Space growth. Challenges: capacity limits; grantee Oakland Schools has not offered access for additional GSRP slots; stigma around Career Readiness.

## Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being
Objectives: safely reopen schools and support students disproportionately impacted by the pandemic; fund whole-child investments including community schools with wraparound services and more counselors, social workers and school psychologists; assess and act on facility upgrades. Results reported: 1.0 SW at every elementary, increased psychologist support and counseling at secondary; data reviews with interventions in progress; monthly staff topics; a District Level Team established; a 2nd annual equity and inclusion stakeholder survey. Recommendations include SEL pilots for 2022-23.

## Blue Pillar - Deep Learning
MTSS build-out in mathematics: elementary Tier 1 early adopters (70+ teachers) and Tier 2/3 Math Recovery training for 9 teachers; secondary Tier 1 teacher pilot team and Tier 2/3 Math Recovery training for 6 teachers; Math Specialists coaching PD; a Troy High visit to Troy Athens for job-embedded learning. Broader objectives cover technology access, NPDL and The 6 C's, and facilities.

## Gold Pillar - Building Capacity
Educator preparation, pipelines for underrepresented educators, and job-embedded learning. Reported partnerships include MSU Create for Stem, Teachers College, National Equity Project, and Oakland University as exclusive Elementary COE partner. Challenges include teacher coverage, calendar time for collaboration, and teacher shortage particularly in special education.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Project 2026 Blueprint is a 37-slide Troy School District staff presentation to the Board of Education carried on the June 14, 2022 agenda under the title June 22 Accountability Plan BOE Presentation. Its title slide reads Project 2026 Blueprint / District / School / Troy. The deck is organized as an Introduction (2026 Troy School District Blueprint), Key Themes and Next Steps, four pillar sections, and a Summary. Slides 23 through 30 and slide 37 contain no extracted text.

Mission and Vision (Re) Fresh. The framing slide places the Troy School District mission at the center - Mission: Ensuring learning for all. Centers ONETROY community - surrounded by four pillars, each with a one-line refresh: EARLY CHILDHOOD TO CAREER expands on research with access through career; EQUITY AND WELL-BEING ensures safety, belonging, and connection; DEEP LEARNING ensures learning for all throughout the system; BUILDING CAPACITY expands to include students, staff, and community as learners.

Core Values and Accountability Plan. The World Class for All Pillars are described as carefully aligned to the district core values of Collaboration, Deep Learning and Focus. The Accountability Plan slide states that the World Class for All Pillars hold the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results.

Green Pillar - Early Childhood to Career. The section covers Overview, Objectives and Key Results. Objectives are to continue to invest in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for access to universal preschool for all three and four-year-olds; and to expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students, with a plan aimed at providing more students access to high-quality career and technical education programs that expand access to computer science, connect underrepresented students to careers in demand in high-growth industry sectors, and include partnerships with institutions of higher education, employers and other stakeholders allowing students to engage in quality work-based learning opportunities, earn a credential, and/or earn college credit.

Green Pillar Key Results: apply for 16-32 additional GSRP slots from the state of Michigan in the 2021-22 school year; open an additional 2-3 PreK classrooms (40-60 students) in the 2021-22 school year; schedule two meetings and/or site visits with local legislators regarding free preschool for all during the 2021-22 school year; building leaders will participate in Career Readiness meetings led by district CR team leaders and report back to their respective building teams two times during the 2021-22 school year; the Green Pillar Team will research the Portrait of a Graduate framework to implement the process in TSD during two Career Readiness meetings; and the Green Pillar Team will develop a Portrait of a Graduate survey by the close of the 2021-22 school year.

Green Pillar January-June 2022 Celebrations: current Early Childhood enrollment at a record high, with waitlists for PreK, GSRP, tuition and before and after school programs; Portrait of a Graduate work investigating other districts, with the team having met and created a timeline for the process and for engaging all stakeholders; CTE program growth that has provided almost triple the funding from year 20/21 to 21/22 for program improvements, creating new learning opportunities for students; Career Readiness engagement opportunities in k-5 partnered with Media Specialists and Maker Space growth; and continued prioritization of post-secondary learning partnerships in various ways throughout k-12.

Green Pillar January 2022 Challenges: the current capacity limit for early childhood programs; grantee Oakland Schools has not offered access for additional GSRP slots; alignment of Media/Maker with Career Readiness in terms of time and consistency; the need to mindshift the stigma of CR to help prioritize relevance to learning in classrooms; and balancing Portrait of a Graduate work with current top priorities.

Green Pillar January 2022 Recommendations: early and frequent Early Childhood recruitment for 2022-23; align PreK enrollment with Kindergarten enrollment; continued advocacy for universal funding; prioritize messaging Career Readiness as a tool for students aligned with academic planning and college readiness with administrators, teachers and counselors; and Portrait of a Graduate work through ILT team partnerships.

Red Pillar - Equity and Well-Being. Objectives: safely reopen schools and support students, particularly those disproportionately impacted by the pandemic; fund additional investments to support the needs of the whole child, including community schools that provide wraparound services like afterschool programs and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists; and assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities.

Red Pillar Key Results: increase Social Work and Counseling support in all buildings; review and monitor student data; emphasis on adult learning in the areas of well-being and equity; create common understanding of a system of support at all levels; and development of a district level Equity Leader network. The January-June 2022 status slide reports 1.0 SW at every elementary with increased psychologist support and counseling at secondary; data reviews conducted with interventions in progress; monthly staff topics; and a District Level Team established. A second January-June 2022 slide adds a presentation to the board on Social Work, Counseling and Psychologist support; continued reviews and exploration of additional intervention options; conducting a 2nd annual equity and inclusion stakeholder survey; monthly staff topics plus district-wide learning on Equity; and a District Level Team that will create systems to support well being.

Red Pillar Recommendations: continue Social Work, Psychologist and Counseling support in all buildings; resource implementation for support tied to student data review; monthly staff topics, district-wide learning on Equity, and evaluation of progress and future goals through equity data analysis; SEL pilots for 2022-23; and development of the district level Equity Leader network.

Blue Pillar - Deep Learning. Objectives: create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice (MTSS), with access to deep learning described as imperative for all children; improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage technology to deepen learning; continue to pursue the global best practices of all content areas (NPDL, The 6 C's, Learning partnerships); and assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities.

Blue Pillar Key Results center on mathematics MTSS. For Elementary Math MTSS: Tier 1 Early Adopters (70+ teachers); Tier 2/3 Math Recovery Training for 9 teachers; a Board visit to observe; and principal learning. For Secondary Math MTSS: a Tier 1 teacher pilot team with early research classrooms; Tier 2/3 Math Recovery Training for 6 teachers; and principal learning. Also listed are Math Specialists Coaching PD, a visit to elementary to observe coaching, a Troy High visit to Troy Athens for job-embedded learning, and middle school math specialists planning colleague observations.

Blue Pillar Recommendations: formalize review of data at the building level for both elementary and secondary; next level training in Math Recovery for elementary and middle school math specialists; continue course offerings for elementary and special-education teachers; support the early adopter team with job-embedded learning; support the middle school pilot team with job-embedded learning; and have Math Specialists expand classroom coaching.

Gold Pillar - Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families. Objectives: improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, and supporting current educators; continuing to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff; and providing professional learning opportunities for staff, community and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.

Gold Pillar Key Results and January-June 2022 Celebrations: all elementary staff had two job-embedded learning experiences utilizing technology to enhance teaching and learning; Elementary Math Specialists trained in MSRP1, the Math Recovery Intensive Intervention Course; Middle and High School Math Specialists trained in AVMR, the Fractions Math Recovery Course; high school chemistry job-embedded learning with the MSU Create for Stem Partnership; a PreK-12 Coaching Institute with Teachers College including classroom visits at Larson and Troy High; buildings partnered with the National Equity Project to conduct student leadership and student voice sessions; Board of Education learning at Costello; an Equity Parent Advisory Committee; and an Oakland University partnership with the Elementary COE as exclusive partner.

Gold Pillar Challenges: teacher coverage for job-embedded learning; the need for time built into the calendar for teacher collaboration; parent education around changes in teaching and learning in the Troy School District; finding candidates with diverse backgrounds who want to apply or relocate for positions in the area; and teacher shortage, particularly in special education.

Gold Pillar Recommendations: host meetings that do not occur in classrooms after or before school at the curriculum rate; host a parent learning series around deep learning and changes to education; extend the conversation with Oakland University into secondary, in particular AP and science candidates; establish a partnership with Eastern Michigan's Special Education COE; join the PTO Advisory Board for more in-depth learning around mathematics; and work as a teaching and learning team to create a workplan based on the biggest priorities, named as Secondary Technology Support, Math Early Adopter Team, and Elementary Social Studies. The deck closes with a Summary slide for the 2026 Troy School District Blueprint.

## Document type
Michigan Department of Treasury Form 614 (Rev. 02-22), designated L-4029, titled 2022 Tax Rate Request / MILLAGE REQUEST REPORT TO COUNTY BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. Routing is printed at the top: ORIGINAL TO County Clerk(s) and the Michigan Department of Treasury; COPY TO Equalization Department(s); COPY TO each township or city clerk. The form must be completed and submitted on or before September 30, 2022. It is issued under authority of MCL Sections 211.24e, 211.34 and 211.34d; filing is mandatory and a penalty applies, with the penalty for non-filing provided under MCL Sec 211.119.

## Header fields
County(ies) where the local government unit levies taxes; 2022 Taxable Value of ALL Properties in the Unit as of 5-23-2022; Local Government Unit Requesting Millage Levy; and, for LOCAL school districts, the 2022 Taxable Value excluding Principal Residence, Qualified Agricultural, Qualified Forest, Industrial Personal and Commercial Personal Properties. In this copy all header fields are blank.

| Col | Heading |
|---|---|
| 1 | Source |
| 2 | Purpose of Millage |
| 3 | Date of Election |
| 4 | Original Millage Authorized by Election, Charter, etc. |
| 5 | 2021 Millage Rate Permanently Reduced by MCL 211.34d Headlee |
| 6 | 2022 Current Year Headlee Millage Reduction Fraction |
| 7 | 2022 Millage Rate Permanently Reduced by MCL 211.34d Headlee |
| 8 | Sec. 211.34 Truth in Assessing or Equalization Millage Rollback Fraction |

Signature blocks are provided for Prepared by, Telephone Number, Title of Preparer and Date; for the Clerk or Secretary; and for the Chairperson or President. The certification states that representatives of the local government unit certify the requested tax levy rates have been reduced if necessary to comply with the state constitution (Article 9, Section 31) and with MCL Sections 211.24e and 211.34, and, for LOCAL school districts levying a Supplemental (Hold Harmless) Millage, MCL 380.1211(3). A footnote adds that under Truth in Taxation, MCL Section 211.24e, the governing body may levy a rate not exceeding the maximum authorized rate in column 9.

## Local school district section
A Local School District Use Only block, to be completed if requesting millage to be levied per STC Bulletin 2 of 2022, captures Total School District Operating Rates to be Levied (HH/Supp and NH Oper ONLY) broken out for Principal Residence, Qualified Ag., Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal; for Commercial Personal; and for all Other.

## Instructions
Page 2 provides column-by-column instructions issued under MCL Sections 211.24e (truth in taxation), 211.34 (truth in county equalization and truth in assessing), 211.34d (Headlee), and 211.36 and 211.37 (apportionment), including references to Form 2166 (L-4034) millage reduction fraction calculations, STC Bulletin No. 11 of 1999 as supplemented by letter of 6/7/2000, and a memo to assessors dated October 26, 2004 regarding the change in the collection date of certain county taxes.

A starred footnote explains that under Truth in Taxation, MCL Section 211.24e, the governing body may decide to levy a rate which will not exceed the maximum authorized rate allowed in column 9, and that the requirements of MCL 211.24e must be met prior to levying an operating levy larger than the base tax rate but not larger than the rate in column 9.

Local School District Use Only. A separate block, to be completed if requesting millage to be levied and following STC Bulletin 2 of 2022, records Total School District Operating Rates to be Levied (HH/Supp and NH Oper ONLY), with separate rate lines For Principal Residence, Qualified Ag., Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal; For Commercial Personal; and For all Other. A double-starred note directs the filer to the page 2 instructions regarding where to find the millage rate used in column (5).

Instructions for completing Form 614 (L-4029). The instructions are provided under MCL Sections 211.24e (truth in taxation), 211.34 (truth in county equalization and truth in assessing), 211.34d (Headlee), and 211.36 and 211.37 (apportionment).

Column 1, Source: enter the source of each millage, for example allocated millage, separate millage limitations voted, charter, approved extra-voted millage, or public act number; taxes levied on the Industrial Facilities Tax Roll are excluded.

Column 2, Purpose of millage: examples given are operating, debt service, special assessments, school enhancement millage and sinking fund millage. A local school district must separately list operating millages by whether they are levied against ALL PROPERTIES in the school district or against the NON-HOME group of properties, per State Tax Commission Bulletin 2 of 2022. Permitted abbreviations are Operating ALL, short for operating millage levied on ALL PROPERTIES in the local school district such as Supplemental (Hold Harmless) Millages and Building and Site Sinking Fund Millages, and Operating NON-HOME, short for operating millage levied on all properties excluding principal residence, qualified agricultural, qualified forest and industrial personal properties, such as the 18 mills in a district which does not levy a Supplemental (Hold Harmless) Millage.

Column 3, Date of Election: the month and year of the election for each millage authorized by direct voter approval.

Column 4, Millage Authorized: the allocated rate, charter aggregate rate, extra-voted rate authorized before 1979, each separate rate authorized by voters after 1978, debt service rate and similar, stated before any reductions.

Column 5: the 2021 millage rate permanently reduced by MCL 211.34d Headlee rollback. Starting with taxes levied in 1994 the Headlee rollback permanently reduces the maximum rate or rates authorized by law or charter. The 2021 permanently reduced rate is found in column 7 of the 2021 Form L-4029. For operating millage approved by voters after April 30, 2021, the millage approved by voters is entered. For debt service or special assessments not subject to a millage reduction fraction, enter NA.

Column 6, Current Year Millage Reduction Fraction: the fraction certified by the county treasurer for the current year as calculated on Form 2166 (L-4034), 2022 Millage Reduction Fraction Calculations Worksheet, rounded to four decimal places. The fraction shall not exceed 1.0000 for 2022 and future years, preventing any increase or roll up of millage rates. Use 1.0000 for new millage approved by voters after April 30, 2022, and 1.0000 for debt service or special assessments not subject to a millage reduction fraction.

Column 7: the 2022 millage rate permanently reduced by MCL 211.34d Headlee rollback, found by multiplying column 5 by column 6 on the 2022 Form L-4029, rounded DOWN to four decimal places, citing STC Bulletin No. 11 of 1999 as supplemented by letter of 6/7/2000. Enter NA for debt service or special assessments not subject to a millage reduction fraction.

Column 8, Section 211.34 Millage Rollback Fraction (Truth in Assessing or Truth in Equalization): listed for each operating rate and rounded to four decimal places. Use 1.0000 for school districts, special assessments and bonded debt retirement levies. Counties, villages and authorities enter the Truth in Equalization Rollback Fraction calculated on STC Form L-4034 as total taxable value based on CEV for all classes divided by total taxable value based on SEV for all classes; use 1.0000 for an authority located in more than one county. Townships and cities enter the Truth in Assessing Rollback Fraction calculated on STC Form L-4034 as total taxable value based on assessed value for all classes divided by total taxable value based on SEV for all classes. The Section 211.34 Millage Rollback Fraction shall not exceed 1.0000.

Column 9, Maximum Allowable Millage Levy: multiply column 7 by column 8 and round DOWN to four decimal places, again citing STC Bulletin No. 11 of 1999 and the letter of 6/7/2000. For debt service or special assessments not subject to a millage reduction fraction, enter the millage from column 4.

Columns 10 and 11, Millage Requested to be Levied: enter the tax rate approved by the unit of local government provided it does not exceed the maximum allowable millage levy in column 9. A millage rate exceeding the base tax rate under Truth in Taxation cannot be requested unless the requirements of MCL 211.24e have been met. A LOCAL school district levying a Supplemental (Hold Harmless) Millage shall not levy a Supplemental Millage in excess of that allowed by MCL 380.1211(3). Filers are referred to the memo to assessors dated October 26, 2004 regarding the change in the collection date of certain county taxes.

Column 12, Expiration Date of Millage: enter the month and year on which the millage will expire.

**Document and authorship**
Draft "Report to the Board of Education," Troy School District, June 30, 2022, prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC; signed by Donna Hanson, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Senior Manager); dated October 4, 2022. Sections: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), Informational Items (pages 7-16). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office.

**Results of the audit**
Engagement letter dated June 1, 2022; planning matters discussed at a meeting on July 29, 2022; audit performed under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards and Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States. A separate letter dated October 4, 2022 addresses internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing, and a report on federal programs under 2 CFR Part 200 is likewise dated October 4, 2022. The management representation letter is dated October 4, 2022. The School District adopted GASB Statement No. 87, Leases, as of July 1, 2021, as described in Note 2. The auditors report no transactions lacking authoritative guidance, no significant transactions recorded in a different period, no significant difficulties, no disagreements with management, no consultations with other accountants, and that management corrected all immaterial misstatements. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of MPSERS net liabilities under GASB 68 and GASB 75, estimated at June 30, 2022 as $210,869,230 (pension) and $13,509,781 (OPEB), based on data from the Office of Retirement Services.

**Other recommendations and observations**
- GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that items purchased in a group that fall below the capitalization threshold individually but exceed it in aggregate belong in fixed asset records; effective for the year ending June 30, 2024.
- Food Service Fund balance exceeds the U.S. Department of Agriculture maximum of three months of operating expenditures; a spend-down plan must be submitted to the Michigan Department of Education.

**School funding highlights**

| Item | Figure |
| --- | --- |
| 2021/2022 target foundation allowance | $8,700 per pupil |
| Prior target level | $8,529 per pupil |
| Minimum 2021/2022 increase, all districts | $171 per pupil |
| Troy foundation allowance 2021/2022 | $9,430 per pupil, up $115 |
| 2022/2023 target foundation allowance | $9,150 per pupil, a $450 / 5.2 percent increase |
| MPSERS overall contribution rate 2022 | 43 percent, from 42 percent |
| MPSERS overall contribution rate 2023 | 45 percent, from 43 percent |
| District net MPSERS cost | approximately 28 percent |

State retirement support received by the District: $1,062,198 under Section 147a1, $1,841,462 under 147a2, $13,922,709 under 147c1, and $311,632 under 147e. Other state actions cited include $475 million for a school consolidation and infrastructure fund, 1,300 new GSRP openings, $10,000 in tuition support for future teachers, $9,600 per-semester stipends for student teachers, full funding of Section 31a At-Risk, and a 5.2 percent ISD operations increase. Pupil counts use the 90 percent fall / 10 percent spring blend.

**Fund balance**
General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $247,000 in 2021-2022, with fund balance at approximately $33,000,000 at June 30, 2022 - 19.12 percent of expenditures, about 9.9 weeks of operations. **MPSERS plan status and future standards**
At September 30, 2021 the MPSERS net pension liability was approximately $24.2 billion (down about 30 percent from $35 billion) and net OPEB liability approximately $1.5 billion (down about 72 percent from $5.4 billion), driven by a 27.2 percent investment return. Coming changes: the GASB financial reporting model exposure draft (final standard targeted December 2023, adoption June 30, 2025 for districts over $75 million in revenue), GASB 96 on subscription-based IT arrangements (June 30, 2023), and GASB 101 on compensated absences (June 30, 2025). https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Plante & Moran, PLLC prepared this draft "Report to the Board of Education" for Troy School District covering the audit of the basic financial statements as of and for the year ended June 30, 2022. The letter is dated October 4, 2022 and is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Senior Manager. It is organized into three parts: Results of the Audit (pages 1-4), Other Recommendations and Observations (pages 5-6), and Informational Items (pages 7-16). The cover letter extends thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit.

**Results of the audit.** The auditors state their responsibility under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management under the Board's oversight are fairly presented in all material respects in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles, obtaining reasonable but not absolute assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on such control. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, and a separate letter dated October 4, 2022 was issued on the consideration of internal control over financial reporting and on tests of compliance with laws, regulations, contracts, and grant agreements. The engagement letter is dated June 1, 2022, and planning matters were communicated at a meeting on July 29, 2022; the audit was performed according to that planned scope and timing.

**Significant audit findings.** Significant accounting policies are described in Note 2; as described there, the School District adopted Governmental Accounting Standards Board Statement No. 87, Leases, as of July 1, 2021, as required by the standard. The auditors noted no transactions entered into during the year for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions recognized in a period different from when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates affecting the financial statements were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75; the District's estimates as of June 30, 2022 were $210,869,230 for pension and $13,509,781 for OPEB, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, management corrected all immaterial misstatements identified, disclosures are described as neutral, consistent, and clear, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants. A management representation letter dated October 4, 2022 was obtained. An audit of federal programs required by 2 CFR Part 200 was completed, with the compliance report to the Board dated October 4, 2022. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and nothing came to their attention suggesting the other information is materially misstated or inconsistent. The information is intended solely for the use of the Board of Education and management.

**Other recommendations and observations.** Two items are raised. First, GASB Implementation Guide Update 2021-1 clarifies that items purchased in a group that are individually below a district's capitalization threshold but exceed the threshold in the aggregate should be reported in fixed asset records; this clarified guidance takes effect commencing with the year ending June 30, 2024, and the District should review its practices and written policies. Second, the fund balance of the Food Service Fund exceeds the U.S. Department of Agriculture's maximum allowance of three months' worth of operating expenditures, and the District will be required to develop a spend-down plan and submit it to the Michigan Department of Education.

**Informational items - school funding.** The report describes movement from projected pandemic hardships to the largest level of funding since the start of Proposal A (1994/1995). Highlights include elimination of the gap between base and target foundation levels in 2021/2022, the largest per-pupil funding increase since Proposal A in 2022/2023, increased state contributions above constitutional minimums for special education, increased contributions to reduce long-term retirement system cost, state and federal resources for learning support, federal contributions toward pandemic staffing costs, one-time investments in education resources and technology, and federal investments to address learning loss.

For 2021/2022, the School Aid Fund had a surplus for fiscal 2021 and the Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference predicted sustainable revenue. All schools moved to the target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap, and all schools including hold harmless districts received an increase of at least $171 per pupil from the former target of $8,529. Troy's foundation allowance per pupil was $9,430, an increase of $115 from the 2021 level. Funding progress was also made on School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations covering special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and Great Start Readiness (GSRP).

For 2022/2023, the target foundation allowance rose by $450 per pupil to $9,150, a 5.2 percent increase, with hold harmless districts also receiving the $450 increase. The traditional blended pupil count continues at 90 percent weighting for the October 2022 count and 10 percent for the February 2022 count. Other items: continued increases in special education cost reimbursement, with 2022 and 2023 the first years since Proposal A that special education allocations exceeded state constitutional minimums; increased GSRP funding creating 1,300 new student openings; full funding of Section 31a At-Risk programs after prior prorations; increased career and technical education funding; increased student mental health funding; teacher recruitment resources including $10,000 in tuition support for future teachers, $9,600 stipends per semester for student teachers, and "Grow Your Own" programs; expansion of before- and after-school programs; dedicated school safety funding for school resource officers, intervention systems, and a school safety commission; increased retirement system contributions; $475 million of state aid allocated to a school consolidation and infrastructure fund, the first such state allocation; and an ISD operations allocation increase of 5.2 percent to mirror the foundation increase.

**Federal resources.** Federal assistance has arrived in waves beginning in 2020 with most funding ending in 2024. ESSER III, made available during 2021/2022, comprises ESSER III formula and ESSER III equalization (Section 11t of PA 48 of 2021), is funded under the American Rescue Plan, and carries more restrictions than ESSER I and II; its funding period ends during 2024 and it is the last iteration of pandemic funding expected. In 2021/2022 the "super blend" was not used and the historic 90/10 blend applied. Summer school and learning assistance funding from ESSER II and state appropriations spanned the 2021 and 2022 fiscal years.

**MPSERS costs.** For 2022, the overall contribution rate increased to 43 percent from 42 percent, with the net cost to the District approximating 28 percent. State support flows through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e; the District received $1,062,198 in 147a1, $1,841,462 in 147a2, $13,922,709 in 147c1, and $311,632 of 147e funding. For 2023, the overall rate rises to 45 percent from 43 percent with the District's net cost continuing at up to approximately 28 percent; by comparison, the total contribution rate when Proposal A was adopted was 11 percent. Beginning in 2021/2022 the State increased its share of special education costs by 3 percent of those costs, continuing into 2022/2023 with a reduction in the foundation allowance credited against required state support.

**Enrollment and outlook.** Statewide enrollment has historically been slightly under 1.5 million students, declining about 10,000 per year before the pandemic, then falling in excess of 50,000 during the pandemic; some recovery is expected but not to pre-pandemic levels. The May 2022 Consensus Revenue Estimating Conference projected surpluses for 2023, 2024, and 2025; the next conference is set for January 2023. Inflation and a potential recession are cited as the key risks, and the window for using the majority of federal pandemic funds closes by September 30, 2024.

**Grants management and budgeting.** The report describes increased grants management workload and risk across superintendents and leadership, board members, the business office, staff, procurement, information technology, and facilities, arising from ESSER, GEER, and CRF programs alongside traditional Title I, Special Education, and Child Nutrition grants, and recommends continued assessment of compliance risks moving into fiscal 2023.

**Fund balance.** During the 2021-2022 school year the School District's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $247,000, leaving General Fund fund balance at approximately $33,000,000 at June 30, 2022. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2021 was approximately 19.30 percent of expenditures and outgoing transfers, equal to about 10.0 weeks of average operating costs. The School District's fund balance percentage is 19.12 percent, equal to approximately 9.9 weeks of operation. Consumer Price Index growth and decisions on spending COVID-19 relief funds are named as pressures on 2022-2023 fund balance.

**MPSERS plan net liabilities.** The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2021 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $24.2 billion, a decrease of approximately 30 percent from $35 billion at September 30, 2020, driven largely by net investment gains; the plan's annual investment rate of return was 27.2 percent for the year ended September 30, 2021 compared with 5.0 percent for the year ended September 30, 2020. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $1.5 billion at September 30, 2021, down from $5.4 billion at September 30, 2020, a decrease of approximately 72 percent, reflecting the 27.2 percent return versus 4.9 percent the prior year. Because markets declined after the valuation date, both net liabilities are expected to increase significantly next year.

**Future GASB standards.** The financial reporting model project began in August 2013, with an exposure draft titled "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" issued in June 2020 and a comment period ending February 2021; Plante & Moran submitted comments, and the GASB's goal is a final standard by December 2023. Proposed changes include expanded management's discussion and analysis, a budget-to-actual column showing variances between original and amended budgets, terminology changes ("revenue" to "inflows of resources," "expenditures" to "outflows of resources"), and replacement of modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" recognizing transactions expected to be converted to or paid in cash within 12 months of year end, versus today's general 60-day receivable rule. Phased adoption would apply to districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million in the year ending June 30, 2025, and to those under $75 million in the year ending June 30, 2026. A related project, the June 2020 preliminary views on "Revenue and Expense Recognition," could produce a standard during 2027. GASB Statement No. 96 on subscription-based information technology arrangements is effective for the District's June 30, 2023 financial statements and mirrors GASB 87, requiring a right-to-use subscription asset and subscription liability measured at net present value for arrangements generally exceeding one year, with fund-level expenditures reclassified as debt service payments. GASB Statement No. 101 on compensated absences, effective for the year ending June 30, 2025, requires a full accrual liability for leave attributable to services already rendered that accumulates and is more likely than not to be used or paid, measured at each employee's pay rate at the statement date, while removing gross addition and reduction disclosure and the requirement to disclose liquidating funds.

**Cybersecurity.** Education remains a top target for ransomware; the "K-12 Cybersecurity Act of 2021" was signed into law in October 2021. The letter notes that the human element is the weakest link, citing easily guessed passwords such as "August2022," raises questions about phishing awareness, data location, personally identifiable information and FERPA data on file-sharing sites or flash drives, and remote access security, and offers an external vulnerability assessment.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Biographical sketches prepared for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of September 21, 2021 profile newly hired certified staff, giving each person's FTE and assignment, degrees and granting institutions, teaching certificate, prior teaching or clinical experience, and community of residence. The hires cover elementary, middle and high school classroom positions plus counselors, social workers, a school psychologist, speech pathologists, special education teachers and Troy Preschool early childhood educators, staffing buildings including Athens High School, Troy High School, Boulan Park, Baker, Larson and Smith middle schools, and Barnard, Bemis, Costello, Hamilton, Hill, Leonard, Martell, Morse, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wass and Wattles elementary schools. Oakland University, Michigan State University, Wayne State University, Central Michigan University and the University of Michigan recur as degree sources, and several appointees are Troy residents.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held February 15, 2022 at the Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m. before an audience of approximately 80. The Board adopted resolutions 22-015 through 22-026, each on a 7 to 0 vote, covering Principal Appreciation Month, the consent agenda, a new hire, open-enrollment closures, Schools of Choice numbers, several construction and technology awards, an IDEA Full Funding Act resolution, and a MASB ballot. The largest single action was the Site Work Paving Program awarded to Nagle Paving at a total of $2,048,607.75 from the Building Site Sinking Fund and Capital Projects Fund. The meeting adjourned at 9:03 p.m.

**Meeting**
Troy Board of Education regular meeting, February 15, 2022, Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Also present: Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson; Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, and West. Approximately 80 members of the audience attended. Adjourned 9:03 p.m. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary.

**Recognitions**
Fall 2021 All-State Athletes were named across boys tennis, boys soccer, and girls golf. Athletic Director Tim Fulcher recognized the Troy High School Boys Tennis Team as MHSAA Division 1 State Champions for fall 2021 and presented certificates. The Board honored Melissa Verduyn, Systems Analyst/Admin Webmaster, for artwork visualizing the District pillars of World Class; Kerry Birmingham introduced her and presented a framed photograph of her artwork plus a certificate of appreciation.

**Resolutions and Votes** (all 7 Yes, 0 No)

| No. | Subject | Moved / Supported |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 22-015 | February as Principal Appreciation Month | Philippart / Hammond |
| 22-016 | Consent agenda items A-D | Hauff / Anne |
| 22-017 | Personnel, new hire Samantha Morgan | Wilson / Hauff |
| 22-018 | Schools closed to open enrollment 2022-2023 | Anne / Gottlieb |
| 22-019 | Schools of Choice 105 and 105c | Philippart / Anne |
| 22-020 | Site Work Paving Program | Anne / Hauff |
| 22-021 | Asbestos abatement | Wilson / Hammond |
| 22-022 | Network firewall replacement | Hammond / Gottlieb |
| 22-023 | Fiber connectivity to TLC | Gottlieb / Philippart |
| 22-024 | Replacement ovens, Athens | Hammond / Anne |
| 22-025 | IDEA Full Funding Act resolution | Hauff / Wilson |
| 22-026 | 2022 MASB Board of Directors ballot | Philippart / Anne |

**Consent Agenda (22-016)**
Minutes of the January 4, 2022 Workshop; minutes of the January 18, 2022 Organizational and Regular Meeting; Treasurer's Report for December 2021; and cancellation of the March 12, 2022 Winter Retreat with the July 19 Board Meeting rescheduled to July 26, 2022 at 9:00 a.m.

**Enrollment Actions**
22-018 closed Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder, and Boulan Park Schools, plus Athens and Troy High Schools, to open enrollment for 2022-2023, excepting not more than twenty-five (25) incoming ninth grade students residing in the Troy High attendance area who wish to attend Athens; siblings currently in grades 9-11 at Athens and Troy High may remain. 22-019 accepted a Limited Schools of Choice program under Section 105 and 105c of the State School Aid Act of 1979 as amended by Public Act 300 of 1996 for eighteen (18) kindergarten, three (3) first grade, and sixteen (16) total 6th-8th grade nonresident students.

**Business Awards**

| Site Work Paving Program | Nagle Paving | $2,048,607.75 total | Building Site Sinking Fund and Capital Projects Fund |
| Asbestos abatement | Quality Environmental | $85,600.00 | Capital Projects Fund |
| Network firewall replacement | Delta Networks | $343,720.69 total | 2019 Capital Projects Fund |
| Fiber connectivity | Fiber Link, Inc. | $137,562.60 total | 2019 Capital Projects Fund |
| Two UNOX ovens | Stafford Smith | $58,524.00 | Food Service Fund |

**Public Communication**
No comment on agenda items. Twelve speakers addressed non-agenda items, raising equity versus equality, classroom volunteers, curriculum, media center content, diversity and inclusion, mask mandates and their lifting, and library books.

**Other**
22-025 supported the IDEA Full Funding Act. 22-026 cast the District ballot for Melandie Hines, Wayne Westland Community Schools, Region 8, three-year term, on the 2022 MASB Board of Directors. President Schmidt announced the next Board Workshop for March 1st at 6:00 p.m. and the next Board Meeting for March 15th at 7:00 p.m., both at the Services Building.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Official minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held February 15, 2022 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, Troy, Michigan. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Fulcher, and West. There were approximately 80 members of the audience. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, and bear the initials GH/jh.

RECOGNITION - ALL-STATE ATHLETES FALL 2021. The following students received the distinction of being named All-State Athletes in their respective sports: Srihari Ananthalwan (Boys Tennis), Aiden Baraiac (Boys Soccer), Derek Blackwell (Boys Tennis), Matthew Gawthrop (Boys Soccer), Rintaro Goda (Boys Tennis), Ryan Gruca (Boys Soccer), Mayank Gudi (Boys Tennis), Aryan Gupta (Boys Tennis), Olivia Hemmila (Girls Golf), John Palomino (Boys Soccer), Rishi Shetty (Boys Tennis), Nikhil Tatineni (Boys Tennis), Andrew Wang (Boys Tennis), Ava Weeks (Girls Golf), and Nicholas Worrell (Boys Soccer).

TROY HIGH BOYS TENNIS STATE CHAMPIONS. Director of Athletics Mr. Tim Fulcher recognized the Troy High School Boys Tennis Team for being named MHSAA Division 1 State Champions for the fall of 2021. Athletes called up to receive a certificate and congratulations were Haresh Anand (Sophomore), Srihari Ananthalwan (Junior), Pranav Bellad (Senior), Derek Blackwell (Sophomore), Yashwant Dubbaka (Junior), Aryan Gupta (Senior), Dhruv Gupta (Freshman), Sai Rushil Kagithala (Junior), Shalin Kakasani (Senior), KyungJin Kim (Sophomore), Nishit Palepu (Sophomore), Eric Rymkiewicz (Senior), Zachary Saad (Senior), Joshua Samuelsen (Sophomore), Rishi Shetty (Senior), Sachin Sridhar (Senior), Nikhil Tatineni (Senior), and Andrew Wang (Senior). Srihari Ananthalwan and Aryan Gupta were noted as Flight State Champions at #2 Doubles; Pranav Bellad and Zachary Saad were noted as Flight State Champions at #3 Doubles.

TSD MISSION MOMENT. The Board honored Melissa Verduyn, Systems Analyst/Admin Webmaster, who works in both the Technology Department and on the creative team. When the District began the process to evolve the characteristics of a world class school district, it ran into challenges producing a visual image similar to the pillars that could accurately communicate the vision; Verduyn brought it together in a way that helps the community understand and connect. Kerry Birmingham introduced Melissa, described her contributions, and presented her with a framed photograph of her artwork along with a certificate of appreciation.

PRINCIPAL APPRECIATION MONTH, RESOLUTION 22-015. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Hammond. The resolution recited that energetic and inspiring school leadership is essential if teachers, schools and districts are to ensure that all Troy students are college and career ready; that K-12 school principals play a vital role in student success and act as liaison between school and community; that Troy School District principals are dedicated, quality educational professionals; and that during February the District joins educators, parents and students throughout Michigan to raise awareness of the importance of educational leadership. It resolved that the Troy Board of Education officially recognizes February as Principal Appreciation Month in Troy. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS): None.

GENERAL CONSENT AGENDA, RESOLUTION 22-016. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne to approve items A, B, C, and D: minutes of the January 4, 2022 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the January 18, 2022 Board of Education Organizational and Regular Meeting; Treasurer's Report for December 2021; and cancellation of the March 12, 2022 Winter Retreat together with rescheduling of the July 19 Board Meeting to July 26, 2022, to be held at 9:00 a.m. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

PERSONNEL, RESOLUTION 22-017. Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff to approve the elementary and secondary personnel recommendation, a new hire, Samantha Morgan. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

CURRICULUM - SCHOOLS CLOSED TO OPEN ENROLLMENT FOR 2022-2023, RESOLUTION 22-018. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, adopting a resolution to close Barnard, Bemis, Schroeder and Boulan Park Schools as well as Athens and Troy High Schools to open enrollment for the 2022-2023 school year, with the exception of not more than twenty-five (25) incoming ninth grade students who reside in the Troy High School attendance area but wish to attend Athens High School. Students with siblings attending Athens and Troy High and currently enrolled in grades 9 through 11 will be allowed to open enroll to remain for the 2022-2023 school year. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

SCHOOLS OF CHOICE REPORT. Ms. Griffor shared that the Board had the opportunity to review the Schools of Choice data and information at the March 1, 2022 Board of Education Workshop, and that the Board would be asked to pass a resolution approving the suggested Schools of Choice numbers for the 2022-2023 school year.

SCHOOLS OF CHOICE 105 AND 105C, RESOLUTION 22-019. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne. ASBESTOS ABATEMENT PROJECT, RESOLUTION 22-021. Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Hammond, awarding the asbestos abatement bid to Quality Environmental in the amount of $85,600.00, approved as an expenditure from the Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

NETWORK FIREWALL REPLACEMENT, RESOLUTION 22-022. Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, awarding the network firewall replacement and approving the amount as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. Delta Networks base bid $327,353.04; Contingency $16,367.65; TOTAL $343,720.69. Vote: Yes 7, No 0.

FIBER CONNECTION TO TLC, RESOLUTION 22-023. Moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Dr. Philippart, awarding fiber connectivity services and approving the amount as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). President Schmidt described how Public Participation would be conducted in compliance with the Open Meetings Act and reviewed the guidelines for public comment. Speakers: Mrs. Katie MacFarland, TSD parent and resident, on the difference between equity and equality; Kristina Sosnoski, TSD parent and resident, on allowing parents to volunteer in classrooms again; Mrs. Kacy Bailey, parent of two students, on curriculum being taught in the District; Mr. Ollie Apahidean, TSD parent, on media content in school media centers; Mr. Christopher Henne, TSD parent, on diversity, equity and inclusion and arming kids with tools to be good quality citizens; B.J. Lennon, TSD parent, on the mask mandates being lifted; Mrs. Diana Magiera, TSD parent, on mask enforcements and effects on children; Stephanie Margilaj, TSD parent, on explicit books in school libraries; Kelly Jones, TSD parent, on the use of pronouns as a way to show respect; Dr. Stephanie Mikulski, TSD parent, on the mask requirement being discontinued prematurely; Ms. Ashleigh Jennings, TSD parent, on lifting the mask mandate and whether past mitigation measures will be reinstated; and Susan Tompkins, TSD resident, on masks and how teachers struggle to help students read with masks on.

OTHER - RESOLUTION IN SUPPORT OF IDEA FULL FUNDING ACT, RESOLUTION 22-025. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Dr. Wilson. The resolution recited that the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act was first enacted in 1975 to help ensure all students with disabilities have access to a free appropriate public education; that with IDEA's enactment the United States Congress committed to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost of special education, promising up to 40 percent of the national average per pupil expenditure, currently estimated at $13,828 by the U.S. Department of Education; that more than 45 years after enactment the current federal investment in IDEA is less than 14 percent; that Troy and many other districts educate a growing number of children with disabilities now numbering more than seven million; that districts face increased demand for greater resources, including for students with multiple disabilities whose individual education plans require more resources; and that with each increase in the IDEA child count boards adjust budgets, with some school districts dedicating forty percent or more of their general education budgets to special education services. The Board resolved to support the IDEA Full Funding Act authorizing a ten year plan to fully fund the federal share of IDEA, to urge Congress's strong bipartisan support and passage, and to remain committed to providing students with disabilities and their families the supports they need while acknowledging the intergovernmental partnership among local, state, and federal levels of government. Vendor sales deck from Arctic Wolf Networks, Inc. titled Managed Detection and Response and Managed Security Awareness Training Proposal Overview, dated 3/21/22 and carried on the Troy School District Board agenda as item 3.a. The cover slide is marked Classification: Public; most interior slides carry the notice Classification: Confidential with copyright lines for 2020 and 2021 Arctic Wolf Networks, Inc. Presented To: Beth Soggs, IT Director, and Alan Wilson, Network Manager. Prepared By: Nick Hankins, Account Executive, Arctic Wolf, and Chris Pittman, Sr. Systems Engineer, Arctic Wolf. People Driven, the partner organization, is represented by Bryan Teipel, President, and Dave Benham, Solution Architect. The proposal contents are enumerated as six sections: Executive Summary, Current Assessment, Why Arctic Wolf, Security Risk Quantification, Pricing Proposal, and Partnership and Enablement.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY. The strategic initiative is stated as Enhance Security and Visibility. The problem statement holds that Troy Schools has a distributed network across multiple physical buildings with most traffic backhauled to the central hub, making visibility across the environment and monitoring of network traffic a challenge; that Troy Schools has multiple security tools in place with limited staff to monitor and correlate alerts or identify and respond to potential malicious activity; and that a lack of a broad detection and response mechanism could prevent the ability to quickly identify, contain and remediate sophisticated threats. The desired outcomes are to operationalize a full-feature SIEM solution leveraging existing IT and security controls, to obtain a full-functioning cloud-integrated SOC service, and to leverage a service-based solution that can identify, evaluate, and provide quarantine and remediation guidance for threat indicators in real time. The proposed solution is Arctic Wolf's security operations as-a-concierge service ingesting Troy Schools environmental telemetry to perform 24x7x365 observations, investigations, and incident response guidance; an open, vendor-agnostic SIEM platform ingesting standardized log sources and live network traffic analysis; and three dedicated Security Operations FTEs using the Arctic Wolf Cloud Platform for proactive threat hunting and continuous improvement.

CURRENT ASSESSMENT. Current challenges reported from the Troy team: IT and security resources are constrained and the cost and complexity of building a 24x7x365 cybersecurity team in-house is probably unrealistic; endpoint and network security tools are in place and seasoned security professionals are desired for guidance in environmental hardening and continuous improvement; and there is interest in human-led, proactive threat hunting over basic alert-response services. Negative business impacts listed include risk from cyber attack, reactive response distracting burdened IT staff from existing initiatives, and inability to identify dormant vulnerabilities and threats. Value drivers are described as Benchmark Your Business, Team Enhancement, Faster Intrusion Detection, and Harden Your Environment, the latter via the CST evaluating vulnerability and risk data and presenting on-demand executive reports and personalized risk remediation plans.

SERVICE OFFERINGS. Managed Risk (Discover, Benchmark, Harden) is framed against the Center for Internet Security statement that 80% of breaches could have been prevented if the organization had met the top 5 CIS controls. Managed Detection and Response covers Detect, Respond, and Recover. Managed Cloud Monitoring covers Identify, Monitor, and Simplify, including unsecured S3 buckets and unauthorized cloud deployments, IaaS configuration risks, and SaaS indicators of compromise. Managed Security Awareness covers Engage, Measure, and Transform. A statistics band on the same slide prints the figures 47%, 80%, 85% and 70% alongside claims regarding incidents including a cloud component, threats preventable by meeting the top 5 CIS controls, data breaches resulting from employee actions, and new customer environments containing latent threats.

TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT MDR ARCHITECTURE. The scoped environment is stated as 1200 Users, 12,500 Student Users, 100 Servers, 1 300 Series Sensor, and 90 Day Log Retention, using AWN301 sensors and Secure Transport with API and platform integration to the Arctic Wolf Concierge Security Team. Monitored inputs include client monitoring agent and quarantine, firewall/UTM, Active Directory, server logs, anti-virus, Arctic Wolf Agent, DNS logs, HTTP and TLS, wireless APs, Cisco AMP for Endpoints, network monitoring with log collection and NTA, wireless networks, Windows event logs, system vulnerabilities, rootkit/compromise checks, process tables, installed patches, configuration benchmarks, asset information, and cloud monitoring of SaaS and IaaS.

WHY ARCTIC WOLF. Industry framing figures: 3,000 vendors, $120B total spend, and 3,950 reported breaches. Company facts: 1,200+ employees, 3,300+ customers, founded 2012. Audit and compliance drivers named are PCI DSS, FFIEC-NCUA, HIPAA, NIST 800-171, and 23 NYCRR 500. Better Protection statistics: Dwell Time 0:30, with the industry average time to identify an intrusion given as 206 days versus 30 minutes or less for Arctic Wolf; Phishing 18% of customers have phishing activity missed by email security but caught by Arctic Wolf; Advanced Threats 43% of customers have advanced threat activity missed by security tools; Account Takeover 70% of customers have some PII exposure, with 5.5% having plaintext passwords exposed online; and Unpatched Vulnerabilities 35% reduction in time to patch critical vulnerabilities after activating Arctic Wolf. The top five attack vectors listed are malware/ransomware, phishing, PUP adware, account hijacking, and unpatched outdated software. Citing the 2019 Ponemon Cost of Data Breach Incident Report, the deck prints 84 Days Mean Time to Contain (MTTC), 230 Days Mean Time to Identify (MTTI), and 314 DAYS. Citing Gartner, 70% of organizations are unable to process more than 60% of their security data, and the security skills gap through 2020 is given as 1.5M.

SECURITY OPERATIONS SCALE. The platform slide prints approximately 165M observations per week, approximately 765 investigations per week, and approximately 1-2 tickets per week, with an illustrative environment of 450 Users, 150 Servers, and 4 Sensors, flowing through Arctic Wolf Triage, the Concierge Security Team, a data lake and correlation database, threat intelligence and IOCs, and a real-time correlation engine.

SECURITY MONITORING BREAKDOWN. The general observation breakdown is given as Network/IDS 30%, SaaS/O365 15%, Active Directory/Domain Controllers 10%, Firewall 10%, EDR/AV 10%, Arctic Wolf Agent 10%, External Vulnerabilities 5%, Account Takeover 5%, and Other (VPN, Darktrace, Varonis) 5%. A comparison table asserts that NTA is included with the Arctic Wolf sensor while others offer NIDS/HIDS only, that asset inventory across endpoint and network is included, that vulnerability scanning is included, and that integrations, engagement with the CST, remote incident response, security guidance, custom rules, log ingestion and volume, log bandwidth, and security posture reviews are unlimited, with security posture reviews defaulting to once per month.

PRICING PROPOSAL. Arctic Wolf MDR is described as including a fully managed and hosted SIEM, 24x7 monitoring, a named Concierge Security Team, Managed Cloud Monitoring for O365 and Azure, monthly external vulnerability scanning, host-based isolation and managed containment, monthly and quarterly reporting, ad hoc reports on request, unlimited log volume and events per second, 90 days log retention, unlimited custom rules, and managed IDS. Arctic Wolf Service Assurance protects Troy Schools with up to $500,000 in financial assistance for a covered security event, itemized as Compliance $100,000, Ransomware and BEC $100,000, Cyber Legal Liability $250,000, and Business Income $50,000; eligibility requires purchasing MDR and Managed Awareness or Managed Risk and committing to standard terms of an annual contract paid upfront with an 8% annual renewal increase. A separate slide states a multi-year deal with all products is required to qualify for the $1,000,000 level. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Board presentation on the English Language Arts Curriculum Review and Revision for Grades 9-12 during 2021-2022, laying out the rationale for moving the high school program to a workshop model already used in elementary and middle school. District data on SAT college level reading readiness show Cohort 1 (2016-2018) at 82.47 in 9th grade, 83.50 in 10th, and 76.85 in 11th, a stated decrease of 5.62%, and Cohort 2 (2017-2019) at 86.80, 84.70, and 81.44, a stated decrease of 5.36%. A 9th Grade Curriculum Development Team is writing six workshop-style, skill-based units for piloting in 2022-2023, with a new 9th Grade English course in 2023-2024 and 10th Grade English in 2024-2025.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Topic**
ELA Curriculum Review and Revision, Grades 9-12, 2021-2022, presented to the Troy Board of Education.

**Collectively Developed Priorities**
The need to effectively serve ALL students; recent SAT college level reading readiness data meriting consideration; addressing the gap between high and low performing students; adequate training for teachers in advancing readers; a priority placed on the blue and red pillars; protected practice time for reading, writing, and critical thinking; learning environments conducive to responsive teaching; building student independence in college and career readiness skills; a commitment to rich, student-centered discussion and critical thinking; and choice, rigor, and diversity of text selection in all courses.

**District Data: SAT College Level Reading Readiness**

| Cohort | 9th Grade | 10th Grade | 11th Grade | Stated change |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cohort 1: 2016-2018 | 82.47 | 83.50 | 76.85 | Decrease of 5.62% |
| Cohort 2: 2017-2019 | 86.80 | 84.70 | 81.44 | Decrease of 5.36% |

**Rationale**
The presentation cites Michael Fullan et al (2006), Breakthrough, for the proposition that the old mission of schools was universal access to basic education plus university access for a small elite, and that whereas twenty years ago 95% of jobs were low-skilled, today those jobs constitute only 10% of the entire economy. The new mission is to get all students to meet high standards and equip them as lifelong learners. Capacities of the literate individual are excerpted from the Michigan Common Core State Standards: demonstrate independence; build strong content knowledge; respond to the varying demands of audience, task, purpose and discipline; comprehend as well as critique; value evidence; use technology and media strategically and capably; and come to understand other perspectives and cultures.

**Course Pathways**
Current trajectory, described as limited options and a linear path: 9 Lit and Comp, 10 Lit and Comp, 11 LC/Elective, 12 Lit and Comp, with an honors strand of 9 LC Honors, 10 LC Honors, 11 AP Language, 12 AP Literature. Preferred future, described as more options with all students prepared for choice: 9th Grade English in 2023-2024 and 10th Grade English in 2024-2025, opening into American Lit, World Lit, AP Language, AP Literature, and Electives.

**Workshop Model Experience**
The literacy journey runs from elementary through middle school to high school, with curricular coherence aligning to Workshop in elementary at 5th and 6th grade. Middle school teachers report that avid readers are plowing through books and reluctant readers are reading more than in past years, that students are writing more daily through jots, long writes and flash drafts, that current students are performing well and challenge themselves with higher level books through book clubs, and that students are more engaged and thinking deeply. Areas for growth identified by middle school colleagues are conferring, resources and professional development, and small group resources and professional development.

**Professional Development**
5 teachers participated in the Teachers College Writing Institute in July 2021. 8 teachers participated in the Teachers College HS Book Club Institute in December 2021. 11 teachers participated in a webinar with Penny Kittle and Kelly Gallagher in December 2021. A full day of PD was provided in August, led by fellow teachers. During the November late start, a TC Staff Developer led PD on using on-demand writing samples to inform small groups and conferring. 9th grade teachers and coaches continue to visit middle school classrooms. Coaches participated in an on-site day with Teachers College in March 2022 and secondary administrators in February 2022, both with TC Staff Developer Natalie Louis.

**Current Work and Next Steps**
A 9th Grade Curriculum Development Team was created, prioritized skills for 9th grade, and outlined skills for all 6 units; the team has met twice to unpack vertical alignment of skills from 6-8, will visit middle school classrooms to observe through the lenses of 3 workshop commitments, and will spend time with a TC Staff Developer in lab settings receiving guidance for Units 1-3. The goal is to write 6 workshop-style, skill-based units to be piloted in 2022-2023. Next steps: summer learning through the Teaching Writing in High School Institute and a Summer Homegrown Institute on Creating Teacher Toolkits to Support a Wide-Range of Writers, followed by targeted piloting of 9th grade units in Fall 2022.

**Ask of the Board**
Target professional development to meet teacher needs, specifically centered around responsive teaching and differentiation at both middle school and high school, and continue to honor the workshop commitment of choice by funding access to fascinating texts.

COLLECTIVELY DEVELOPED PRIORITIES. The presentation opens with a list of priorities developed collectively: the need to effectively serve ALL students; recent data in SAT college level reading readiness that merits consideration; addressing the gap between high and low performing students; adequate training for teachers in advancing readers; a priority placed on the blue and red pillars; protected practice time for reading, writing, and critical thinking; learning environments conducive to responsive teaching; building student independence in college and career readiness skills; a commitment to rich, student-centered discussion and critical thinking; and choice, rigor, and diversity of text selection in all courses.

DISTRICT DATA, DECREASE IN SAT COLLEGE LEVEL READING READINESS. Two cohorts are tracked. Cohort 1, spanning 2016-2018, shows 9th Grade 82.47, 10th Grade 83.50, and 11th Grade 76.85, labeled as a Decrease of 5.62%. Cohort 2, spanning 2017-2019, shows 9th Grade 86.80, 10th Grade 84.70, and 11th Grade 81.44, labeled as a Decrease of 5.36%.

RATIONALE AND RESEARCH BASE. The deck quotes the argument that study after study shows globalization and new information technologies have made it especially urgent for schools to chart a new mission. It cites Breakthrough by Michael Fullan and colleagues (2006) for the point that the old mission for schools was to provide universal access to basic education and then to provide a small elite with access to university education. It states that the world has changed: whereas twenty years ago 95% of jobs were low-skilled, today those jobs constitute only 10% of the entire economy. The new mission is described as getting all students to meet high standards of education and providing them with a lifelong education that does not have the built-in obsolescence of so much old-style curriculum but that equips them to be lifelong learners.

STANDARDS FRAMING. Excerpted from the Michigan Common Core State Standards, the presentation lists the capacities of the literate individual that students exhibit with increasing fullness and regularity as they advance through the grades and master the standards in reading, writing, speaking, listening, and language: demonstrate independence; build strong content knowledge; respond to the varying demands of audience, task, purpose and discipline; comprehend as well as critique; value evidence; use technology and media strategically and capably; and come to understand other perspectives and cultures.

CURRENT COURSE TRAJECTORY. The present high school pathway is characterized as limited options on a linear path. The general sequence runs 9 Lit and Comp, 10 Lit and Comp, 11 LC/Elective, and 12 Lit and Comp. The accelerated sequence runs 9 LC Honors, 10 LC Honors, 11 AP Language, and 12 AP Literature.

PREFERRED COURSE STRUCTURE. The preferred model is described as more options with all students prepared for choice. It begins with a redesigned 9th Grade English course in 2023-2024 followed by a redesigned 10th Grade English course in 2024-2025, after which students may select from American Lit, World Lit, AP Language, AP Literature, and Electives.

LITERACY JOURNEY AND CURRICULAR COHERENCE. The presentation traces the literacy journey from elementary to middle school to high school, noting curricular coherence that aligns with Workshop in elementary, with slides addressing 5th Grade and 6th Grade and the movement of Workshop into the middle school.

WHAT THE DISTRICT HAS LEARNED FROM WORKSHOP IN MIDDLE SCHOOL. The stated lessons are that the student is at the center of the work; that skills are at the forefront with content used to achieve those skills; that choice in reading and writing allows for the engagement necessary for growth; that time to practice is the hallmark of the workshop model; and that normalizing feedback in the moment to meet students where they are promotes progress for all.

POSITIVE ASPECTS REPORTED BY MIDDLE SCHOOL TEACHERS. Teachers report that avid readers are plowing through books and reluctant readers are reading more than in past years. Students are writing more, with daily jots, long writes, or flash drafts, and fewer students sit and say they do not know what to write about; notebooks are filled with drafts, revisions, and edits. Current students are performing well, with some challenging themselves through reading higher level books, and teachers report doing a good job encouraging reading more difficult books through book clubs. Students are described as more engaged and thinking deeply about what they are reading.

AREAS FOR GROWTH IDENTIFIED BY MIDDLE SCHOOL COLLEAGUES. Three areas are named: conferring; resources and professional development; and small group resources and professional development.

WHAT TEACHERS NEED AS THE WORK EXTENDS TO HIGH SCHOOL, AND THE ASK OF THE BOARD. The presentation asks the Board to target professional development to meet teacher needs, specifically centered around responsive teaching and differentiation at both the middle school and high school levels, and to continue to honor the workshop commitment of choice by funding access to fascinating texts.

ONGOING SUPPORT FOR TEACHERS THROUGHOUT THE TRANSITION. 5 teachers participated in the Teachers College Writing Institute in July 2021. 8 teachers participated in the Teachers College HS Book Club Institute in December 2021. 11 teachers participated in a webinar with Penny Kittle and Kelly Gallagher in December 2021. A full day of professional development was provided in August and led by fellow teachers. During the November late start, a Teachers College Staff Developer led professional development on how to use on-demand writing samples to inform small groups and conferring. 9th grade teachers and coaches continue to visit middle school classrooms. Coaches participated in an on-site day with Teachers College in March 2022, and secondary administrators participated in an on-site day with Teachers College in February 2022. Teachers shared their learning with the 9-12 ELA team, and teachers learned more about engaging students in writing to increase volume. The Administrators' Day and the Coaches' Day were both conducted with Teachers College Staff Developer Natalie Louis.

CURRENT WORK WITH HIGH SCHOOL. A 9th Grade Curriculum Development Team (CDT) was created. The team prioritized skills for 9th grade and outlined skills for all 6 units. The CDT will visit middle school classrooms to observe through the lenses of the 3 workshop commitments. The stated goal is to write 6 workshop-style, skill-based units that will be piloted in 2022-2023. The team has already met twice to unpack the vertical alignment of skills from grades 6 through 8. The CDT will spend time with a Teachers College Staff Developer in lab settings and receive guidance for Units 1-3. Summer learning for the team includes creating teacher toolkits to support a wide range of writers and a Teaching Writing in High School Institute. A slide is devoted to the 9th Grade CDT's work on vertical alignment of skills.

NEXT STEPS. Summer learning consists of the Teaching Writing in High School Institute and a Summer Homegrown Institute titled Creating Teacher Toolkits to Support a Wide-Range of Writers. For Fall 2022, the next step is targeted piloting of the 9th grade units.
