Arctic Wolf Networks, Inc. proposal overview titled Managed Detection and Response and Managed Security Awareness Training Proposal Overview, dated 3/21/22, appearing on the Troy Board of Education agenda as item 8.A. for the April 19, 2022 meeting. The cover slide is marked Classification: Public, with interior slides marked Classification: Confidential and bearing 2020 and 2021 Arctic Wolf Networks, Inc. copyright notices. Presented To: Beth Soggs, IT Director, and Alan Wilson, Network Manager. Prepared By: Nick Hankins, Account Executive, Arctic Wolf, and Chris Pittman, Sr. Systems Engineer, Arctic Wolf. People Driven is represented by Bryan Teipel, President, and Dave Benham, Solution Architect. The proposal contents are Executive Summary, Current Assessment, Why Arctic Wolf, Security Risk Quantification, Pricing Proposal, and Partnership and Enablement.

EXECUTIVE SUMMARY. Under the strategic initiative Enhance Security and Visibility, the stated problems are that Troy Schools has a distributed network across multiple physical buildings with most traffic backhauled to the central hub, making visibility across the environment and monitoring of network traffic for security relevant perspectives a challenge; that Troy Schools has multiple security tools in place with limited staff to monitor and correlate alerts or identify and respond to potential malicious activity; and that a lack of a broad detection and response mechanism could prevent the ability to quickly identify, contain and remediate sophisticated threats. Desired outcomes are to operationalize a full-feature SIEM solution leveraging existing IT and security controls, a full-functioning cloud-integrated SOC service, and a service-based solution providing quarantine and remediation guidance in real time. The proposed solution is Arctic Wolf's security operations as-a-concierge service ingesting Troy Schools environmental telemetry for 24x7x365 observations, investigations, and incident response guidance; an open, vendor-agnostic SIEM platform ingesting all standardized log sources plus live network traffic analysis; and three dedicated Security Operations FTEs providing proactive threat hunting and continuous improvement.

CURRENT ASSESSMENT. Challenges heard from the Troy team: IT and security resources are constrained and the cost and complexity to build a 24x7x365 cybersecurity team in-house is probably unrealistic; endpoint and network security tools are in place and seasoned security professionals are wanted to guide environmental hardening and continuous improvement; and there is interest in human-led, proactive threat hunting over basic alert-response and typical operational-level services. Negative impacts listed are risk from cyber attack and inability to prevent, detect, respond and remediate quickly; reactive response distracting already burdened IT staff from existing initiatives and projects; and inability to identify dormant vulnerabilities and threats risking a larger and longer-term breach. Business value drivers are Benchmark Your Business, Team Enhancement, Faster Intrusion Detection, and Harden Your Environment.

SERVICE OFFERINGS. Managed Risk (Discover, Benchmark, Harden) is framed by the Center for Internet Security statement that 80% of breaches could have been prevented if the organization had met the top 5 CIS controls. Managed Detection and Response covers Detect, Respond, and Recover. Managed Cloud Monitoring covers Identify, Monitor, and Simplify, including unsecured S3 buckets and unauthorized cloud deployments. Managed Security Awareness covers Engage, Measure, and Transform. The accompanying statistics band prints 47%, 80%, 85% and 70% against claims concerning incidents including a cloud component, threats preventable by meeting the top 5 CIS controls, data breaches resulting from employee actions, and new customer environments containing latent threats.

TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT MDR ARCHITECTURE. The environment is stated as 1200 Users, 12,500 Student Users, 100 Servers, 1 300 Series Sensor, and 90 Day Log Retention, with AWN301 sensors and Secure Transport feeding the Arctic Wolf Concierge Security Team through API and platform integration. Data sources include client monitoring agent and quarantine, firewall/UTM, Active Directory, server logs, anti-virus, Arctic Wolf Agent, DNS logs, HTTP and TLS, wireless APs, Cisco AMP for Endpoints, network monitoring with log collection and NTA, wireless networks, Windows event logs, system vulnerabilities, rootkit/compromise detection, process tables, installed patches, configuration benchmarks, asset information, and cloud monitoring of SaaS and IaaS.

WHY ARCTIC WOLF. Industry framing: 3,000 vendors, $120B total spend, 3,950 reported breaches. Company: 1,200+ employees, 3,300+ customers, founded 2012. Compliance drivers named are PCI DSS, FFIEC-NCUA, HIPAA, NIST 800-171, and 23 NYCRR 500. Protection statistics: Dwell Time 0:30 against an industry average time to identify an intrusion of 206 days; Phishing 18% of customers have phishing activity missed by email security but caught by Arctic Wolf; Advanced Threats 43% of customers have advanced threat activity missed by security tools; Account Takeover 70% of customers have some PII exposure with 5.5% having plaintext passwords exposed online; Unpatched Vulnerabilities 35% reduction in time to patch critical vulnerabilities after activating Arctic Wolf. Top five attack vectors: malware/ransomware, phishing, PUP adware, account hijacking, and unpatched outdated software. From the 2019 Ponemon Cost of Data Breach Incident Report the deck prints 84 Days Mean Time to Contain (MTTC), 230 Days Mean Time to Identify (MTTI), and 314 DAYS. From Gartner it prints that 70% of organizations are unable to process more than 60% of their security data and that the security skills gap through 2020 is 1.5M.

PLATFORM SCALE. The security operations slide prints approximately 165M observations per week, approximately 765 investigations per week, and approximately 1-2 tickets per week, with an illustrative environment of 450 Users, 150 Servers, and 4 Sensors, routed through Arctic Wolf Triage, the Concierge Security Team, a data lake and correlation database, threat intelligence and IOCs, and a real-time correlation engine, supporting Identify, Act, and Improve functions including the Security Journey program.

SECURITY MONITORING BREAKDOWN. General observation breakdown: Network/IDS 30%, SaaS/O365 15%, Active Directory/Domain Controllers 10%, Firewall 10%, EDR/AV 10%, Arctic Wolf Agent 10%, External Vulnerabilities 5%, Account Takeover 5%, and Other (VPN, Darktrace, Varonis) 5%. The deck argues that EPP focuses on preventing well-known attacks but cannot detect unknown or zero-day threats, that EDR detects and responds to unknown threats on endpoints but does not provide network visibility, and that MDR leverages existing endpoint, network and cloud solutions to create a unified view. A capability comparison lists NTA included with the Arctic Wolf sensor versus NIDS/HIDS only elsewhere, asset inventory across endpoint and network included, vulnerability scanning included, holistic visibility included, unlimited integrations, unlimited direct CST engagement, unlimited remote incident response, unlimited security guidance and analysis, unlimited custom rules, unlimited log ingestion, volume and bandwidth, unlimited security posture reviews defaulting to once per month, and dark web scanning and account takeover monitoring included.

PRICING PROPOSAL AND INCLUSIONS. Arctic Wolf MDR includes a fully managed and hosted SIEM, 24x7 monitoring, a named Concierge Security Team, Managed Cloud Monitoring for O365 and Azure, monthly external vulnerability scanning, host-based isolation and managed containment, monthly and quarterly reporting, ad hoc reports on request, unlimited log volume and events per second, 90 days log retention, unlimited custom rules, and managed IDS. Arctic Wolf Service Assurance protects Troy Schools with up to $500,000 in financial assistance should a covered security event occur, allocated as Compliance $100,000, Ransomware and BEC $100,000, Cyber Legal Liability $250,000, and Business Income $50,000. Eligibility requires purchasing MDR and Managed Awareness or Managed Risk, and committing to standard terms of an annual contract paid upfront with an 8% annual renewal increase. A separate slide states that a multi-year deal with all products is required to qualify for the $1,000,000 level. Arctic Wolf Managed Security Awareness includes a fully managed awareness program, awareness program coaching, multiple integration options, a friction free user experience, gamification, positive education and reinforcement, ongoing microlearning, integrated phishing simulations, 24x7 account takeover monitoring, and performance analytics.

MDR PRICING OVERVIEW, ANNUAL CONTRACT. MDR User License, AW-MDR-USER, quantity 1200, $77,760.00. MDR Student User License, AW-MDR-STUDENT, quantity 12,500, $40,500.00. MDR Server License, AW-MDR-SE, quantity 100, $6,480.00. MDR 300 Series Sensor, AW-MDR-3XX-S-10GC, quantity 1, $2,160.00. MDR Log Retention 90 Days, AW-MDR-90DAY, quantity 1346, $13.00. AW Platform, AW-PLATFORM, quantity 1346, $7,020.00. Subscription Fee Total $133,933.00, with a footnote that upon renewal of equal or greater quantities and subscription terms the net total will increase by 8.0 percent annually. One-time setup items: Arctic Wolf MDR Onboarding, AW-MDR-OB, quantity 1, $9,091.48; Arctic Wolf Sensor Shipping, AW-SHP, quantity 1, $144.00; One-time Setup Fees Total $9,235.48. Total Fees for 1 Year: $143,168.48. Pricing expires on 4/22.

MSAT PRICING OVERVIEW, ANNUAL CONTRACT. Managed Security Awareness Service, AW-MSAT-MA, quantity 1200, $12,972.00; Subscription Fee Total $12,972.00, with a footnote that renewal increases the net total by 5.0 percent annually. Pricing expires on 4/22.

COMBINED MDR PLUS MSAT PRICING OVERVIEW, ANNUAL CONTRACT. MDR 1YR Total, quantity 1, $143,168.48; MSAT 1YR Total, quantity 1, $12,972.00; Subscription Fee Total $156,140.48, with a 5.0 percent annual renewal increase footnote. Pricing expires on 4/22.

SECURITY TALENT GAP IN MICHIGAN. Citing ziprecruiter.com salary data for Cybersecurity Engineer in Detroit, MI, and cyberseek.org, the deck states that hiring and retaining cybersecurity professionals is challenging and expensive, that the U.S. cybersecurity workforce currently consists of 715,000 people with 314,000 unfilled job openings, and that cybersecurity professionals are receiving larger than average salary increases at 8-10% annually, with salary averages shown for Detroit, MI Cyber Security Engineer and Cyber Security Analyst.

DIY VS. ARCTIC WOLF TCO/ROI ESTIMATE. For a DIY in-house SOC, described as average SOC costs across major vendors: annual SIEM costs with an 8% year-over-year increase at $80,000 in Year 1, $86,400 in Year 2, and $93,312 in Year 3, totaling $259,712; professional services for install, training and maintenance at $25,000, $5,000, and $5,000, totaling $35,000; SOC staffing for analysis and forensics covering 1 FTE and 1 analyst with an 8% year-over-year increase at $282,746.10, $302,538.33, and $323,716.01, totaling $909,000.44; threat intelligence at $19,800 per year, totaling $59,400; and vulnerability scanning for 2 point-in-time scans at $20,000 per year, totaling $60,000. The DIY SOC cost estimate is $427,546.10, $433,738.33, and $461,828.01, totaling $1,323,112.44. The Arctic Wolf line, all-inclusive MDR costs with 24x7x365 coverage, is $143,168.48, $144,647.64, and $156,219.45, totaling $444,035.57, with SIEM appliance costs, professional services, Arctic Wolf security staff costs, threat intelligence costs, and existing SOC staff all shown at $0. Stated cost savings of the Arctic Wolf solution over DIY are $284,377.62, $289,090.69, and $305,608.56, totaling $879,076.87, with a note that years 2 and 3 go to the renewals team and have an 8% increase.

EVALUATION HIGHLIGHTS AND CONTRACT DATES. 11/17 initial discovery call held between TSD and AW. 11/19 technical walkthrough completed with TSD and AW to confirm scope and build pricing. 12/10 first scope and proposal exercise held with TSD, AW, and People Driven. 4/22 technical selection made and budget secured, initial order entered. 4/26 CST onboarding experience begins, 30 to 45 days before the contract start date. 5/30 full ramp including all sensors in place, data properly aggregating, and initial determinations being performed by the iSOC and CST team. Signature Date: 4/22/2022. On-boarding Start Date: 4/26/2022. Subscription Start Date: 5/30/2022, with onboarding typically completed in 4-6 weeks.

PARTNERSHIP AND ENABLEMENT. The Concierge Security Team is presented under Expertise (security operations experts with accreditations such as CISSP, HCISPP, CCSP, CISM, and CRISC; daily proactive threat hunting; informed incident insights), Coverage (24x7 continuous monitoring; rapid response detecting and investigating critical events within five minutes; real-time remediation), and Strategy (security posture reviews, named advisors, and Security Journey guidance delivered through quarterly reviews). The Concierge Engagement Model splits duties between Troy School District and Arctic Wolf across Deployment, Activation, Customization, Service Delivery, Scheduled reviews, and Ad-Hoc requests, with district responsibilities including deploying the agent, receiving and installing sensors and scanners, configuring log sources, engaging with tickets, executing remediation, calling for emergencies, and notifying Arctic Wolf of architecture changes. Closing slides cover Arctic Wolf customers, Q&A, and a comparison of approaches to security operations spanning SIEM, MSSP, EDR, MDR, and XDR, with Arctic Wolf claiming coverage across the security operations framework, use of existing or Arctic Wolf technology, visibility across endpoint, network, cloud, apps, identity and people, unlimited and unmetered data pricing, and having invented the Concierge Security Team.

GENERAL FUND AMENDMENT RATIONALE. Four drivers are listed: categorical funding adjusted to reflect the state aid status report; federal grant funding adjusted to reflect final allocations; ISD related funding sources adjusted to reflect final allocations; and purchased services, salaries and benefits budgets adjusted to reflect anticipated final expenditures.

REVENUE EXPECTATIONS. Comparing 2025-2026 original to 2025-2026 Amendment #1 with the difference: Enrollment 12,074.00 to 12,071.23, a difference of (2.77); Foundation 130,230,164 to 130,788,472, a difference of 558,308; 27L(4) MPSERS 0 to 1,326,153, a difference of 1,326,153; 147A(1) MPSERS 1,007,246 to 0, a difference of (1,007,246); 35(A) Early Literacy 176,655 to 0, a difference of (176,655).

MPSERS UPDATES, FISCAL YEAR 2025. The state provided 147a(4) funds to offset retirement expenses in the amount of $5,055,278. That funding would be eliminated for fiscal year 2026. The presentation stresses that the payment was a categorical payment that does not roll into future foundation allowance and was essentially one-time money.

MPSERS UPDATES, FISCAL YEAR 2026. The state eliminated 147a(1) at the last minute, a loss shown as ($1,007,246). Employees are no longer contributing the 3% healthcare premium, which has been absorbed by the employer this year. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Purpose**
The High School Course Description Book (CDB) shows course requirements and elective opportunities for students, organized by department so students and families understand the offerings. It is a OneTroy document developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools along with the Teaching and Learning team, and is updated annually as part of the curriculum review process. Department teams determine where descriptions should be updated to reflect new curriculum and instruction and where courses should be added or deleted. The changes listed apply to the 2026/2027 school year.

**Courses added**

| Course | Grades | Length / credit |
|---|---|---|
| AP Business with Personal Finance | 9-12 | Full year, 1.0 credit |
| AP Cybersecurity | 9-12 | Full year, 1.0 credit |
| AP Precalculus AB | 9-12 | Full year, 1.0 credit |
| AP Precalculus BC | 9-12 | Full year, 1.0 credit |
| Career Capstone | 11-12 | 1 semester, 1/2 credit |
| English 11 1 - Great American Stories | 11 | 1 semester, 0.5 credit |
| English 11 1 - Contemporary American Literature | 11 | 1 semester, 0.5 credit |
| English 11 1 - American Dramas and Musicals | 11 | 1 semester, 0.5 credit |
| English 11 2 - Persuasive Writing | 11 | 1 semester, 0.5 credit |
| English 11 2 - Writing Imaginative Fiction | 11 | 1 semester, 0.5 credit |
| English 11 2 - Writing Personal Memoirs | 11 | 1 semester, 0.5 credit |
| Mathematics of Tabletop Games | 11-12 | 1 semester, 0.5 credit |
| Sports Officiating | 9-12 | 1 semester, 0.5 credit |

**Course replacement notes**
AP Cybersecurity replaces and builds upon the previously offered Cybersecurity course and is part of the AP Career Kickstart group. AP Precalculus AB replaces the previously offered Precalculus; AP Precalculus BC replaces the previously offered Honors Precalculus. Both AP Precalculus courses require completion of Algebra 2. AP Business with Personal Finance satisfies 1 credit of the math related graduation requirement; Mathematics of Tabletop Games satisfies 0.5 credit of the math related graduation requirement and requires Geometry.

**English 11 structure**
Semester 1 is Literary Analysis in Reading; Writing about Reading, with students choosing one of three courses. Semester 2 is Writing with a Purpose and Exploring Mentor Texts, again choosing one of three. All six include focused sessions tied to the SAT.

**Courses removed** (none of these offerings has run in the past five years)
Social Studies: Political Science, Stories of Yourself and Others, Psychology 2, Conflicts of the 20th Century, Philosophy. English: Literature of Suspense, Science Fiction, Voices in Literature, Modern Shakespeare. Life Skills: Interior Design, Stitchery.

**Other changes**
Achievement Skills III will now be called Integrated Studies III; increased math-related and NCAA course approvals; the format changed from PDF to PaperTurn.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Administrative memorandum describing updates to the Troy School District High School Course Description Book (CDB) for the 2026/2027 school year. The CDB shows the course requirements and elective opportunities for students and is organized by department so that students and families understand the offerings. It is described as a OneTroy document developed collaboratively by administrators and department heads from both high schools along with the Teaching and Learning team, and is updated annually as part of the curriculum review process, with department teams determining where course descriptions should be updated to reflect new curriculum and instruction and where courses should be added or deleted.

COURSES ADDED.

AP Business with Personal Finance, grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit. The course satisfies 1 credit of the math related graduation requirement. It introduces students to the knowledge and skills needed to grow careers, manage money, and get a head start toward the most popular college major in the U.S. Developed in partnership with college faculty and industry leaders, the yearlong course offers the opportunity to earn college credit and an employer-endorsed credential. Students who participate meet the introductory requirement to have the potential to compete in DECA the following year.

AP Cybersecurity, grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit. A yearlong course offering a broad introduction to the field, aligned closely with a college-level introductory cybersecurity course. It replaces and builds upon the previously offered Cybersecurity course. Students learn about common threats and vulnerabilities and how they combine to create risk, how individuals and organizations manage risk, and how risk can be mitigated through a defense-in-depth strategy. They explore vulnerabilities, attacks, mitigations, and detection measures across physical spaces, computer networks, devices, and data and applications, and consider the impact of cybersecurity on individuals, organizations, societies, and governments. Content and skills align with the professional skills outlined in the National Initiative for Cybersecurity Education Workforce Framework. The course is part of the AP Career Kickstart group of courses, designed to accelerate high school students on their paths to in-demand careers, and offers the opportunity to earn an employer-endorsed credential in the cybersecurity field.

AP Precalculus AB, grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit. Students must have completed Algebra 2. The course replaces the previously offered Precalculus. Major topics include polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions; polar and parametric equations; and the analysis of rates of change. Students may take the AP Precalculus exam and are prepared to take AP Calculus AB.

AP Precalculus BC, grades 9-12, full year, 1.0 credit. Students must have completed Algebra 2. The course replaces the previously offered Honors Precalculus and covers the same major topics plus the additional content of limits and derivatives and vectors. Students may take the AP Precalculus exam and are prepared to take AP Calculus BC.

Career Capstone, grades 11-12, 1 semester, 1/2 credit. Students must be a completer in a business pathway (Finance, BAMO or Marketing). Described as the CTE Professional Capstone, a culminating experience preparing students for college, careers, and real-world professional environments. Students build a professional identity by developing a resume, LinkedIn profile, and digital portfolio showcasing their CTE work, engage in professional-based learning projects that mirror authentic industry challenges, and collaborate with business partners. They refine employability skills through formal interview practice, career coaching, job-shadow opportunities, and reflective activities, graduating with a polished professional toolkit supporting job applications, internships, apprenticeships, and postsecondary pathways.

English 11 Semester 1 is titled Literary Analysis in Reading; Writing about Reading, with students choosing one of three courses, each grade 11, 1 semester, 0.5 credit. English 11 1 - Great American Stories introduces influential and enduring works of American literature through short stories, novels, dramas, and historical texts, exploring identity, freedom, justice, the American Dream, and societal change; texts may include The Great Gatsby, A Raisin in the Sun, and Fences. English 11 1 - Contemporary American Literature examines the contemporary landscape of American literature and themes of freedom, equality, justice, identity, race, immigration, and belonging; texts may include Kindred, King James, and Sweat. English 11 1 - American Dramas and Musicals introduces dramas by American playwrights about the American Dream, American identity, and the American experience in 20th and 21st century plays, along with musicals; texts may include Hamilton, View from the Bridge, and King James. All three include focused sessions on preparing for the SAT.

English 11 Semester 2 is titled Writing with a Purpose and Exploring Mentor Texts, again choosing one of three, each grade 11, 1 semester, 0.5 credit. English 11 2 - Persuasive Writing develops critical thinking, evidence-based argument, and oral presentation, with students forming claims, selecting evidence, addressing counterarguments, and adapting messages to diverse audiences. English 11 2 - Writing Imaginative Fiction develops creative voice through storytelling elements of character, setting, plot, dialogue, and narrative structure, along with poetic techniques such as imagery, metaphor, rhythm, and form, and prepares students to take Creative Writing 2 in senior year. English 11 2 - Writing Personal Memoirs uses close reading of mentor texts including memoirs, personal essays, and narrative nonfiction, teaching sensory detail, structure, reflection, and voice, with each student producing a polished memoir and a collection of shorter writings. All three include focused sessions on writing a rhetorical essay in response to the SAT prompts and creating a working draft of a personal essay.

Mathematics of Tabletop Games, grades 11-12, 1 semester, 0.5 credit. The course qualifies as a 1/2 math-related credit and requires completion of Geometry. Students collaboratively investigate the mathematical foundation of various tabletop games through theorycrafting, experiential observation, and empirical analysis, connecting combinatorics, geometry, probability, game theory, and logic with the medium of tabletop games. The course satisfies 0.5 credit of the math related graduation requirement.

Sports Officiating, grades 9-12, 1 semester, 0.5 credit. Students learn to officiate sports and become certified high school officials upon course completion. The course covers three sports per semester: football, basketball, and a sport of students' choice in the Fall semester; baseball, softball, and soccer in the Spring semester along with a sport of students' choice. Students will earn referrals to local recreational leagues, middle schools, and sub-varsity scholastic assignors.

COURSES REMOVED. The memorandum states that none of these offerings has run in the past five years. Social Studies: Political Science, Stories of Yourself and Others, Psychology 2, Conflicts of the 20th Century, and Philosophy. English: Literature of Suspense, Science Fiction, Voices in Literature, and Modern Shakespeare. Life Skills: Interior Design and Stitchery.

OTHER CHANGES. Achievement Skills III will now be called Integrated Studies III. There are increased math-related and NCAA course approvals. The format of the book changed from PDF to PaperTurn.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Board of Education resolution, drafted for adoption at the regular meeting of February 24, 2026 at 7:00 p.m., requesting that Oakland Schools Intermediate School District place a regional enhancement millage question before voters. The resolution asks for 1.50 mills for a period of six years, 2026 to 2031 inclusive, at the school election to be held August 4, 2026, under Section 705 of the Revised School Code (MCL 380.705). The attached Exhibit A ballot language states the levy would raise an estimated $125,756,247 if approved and first levied in 2026, with proceeds distributed by Oakland Schools on an equal per-pupil basis to eligible constituent districts and public school academies.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Instrument**
Minutes and resolution of a Regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, held on the 24th day of February 2026 at 7:00 p.m., local time. The document is a template with blanks for present and absent members, the offering and supporting members, and the ayes and nays.

**Statutory basis**
Section 705 of the Revised School Code of 1976, as amended (MCL 380.705), provides for the levy of a regional enhancement property tax by an intermediate school district at a rate not to exceed 3 mills, to enhance other state and local funding for local school operating purposes, if approved by a majority of the intermediate school district electors. Proceeds are paid to each constituent school district, including eligible public school academies, on a per pupil basis. A constituent school district may request that the ISD submit the question, and the ISD is required to submit it if it receives requests from constituent districts representing a majority of combined membership as of the most recent membership count date.

**Rationale recited**
The intermediate school districts in both Wayne and Macomb County are currently authorized to levy a voter-approved regional enhancement millage, which provides greater student opportunities that may include reduced class sizes, enhanced program offerings, improved school safety, and increased staff retention and attraction, benefits Oakland County currently does not receive. The resolution states that Oakland County residents deserve the opportunity to provide competitive educational opportunities and similar resources to those available in neighboring Wayne and Macomb counties.

**Operative provisions**
1. Requests that Oakland Schools submit to its electors a regional enhancement millage proposal for 1.50 mills for a period of six (6) years, 2026 to 2031 inclusive, at the school election to be held August 4, 2026, in substantially the form of Exhibit A.
2. Approves the Exhibit A ballot wording, subject to revision and finalization by Oakland Schools as necessary.
3. Directs the Superintendent to deliver a certified copy of the resolution to the Secretary of the Board of Education of Oakland Schools.
4. States the resolution is only a request; the proposal will be submitted to voters only if Oakland Schools receives requests from constituent districts representing a majority of combined membership on or before March 31, 2026.
5. Rescinds conflicting resolutions and parts of resolutions.

**Exhibit A ballot language**
Oakland Schools Intermediate School District regional enhancement millage proposal: an increase in the ad valorem tax limitation of 1.5 mills ($1.50 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation) for a period of six (6) years, 2026 to 2031 inclusive, as new additional millage to provide funds to enhance other state and local funding for public school operating purposes. The proposal states the millage would raise an estimated $125,756,247 if approved and first levied in 2026, with YES and NO options. Revenue will be disbursed on an equal per-pupil basis to the listed school districts and public school academies within Oakland Schools boundaries that are eligible under the Revised School Code.

**Certification**
A secretary's certification attests the resolution is a true and complete copy adopted at a Regular meeting held February 24, 2026, conducted with public notice in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Minutes and accompanying resolution for a Regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, held on the 24th day of February 2026 at 7:00 p.m. local time. The document is presented in template form with blank lines for the members present and absent, for the member offering the resolution and the member supporting it, and for the ayes and nays, and is titled RESOLUTION REQUESTING REGIONAL ENHANCEMENT MILLAGE ELECTION.

WHEREAS CLAUSES. The first clause recites that Section 705 of the Revised School Code of 1976, as amended (MCL 380.705), referred to throughout as Section 705, provides for the levy of a regional enhancement property tax by an intermediate school district at a rate not to exceed 3 mills, for the purpose of enhancing other state and local funding for local school operating purposes, if approved by a majority of the intermediate school district electors. The second clause recites that proceeds of a millage levied pursuant to Section 705 are paid to each constituent school district, including eligible public school academies and referred to as a Constituent School District, by the intermediate school district in an amount calculated on a per pupil basis as provided in Section 705. The third clause recites that a Constituent School District may request an intermediate school district to submit the question of a regional enhancement property tax to the voters at a school election held in each Constituent School District that is a school district. The fourth clause recites that the intermediate school district is required to submit the question to the voters if it receives a request from its Constituent School Districts representing a majority of the combined membership of the Constituent School Districts as of the most recent membership count date.

The fifth clause recites that the intermediate school districts in both Wayne and Macomb County are currently authorized to levy a regional enhancement millage approved by the voters, which provides greater student opportunities that may include, but are not limited to, reduced class sizes, enhanced program offerings, improved school safety, and increased staff retention and attraction, and states these are benefits that Oakland County currently does not receive. The sixth clause states that Oakland County residents deserve the opportunity to provide competitive educational opportunities and similar resources to those available in the neighboring counties of Wayne and Macomb, and that voters should have the ability to determine whether to support these efforts for the benefit of their students. The seventh clause states that the Board of Education has determined that it is in the best interest of the School District to allow voters an opportunity to consider a ballot proposal that enhances educational opportunities by requesting the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District, referred to as Oakland Schools, to submit a regional enhancement millage proposal to the electors at the school election on August 4, 2026, in accordance with Section 705.

RESOLVED PROVISIONS. Paragraph 1 states that the School District requests that Oakland Schools submit to its electors the question of a regional enhancement millage proposal for 1.50 mills for a period of six (6) years, 2026 to 2031 inclusive, at the school election to be held on August 4, 2026, pursuant to a ballot proposal substantially in the form attached as Exhibit A. Paragraph 2 approves the ballot wording substantially in the form attached at Exhibit A, provided that the wording is subject to revision and finalization by Oakland Schools as may be necessary. Paragraph 3 authorizes and directs the Superintendent to deliver a certified copy of the resolution to the Secretary of the Board of Education of Oakland Schools. Paragraph 4 states that the resolution is only a request to Oakland Schools and that the regional enhancement millage proposal will only be submitted to the voters if Oakland Schools receives a request to submit the question from its Constituent School Districts representing a majority of the combined membership of its Constituent School Districts on or before March 31, 2026. Paragraph 5 rescinds all resolutions and parts of resolutions insofar as they conflict with the provisions of this Resolution. The document then records AYES, NAYS, and RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED, with a signature line for the Secretary, Board of Education.

CERTIFICATION. The Secretary of the Board of Education certifies that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a resolution adopted by the Board of Education of Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, at a Regular meeting held on February 24, 2026, and that the meeting was conducted and public notice of the meeting was given pursuant to and in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, being Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, and that the minutes of the meeting were kept and will be or have been made available as required by the Act.

EXHIBIT A - BALLOT LANGUAGE. Headed OAKLAND SCHOOLS INTERMEDIATE SCHOOL DISTRICT, STATE OF MICHIGAN, REGIONAL ENHANCEMENT MILLAGE PROPOSAL. It opens with the statutory explanation that, pursuant to state law, revenue raised by the proposed regional enhancement millage will be collected by the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District and distributed on an equal per-pupil basis to local public school districts and eligible public school academies within the boundaries of the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District.

The proposition reads: Shall the limitation on the amount of ad valorem taxes which may be imposed on taxable property in the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District, State of Michigan, be increased by 1.5 mills ($1.50 on each $1,000 of taxable valuation) for a period of six (6) years, 2026 to 2031, inclusive, as new additional millage to provide funds to enhance other state and local funding for public school operating purposes? This millage would raise an estimated $125,756,247 if approved and first levied in 2026. The ballot then provides YES and NO options.

A closing paragraph states that the revenue from the regional enhancement millage will be disbursed on an equal per-pupil basis to the listed school districts and public school academies within the boundaries of Oakland Schools Intermediate School District which are eligible to receive regional enhancement millage revenue under the Revised School Code; the list itself follows in the source document. The key operative facts are the 1.50 mill rate, the six-year term of 2026 to 2031 inclusive, the August 4, 2026 election date, the March 31, 2026 deadline for the ISD to have collected majority-membership requests, and the estimated first-year yield of $125,756,247 across the ISD.

PROJECT AND NECESSITY. The Troy School District, a Michigan general powers school district acting by and through its Board of Education, is undertaking a project for construction and operation of the new Smith Middle School located on Livernois Road in the City of Troy, Oakland County, Michigan, which includes roadway and sidewalk improvements necessary for the benefit of the public and to improve road conditions, safety, and mobility and accessibility to the school and for road users. As part of the project it is necessary to construct driveway approaches and a deceleration lane on the east side of Livernois Road, including widening the road and making traffic signal and sidewalk improvements, collectively the Livernois Road Improvements. The UCPA establishes procedures for taking property by eminent domain. The district reserves the right to bring federal or state cost recovery actions against the owner for costs incurred as a result of the release of hazardous or toxic substances or materials which may have occurred on the easement. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Troy School District's Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 states the district's middle school philosophy, nine program goals, five graduate outcomes, and the complete course catalog for grades 6, 7 and 8. Sixth graders take five academic classes plus required every-other-day physical education, while seventh and eighth graders take four academic classes plus required half-year Health/Physical Education and Digital Applications 1.0. Algebra 1 Honors, Geometry Honors and World Language I are taken in eighth grade, each earning high school credit and counting toward the high school GPA. The 18-page guide also catalogs more than two dozen half-year and full-year electives in visual art, music, computer science, engineering, media and life skills.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Publication**
Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide, 2024-2025, 18 pages, presented to the Board of Education on February 11, 2025.

**Philosophy and Goals**
Troy middle schools provide a program that recognizes, accepts, respects and meets the diverse needs of young adolescents, characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation; a shared vision fostering respect for learning, diversity and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community. Nine goals are listed, covering developmentally appropriate programs, meeting the needs of a diverse student population, core-subject skills and knowledge, discovery of special interests and aptitudes, diversified cultural/social/civic/vocational/recreational experiences, guidance services promoting self-esteem and responsible behavior, community partnerships, transition from elementary to high school, and modeling healthy lifestyles.

**Outcomes**
Five student outcomes: a self-directed learner, a quality worker, a positive communicator, a collaborative and cooperative contributor, and an involved and visionary citizen.

**Three-Year Overview**

| Grade | Academic load | Additional requirements |
|---|---|---|
| 6 | Five academic classes | Physical Education EOD required; music students may add Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, Band EOD, Art EOD |
| 7 | Four academic classes | Health/Physical Education half year; Digital Applications 1.0 half year; music option of Concert Band, Chamber Orchestra or Choir full year; elective total of one full year |
| 8 | Four academic classes | Music option of Symphonic Band, Advanced Orchestra or Choir full year; elective total of one full year for music students, two full-year classes for non-music students |

EOD is defined as Every Other Day.

**Grade 6 Courses**
Required: ELA 6, Language Arts 6, Mathematics 6 (or another math class), Physical Education 6, Science 6, Social Studies 6. Mathematics 6 is organized into ten units: Area and Surface Area; Introducing Ratios; Linear Relationships; Unit Rates and Percentages; Dividing Fractions; Arithmetic in Base Ten; Expressions and Equations; Rational Numbers; Data Sets and Distributions; Putting it all Together. Grade 6 electives meet every other day alternating with PE: Art 6, Band 6 or Orchestra 6, and 6th Grade Choir.

**Grade 7 Courses**
Digital Applications 1.0 (half year, required), English 7, Health and Physical Education 7 (half year, a ten-week course covering nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality and choosing healthy behaviors, with parental excusal permitted), Mathematics 7, Science 7, and Social Studies 7, which surveys ancient world history and geography from the beginning until around 1500.

**Grade 8 Courses**
Algebra 1 Honors (five critical areas), English 8, Geometry Honors (six critical areas), Mathematics 8, Science 8, and United States History 8, which surveys U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877. Algebra 1 Honors and Geometry Honors count toward high school credit and the high school GPA.

**Electives**
Half-year electives for grades 7 and 8: 2D Visual Art, 3D Visual Art, Applied Engineering, Art Expressions, Ceramics, Communication Arts, Computer Programming, Computer Science Discoveries, Creation Lab, Digital Applications 2.0, Innovation Incubator, Life Skills, LINKS (teacher recommendation only), Money Matters, Science and Engineering Explorations, Theatre Arts, Video Technology, and Video Technology 2. Grade 7 full-year electives: Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, Graphic Design/Yearbook. Grade 8 electives: 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra, Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band, Physical Education, Symphonic Band, WEB Leadership, and World Language I in Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I and Spanish I.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The Troy School District Middle School Curriculum Guide for 2024-2025 is an 18-page publication appearing on the Board of Education agenda of February 11, 2025. It opens with the district's middle school philosophy: Troy middle schools provide a program that creates an environment recognizing, accepting, respecting and meeting the diverse needs and characteristics of young adolescent students, committed to academic excellence and to being developmentally responsive to adolescents' innate curiosity, desire to expand their environment, and need for recognition and personal achievement. The program is characterized by a research-based curriculum with effective assessment and evaluation that is challenging, integrative and exploratory; a shared vision with all members of the educational community fostering respect for learning, diversity and responsible behavior; and a cooperative partnership with parents and community members.

Nine Middle School Goals are enumerated. Goal 1: all programs will be developmentally appropriate. Goal 2: ensure all programs meet the needs of a diverse student population. Goal 3: ensure all students develop skills and knowledge in the core subject areas. Goal 4: provide opportunity to discover special interests, attitudes, aptitudes and abilities. Goal 5: provide diversified experiences in cultural, social, civic, vocational and recreational programs. Goal 6: provide guidance services and programs promoting self-esteem, independence and responsible behavior. Goal 7: provide opportunity to establish partnerships with the community. Goal 8: provide a transition from elementary to high school. Goal 9: provide a model for healthy lifestyles.

Five Middle School Outcomes follow: a self-directed learner who is responsible, enthusiastic, thinks independently and is open-minded and intellectually curious; a quality worker who designs a plan, applies resources, technologies and organizational strategies, creates products and performances, monitors development, maintains high standards and assesses results; a positive communicator; a collaborative and cooperative contributor who creates and sustains productive group relationships, respects the contributions of others, helps resolve conflicts and stays focused and task oriented; and an involved and visionary citizen who develops awareness of global issues, contributes to local and world communities, advocates for the environment and prepares to meet future challenges.

The three-year middle school overview specifies that all sixth graders take five academic classes; seventh and eighth graders each take four academic classes. Sixth grade requires Physical Education on an every-other-day (EOD) basis for both music and non-music students, with Orchestra EOD, Choir EOD, Band EOD and Art EOD listed as the alternating options. Seventh grade requires Health/Physical Education for a half year and Digital Applications 1.0 for a half year, plus, for music students, one of Concert Band (full year), Chamber Orchestra (full year) or Choir (full year); the elective load totals one full year, taken as two half-year classes or one full-year class. Eighth grade music students choose among Symphonic Band (full year), Advanced Orchestra (full year) and Choir (full year); non-music eighth graders carry an elective total of two full-year classes, taken as four half-year classes, two half-year classes plus one full-year class, or two full-year classes.

Grade 6 required courses are ELA 6 (full year), which studies literature of various genres and informational text including literary nonfiction with emphasis on inference from textual evidence, thematic and character development, claims and evidence, academic vocabulary and independent choice reading; Language Arts 6 (full year), covering narrative, informational and argumentative writing using mentor texts and the writing process; Mathematics 6 (full year, or another math class), covering ratio and rate, dividing fractions by fractions, negative numbers and variables; Physical Education 6 (full year EOD), run either as a yearlong every-other-day program or an everyday semester class; Science 6 (full year), with units on cells and heredity, ecology, Earth's changing surface, and species adaptation and survival; and Social Studies 6 (full year), a geography-based course covering physical and human geography, migration and settlement, culture and cultural diffusion, population and demographic changes, resource use, and trade and economic interdependence. Mathematics 6 lists ten units: Unit 1 Area and Surface Area; Unit 2 Introducing Ratios; Unit 3 Linear Relationships; Unit 4 Unit Rates and Percentages; Unit 5 Dividing Fractions; Unit 6 Arithmetic in Base Ten; Unit 7 Expressions and Equations; Unit 8 Rational Numbers; Unit 9 Data Sets and Distributions; Unit 10 Putting it all Together.

Grade 6 elective courses meet every other day, alternating with PE: Art 6 (full year EOD), Band 6 or Orchestra 6 (full year EOD, with fifth-grade band or orchestra or prior formal instruction expected), and 6th Grade Choir (full year EOD), which follows the National Core Arts Standards of Perform, Create, Respond and Connect.

Grade 7 required courses are Digital Applications 1.0 (half year), covering 21st Century and Web 2.0 online tools; English 7 (full year); Health and Physical Education 7 (half year), a combined ten-week course covering nutrition, recognizing influences, human sexuality and choosing healthy behaviors, with units countering messages encouraging tobacco, alcohol and other drug use and information on the spread of AIDS and sexually transmitted diseases, and with parents permitted to excuse their child from sessions on human sexuality and AIDS; Mathematics 7 (full year, or another math class), extending rates and ratios to proportional relationships and all rational numbers; Science 7 (full year), covering Earth's waters, weather and climate, astronomy, waves, energy, physical and chemical changes, and chemical properties; and Social Studies 7 (full year), focused on ancient world history and geography with content literacy, investigating human history from the beginning until around 1500.

Grade 8 courses are Algebra 1 Honors (full year, or another math class), a first-year high school algebra course for advanced students with five critical areas covering linear equations and inequalities, functions and sequences, regression techniques, exponential/quadratic/rational equations and systems, and specialized functions including absolute value, step and piecewise-defined; English 8 (full year); Geometry Honors (full year, or another math class) for advanced students who have completed Algebra 1 Honors, with six critical areas covering congruence and rigid motions, similarity and right triangle trigonometry, coordinate geometry, circles, geometric measurement in two and three dimensions, and geometric modeling; Mathematics 8 (full year, or another math class), covering linear relationships, linear equations in one and two variables, functions and irrational numbers; Science 8 (full year), covering energy, biogeochemical cycles, resources and human impacts, the rock cycle, Earth's interior, plate tectonics, earthquakes, volcanoes, hydrogeology, severe weather, Earth in space, the sun, Earth history and geologic time and climate change, including an online Moodle project; and United States History 8 (full year), surveying U.S. history from the time of the Native Americans to 1877, with detailed study of the American Revolution, formation of the national government, westward movement, and the Civil War and Reconstruction, and periodic study of Michigan history and U.S. foreign affairs. Both Algebra 1 Honors and Geometry Honors count toward high school credit and are figured into the high school GPA.

Half-year elective courses for grades 7 and 8 are 2D Visual Art; 3D Visual Art (papier-mache, clay, batik and mixed media); Applied Engineering (stress analysis, mechanical engineering, renewable energy systems, aerodynamics, space and rocketry); Art Expressions; Ceramics (pinch, coil and slab construction); Communication Arts (public speaking, pantomime, roleplaying, interviews, listening skills, improvisation); Computer Programming (Introduction to JavaScript: Drawing and Animation, JavaScript: Games and Visualizations, HTML/CSS: Making Webpages, HTML/JS: Making Webpages Interactive, plus building and programming a robot); Computer Science Discoveries; Creation Lab (bridge building, soldering, coding, game creation, projectiles, S.T.E.A.M. focus); Digital Applications 2.0 (Adobe Creative Suite, video production, animation, digital imaging, Dreamweaver; prerequisite is successful completion of Digital Applications 1.0); Innovation Incubator, whose cornerstone is the Larson Innovation Shark Tank project in which teams pitch inventions to members of the Metro Detroit business community including market researchers, patent attorneys and engineers; Life Skills (food preparation and hand and machine sewing); LINKS, a peer-to-peer support program pairing general education students with students with Autism Spectrum Disorder and other special needs, by teacher recommendation only; Money Matters (Michigan Career Pathways, budgets, bank accounts, credit, interest, investing and responsible spending); Science and Engineering Explorations, which prepares work for competitions such as the Science and Engineering Fair of Metro Detroit (SEFMD); Theatre Arts, which includes a public performance; Video Technology, using Windows Movie Maker and Apple iMovie with live morning news broadcasts and media literacy and copyright ethics; and Video Technology 2.

Grade 7 full-year electives are Chamber Orchestra, Choir 7, 7th/8th Choir, Concert Band, and Graphic Design/Yearbook, the latter connecting students with the Boulan Park School Community. Grade 8 electives are 7th/8th Choir, Advanced Orchestra (which requires many evening performances plus a Saturday performance at the MSBOA Orchestra Festival), Choir 8, Fundamentals of Fitness, Graphic Design/Yearbook, Jazz Band (by audition or teacher approval, with members also participating in a concert band ensemble), Physical Education, Symphonic Band (requiring many evening performances plus two Saturday performances including MSBOA Band Festival), WEB Leadership (Where Everyone Belongs, covering sixth grade orientation, school character and culture programs, charity opportunities and student mentoring), and World Language I. World Language I is a full-year, every-day course counting toward high school credit and the high school GPA, offered in Chinese I, French I, German I, Japanese I and Spanish I; the guide warns the class may only be offered at the high school during 1st hour, that parents would need to provide transportation to the high school, and that a shuttle will bring students back to the middle school.

**Understanding School Funding (2024-25)**
The foundation allowance is built from state aid, a Non-Homestead Levy of $2,804 per pupil, and a Hold-Harmless Levy of $786 per pupil, with the amount dependent upon voter approval given as $3,590. Meeting and Attendance
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, October 19, 2021, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m.; adjournment was at 8:57 p.m. Present with Mr. Schmidt were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson, plus Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, Carrier, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Fulcher, Brinks, Cottone, DiPonio, Godfrey, Whan and West. Approximately 90 members of the audience attended. Minutes submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary; footers are marked "corrected JH."

Recognition
The TSD Mission Moment honored Hill Elementary School's schoolwide "Color Run" of Friday, October 1st, designed to be inclusive of students with sensory issues; Principal Shari Pawlus and her PTO board members received a certificate. Resolution 21-081 commended seventy-four 2022 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists; per the resolution, more than one million students nationwide from some 21,000 high schools entered the program and only 16,000 seniors are selected as semifinalists, by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT with comparable SAT scores. Copies were to be presented at a reception on November 3rd.

Actions Taken

| Res. | Item | Moved / Supported | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 21-081 | 2022 National Merit Semifinalists resolution | — | Yes 7, No 0 |
| 21-082 | Consent agenda items A, B, C | Hauff / Gottlieb | Yes 7, No 0 |
| 21-083 | Accept audited 2021 financial statements | Wilson / Philippart | Yes 7, No 0 |
| 21-084 | Operating-All (Hold-Harmless) millage amendment | Philippart / Anne | Yes 7, No 0 |

Consent agenda 21-082 covered minutes of the September 7, 2021 Board Workshop, minutes of the September 21, 2021 Board Meeting, and the Treasurer's Report - August 2021.

Business
2020/2021 Audit: Ms. Donna Hanson and Mr. Michael Walsh of Plante Moran presented the audit of the 2020-2021 fiscal year, a draft of which had been detailed at the October 5, 2021 Board Workshop. There were no findings or questioned costs. Governmental funds revenue and expenditures, student population and foundation allowance were reviewed.

Millage amendment: The June 15, 2021 Budget Appropriations Resolution had authorized 4.4575 mills on Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal Properties and 13.5425 mills on all Non-Homestead Properties, a total levy of 18 mills for general operating purposes. The FY22 state school aid act, 2021 PA 48 (HB 4411), reduces hold-harmless (OPR ALL) millage; under section 1211 of the state school code per-pupil hold-harmless revenue is limited to the difference between the district's foundation allowance and $8,700. The amended 2021 Tax Rate Request (Form L-4029) sets a Principal Residence request of 3.3878 mills, 1.1591 of them levied December 1, 2021, and a Non-Homestead operating request of 14.6122 mills, 7.8409 of them levied on the December 1, 2021 levy date, and goes to the Oakland County Clerk and City of Troy Clerk.

Public Comment and Reports
Non-agenda speakers were split between opposition to and support for the mask mandate and Covid protocols, with further comment on library books, parental rights, a Schroeder Elementary drop-off incident, the Covid Family Guidebook and the "Moms for Liberty" organization. Student representatives Yara Mashal (International Academy-East), Sasha Palmkoeck (Athens High School) and Sarayu Bethamcherla (Troy High School) reported; Alyssa McLarty (Troy College and Career High School) was not in attendance. Additions & Deletions, agenda-item public communication, Personnel and Curriculum were all "None."

Other
Board members congratulated Rick West and the Business Office for the audit. Dr. Machesky reported the Facilities Review Committee (FRC) held its first meeting, comprised of 54 community members and three Board members. Mr. Schmidt announced the next Board Workshop for Tuesday, November 9th at 6:00 p.m. and the next regular Board Meeting for Tuesday, November 16th at 7:00 p.m., both at the Services Building.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Corrected minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, Troy, Michigan, held October 19, 2021 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. Every page footer carries the notation "Board of Education Meeting [page] October 19, 2021 - corrected JH," identifying this as the corrected version of the October 19 minutes. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

Call to Order and Attendance
President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, Carrier, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Fulcher, Brinks, Cottone, DiPonio, Godfrey, Whan and West. There were approximately 90 members of the audience. The meeting adjourned at 8:57 p.m.

Recognition - TSD Mission Moment: Hill Elementary School "Color Run"
Hill Elementary students participated in a schoolwide Color Run event on Friday, October 1st. The Fun Run was specifically designed to be inclusive and mindful of students who might have sensory issues. The Color Run involves colorful chalk being thrown into the air and decorating the shirts of those running by, and Fun Runs typically involve lots of cheering, music, loud audio and visual stimulants. For a portion of Hill's Color Run the music was turned off and cheering consisted of hands in the air and thumbs up instead of clapping and raised voices; the quiet allowed students who have sensory issues to fully enjoy the Fun Run, and the entire 5th grade was there to quietly but enthusiastically cheer them on. The minutes characterize the event as an example of the district's Red Pillar (Equity & Well-Being) "at its finest," thanking Hill Elementary for demonstrating that "ALL means ALL in the TSD." The Board invited Principal Shari Pawlus up along with her PTO board members to receive a certificate of recognition.

Recognition and Resolution 21-081 - 2021-22 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists
The minutes state that more than one million students nationwide, from some 21,000 high schools, entered the National Merit Scholarship Program, but only 16,000 of these seniors are selected to be semifinalists. The Board passed a resolution to commend and congratulate the district's seventy-four National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists, named as: Prisha Agnihotri, Frederick Aldinger, Sreenand Anumolu, Akshat Arya, Seo Hyun Baek, Cole Balintfy, Sarayu Bethamcherla, Shreya Bhargava, Kevin Chang, Sanya Chawla, Emily Chen, Reagan Choi, Shiham Chowdhury, Abhishek Dahad, Raaga Dandavolu, Atharva Dharphale, Malina Dumitrascu, Nikita Ganesh, Rittik Ghosh, Mariska Goswami, Navya Gullapuram, Albert Hua, Nicolas Hung, Jemi Isaac, Neha Jaisankar, Udayvir Jalf, Victoria Jan, Agastya Jayanthi, Sachin Karatha, Hyun Kim, Havesh Kolli, Rishi Konduru, Aileen Liu, Allison Liu, Aditi Locula, Iris Ma, Mlahat Mahmood, Meera Manek, Anay Modi, Brandon Nguyen, Abel Noble, Tanisha Panchal, Esha Patel, Avani Prasad, Ayush Pujara, Vandhana Purushothaman, Yahya Qamar, Eric Qiao, Katie Qu, Danny Samuel, Mohammad Shaik, Navya Shankar, Sanjana Sharma, Rishi Shetty, Heejin Shyn, Kishan Soni, Saakshi Sovani, Sachin Sridhar, Vidhya Harini Srinivas, Smriti Suresh, Dilan Swami, Sharanya Swaminathan, Areej Tahir, Jordan Tansingco, Cole VanAmberg, Rebecca Varghese, Akshay Vasudevan, Andrew Wang, Roger Wang, Claire Wu, Angela Xu, Gary Xu, Rachel Yang and Nancy Yao. The minutes call this a remarkable number of semifinalists and a tribute to the staff and parents of the Troy School District; copies of the resolution were to be presented to the students at a reception on November 3rd.

The resolution recites that student achievement is honored through the National Merit Scholarship semifinalist and finalist recognition programs, and that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test (PSAT) and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). It resolves that the Troy School District Board of Education adopts the resolution in honor of the students for their selection as 2022 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists. The vote was Yes 7, No 0, recorded as item 21-081.

Additions & Deletions; Public Communication (Agenda Items)
Both were recorded as None.

General - Consent Agenda, Resolution 21-082
It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Gottlieb that the Troy Board of Education take action to approve items A, B and C on the consent agenda: (A) Minutes of the September 7, 2021 Board of Education Workshop; (B) Minutes of the September 21, 2021 Board of Education Meeting; and (C) Treasurer's Report - August 2021. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Personnel and Curriculum
Both sections were recorded as None.

Business - 2020/2021 Audit Report, Resolution 21-083
Ms. Donna Hanson and Mr. Michael Walsh from Plante Moran provided a presentation to the Board of Education on the audit of the 2020-2021 fiscal year. A draft copy of the District's Audit Report had been presented in detail to the Board at the October 5, 2021 Board Workshop. Ms. Hanson and Mr. Walsh provided highlights of the audit and shared that there were no findings or questioned costs. Governmental funds revenue and expenditures were reviewed, as were student population and foundation allowance. The economic impact of the pandemic challenges, as well as the changes in federal funding, was also discussed at length. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Board of Education accept and approve the Troy School District's audited 2021 financial statements as presented by Plante Moran. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Business - 2021-2022 Amendment of the Operating-All (Hold-Harmless) Millage, Resolution 21-084
It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne. The resolution recites that the Board, pursuant to a 2021-22 Budget Appropriations Resolution adopted on June 15, 2021, approved the School District's operating, debt and sinking fund millage rates for the 2021-22 school year, which included the authority to levy 4.4575 mills on Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal Properties and 13.5425 mills on all Non-Homestead Properties for a total levy of 18 mills for general operating purposes. It further recites that the FY 22 state school aid act, 2021 PA 48, HB 4411, reduces the amount of hold harmless (OPR ALL) millage districts may levy in 2021 for FY 22; that under section 1211 of the state school code the per pupil hold-harmless revenue is limited to the difference between the district's foundation allowance and $8,700; and that the Board desires to comply with section 1211 of the FY22 state school aid act.

The Board resolved to approve an amendment to the 2021-22 Budget Appropriations Resolution to approve and authorize the School District to modify the Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal and the Non-Homestead Properties millage rate levies for a total levy of 18 mills for general operating purposes. It further resolved to authorize the President and Secretary to sign an amended 2021 Tax Rate Request (Form L-4029) with a Principal Residence, Qualified Agriculture, Qualified Forest and Industrial Personal Properties millage request of 3.3878, with 1.1591 mills of the 3.3878 to be levied on December 1, 2021, and a Non-Homestead operating millage request of 14.6122, with 7.8409 mills of the 14.6122 mills to be levied on the December 1, 2021 levy date, and that the amended 2021 Tax Rate Request be submitted to the Oakland County Clerk and City of Troy Clerk. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Reports from Student Representatives to the Board
Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East; Sasha Palmkoeck, student representative for Athens High School; and Sarayu Bethamcherla, student representative for Troy High School, each shared a report on events and activities happening in their schools. Alyssa McLarty, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, was not in attendance.

Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items)
President Schmidt shared a statement providing the structure of how the evening's Public Participation would be conducted in compliance with the Open Meetings Act and reviewed the guidelines for public comment. Speakers were: Carrie Leser, TSD parent, on a concerning incident occurring at Schroeder Elementary School during morning drop-off and how it is confusing students; Diana Magiera, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask-wearing mandate; Fabrice Smielianskas, TSD parent, in support of the Covid protocols put in place in the district; Ollie Apahidean, TSD parent, on parental rights, displaying pictures from a book found in the school library; Ana Maria Gould, TSD parent, in support of mask-wearing in schools; Yousef Safah, Co-Founder of Mind Matters Education, on mental health support for students; B.J. Lennon, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate; Ashleigh Jennings, TSD parent, in support of the mask mandate; Kacy Bailey, TSD parent, introducing "Moms for Liberty," an Oakland County organization she represents to defend parental rights; Ryan Johnson, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate and expressing concerns of unlawful activities happening; Kelly Jones, TSD parent, in support of the mask mandate; Sarah Krieger, TSD parent, in opposition to the mask mandate; Peggy Chinoski, TSD parent, in support of the mask mandate; and Thomas Fraser, TSD parent, on the recently published Covid Family Guidebook related to quarantine restrictions for students.

Other
Board members congratulated Rick West and his team in the Business Office for the great audit report and their fiscal stewardship, and congratulated the National Merit Semi-Finalists for their accomplishments. Dr. Machesky shared that the Facilities Review Committee (FRC) kicked off its first meeting; the team is comprised of 54 community members and three Board members. He also shared that the Fall Update presentations had begun to building staff and PTOs. Mr. Schmidt shared that the next Board Workshop would be held on Tuesday, November 9th at 6:00 p.m. at the Services Building and the next regular Board Meeting would be Tuesday, November 16th at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building.

Adjournment
The meeting adjourned at 8:57 p.m.

Minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education of the Troy School District, Troy, Michigan, held November 16, 2021 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

Call to Order and Attendance
President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Detmer, Morey and West. There were approximately 85 members of the audience. The meeting adjourned at 8:38 p.m.

Recognition - TSD Mission Moment: THS Student Receives Perfect Score on AP Physics Exam
The Board recognized Troy High School senior Reagan Choi for receiving a perfect score on the AP Physics C: Mechanics Exam in May 2021. The minutes note that Reagan's performance was so superior that it fell into an extremely select category; Advanced Placement Exams are college-level examinations scored on a scale of 1 to 5, and Reagan not only received the top score of 5 but is "in the 0.00% in the world for an absolute perfect score." He is one of only two students in the world who answered every single question perfectly. The Board invited teacher Brian Glynn to introduce Reagan and share his accomplishment; Reagan received congratulations from the Board along with a certificate.

Recognition - 2021-22 National Blue Ribbon Awards: Barnard & Leonard Elementary Schools
The Board recognized Barnard Elementary School and Leonard Elementary School for their designation as National Blue-Ribbon Schools, an award honoring them as among the very best schools in the United States. Barnard and Leonard were recognized by U.S. Secretary of Education Miguel Cardona at a ceremony in Washington, D.C. on November 4th and 5th. Only 325 schools from around the country were chosen for this honor in 2021. The minutes state the award affirms the hard work of students, staff, parents and the Barnard and Leonard communities, and quote Secretary Cardona: "This year's cohort of honorees demonstrates what is possible when committed educators and school leaders create vibrant, welcoming, and affirming school cultures where rich teaching and learning can flourish," and "I commend our Blue-Ribbon honorees for working to keep students healthy and safe while meeting their academic, social, emotional, and mental health needs. In the face of unprecedented circumstances, you found creative ways to engage, care for, protect, and teach our children. Blue Ribbon Schools have so much to offer and can serve as a model for other schools and communities so that we can truly build back better." The Board invited Melanie Morey, principal of Barnard Elementary School, along with several Barnard staff members, to the podium to say a few words and receive congratulations and a certificate, then invited Dr. Erin Detmer, principal of Leonard Elementary School, along with several Leonard staff members, to do the same.

Additions & Deletions; Public Communication (Agenda Items)
Both recorded as None.

General - Consent Agenda, Resolution 21-085
It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Gottlieb that the Troy Board of Education take action to approve items A, B, C and D on the consent agenda: Minutes of the October 5, 2021 Board of Education Workshop; Minutes of the October 19, 2021 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - September 2021; and Second Reading and Adoption of Board Policies, consisting of revisions to Policy 1000.02 Special Meetings and Policy 2000.06 Student Bullying, and the addition of a policy in Section 8000, Animals on District Property. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Personnel, Resolution 21-086
It was moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Dr. Wilson that the Board of Education approve the personnel recommendations as stated, identified in the minutes as New Hires: Aaron Ducharme and Toby Klein. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Curriculum
Recorded as None.

Business - Bus Purchase, Resolution 21-087
It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that the bid for school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $931,182.00 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2013 Bond Series 3. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Business - CAD Lab Computers, Resolution 21-088
It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for CAD Lab Computers be awarded to Sehi Computer Products in the amount of $66,096 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund and General Fund. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

Reports from Student Representatives to the Board
Sasha Palmkoeck, student representative for Athens High School; Sarayu Bethamcherla, student representative for Troy High School; Alyssa McLarty, student representative for Troy College and Career High School; and Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East, each shared a report on the events and activities happening in their schools.

Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items)

- Ryan Johnson, TSD parent, on diversity and equity and CRT and his opposition to the mask mandate; he demanded the immediate resignation of the superintendent and all Board members and threatened to sue each person for what he considers breaking the law, including the mask mandate, and unenrolling his son from school.

- Mr. Ollie Apahidean, TSD parent, on parental rights, displaying graphic pictures from a book found in the school library and discussing the book review committee.
