Another 18 were course candidates attempting HL credit, 1 student opted to return and take exams in November, and 8 students withdrew from all IB exams.

IB evaluation visit
Scheduled Wednesday, November 10 through Friday, November 12.

Return to school
Thursday, August 12 for new student orientation, new teacher orientation, and schedule pickup with school photos; Monday, August 16 for staff professional development; Tuesday, August 17 as the first day of school for students; Friday, August 27 no school.

Tri-Campus School Improvement Committee
The report proposes reinstituting a tri-campus School Improvement Committee that is both school wide and campus specific. Its responsibilities would be to prepare for IB evaluation visits, meet state professional development requirements, and develop professional development for staff.

School goals
Instruction: instruction will be engaging, innovative, student-centered and inquiry based, with the goal of promoting and supporting effective and innovative pedagogy in the classroom. Curriculum: the curriculum will be in full alignment with the standards of the International Baccalaureate Middle Years and Diploma Programs plus state standards, with interdisciplinary units fully implemented and assessed at all levels, a goal of two units per year for MYP, one each semester. Culture: the culture will balance the social, emotional and physical health of the community and embrace both commonalities and individuality, with goals to build capacity as a community cultivating a global culture of acceptance and inclusion and to foster a culture of service learning. Assessment: assessments will fairly evaluate diverse abilities, with formative assessment used for practice and feedback and summative assessment emphasizing mastery, and a goal of defining and aligning the assessment philosophy and policy within departments and school wide.

Staff survey
Asked which school goal to engage in for the 2021-22 school year, all three campuses chose Culture. Comments cite the need to rebuild culture after a year of uncertainty, student transition back to full face-to-face instruction, continued social-emotional support, and the view that culture is the foundation on which the other goals rest. Suggested secondary goals center on rethinking assessment, focusing on the Diploma Program, analyzing which pandemic-era instructional methods worked, and refining new DP curricula. Practices staff want to carry forward include asynchronous days, Canvas for organizing and collecting assignments, one-to-one device access, the House system and house competitions, the Open House video, and flexible time management. Staff also identified pre-COVID features they could do without, naming intense workload and stress levels and in-person conferences.

Mission statement
The report closes with the International Academy mission: through the International Baccalaureate program, instilling cultural appreciation and global citizenship while promoting personal development and a passion for learning.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Principal's report for the International Academy delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education at its June 23, 2021 meeting. The document is a slide deck covering the close of the 2020-21 school year and planning for 2021-22 across the Academy's three campuses, West, Okma and East.

Graduation. All three ceremonies are reported as a success. West held graduation Wednesday, May 26 at the Lakeland HS Fieldhouse at 7:00pm. Okma held graduation Thursday, June 3 at the BHHS Athletic Field at 7:00pm. East held graduation Saturday, June 5 at DTE at 12:30pm.

IB examinations. The exam window ran April 29 through May 20 and is likewise reported as a success. There were 326 full Diploma Program candidates, stated in the report as 94 percent of the graduating class. Of those, 13 students will have one or more of their exams graded on the non-exam route because of quarantine or other illness. A further 18 students sat as course candidates attempting HL credit. One student opted to return and take exams in November, and 8 students withdrew from all IB exams.

IB evaluation visit. The Academy will host an IB evaluation visit Wednesday, November 10 through Friday, November 12.

Return to school calendar. Thursday, August 12 is set for New Student Orientation, New Teacher Orientation, and Schedule Pickup and School Photos. Monday, August 16 is staff professional development. Tuesday, August 17 is the first day of school for students. Friday, August 27 is a no school day.

Tri-Campus School Improvement Committee. The report calls for reinstituting a tri-campus School Improvement Committee that operates both school wide and campus specific. Its stated responsibilities are to prepare for IB evaluation visits, address state professional development requirements, and develop professional development for staff.

School goals. Four goal areas are set out with accompanying statements.

Instruction. The instruction of the International Academy will be engaging, innovative, student-centered and inquiry based. The goal is to promote and support effective and innovative pedagogy in the classroom.

Curriculum. The curriculum of the International Academy will be in full alignment with the standards of the International Baccalaureate Middle Years and Diploma Programs in addition to state standards. The goal is that interdisciplinary units will be fully implemented and assessed at all levels, with a target of two units per year for MYP, one each semester.

Culture. The culture of the International Academy will balance the social, emotional and physical health of the community, and will embrace and value commonalities and individuality. Two goals are stated: continue to build capacity as a community that cultivates a global culture encouraging acceptance and inclusion, and foster and support a culture of service learning.

Assessment. Assessments will fairly evaluate the unique and diverse abilities and knowledge base of all students. Formative assessments will be used to strengthen skills and provide practice and feedback during the learning process, while summative assessments will emphasize mastery of the skills and content knowledge students have had an opportunity to learn. The goal is to define and align the assessment philosophy and policy within departments and as a school.

Staff survey and conversations, primary goal. Asked which school goal they would most like to engage in for the 2021-22 school year, all three campuses want to pursue Culture. Quoted staff responses include the observation that after a year of uncertainty the culture at IA will need rebuilding because students missed out on much of what makes the Academy distinctive; that IA has excellent educators who will adapt curriculum and instruction to make up for material not covered, but that the most important factors are the cultural pieces, including the culture of commitment to excelling, the culture derived from the Academy's international grounding, and the culture of interpersonal relationships many students have not been able to form; that culture is what students will be looking forward to when they return to full face-to-face instruction in the fall; that staff want to continue guiding students to succeed with the rigor of the IB program; that students and staff face a difficult transition back to real school and will need help balancing physical, emotional, educational and life stressors, with continued focus on SEL rather than a return to business as usual; that culture work is never done and there is much to do before changing priorities, since students will struggle to readjust next fall and supporting that transition should be the greatest priority; and that culture is the foundation upon which the others are built.

Staff survey, secondary goals. Responses on a secondary goal emphasize assessment and curriculum. Staff noted that the year forced a rethinking of assessment, with more creativity and less grade-driven work that was healthy for staff and students, and that high quality authentic assessments that do not overwhelm should continue. Working with digital assessments allowed work outside the box of what a typical summative and formative assessment looks like, prompting a desire to reevaluate assessment style going forward. Other comments call for spending time focusing on the Diploma Program; for more focus on in-person instruction after a year and a half on Zoom; for space and time to analyze which instructional methods introduced during the year worked and how they might improve overall instruction; for continued curriculum improvement, noting that large curricular hurdles were cleared during the year and that some choices favored ease during a stressful time over better curricular choices that now need correction; and for retaining classroom technologies, particularly methods that allowed more immediate feedback than traditional approaches, with interest in using them to differentiate assignments and assessments or to create a semi-self-paced course allowing more personal preference and interest. Additional responses ask for consistency between departments regarding assessment or a school-wide grading and percentage policy for tests, note that some teachers sit at polar ends of the assessment spectrum and that the whole staff should discuss the topic, and observe that new DP curricula in several subjects would benefit from extra time to iron out wrinkles.

Practices to carry forward and new ideas. Staff suggested exploring how asynchronous days could work, based on feedback gathered from numerous freshmen and sophomores met with during second semester, on the grounds that students and staff work very hard and would benefit from set-aside time. Continuing to use Canvas to organize and to an extent collect assignments was cited as useful, as was using Canvas to cut down on paper and communicate with absent students. Staff asked for easy and consistent student access to a device in class, describing one-to-one as a goal, and expressed enthusiasm for the House system, friendly house competitions and team building, more field trips after a year indoors, and connecting alumni with students. The Open House video was praised, and the picnic was reported to be better without grilling and with a focus on fun activities. Staff also valued professional consideration of time management, with flexibility to leave when not teaching or meeting described as crucial to mental health and to fulfilling work and home obligations, noting a high level of trust during the year that the job would get done.

Aspects of pre-COVID school life to do without. Staff named the intense workload and high levels of stress before COVID as detrimental to student and staff health, calling for additional and focused or protected time, and suggested that in-person conferences may not be necessary.

Additional comments. Staff asked that more teachers understand program expectations beyond their own disciplines, and suggested a workshop or professional development session on Canvas functionality since its many features can be confusing or unobvious to new users. Closing comments thank the principal for support and grace during a difficult year and for seeking staff input, express anticipation for the new school year, and state that culture and instruction are key to next year's success, with investment there also taking care of curriculum and assessments.

Mission. The report closes with the Academy's mission statement: the International Academy community, through the International Baccalaureate program, instills cultural appreciation and global citizenship while promoting personal development and a passion for learning.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) circulated a proposed new resolution for member district consideration in May 2026, stating that OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege. The rationale cites the FY26 school aid budget's section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding, which required districts to opt in and, in doing so, to agree to cooperate with an investigation including waiving attorney-client privilege following a mass-casualty incident. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Proposed new resolution (May 2026)**
OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege.

**Rationale**
In the FY26 school aid budget, section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding required districts to "opt in." Any district that opted in to receive 31aa funds agreed to cooperate with an investigation, including waiving the attorney-client privilege, following a mass-casualty incident. The rationale argues that while cooperation with investigations after a mass casualty event is necessary to prevent another event, the attorney-client privilege must remain sacred, that the courts have ruled on this issue, and that nothing would stop the legislature from tying waiver of the privilege to other funding in the future.

**Adoption threshold**
OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, Resolution Adoption: resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors. The continuing resolutions that follow are provided for reference only, with adoption and amendment dates noted.

**Continuing resolutions**

| Resolution | Adopted / amended |
| --- | --- |
| Accountability and Transparency | 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Broadband Access and Devices | 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Early Childhood | 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Early On Michigan | 1/26/2026 |
| Evidence-Based Decision Making | 9/24/2019 |
| Lame Duck | 9/24/2019 |
| Local Control | 9/24/2019 |
| Mental Health | 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Non-Partisan Elections | 1/9/2026 |
| School Aid | 9/24/2019; amended 6/5/2025 |
| School Finance Research Collaborative | 9/24/2019; amended 9/11/2021, 3/3/2023, 6/5/2025 |
| School Nutrition | 3/3/2023; amended 6/5/2025 |
| School Safety | 3/3/2023 |
| Special Education | 9/24/2019 |
| Teacher Shortages | 9/11/2021; amended 6/5/2025 |
| Unfunded Mandates | 9/24/2019 |

**Selected positions**
Accountability and Transparency applies the same standards, including FOIA and the Open Meetings Act, to local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (charter schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities. Early Childhood supports new dollars for universal public preschool for all four-year-olds and mandatory kindergarten for all five-year-olds. School Aid asks that the School Aid Fund be constitutionally restricted to Pre-K through 12th grade public education, opposes private school vouchers or tax credit programs, supports added funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students, protects the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes, and urges enactment of the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts can meet the June 30 budget deadline. Special Education supports full funding of IDEA, noting federal legislation initially promised 40 percent of the excess cost. The School Finance Research Collaborative resolution supports implementing SFRC recommendations while holding higher funded districts harmless.

**Aligned agendas**
When aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the NSBA, MASB, Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) and COSSBA legislative agendas.

This three-page Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) packet, labeled "Proposed NEW Resolution May, 2026" and carried as item 6I on the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for the meeting dated June 16, 2026, presents one proposed new resolution for member district consideration together with the association's full slate of continuing resolutions.

PROPOSED NEW RESOLUTION: "OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege." The stated rationale is that in the FY26 school aid budget, section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding required districts to "opt in," and any district that opted in to receive 31aa funds agreed to cooperate with an investigation, including waiving the attorney-client privilege, following a mass-casualty incident. The rationale continues that while cooperation with investigations after a mass casualty event is necessary to prevent another event, the attorney-client privilege must remain sacred, that the courts have ruled on this issue, and that in the future there is nothing to stop the legislature from tying waiver of the attorney-client privilege to other funding.

ADOPTION MECHANISM. The continuing resolutions are stated to have been adopted by member school districts and are provided for reference only, with adoption and/or amendment dates noted for each. OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, Resolution Adoption, provides that resolutions approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors.

ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]: OCSBA supports holding every school that receives public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act, covering local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (aka Charter Schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities. Cited as MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f).

BROADBAND ACCESS AND DEVICES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021; Amended 6/5/2025]: broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; OCSBA supports additional federal and state funding opportunities to expand affordable and reliable broadband access; supports federal and state programs for purchase of internet capable devices and software; and supports dedicated resources for cybersecurity. Cited as MASB Resolution A-10.30 (2021 amendment).

EARLY CHILDHOOD [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]: supports additional new dollars to fund universal, public preschool for all four-year-old children, and mandatory kindergarten for all five-year-old children. Cited as MASB Resolution A 6.15 (c).

EARLY ON MICHIGAN [OCSBA Adopted 1/26/2026]: supports full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or who are at risk for delays due to certain health conditions.

EVIDENCE-BASED DECISION MAKING [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: supports evidence-based education policy that will maximize opportunities for the highest achievement of each student. Cited as MASB Resolution G 11.01.

LAME DUCK [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: supports lame duck parameters addressing introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election.

LOCAL CONTROL [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: supports local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards. Cited as MASB Resolutions A 10.10, A 10.55, A 12.70.

MENTAL HEALTH [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]: supports increased mental health services and professionals in schools and providing, at a minimum, annual inflation adjusted state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe; help staff identify potential mental health issues for students; encourage MDE to develop a model policy for staff regarding identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response. Cited as MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05, G 9.50.

NON-PARTISAN ELECTIONS [OCSBA Adopted 1/9/2026]: supports non-partisan school board elections.

SCHOOL AID [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025], four parts: (A) specify that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education in Michigan's Constitution and oppose any attempts to create private school vouchers or tax credit programs [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (a) and A 10.05]; (B) support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (g) and (j); A 10.55]; (C) protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes [MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (c); A 10.55]; (D) support enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so that school districts have factual information to meet their constitutional/statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30 [MASB Resolution A 10.25 (h)].

SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC) [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 9/11/2021; 3/3/2023; 6/5/2025]: supports implementation of the recommendations of the SFRC, while requiring that higher funded districts be held harmless. Cited as MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25 (2021 amendment).

SCHOOL NUTRITION [OCSBA Adopted 3/3/2023; Amended 6/5/2025]: supports codification of free universal meals.

SCHOOL SAFETY [OCSBA Adopted 3/3/2023]: supports adequate state resources to allow schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

SPECIAL EDUCATION [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: supports full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), noting that although federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities, appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local school districts to make up the difference. Cited as MASB Resolution A 5.01 and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA.

TEACHER SHORTAGES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021; Amended 6/5/2025]: supports statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, potentially including incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process to obtain Michigan certification for teachers certified in other states. Cited as MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority.

UNFUNDED MANDATES [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]: opposes any state or federal legislation that results in increased costs for school districts without full funding, and encourages the Michigan Legislature to oppose any federal laws or programs that are not fully funded and thus cost the state valuable resources. Cited as MASB Resolution A 10.20.

WHEN ALIGNED WITH OCSBA LEGISLATIVE PRIORITIES, OCSBA ALSO SUPPORTS [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]: the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda; the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda; the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda; and the Consortium of State School Board Associations (COSSBA) Legislative Agenda.

LINKS provided: MASB Resolutions at https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA at https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy; COSSBA Advocacy at https://www.cossba.org/advocacy.

The packet reproduces MHSAA Handbook Regulation I, Section 1(E) and 1(F) and their interpretations, the procedures for application, renewal and dissolution, advance preparation materials, and the blank two-page Senior High Application to Form and Support a Cooperative Team. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What this is**
MHSAA "High School Cooperative Agreement Regulations, Procedures and Advance Preparation Material to Assist Schools," together with the blank two-page Senior High Application to Form and Support a Cooperative Team, submitted with a Troy Athens boys lacrosse cooperative request for 2026-27. Completed forms are emailed to coops@mhsaa.com.

**Enrollment thresholds (Regulation I, Section 1)**

| Provision | Enrollment ceiling | Scope |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Sect. 1(E) | 1,000 combined | Any sport |
| Sect. 1(E-1) | none | Subvarsity only, any sport |
| Sect. 1(E-2) | none | Named sports, same public school district |
| Sect. 1(F-1) | 3,500 combined | Sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools |
| Sect. 1(F-2) | 5,500 combined | Ice hockey |
| Sect. 1(F-3)/(F-4) | waiver, four years | New or previously dropped sponsorship |

The Section 1(F)(1) sport list is field hockey, gymnastics, boys lacrosse, girls lacrosse, boys alpine skiing, girls alpine skiing, boys swimming & diving, girls swimming & diving, boys tennis, girls tennis and boys volleyball. Section 1(E-2) names baseball, bowling, competitive cheer, cross country, field hockey, golf, boys and girls lacrosse, soccer, softball, tennis, boys volleyball and wrestling for two or more schools of the same public school district.

**Deadlines**
New cooperative programs: May 1 for fall sports, Aug. 15 for winter sports, Oct. 15 for spring sports. Dissolution deadlines are the same three dates. Renewal forms for agreements including a Class A or B school, or three or more schools, are due every two years prior to May 1, emailed to the primary school in March/April. A league may void an agreement at renewal by notification prior to April 1 of the previous school year. Section 1(F-3)/(F-4) four-year programs must report plans to the MHSAA by February 1 of the final year.

**Application requirements**
Application must be made on MHSAA forms by the administration of the cooperating member schools and be accompanied by (1) a resolution of authorization by each board of education describing the purpose for sponsoring the program and the Advance Preparation Materials, indicating which school or district administers it locally, and (2) a resolution of support from each league or conference, or support from at least four future opponents if there is no league. One school must be designated primary host and becomes the official team name. Enrollment figures come from the most recent Enrollment Declaration Form. Agreements are effective for two years.

**Executive Committee criteria**
Lack of numbers of students to support a program; lack of qualified staff to coach; lack of facilities; and evidence of a desire to increase opportunities for participation in new programs rather than win/loss records of existing programs.

**Advance preparation and guidelines**
Schools are asked to settle in writing who pays for and maintains uniforms, equipment and facilities; travel to practices and contests; selection, supervision and payment of coaches; cheerleaders; training rules and letter award guidelines; academic regulations; class schedule coordination; gate receipts; practice and game sites; hosting and supervision; athletic accident insurance and liability notification; and school identity, mascot and colors. A Cooperative Program Board of Control including at least an administrator and the athletic director of each school should oversee the program. The MHSAA Representative Council reaffirms its preference that Class A and B schools sponsor separate teams rather than repeatedly renew cooperative programs.

**Signatures required**
Superintendent, Board of Education, Principal and Athletic Director signatures plus date for each cooperating school.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
The document attached to the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for July 22, 2026 under the title "MHSAA Cooperative Agreement Request - Troy Athens - Boys Lacrosse - 26-27" is the Michigan High School Athletic Association's standard packet, "High School Cooperative Agreement Regulations, Procedures and Advance Preparation Material to Assist Schools," followed by the blank two-page Senior High Application to Form and Support a Cooperative Team with its Board of Education resolution page.

MHSAA HANDBOOK REGULATION I, SECTION 1(E). In any sport, two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 1,000 students may conduct, with Executive Committee approval, a Cooperative Program in the specific sports applied for. Subsection 1 allows the Executive Committee to approve a cooperative program at the subvarsity level only, in any sport, for two or more member high schools regardless of enrollment; there must be a demonstrated history of inadequate numbers of participants and approval will not be granted based on financial concerns. Students in such programs hold varsity eligibility only with their school of actual enrollment if brought up to a varsity team during the regular season or MHSAA Tournament. A student who participates in a subvarsity cooperative program and transfers into another school in that program may not be the subject of a waiver request under Regulation I, Section 9(C). Deadlines for high school cooperative programs and the two-year minimum operating length do not apply, but board of education, league (or four future opponents) and Executive Committee approvals are required. Subsection 2 allows approval regardless of combined enrollment maximum in baseball, bowling, competitive cheer, cross country, field hockey, golf, boys and girls lacrosse, soccer, softball, tennis, boys volleyball and wrestling for two or more schools of the same public school district under the same governing board; a demonstrated history of low participation is required, financial concerns are not a basis, the allowance does not apply to public school academies, approval is case-by-case, league or conference approval is required, and the standard deadlines apply.

SECTION 1(F). (1) Two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 3,500 students may conduct, with Executive Committee approval, a Cooperative Program in specific sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools: field hockey, gymnastics, boys lacrosse, girls lacrosse, boys alpine skiing, girls alpine skiing, boys swimming & diving, girls swimming & diving, boys tennis, girls tennis and boys volleyball. (2) Two or more member high schools whose combined enrollment does not exceed 5,500 students may conduct a Cooperative Program in ice hockey. (3) For those 12 sports, if none of the schools involved sponsored the sport at any level on an interscholastic basis during the previous school year, the 3,500 or 5,500 (ice hockey only) maximum may be waived by the Executive Committee, but the cooperative agreement may not exist beyond four school years. (4) The Executive Committee may approve an agreement in excess of the 3,500 or 5,500 maximum for up to four years in sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools if during the previous year the school, or the cooperative program the school was part of, dropped the sport because of demonstrated lack of participation; again limited to four school years.

INTERPRETATIONS (items 12-14). Cooperative Programs are arrangements made for a minimum of two years but may be voided at any time by resolutions of any cooperating board of education; if voided before completion of the second year, the terminating school or schools may not enter another cooperative program in the sports involved until another two-year period has transpired. Deadlines for dissolution are May 1 for fall sports, Aug. 15 for winter sports and Oct. 15 for spring sports; dissolutions after those dates may not permit changes to tournament divisions or assignments. Agreements established under Section 1(E) whose combined enrollments later rise above 1,000 students as established each February will be dissolved prior to the start of the school year in which the new enrollment is effective. If combined enrollment exceeds the original Division in the second year of an agreement, the schools play in the higher Division of MHSAA tournaments in the cooperative sports. A new MHSAA member school otherwise ineligible for tournaments until its second full year may participate sooner if it joins a Cooperative Program with a tournament-eligible member school. If the MHSAA Membership Resolution for a school in a cooperative agreement is not submitted on or before the fourth Friday after Labor Day, students of that school may not participate in any MHSAA tournament, including cooperative sports. Agreements including a Class A or B school, or three or more schools, must submit a renewal form every two years prior to May 1; the form is emailed to the primary school in March and requires league approval and statistics on participation levels and win/loss records. Agreements involving only two Class C or D schools need not submit renewal forms and continue until the MHSAA is notified of dissolution or a league withdraws support. After the initial two years, a league may by vote of its membership void an agreement at renewal by notifying all schools and the MHSAA prior to April 1 of the previous school year. Adding new schools requires a new application with all approvals. Programs started in newly sponsored sports under Section 1(F) over the 3,500 limit complete the two-year renewal process and are automatically dissolved after the fourth year. Cooperative Programs in sports sponsored by 250 or fewer schools are assigned tournament classification corresponding to total enrollment of the cooperating schools. When a sport is removed from the Section 1(F) list, existing programs are grandfathered subject to Executive Committee review at each renewal. Section 1(F) four-year programs must report to the MHSAA by February 1 of the final school year how the schools and teams will operate under 3,500/5,500 students subsequently. Programs whose combined enrollment on the February Enrollment Declaration Form exceeds 3,500/5,500 or the Section 1(E) limit may not operate in the coming school year. Deadlines for newly forming programs are May 1 (fall), Aug. 15 (winter) and Oct. 15 (spring); where a school is established and opened after the fall and winter deadlines, application may be made until MHSAA tournament assignments are made or Oct. 15, whichever occurs first.

PROCEDURES. Applications must be made on MHSAA forms by the administration of the cooperating member schools and received, even if partially completed, by the stated deadline; subvarsity-only and middle school applications have no established deadline but need board, league and Executive Committee approval before operating. Each application must include a resolution of authorization by each board of education describing the purpose for sponsoring the program and the Advance Preparation Materials and indicating which school or district will oversee local administration, plus a resolution of support from each league or conference, or from at least four future opponents if the schools do not belong to a league. One school must be designated primary host on the application and is considered the official team name; all signatures and enrollment figures from the most recent Enrollment Declaration Form must be provided. The Executive Committee considers lack of numbers of students to support a program, lack of qualified staff to coach, lack of facilities, and evidence of a desire to increase opportunities for participation in new programs rather than win/loss records of existing programs. Agreements are effective for two years, and no other cooperative agreement in the same sports may be made with another school until the original two-year period lapses; agreements may be voided in writing or via the Cooperative Program Dissolution Form. Renewal rules mirror the interpretations above, with the renewal form emailed to the primary school each April. A note records that the MHSAA Representative Council reaffirms its preference that Class A and B schools sponsor separate teams rather than continue to renew cooperative programs over a period of years without careful evaluation, and that schools should review participation numbers annually.

ADVANCE PREPARATION MATERIALS. Schools are asked to consider whether students from another school will replace students from their own community in an existing program, and, where two or more schools are creating a program where none existed, who pays for and maintains or launders uniforms, equipment and facilities; who pays travel to practices and contests; who selects, supervises and pays coaches; whose cheerleaders will cheer; whose training rules and letter award guidelines apply; whose local academic and other regulations apply; whether daily class schedules can be coordinated; how gate receipts are handled; where practices and games are held and who pays those expenses; who hosts and supervises events; whether athletic accident insurance is provided, who pays for it and whether liability insurers have been notified; and whose school identity, mascot and colors will be used. Schools must also consider whether an existing sport will suffer from creation of a cooperative program in another sport that season.

GUIDELINES. All issues should be addressed in writing in advance and submitted with the application for future reference. A "Cooperative Program Board of Control" consisting of at least an administrator and the athletic director of each cooperating school should be appointed to initiate the program and resolve disputes. Cooperating districts should be adjacent, though not required, with reasonable travel distance. Cooperative arrangements should be sought only where opportunities are limited and students are not expected to be cut. Agreements are intended for a significant group of students over several years, not a single participant for a year or two. There is no limit on the number of schools in an agreement, but programs with several schools tend to resemble non-school sports and may blur the philosophy of school sports.

APPLICATION FORM. The blank Senior High application collects the sport(s) with boys/girls designation, the primary and up to five secondary high schools with city, enrollment and class, the Handbook regulation under which the agreement is formed (Sect. 1[E], 1[E-1], 1[E-2], 1[F-1], 1[F-2], 1[F-3], 1[F-4]), the team levels sponsored (V, JV, Freshman), whether any school sponsored the sport last year, whether the schools have a current agreement in another sport, an acknowledgment that the agreement commences and continues for a minimum of two years, attached written support from the applicable league or four future opponents, certification that all approvals, required study, planning and review are complete, and whether the team will be known by a name other than a school name (the MHSAA generally uses the primary school as the designated team title). Page 2 is the Cooperative Program Board of Control resolution, submitted with the application and letter of league support, requiring Superintendent, Board of Education, Principal and Athletic Director signatures and dates for each cooperating school, plus the name, school represented, phone and email of the person completing the application. Completed forms are emailed to coops@mhsaa.com.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A twenty-slide Troy School District presentation titled "TSD Equity & Inclusion," delivered as a Board of Education workshop on May 18, 2021, tracing the district's equity work from the 2009 TSD Diversity Study to a newly created Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships position built around three priorities: Assess, Connect and Engage. The centerpiece finding is from the Equity & Inclusion Survey conducted by Hannover Research, which captured 7,448 stakeholder perceptions and identified the greatest opportunity for improvement in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Framing**
Presented under the title "TSD Equity & Inclusion" as a Board of Education workshop item for the meeting of May 18, 2021. Twenty slides, authored around five guiding principles attributed to Cornelius Godfrey.

**Guiding Principles**
1. Radical Equity: dismantling systems of inequity takes courage, imagination and a high tolerance for discomfort.
2. Gracious Inclusion: invitations to "the table" extended not on the basis of perceived merit, but because it's time to eat.
3. Abundance Mentality: belief that available resources are sufficient to meet the needs of every child, everyday.
4. Fearless Feedback: an honest look at ourselves and actively seeking critique, without threat of reprisal.
5. Many Hands: the work can never be "my work," "your work" or "their work" — it must always be "our work."

**Where we've been**
The 2009 TSD Diversity Study, conducted by R&J Consulting Group (Rosalind Cox), produced findings and recommendations in four areas: Personnel Diversity (review hiring and recruiting practices with a focus on retention), Cultural Awareness (appoint a Diversity Council, establish staff-wide competencies and incorporate them into evaluation), Curriculum (review data for gaps in achievement and access; review materials for inclusivity), and Parent Outreach (establish parent networks). A Diversity Council convened meetings between 2011 and 2012.

**Where we are**

| Initiative | Participants |
| --- | --- |
| National Equity Project | District and building administrators, teachers, students |
| Teacher's College: TRWP | Teachers |
| Book Clubs | Elementary and secondary teachers, administrators, support staff |
| Excellence in Equity Statement | Board of Education |
| Leading for Equity | Teachers, support staff (early adopters) |
| Building-level training on Culturally Responsive Teaching | Dr. Jay Marks of Oakland Schools |
| Equity Survey by Hannover Research | All stakeholders (staff, students, parents) |

**Where we're going**
System-wide integration across all pillars, departments and content areas, with significant investment from Teaching & Learning; community voice through collaborative meetings and quantitative evidence; creation of a new Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships role with three priorities; and an equity agenda calling for a comprehensive framework of supports at building and district levels (BELE), a learning continuum for all TSD employees, capacity building through stakeholder partnerships, transparency and reporting mechanisms, and a co-designed action plan with parent and student advisory support.

**Survey results**

| Respondent group | Count |
| --- | --- |
| Students (grades 5-12) | 5,520 |
| Parents | 1,503 |
| TSD staff members | 425 |
| Total stakeholder perceptions reflected | 7,448 |

Key finding: the greatest opportunity for improvement exists in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents. The final report was expected in late May or early June. Slides compare overall stakeholder perceptions against Black stakeholders, and overall parent perception against Black parents.

**Connecting**
Focused conversations with community members; Michigan Seal of Biliteracy; 70 scheduled connections via Calendly; an affinity group for TSD employees of color; postings shared to HBCUs via Handshake; MI Roundtable connections.

**Learning continuum**
A "house analogy" positions employees along three stages — Listening, Learning, Leading — described as a non-judgmental method of placing TSD employees along the continuum of learning for equity and inclusion.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document and occasion**

A Troy School District PowerPoint presentation of twenty slides titled "TSD Equity & Inclusion," prepared for an Equity and Inclusion Board Workshop held in connection with the Board of Education meeting of May 18, 2021. It narrates the district's equity history, current initiatives, survey results, planned structure, and a staff learning continuum.

**Guiding Principles**

Five numbered principles are presented, attributed on the slide to Cornelius Godfrey. Radical Equity holds that the work of dismantling systems of inequity takes courage, imagination and a high tolerance for discomfort. Gracious Inclusion states that invitations to "the table" are extended not on the basis of perceived merit, but because it is time to eat. Abundance Mentality asserts that to effectively engage in the work of equity one must believe available resources are sufficient to meet the needs of every child, everyday. Fearless Feedback holds that achieving equity requires an honest look at ourselves and actively seeking critique, without the threat of reprisal. Many Hands states that improving outcomes for the marginalized means the effort can never be "my work," "your work" or "their work" — it must always be "our work."

**Where we've been**

The historical anchor is the 2009 TSD Diversity Study conducted by R&J Consulting Group, with Rosalind Cox named as the consultant. A Diversity Council convened meetings between 2011 and 2012. The study's findings and recommendations are grouped into four areas. Personnel Diversity: review hiring and recruiting practices with a focus on retention. Cultural Awareness: appoint a Diversity Council, establish staff-wide competencies and incorporate them into the evaluation process. Curriculum: review data to identify gaps in achievement and access, and review materials for inclusivity. Parent Outreach: establish parent networks to review concerns and recommendations.

**Where we are**

Current initiatives are paired with the audiences engaged in each. The National Equity Project involves district and building administrators, teachers and students. Teacher's College TRWP involves teachers. Book Clubs involve elementary and secondary teachers, administrators and support staff. The Excellence in Equity Statement is attributed to the Board of Education. Leading for Equity involves teachers and support staff described as early adopters. Building-level training on Culturally Responsive Teaching is associated with Dr. Jay Marks of Oakland Schools. The Equity Survey by Hannover Research reaches all stakeholders — staff, students and parents.

**Where we're going and what's different now**

Five forward-looking themes are listed. System-wide integration means a place in all pillars, departments and content areas, with significant investment from Teaching & Learning. Community Voice covers collaborative meetings and quantitative evidence to support the work. The creation of a new equity role — Supervisor of Educational Equity, Inclusion and Community Relationships — carries three priorities: Assess, Connect and Engage. The Equity Agenda calls for implementing a comprehensive framework of supports at the building and district levels, identified as BELE; establishing a learning continuum for all TSD employees; building capacity for equity leadership through stakeholder partnerships; transparency and reporting mechanisms; and a co-designed action plan with parent and student advisory support.

**Three Priorities in detail**

Assess: establish a baseline for current equity, inclusion and community relations; center the perspectives of marginalized stakeholders; gauge efficacy and implementation fidelity regularly. Connect: build dynamic stakeholder coalitions; empower stakeholders to advance equity and inclusion within their various spheres of influence; elevate the voices of marginalized students and families. Engage: focused action oriented toward positive outcomes for marginalized students and families; proactively respond to community concerns; enact practices aimed at systematizing equity and inclusion. Three source citations are footnoted: Bustamante, R. and J. Nelson, "The School-Wide Cultural Competence Checklist," 2007, at cnx.org; "Recommendations for Diversity Training," Arlington Public Schools, at apsva.us; and "Strategies for Promoting Culturally Responsive Classrooms," Alexandria City Public Schools, page 14, at acps.k12.va.us/equity/strategies.

**The Pulley Analogy**

A slide frames assessment, connections and engagement through a pulley. Assessment represents an accurate understanding of the size, weight and dimensions of the load. Connections are represented by the pulley itself, used to multiply and change the direction of effort. Engagement represents the work being done, aided by the mechanical and relational advantage of the pulley. A note adds that the work of advancing equity and inclusion must always be focused on improved outcomes for marginalized individuals and community members, and that efforts with no observable positive impact on the marginalized may be necessary as prerequisites for the work but are not themselves the work.

**Planned activities under each priority**

Under Assess: a comprehensive "Listening Tour" using qualitative methods (surveys, interviews, questionnaires, focus groups) and quantitative methods (a data deep dive for disparities in perceptions, discipline and academic outcomes), a community connections review, and a curriculum review. Under Connect: assemble a Community Advisory Board and a Student Advisory Board; develop a staff coalition district-wide and at building, subject-area and administration levels; establish feedback channels for staff and students; and partner with equity and inclusion exemplars at the district and ISD level. Under Engage: draft vision and mission statements; implement an accountability and transparency platform; develop a three-to-five-year strategic plan for equity and inclusion; develop research-based criteria for equity and inclusion; provide professional development; and establish norms for dialogue.

**Equity & Inclusion Survey results**

The assessment slide reports that the Equity & Inclusion Survey reflected 7,448 stakeholder perceptions, comprising 5,520 students in grades 5 through 12, 1,503 parents and 425 TSD staff members. The stated key finding is that the greatest opportunity for improvement exists in the perceptions and experiences of Black students and Black parents. The final report was expected in late May or early June. Two subsequent slides are given over to comparisons: overall stakeholder perceptions versus Black stakeholders, and overall parent perception versus Black parents.

**Connecting activity to date**

Reported connection work includes focused conversations with community members, the Michigan Seal of Biliteracy, 70 scheduled connections via Calendly, an affinity group for TSD employees of color, job postings shared to HBCUs via Handshake, and MI Roundtable connections.

**Equity & Inclusion Learning Continuum**

The final section presents a Troy School District learning continuum with three stages — Listening, Learning, Leading — introduced through a house analogy described as a non-judgmental method of positioning TSD employees along the continuum of learning for equity and inclusion. Listening involves examining practice for compliance with district equity and inclusion standards, establishing a working knowledge of key terms and definitions, and considering available on-ramps for additional learning. Learning involves reflection on practice to implement cultural competencies, taking responsibility for professional learning, identifying and confronting personal biases, and understanding the role of culture and identity in learning. Leading involves reflection on systems and practices, identifying equity challenges, analyzing data for disparities, and taking responsibility for the learning of others within one's sphere of influence.

**Continuum examples**

Listening examples include following district policy for course recommendation, completing an online training module on cultural competence, reviewing evaluation criteria with a direct supervisor, reading context-specific articles focused on equity, inclusion or diversity, and reviewing policies released by neighboring districts relating to equity and anti-racism. Learning examples include participating in a district-sponsored book study, viewing a documentary film and participating in a discussion group, attending trainings offered by TSD or other local organizations, designating an accountability partner to encourage engagement and learning, and engaging in county-level organizations with equity as a central focus. Leading examples include participating in the district's Leading for Equity learning series, developing systems of group reflection and accountability, leading discussion groups and book clubs to support learning and growth, identifying and addressing system-level barriers to equitable access and practice, and adopting policies that advance equitable and anti-racist practices.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education meeting held September 21, 2021 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, with Acting Vice President Wilson presiding in the absence of President Schmidt and Superintendent Machesky. The Board adopted resolutions 21-076 through 21-080, the most consequential being approval of the 2021-2026 Strategic Plan, built from more than 50 listening sessions and Board sessions on March 13, May 4 and September 7, 2021. Every vote carried with 6 yes, 0 no, Schmidt absent. Residents dominated non-agenda public comment with objections to and support for the district mask requirement.

**Meeting and attendance**
Held September 21, 2021 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. Acting Vice President Wilson called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; President Schmidt and Superintendent Machesky were not in attendance. Present with Dr. Wilson were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff and Philippart, plus administrators Birmingham, Carrier, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Fulcher, Brinks, Cottone, DiPonio, Godfrey, Whan and West. Approximately 90 members of the audience attended. The meeting adjourned at 9:13 p.m.; Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, submitted the minutes.

**Recognitions**
Student representatives to the Board for 2021-2022 were introduced: Alyssa McLarty (Troy College & Career High School), Yara Mashal (International Academy - East), Sasha Palmkoeck (Athens High School) and Sarayu Bethamcherla (Troy High School). Mr. Fulcher and the Board recognized 2021 spring-sports all-state athletes Angela Anderanin, Elizabeth Bultynck, Alyssa Carnes, Zachary Hanoosh, Zachary LaRochelle, Abigail Mayne, Stephanie Ochoa, Sabrina Song and Tianhui Zhu. The Association of School Business Officials International awarded the district its Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for the Comprehensive Annual Financial Report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2020, crediting Rick West, Assistant Superintendent for Business Services, and Finance Director Kandice Moynihan. Bemis and Troy Union Elementary Schools, led by Principals Jeremey Whan and Mike Cottone, were honored as 2021 National Schools of Character, two of 47 schools nationally recognized by Character.org. Michigan Association of School Boards honors went to Vital Anne (Award of Merit), Elizabeth Hammond (Advocacy Skills Specialty Award) and Dr. Nancy Philippart (Data Skill Specialty Award), with the full Board earning the Honor Board Award and Standard of Excellence Award.

**Consent agenda (21-076)**
Moved by Hauff, supported by Gottlieb: approval of items A through D - minutes of the August 17, 2021 meeting; Treasurer's Report for July 2021; Troy Career Center Lease; and the Public Education Leaders Advocacy Institute & Professional Learning Seminar. Yes 6, No 0, Absent Schmidt.

**Personnel (21-077, 21-078)**
Jordan Harris, Assistant Superintendent for Employee Services, reported on the hiring process and the factors driving annual teacher hiring: retirements and resignations, full-year leaves of absence, FTE status and student enrollment. Moved by Anne, supported by Philippart, the Board approved the elementary and secondary personnel recommendations including a large slate of new hires. The Board also issued a two-year administrative contract without tenure to Patrick Griffin, who begins transitioning into the Assistant Principal role at International Academy East on September 22, 2021.

**Strategic Plan 2026 (21-079)**
Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent for Elementary Instruction, presented the planning process and findings from over 50 listening sessions. The four pillars were refreshed: green Early Childhood to Career, red Equity and Well-Being, blue Deep Learning, gold Building Capacity, under the vision World Class for ALL. The adopting resolution (Philippart/Hammond) recited the March 13, 2021 winter retreat session, the May 4, 2021 workshop and the September 7, 2021 workshop that produced the final draft, and was adopted on the 21st day of September 2021.

**Business, public comment and other**
Rick West presented a 2013 Bond Work/Sinking Fund update covering summer capital projects - concrete, door and window replacement, fencing, flooring, paving, roofing and remodeling. The Troy Board of Education met on September 21, 2021 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. In addition to Dr. Wilson, Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff and Philippart were present. Administrators present were Birmingham, Carrier, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Fulcher, Brinks, Cottone, DiPonio, Godfrey, Whan and West. Approximately 90 members of the audience attended. Vice President Wilson opened with a statement describing how the evening's meeting would proceed in compliance with the Open Meetings Act and reviewed the guidelines for public comment.

**Student representatives introduced**

Alyssa McLarty of Troy College & Career High School, a senior and student athlete, led initiatives including a food pantry for TCCHS families, competes on the Athens swim team and dual enrolls at Oakland Community College. Yara Mashal, a junior at International Academy East, has served on student council and as a board member of the Insight Club and the Relay for Life Club, is fluent in Arabic, is studying French, has traveled to five continents and interned at Wayne State University's School of Medicine doing neurological research. Sasha Palmkoeck, a senior at Athens High School, is a lead dancer with Eisenhower Dance Detroit, works at Grabbagreen, and is a Summa Cum Laude, AP and NHS Scholar who will major in Behavioral Neuroscience. Bemis and Troy Union Elementary Schools were honored with the 2021 National Schools of Character Award, one of 47 schools across the country receiving the distinction from Character.org; Principals Jeremey Whan and Mike Cottone, along with a representative from each building, accepted awards from the Board. Yes: 6. No: 0. Absent: Schmidt.

**Administrative appointment - resolution 21-078**
Moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Mrs. Hammond, the Board issued a two-year administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mr. Patrick Griffin, who will begin transitioning his duties as Assistant Principal, International Academy East, starting September 22, 2021. Yes: 6. No: 0. Absent: Schmidt.

**Curriculum - Strategic Plan 2026 and resolution 21-079**
Kris Griffor, Assistant Superintendent, Elementary Instruction, presented a PowerPoint on the district's strategic planning process through 2026 and shared findings collected from over 50 listening sessions with students, parents, community members, staff and the Board. The mission and vision are being refreshed to enhance the pillars: the green pillar Early Childhood to Career will expand research with access through career; the red pillar Equity and Well-Being will focus on ensuring safety, belonging and connection; the blue pillar Deep Learning will center on ensuring learning for all throughout the system; and the gold pillar Building Capacity will expand to include students, staff and community as learners. The leadership team committed to the mission of ensuring learning for ALL, with the vision World Class for ALL and newly established goals in cultivating a collaborative culture, deepening learning and focusing direction. Background recited that in the 2015-2016 school year the Board joined the Superintendent and his team to introduce the vision of World Class 2020, whose Strategic Plan Pillars led the work across oneTROY for the last 5 years. Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Hammond, the resolution recited information-gathering interviews with the Board, Central Office administration, building administrators, teachers, professional and support staff, students, parents and community members; a strategic planning session during the Board's winter retreat on March 13, 2021; an additional workshop on May 4, 2021 that addressed key issues and priorities; and the September 7, 2021 workshop whose input produced the final draft. Daniel Karg, an Athens High School alumnus, spoke on the importance of typing classes at the secondary level. Diana Magiera, a parent of two, spoke about a mask exemption for her son. Sarah Krieger, a parent of three, raised the effects of wearing masks and asked whom she could contact. Katie MacFarland raised concerns about critical race theory and Marxism in public schools. Ollie Apahidean raised concerns about teaching racism and books that promote division and hate. Joe Scott, a parent of two, cited social, emotional, academic and medical effects of children wearing masks. B. J. Lennon, a parent of three, called the mask mandate harmful and a personal choice for parents. Tracy Owens, a parent of three, raised concerns about the Summer Learning Resource letter about race and equity. Ryan Johnson, a parent of one, described attempts to have his son attend school without a mask and argued mandating masks violates the law.

**Other - resolution 21-080 and closing**
Moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne, the Board certified that Mrs. Vital Anne, Mr. Gary Hauff, Mr. Karl Schmidt and Dr. Nancy Philippart will serve as delegates to the MASB 2021 Delegate Assembly on November 11, 2021. Yes: 6. No: 0. Absent: Schmidt. The meeting adjourned at 9:13 p.m. Respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education.

**Bond authorization and details (paragraphs 1–2)**
Bonds may be issued in one or more series, not exceeding $45,000,000 or such lesser amount as determined by the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually (each an “Authorized Officer”). Bonds are registered as to principal and interest in the denomination of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of delivery, numbered by the Transfer Agent, maturing May 1 in years and amounts set at sale. Interest may not exceed four percent (4.00%) per annum, payable semi-annually on May 1 and November 1, provided net present value savings are not less than one percent (1.00%) of projected debt service on the Refunded Bonds absent the refunding, based on Treasury guidelines. Sale price must be not less than 99% and not more than 105% of principal. Serial or term bonds are permitted; term bonds designated by the original purchaser carry mandatory redemption per the Notice of Sale schedule. Interest is paid by check mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month prior to the payment date. Book-entry-only issuance through The Depository Trust Company, New York, New York, is permitted.

**Execution, tax levy, funds, proceeds (paragraphs 3–6)**
Bonds follow Exhibit A, signed by manual or facsimile signatures of the President and Secretary of the Board, valid only upon Transfer Agent authentication, delivered per instructions from the Treasurer of the School District. Commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2020, the District must levy annually a tax sufficient to pay principal and interest when due, without limitation as to rate or amount, as permitted by Article IX, Section 6 and Article IX, Section 16 of the Michigan Constitution of 1963. Unless a Common Debt Retirement Fund exists, the Treasurer opens a 2021 Refunding Bonds Debt Retirement Fund; tax proceeds, accrued interest on delivery, and any net original issue premium are deposited there, and premium may reduce the principal amount issued if federal tax law requires. Proceeds fund a 2021 Refunding Bonds Costs of Issuance Fund, with any surplus transferred to the Debt Retirement Fund; the balance, plus money transferred from the debt retirement fund for the Refunded Bonds, is invested in direct obligations of or obligations unconditionally guaranteed by the United States of America in one or more Escrow Funds held by a bank or trust company as trustee and Escrow Agent under Escrow Agreements irrevocably directing redemption of the specified Prior Bonds.

**Sale, ratings, disclosure, negotiated alternatives (paragraphs 7–12)**
The Authorized Officer may fix a sale date, publish notice in the Bond Buyer, New York, New York, in the form of Exhibit B, award to the bidder producing the lowest true interest cost, and execute a sale order without further Board direction. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Official minutes of the regular meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, held Tuesday, December 14, 2021 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:02 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Anne, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson. Mr. Gottlieb was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Keyser, Young, and West. There were approximately 35 members of the audience. The minutes carry the notation GH/jh and are signed "Respectfully submitted, Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education."

Opening. Mr. Schmidt suggested that in lieu of the Pledge of Allegiance, everyone stand to honor the students lost in the Oxford High School shooting and share in a moment of silence and prayer for all of those affected by the tragedy.

Recognition — TSD Mission Moment: TSD Preschool Inclusion. The Board recognized the TSD Preschool for its inclusion program. The minutes describe inclusive education as a system in which students with special needs attend school with typically developing peers, and an inclusive preschool system as one that integrates special education and related services into all aspects of its program, making it possible to address the needs of all children. In Troy this means collaboration among all stakeholders, including both general education and special education staff as well as families and administration. The minutes note that the Troy School community has invested in ongoing shared learning to ensure best practices are implemented and staff is being responsive to students, and that equity and inclusion remain a priority, with the TSD Preschool committed to ensuring a learning environment where every student feels a sense of belonging. Erin Keyser, Early Childhood Director, was invited to share a video demonstrating examples of the inclusion program and then introduced her team: Lauren DeGrazia, School Social Worker; Elizabeth Neuville, General Education Teacher; Katie Drinkard, Teacher Consultant; and Grace Lynch, Speech & Language Pathologist.

Additions and Deletions. Dr. Machesky indicated that agenda item 10.A, Legislative Report from State Representative Kuppa, needed to be deleted from the agenda because Representative Kuppa was out of the country due to a family emergency. The District and Board planned to meet with Senator McMorrow and Representative Kuppa in January 2022 for a legislative update.

Public Communication (Agenda Items). None.

General — Consent Agenda, Resolution 21-089. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Dr. Wilson that the Troy Board of Education take action to approve items A, B, C, D, E, F, and G on the consent agenda. Those items were: corrected minutes of the October 19, 2021 Board of Education meeting; minutes of the November 9, 2021 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the November 16, 2021 Board of Education meeting; Sex Education Advisory Board for 2021-2023; Treasurer's Report — October 2021; Budget Amendment #1; and Hill Coil & Condensing Unit Replacement. The vote was Yes 6, No 0, Absent Gottlieb.

Personnel. None. Curriculum. None.

Business — Roofing Replacement Program, Resolution 21-090. It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the bid for roof replacement be awarded as follows and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund and Building Site & Sinking Funds. JD Candler was awarded Athens High School and Schroeder for $740,910.00. Royal West Roofing was awarded Troy High School for $623,469.00. A contingency of 5% was set at $68,218.95. The total stated was $1,432,597.95. The vote was Yes 6, No 0, Absent Gottlieb.

Business — Construction, Windows & Doors (Barnard, Bemis & IAE), Resolution 21-091. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mr. Hauff that the bid for bid pack 33 be awarded as follows and that this be approved as an expenditure of the Building Site and Sinking Fund. Environmental Glass Inc. was awarded Exterior Doors at $567,000.00. Triangle Window Fashions, Inc. was awarded Roller Shades at 13,540.00. Environmental Glass Inc. was awarded a Strategic Change Order at 70,000.00. Contingency at 8% was 46,443.00. The total recommended award stated was $696,983.00. The vote was Yes 6, No 0, Absent Gottlieb.

Business — Door Lock Hardware, Resolution 21-092. It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne that the district purchase Nightlock Lockdown hardware in the amount of $162,922.95 from Taylor Brothers Door Lock, LLC, and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the General Fund, the 2019 Capital Projects Bond and/or the Building Site & Sinking Fund. The vote was Yes 6, No 0, Absent Gottlieb.

Reports from Student Representatives to the Board. Alyssa McLarty, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, shared a report on the events and activities happening in her school. Yara Mashal, student representative for International Academy-East, shared a report on the events and activities at her school. Sarayu Bethamcherla, student representative for Troy High School, shared a report on events and activities at her school. Sasha Palmkoeck, student representative for Athens High School, shared a report on events and activities at her school.

Public Communication (Non-Agenda Items). President Schmidt shared a statement providing the structure of how the evening's public participation would be conducted in compliance with the Open Meetings Act and reviewed the guidelines to be followed for public comment. Dr. Dick Young, a Troy resident for 37 years, addressed the Board about his proposal for a school safety review committee made up of sub-committees to keep students safe. Sarah Krieger, a TSD parent of three students, addressed the Board about a book in the high school library and read excerpts from pages in the book. Mrs. Katie MacFarland, a TSD parent, addressed the Board about flaws in the process of selecting books for the school library and read an excerpt from one of the books. Mrs. Kacy Bailey, a TSD parent of two students, addressed the Board about procedures for student quarantines and about her child's iPad and issues with parental controls not working appropriately. Mr. Ollie Apahidean, a TSD parent, addressed the Board about the media content in school media centers and read an excerpt from a book found in the high school library. Mr. Joe Thilman, a Troy resident, addressed the Board about his support of the mask mandate in the District.

Other — Legislative Update from State Representative Kuppa. This item was deleted from the agenda; State Representative Kuppa was out of the country due to a family emergency.

Board Member Comments. Dr. Philippart wished everyone a happy holiday, acknowledged the difficult last few months, and thanked Kerry Birmingham for the continued district communication. Mrs. Hammond echoed Dr. Philippart's sentiments and wished everyone happy holidays. Mrs. Anne shared the same sentiments and thanked the administration, teachers, students, and parents for their patience throughout the challenging times, wishing everyone happy holidays. Mr. Hauff shared a message of hope during the holiday season, asking people to pause, reflect, pray, and extend a hand to all, and wished everyone a Merry Christmas. Dr. Wilson echoed her colleagues and shared how much she appreciates the administrators for their leadership in the challenge of balancing both the tragedy and joy of the season.

Dr. Machesky thanked all employee groups for what they do for students every day. He indicated that it had been a challenging couple of years but that he believes in the community and that it will come through stronger. He also mentioned that Kerry Birmingham had sent out a survey to the district and community for suggestions on how the district should consider spending ESSER funds moving forward.

Mr. Schmidt thanked the TSD cabinet team for its resiliency and how quickly it steps up when there is a crisis. He mentioned that the internal crisis committee met within days of the shooting to make changes where necessary. He talked about the recent shooting and said he appreciates the support the District has provided to staff and students. He shared that he had talked with several students about their feelings and how safe they feel at school after the tragedy and was happy to hear that they felt supported and safe. He announced that the next Board Workshop would be held on Tuesday, January 4 at 6:00 p.m. at the Services Building and that the next Organizational and regular Board Meeting would be Tuesday, January 18 at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building.

Adjournment. The meeting adjourned at 8:13 p.m.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A summary sheet prepared for the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) bylaws review lists each proposed 2025 revision by page, article and section with a short rationale. Four revisions are identified as clerical or grammatical and are stated not to change the meaning of the bylaws, including correcting 'off' to 'office' in Article V, Section 3 and 'Ther' to 'The' in Article VIII, Section 2. Eight further sections are revised for content, among them a new Article VII, Section 10 requiring the Board of Directors to create and maintain Board Operating Procedures, an option to split the Office of Secretary into Corresponding and Recording Secretary roles, and a shift of committee-chair elections from the first meeting after January 31st to the first meeting after July 1st. Overview
OCSBA Bylaws - Amendments at a Glance is a change-log style handout accompanying the Oakland County School Boards Association's proposed 2025 bylaws revisions. Each entry gives the page number, article, section, the revised language and a rationale. The revisions are divided into two groups: four clerical/grammatical changes stated not to change the meaning of the bylaws, and eight sections revised and edited for content.

Clerical and grammatical revisions
| # | Page | Article / Section | Change and rationale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 3 | Article V, Sec. 3 - Place of Meeting | 'off' is supposed to read 'office' (registered office of the Association) |
| 2 | 6 | Article VIII, Sec. 2 - Term of Office | Delete the stray 'r' so 'Ther' reads 'The' |
| 3 | 9 | Article IX, Sec. 4 - Government Relations Committee | Add 'on' after 'information' |
| 4 | 15 | Article XIV, Sec. 2 - Dealing with the Association | Remove a duplicated phrase |

Revisions edited for content
| # | Page | Article / Section | Substance |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | 5 | Article VII, Sec. 4 - Notice | Delete references to notice by U.S. mail and fax as outdated modes of communication; special-meeting notice given at least two days by written notice delivered personally, by phone or email |
| 2 | 6 | Article VII, Sec. 10 - Board Operating Procedures | New section: the Board shall create and maintain Board Operating Procedures to be used with the Bylaws, reflecting procedures recently adopted that define roles, responsibilities and timelines |
| 3 | 7 | Article VIII, Sec. 6 - The Secretary | At the discretion of the Board on an annual basis, the Office of Secretary may be divided into Corresponding Secretary and Recording Secretary; rationale cites a Board of 7-9 directors and added leadership opportunities |
| 4 | 8 | Article IX, Sec. 3 - Committee Chairs | Chair election moves from the first committee meeting after January 31st to the first meeting after July 1st, aligning with the Operating Year of July 1 - June 30; written notice of the election at least seven (7) calendar days in advance |
| 5 | 9 | Article IX, Sec. 4 - Government Relations Committee | Standing committee meeting at least 6 times per year; each Member School District appoints a representative at its annual organizational meeting; chair elected annually at the first committee meeting after January 31st with one (1) vote per district; in the absence of an elected Vice Chair the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the position |
| 6 | 9 | Article IX, Sec. 5 - Resolutions and Bylaws Committee | Standing committee meeting at least once per year; appointments made by the OCSBA President rather than the Board of Directors; the Government Relations Committee Chairperson shall be a member |
| 7 | 16 | Article XV, Sec. 5 - Method of Giving Notices | Notice given by electronic communication to a director's or officer's last known district-provided email address instead of by mailing; OCSBA does not physically mail communications |
| 8 | 17 | Article XVI, Sec. 1 - Amendments | Bylaws altered or amended by vote of Member School Districts on a written ballot with at least a forty (40) day voting period, one vote per district; grammatical errors that do not change meaning or intent may be corrected by the Board of Directors without a membership vote |

Effect
The package modernizes notice practices, formalizes Board Operating Procedures, moves committee leadership elections into the July-June operating year, shifts committee appointments to the OCSBA President, builds a Vice Chair succession path for the Government Relations Committee, and allows routine grammatical corrections during annual review without sending the matter to the Member School Districts.
