**Substance of selected continuing positions**
Accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA and the Open Meetings Act, should apply to every school receiving public funding, including local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies and their authorizers and management companies, and colleges and universities. Broadband should be in any federal or state infrastructure plan, with support for device and software purchase programs and dedicated cybersecurity resources. Early childhood positions support new dollars for universal public preschool for four-year-olds and mandatory kindergarten for five-year-olds; Early On Michigan should be fully funded for infants and toddlers birth to age three. School Aid positions call for constitutionally limiting the School Aid Fund to Pre-K to 12th grade public education, opposing vouchers and tax credit programs, additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students, protection of the School Aid Fund from state tax policy changes, and enactment of the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts can meet the June 30 budget deadline. Special Education seeks full funding of IDEA, noting that federal legislation initially promised 40 percent of the excess cost. The Association also supports the NSBA, MASB, OCSA and COSSBA legislative agendas when aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Ballot and reference packet issued by the Oakland County School Boards Association (OCSBA) for member consideration in spring 2026, footered "Proposed NEW Resolution May, 2026" across three pages, and placed before the Troy School District Board of Education for its June 1, 2026 meeting.

PROPOSED NEW RESOLUTION. The single proposed new resolution reads: "OCSBA opposes tying any school funding to waiving the attorney-client privilege."

RATIONALE. In the FY26 school aid budget, section 31aa school safety and mental health categorical funding required districts to "opt in." Any district that opted in to receive 31aa funds agreed to cooperate with an investigation, including waiving the attorney-client privilege, following a mass-casualty incident. The rationale argues that while cooperation with investigations after a mass casualty event is necessary to prevent another event, the attorney-client privilege must remain sacred; that the courts have ruled on this issue; and that in the future there is nothing to stop the legislature from tying waiver of the attorney-client privilege to other funding.

ADOPTION THRESHOLD. The packet quotes OCSBA Bylaws Article IX, Section 5, Resolution Adoption: resolutions that are approved by at least nineteen (19) member school districts shall be the official position of the association as interpreted and pursued by its board of directors. The continuing resolutions that follow have been adopted by member school districts and are provided for reference only, with adoption and amendment dates noted for each.

ACCOUNTABILITY AND TRANSPARENCY [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]. OCSBA supports holding every school that receives public funding to the same accountability and transparency standards, including FOIA requests and the Open Meetings Act, covering local districts, ISDs, Public School Academies (aka Charter Schools), their authorizers and management companies, and all colleges and universities. Cited as MASB Resolution A 6.65 (c), (d), (f).

BROADBAND ACCESS AND DEVICES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021; Amended 6/5/2025]. Broadband should be included in any federal or state infrastructure plan; OCSBA supports additional federal and state funding to expand affordable and reliable broadband access, federal and state programs for the purchase of internet capable devices and software, and dedicated resources for cybersecurity. Cited as MASB Resolution A-10.30, 2021 amendment.

EARLY CHILDHOOD [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]. Support for additional new dollars to fund universal, public preschool for all four-year-old children, and support for mandatory kindergarten for all five-year-old children. Cited as MASB Resolution A 6.15 (c).

EARLY ON MICHIGAN [OCSBA Adopted 1/26/2026]. Support for full funding of Early On Michigan, an early intervention program for infants and toddlers from birth to age three with disabilities, developmental delays, or who are at risk for delays due to certain health conditions.

EVIDENCE-BASED DECISION MAKING [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. Support for evidence-based education policy that will maximize opportunities for the highest achievement of each student. Cited as MASB Resolution G 11.01.

LAME DUCK [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. Support for lame duck parameters addressing introduction and accelerated passage of legislation after the November election.

LOCAL CONTROL [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. Support local control of community-governed public schools with elected school boards. Cited as MASB Resolutions A 10.10, A 10.55 and A 12.70.

MENTAL HEALTH [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]. Support for increased mental health services and professionals in schools and, at a minimum, annual inflation adjusted state resources so schools can both educate and keep students and staff safe; help staff identify potential mental health issues; encourage MDE to develop a model policy for staff on identifying mental health issues and appropriate staff response. Cited as MASB Resolutions G 9.01, G 9.05 and G 9.50.

NON-PARTISAN ELECTIONS [OCSBA Adopted 1/9/2026]. Support for non-partisan school board elections.

SCHOOL AID [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]. Four parts: (A) specify in Michigan's Constitution that the School Aid Fund is only for Pre-K to 12th grade public education and oppose any attempts to create private school vouchers or tax credit programs (MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (a) and A 10.05); (B) support additional funding for Special Education, At-Risk and ELL students (MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (g) and (j); A 10.55); (C) protect the School Aid Fund and local revenues from state tax policy changes (MASB Resolutions A 10.25 (c); A 10.55); and (D) support enacting the annual School Aid Budget no later than June 1 so districts have factual information to meet their constitutional and statutory requirement to approve a budget by June 30 (MASB Resolution A 10.25 (h)).

SCHOOL FINANCE RESEARCH COLLABORATIVE (SFRC) [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 9/11/2021; 3/3/2023; 6/5/2025]. Support for implementation of SFRC recommendations, with higher funded districts held harmless during implementation. Cited as MASB resolution G 11.01 and A-10.25, 2021 amendment.

SCHOOL NUTRITION [OCSBA Adopted 3/3/2023; Amended 6/5/2025]. Support for codification of free universal meals.

SCHOOL SAFETY [OCSBA Adopted 3/3/2023]. Support for adequate state resources allowing schools to both educate and keep students and staff safe.

SPECIAL EDUCATION [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. Support for full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), noting that federal legislation initially promised to provide 40 percent of the excess cost to educate students with disabilities but that appropriations have fallen short, leaving states and local school districts to make up the difference. Cited as MASB Resolution A 5.01 and NSBA Advocacy: IDEA.

TEACHER SHORTAGES [OCSBA Adopted 9/11/2021; Amended 6/5/2025]. Support for statewide initiatives to address teacher shortages and retain teachers while maintaining quality teacher preparation programs, potentially including incentives to enter and complete a teaching college program, incentives for teachers to remain in the classroom, and easing the process for teachers certified in other states to obtain Michigan certification. Cited as MASB 2021-2022 Legislative Priority.

UNFUNDED MANDATES [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019]. Opposition to any state or federal legislation that increases costs for school districts without full funding, and encouragement for the Michigan Legislature to oppose federal laws or programs that are not fully funded and thus cost the state valuable resources. Cited as MASB Resolution A 10.20.

ALIGNED AGENDAS [OCSBA Adopted 9/24/2019; Amended 6/5/2025]. When aligned with OCSBA legislative priorities, OCSBA also supports the National School Boards Association (NSBA) Legislative Agenda, the Michigan Association of School Boards (MASB) Legislative Agenda, the Oakland County Superintendents Association (OCSA) Legislative Agenda, and the Consortium of State School Board Associations (COSSBA) Legislative Agenda.

LINKS. MASB Resolutions at https://www.masb.org/resolutions.aspx; NSBA Advocacy: IDEA at https://www.nsba.org/Advocacy; COSSBA Advocacy at https://www.cossba.org/advocacy.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Two-page OCSBA packet setting out proposed 2026 bylaws updates for member district consideration. Amendment 1 would add language to Article VI, Section 2 allowing a member district that pays dues directly to the Association to appoint a Trustee to the Board of Directors, specifically entitling the Intermediate School District, which pays annual dues of currently $6,000 per year, to appoint one Trustee to a 3-year term. Amendment 2 would revise Article IX, Sections 3 and 4 so that when an elected committee chair is not a Board member, the Association Board appoints one of its Directors as Vice-Chair.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**What it is**
OCSBA document headed "PROPOSED BYLAWS UPDATES FOR 2026," presenting two proposed amendments with rationales and reference copies of related unchanged bylaw language, prepared for member district voting in May 2026.

**Proposed Amendment 1: ISD appointment to the Board of Directors**
Adds language to Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 2 (Eligibility). The existing text keeps the rule that any Member is eligible for election and only one Member from each Member School District may serve at any given time. The added sentences read that the Intermediate School District pays annual membership dues directly to the Association, and is therefore entitled to appoint one (1) Trustee to a 3-year term on the Board of Directors; if the ISD chooses not to exercise that right, the Board of Directors shall be notified in writing within 30 days of a Board election so the seat can be filled by election.

Rationale: like every other member district the ISD is a member of MASB and therefore of the Association, but it is the only member district that also pays annual dues directly to the Association, currently $6,000 per year. The proposal is described as providing board continuity for a working Board where filling all 9 positions is a struggle, and as consistently filling 1 seat, without altering the total number of Directors or the limit of one director per district. It cites the ISD's in-kind donations of event space with AV support (equipment and staff), legislative affairs/advocacy support, and no-cost employee speakers, and notes that ISD dues cover the entire cost the Association pays the ISD for Event Management services (staff, online registration, collection and processing of meeting fees, onsite event support) and Financial Services support (monthly financial accounting, filing annual tax and state reports).

**Reference language, unchanged**
Article III, Section 1 on Members; Article IV on Dues (annual MASB grant to CASBA members, ISD membership dues not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, contributions and gifts); and Article VI, Section 1 (odd number of Directors, no fewer than 7 nor more than 9).

**Proposed Amendment 2: committee chair or vice-chair on the Board**
Ensures that either the Chair or Vice-Chair of every OCSBA committee is a member of the Board of Directors (BOD), by adding or revising language in two sections of Article IX.

Article IX, Section 3 (Committee Chairs) would add: in the event that the elected committee chair is not a member of the Board of Directors, the Association Board shall appoint one of its Directors to serve as Vice-Chair of the committee. Surrounding provisions are unchanged, including annual election of a Chairperson from appointed representatives as the first order of business at the committee's first meeting after July 1, with written notice not less than seven (7) calendar days before the vote.

Article IX, Section 4 (The Government Relations Committee) keeps annual election of a Chairperson from appointed Members at the first committee meeting after January 31, one vote per Member School District, and the provision that absent an elected Vice Chair the Vice President of OCSBA assumes the position, while adding the same appointment sentence.

Rationale: for Section 3, any member can chair any committee, so assigning a Board member as Vice-Chair provides BOD support, ensures two-way communication with the BOD, and ensures compliance with BOD procedures and bylaws. For Section 4, some Directors never attend Government Relations Committee meetings even though the GRC Vice Chair must attend regularly; both GRC officers need advocacy involvement and attendance at events such as MASB Behind the Scenes and the NSBA Advocacy Institute, so the OCSBA Vice President is not always best suited and the Board should decide which Director serves.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
OCSBA packet titled "PROPOSED BYLAWS UPDATES FOR 2026," two pages, setting out two proposed amendments to the bylaws of the Oakland County School Boards Association for member school district consideration in May 2026, each accompanied by a rationale and, for Amendment 1, reference copies of related bylaw language that would not change. The item appeared on the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for June 1, 2026.

PROPOSED AMENDMENT 1. Headline: a member district that pays dues directly to the Association may appoint a Trustee to a seat on the Board of Directors. The change adds language to ARTICLE VI, ELECTION OF BOARD OF DIRECTORS, Section 2, Eligibility. The section as shown reads that any Member is eligible to be elected to the Association's Board of Directors and that only one Member from each Member School District is allowed to serve on the Board at any given time, followed by the new language: the Intermediate School District pays annual membership dues directly to the Association, and is therefore entitled to appoint one (1) Trustee to a 3-year term on the Board of Directors; if the ISD chooses to not exercise their right to appoint a Director, the Board of Directors shall be notified, in writing, within 30 days of a Board election so that the seat can be filled by election.

RATIONALE FOR AMENDMENT 1. Like every other member district, the ISD is a member of MASB and is therefore a member of the Association. However, to support the Association, the ISD is the only member district that also pays annual dues, currently $6,000 per year, directly to the Association. The proposal is said to help the Association by providing board continuity: the Board of Directors is a working board and it is a struggle to fill all 9 positions, so the proposal will help to consistently fill 1 seat. An appointment by a dues-paying district will not alter the total number of Directors, and the limit of one director per district does not change. Given what the rationale calls the unparalleled financial and in-kind support the ISD provides, an appointed ISD Director is characterized as fair and reasonable. The ISD provides in-kind donations of event space with AV support (equipment and staff) and legislative affairs and advocacy support, and when requested provides employee speakers at no cost to the Association. The ISD's annual dues cover the entire cost that the Association pays to the ISD for service agreements: Event Management services, including but not limited to staff, online registration, collection and processing of meeting fees and onsite event support; and Financial Services support, including but not limited to monthly financial accounting and filing annual tax and state reports.

RELATED LANGUAGE PROVIDED FOR REFERENCE ONLY, WHICH WOULD NOT CHANGE. Article III, Membership, Section 1, Members: the Association is organized upon a membership basis, and any publicly elected Board of Education member of a school district located in Oakland County or any elected Oakland ISD Board of Education member (referred to as "Member School Districts"), that is also a member in good standing in the Michigan Association of School Boards ("MASB"), is an eligible general member of the Association. Article IV, Dues: the Association shall be financed by an annual MASB grant to its County Area School Boards Association (CASBA) members, Intermediate School District membership dues in an amount not to exceed the MASB CASBA grant, and by contributions and gifts accepted by the Association. Article VI, Election of Board of Directors, Section 1, Number of Directors: the Board of Directors shall consist of an odd number of Directors, with no fewer than 7 nor more than 9 members.

PROPOSED AMENDMENT 2. Headline: ensure that either the Chair or Vice-Chair of every OCSBA committee is a member of the Board of Directors (BOD). The change adds or revises language in two sections of ARTICLE IX, COMMITTEES.

Article IX, Section 3, Committee Chairs, as amended: each standing and ad hoc committee shall elect a Chairperson annually from the appointed representatives; in the event that the elected committee chair is not a member of the Board of Directors, the Association Board shall appoint one of its Directors to serve as Vice-Chair of the committee; the election shall be the first order of business at the committee's first meeting after July 1st, unless otherwise specified in the Bylaws; and written notice of the election date, time and place shall be provided to all appointed representatives not less than seven (7) calendar days prior to the meeting at which the vote will occur.

Rationale for adding this language to Section 3: any member can be elected to chair any committee, meaning the chair does not have to be a member of the Board of Directors. When a committee chair is not a BOD member, assigning a BOD member as Vice-Chair will provide BOD support for the committee, ensure direct two-way communication between the committee and the BOD, and ensure compliance with BOD procedures and Association bylaws.

Article IX, Section 4, The Government Relations Committee, Committee Membership/Leadership, as revised: a Committee Chairperson will be elected annually from the appointed Members at the first committee meeting after January 31st, with each Member School District in attendance having one (1) vote cast by its appointed representative; in the absence of an elected Vice Chair, the Vice President of OCSBA will assume the position of Vice Chair; and in the event that the elected committee chair is not a member of the Board of Directors, the Association Board shall appoint one of its Directors to serve as Vice-Chair of the committee.

Rationale for revising the current language in Section 4: while all Directors serve on one or more committees, Directors are not necessarily involved in the Government Relations Committee, and some Directors never attend GRC meetings even though the Vice Chair of the GRC must regularly attend them. Like the GRC Chair, the Vice Chair needs to be knowledgeable and actively involved in advocacy, and both the Chair and Vice Chair of the GRC need to provide leadership for members by regularly attending state and national advocacy conferences and events, such as MASB Behind the Scenes and the NSBA Advocacy Institute. For these reasons the OCSBA Vice President is not always the person best suited to fulfill the role of GRC Vice Chair, and the OCSBA Board of Directors should be allowed to decide which of its Directors is best suited to serve in the role.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: A March 2023 elementary mathematics materials adoption report to the Troy School District Board of Education, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder, recommending Bridges in Mathematics and Number Corner from The Math Learning Center to replace Math Expressions, in place since the 2010 elementary math adoption. The report documents a review begun in September 2019 by the Math Leadership Team, materials piloted by 95 early adopter teachers in 2022-23, and a total projected cost of $535,592.31, of which $443,974.31 is the Math Learning Center quote Q-10092 dated 1/27/2023.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Report**
"Elementary Mathematics Materials Adoption," March 2023, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder to the Troy School District Board of Education (March 7, 2023 meeting).

**Rationale**
The district reviews curricular materials every nine years. The last curricular adoption was Middle and High-School Health in 2020; the last elementary math adoption was conducted in 2010. The review philosophy has shifted from simply seeking new materials to a comprehensive program review covering instructional practices, intervention, assessment and current data, so that curricular, structural and staffing needs can be aligned. Teachers have been supplementing the current resource with three act tasks, number sense routines and additional materials; a resource that fully addresses deep conceptual learning, number sense and mathematical fluency is desired.

**Process**
The Math Leadership Team (MLT), an interdepartmental team with representation from all grade levels and roles, was assembled in September 2019. MLT reviewed student performance data, surveyed all elementary teachers, and studied the NCTM publication Principles to Action, concluding that both a math specialist role and new curricular materials were needed. MLT members and colleagues from the Oakland County Math Leadership Team identified candidate publishers and resources, screened against the Standards for Mathematical Practice, the NCTM 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices, and the Michigan Standards for Mathematics. In January 2021 the list was narrowed and select publishers were invited to Troy to demonstrate online features; materials were piloted in January and February. Ninety-five early adopter teachers volunteered to implement Bridges in Mathematics and Number Corner during the 2022-23 school year.

**Early adopter team by grade**
Kindergarten 13, grade 1 22, grade 2 13, grade 3 15, grade 4 16, grade 5 16; total 95. Building totals: Barnard 6, Bemis 6, Costello 9, Hamilton 18, Hill 6, Leonard 17, Martell 12, Morse 6, Troy Union 9, Wass 4, Wattles 2.

**Materials reviewed**
Illustrative Mathematics (not fully available during the 2021-2022 pilot window, delivered through Google Drive, hands-on materials not integrated, now more available from Kendall Hunt); Math Expressions 2013 Edition, the current resource (limited approach to fluency, did not adequately address differentiation, ELD and students with special needs); and Bridges Mathematics including Number Corner, which integrates Math Recovery learning progressions and a Fluency Pathway in Number Corner.

**Recommendation and implementation**
Bridges Math and Number Corner 3rd edition are recommended. All resources will be available on the first day of school for 2023-24. Optional training on Number Corner and Bridges Unit 1 is offered in June; all teachers participate in a kick-off during back-to-school professional development in August 2023 as part of the OneTroy kick-off, followed by job-embedded PD and math specialist support in each building. Principals will build master schedules incorporating 75-90 minutes of math instructional time per day.

**Cost**

|---|---|
| Bridges Mathematics Second Edition | $443,974.31 |
| Updated Number Corner Third Edition Update Package | $48,000.00 |
| Additional Manipulatives & Number Corner Poster Printing | $32,368.47 |
| For organizing workplaces and additional classroom manipulatives | $11,250 |
| Total Cost | $535,592.31 |

The Math Learning Center quote Q-10092, dated 1/27/2023 and expiring 7/26/2023, shows a subtotal of $425,233.00, a shipping fee of $18,741.31, taxes of $0.00 and a net total of $443,974.31.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Document**
"Elementary Mathematics Materials Adoption," March 2023, submitted by Natalie Haezebrouck and Julia Alder, presented at the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of March 7, 2023.

**Rationale**
Troy School District reviews curricular materials every nine years. Since the last curricular adoption, Middle and High-School Health in 2020, the district has updated its philosophy on curricular review: it is not enough to seek new materials, but necessary to take stock of programming as a whole, including instructional practices, intervention, assessment and current data, so that curricular, structural and staffing needs can be aligned. The last elementary math adoption was conducted in 2010. Since then the district has developed a better understanding of the Michigan Math State Standards, better aligned elementary resources have become available, and the National Council of Teachers of Mathematics (NCTM) has continued to develop guidance on best practice. Teachers have been supplementing the current resource with three act tasks, number sense routines and additional materials to address missed opportunities. A new resource that fully addresses deep conceptual learning, number sense and mathematical fluency is desired.

**Program review timeline (Image 1)**
Timeline entries include comprehensive math program development, developing MTSS, and learning and implementing Math Recovery and Tier 1 research in research classrooms; '19 Bridges early adopters, Tier 1 with a focus on conceptual understanding and modeling; '20 COVID, extending ME and math specialists, supporting intensive intervention in math and researching resources for Tier 1; '21 review of TSD data and focus on math mindset, noting a trend of fewer students proficient in math over time; and 22-23.

**Process and selection**
The review began in September 2019 with the Math Leadership Team (MLT), an established interdepartmental team with representation from all grade levels and roles across the system that meets several times per year to plan and monitor progress toward the district vision. MLT reviewed student performance data and administered a survey to all elementary teachers on their experience with mathematics and on the student experience, and engaged in learning from Principles to Action, an NCTM publication. The team collaboratively identified a need for the role of math specialist as well as a need for new curricular materials. MLT members and colleagues from the Oakland County Math Leadership Team helped identify potential publishers, materials and resources. The team used the Standards for Mathematical Practice (Table 2) and the NCTM Effective Math Teaching Practices to focus the evaluation, with the Michigan Standards for Mathematics as the foundation. Image 2 presents the 8 Effective Math Teaching Practices, cited to NCTM (2014), Principles to Actions: Ensuring mathematical success for all. Once selections were narrowed, the Early Adopter Team was invited to vet resources and try lessons in classrooms; all early adopter teachers spent over a year evaluating materials. In January 2021 the resource list was narrowed and select publishers were invited to Troy to demonstrate online features accompanying the text resources. Materials were piloted by instructors in January and February. Ninety-five early adopter teachers volunteered to implement the recommended curriculum, Bridges in Mathematics and Number Corner, during the 2022-23 school year.

**Table 1, Early Adopter Team and Math Specialists**
Building totals: Barnard 6, Bemis 6, Costello 9, Hamilton 18, Hill 6, Leonard 17, Martell 12, Morse 6, Troy Union 9, Wass 4, Wattles 2. Grade-level totals: kindergarten 13, grade 1 22, grade 2 13, grade 3 15, grade 4 16, grade 5 16. Overall total 95.

**Table 3, Materials reviewed**
Illustrative Mathematics: develops conceptual understanding; tasks call for hands-on learning; the resource was not fully available during the 2021-2022 pilot and review timeline; format was in Google Drive and publishers are not developing more supports for elementary IM; it is now more available from Kendall Hunt and through online modules; hands-on materials and mathematical modeling tools are not integrated; online Google Drive modules for teachers require multiple downloads and integration to Schoology. The publisher describes IM K-5 Math as rigorous, problem-based, fully aligned to the standards, available in print and digital, and highly rated by EdReports for meeting all expectations across all three review gateways.

Math Expressions 2013 Edition, the current resource: approaches to teaching mathematical fluency were limited and only partially addressed number sense; the resource was aligned with grade-level content but did not adequately address differentiation, ELD and students with special needs; the online personal math trainer provided extra online practice; hands-on materials and mathematical modeling tools are not integrated; online teacher resources are available but difficult to use. The publisher describes Math Expressions Common Core as focused, coherent, rigorous and integrated with respect to the Common Core State Standards for Mathematics.

Bridges Mathematics including Number Corner: the approach to fluency is part of Number Corner, with multiple monthly opportunities for students to share models and develop numeracy; aligned with grade-level content and integrates research and models supporting Math Recovery learning progressions; tasks build in opportunities for varying levels of sophistication; modeling tools provide additional access for differentiation including ELD, students with special needs and students with high sophistication in math; teacher website and materials available in PDF; online apps and family supports provided through the Math Learning Center website; an active online support blog; and a Fluency Pathway in Number Corner. Number Corner is described as a skill-building program revolving around the classroom calendar providing 15-20 minutes of additional daily instruction.

**Table 4, Features of recommended materials**
Number Sense Focus (Number Corner); Grade Level Alignment (Bridges Units) addressing the Michigan State Standards; Teacher Implementation Supports through the Math Learning Center Educator Website, which requires an educator login and links all resources in PDF format with videos, author advice, articles and blog topics; Parent Communication through Math At Home and Home Learning Resources; Digital Features via Math Learning Center iPad apps and Work Place games with sharable QR codes; Fluency and Practice via Home Connection and Student Workbook, with an option to print or purchase workbooks; an Assessment System with pre-assessments, check points, post-assessments and checklists, both interview-based and written; support for high aptitude, ELD, special needs and DEI through low-floor, high-ceiling tasks; and Implementation and Support including multiple professional learning sessions included with the purchase and partnership with a local facilitator for job-embedded learning.

**Materials recommendation**
Bridges Math and Number Corner 3rd edition are recommended to move forward.

**Implementation plan**
All resources will be available for instruction on the first day of school for the 2023-24 academic year. Teachers will have the option to receive training on Number Corner and Bridges Unit 1 in June, and all teachers will participate in a kick-off during back-to-school professional development in August 2023 in collaboration with math specialists and the Bridges team during the OneTroy kick-off. **Presentation**
"Summer Professional Learning and Summer School Update," Troy School District Board of Education meeting, September 19, 2023.

**Objective**
Building capacity: to provide professional learning opportunities for staff, community, and students throughout OneTroy.

**OneTroy summer learning for staff**
Components listed are summer curriculum development, an administrative kick-off meeting, a Teaching and Learning Team retreat, a cabinet retreat, literacy and mathematics, Pre-K literacy and math, Troy Institutes K-12, and new teacher orientation.

- TSD Literacy Project: over 80 teachers across K-2, 3-5, 6-8 and 9-10, focused on sustaining the workshop method PreK-10 and responsive teaching.
- Preschool Literacy and Math Institute: 50 staff members, teachers and assistants, present for the Summer Institute; the seventh year of summer learning for preschool staff.
- Mathematics Institutes: Math Recovery Institute, Bridges Institute, Middle School Institute.
- Principal retreats and administrative kick-off: reflection on current state and next steps to sustain vision work; review of mission, vision, values and thematic goals; level-specific meetings for bond engagement covering furniture, playgrounds and Smith Design.
- New Teacher Orientation: four days of professional development with each department, a tour of the district, and time with mentor teachers.
- Staff welcome back August learning.

**Summer learning for students**
Program goals are to provide access to all students in need using a flexible delivery model and grant funding sources when possible, with district level teams working with building teams to design for impact at the local level.

Troy Summer Learning Lab: free summer program for students entering grades 6-8, focused on deep learning through the Stanford design thinking process on a project of the students' own choosing. Students began with two weeks of immersion including guest speakers and field trips, then defined problems, ideated and prototyped solutions. Enrollment was 112 students from all four district middle schools, with 21 TSD staff serving as mentors and teachers.

**Title I summer opportunities**
Morse Summer Nights and Morse Reads, a bi-weekly program with literacy or math focus, available at 4 summer nights events plus a new "Morse to You" program that took books and projects to a local mobile home park. Summer Book Clubs: two sessions for 3rd-5th grade students reading below grade level, meeting virtually on TEAMS Tuesday through Thursday, with students given 5 books at their reading level. Herd of Words Writing and Art Camp for rising grade 1-5 students. Title 1 Summer School for grades K-4 performing at or below grade level in math, reading or writing, including experience with the new Bridges math curriculum. Morse Media Center summer reading, open one hour after each summer school session.

**Programs for multilingual learners**
Morse and Troy Union hosted grades K-7. Morse served 96 students and Troy Union served 72 students, each with a 3 hours, 3 days, 5 weeks program staffed by TSD/EDUStaff certified teachers and assistants. Boulan hosted grades 8-12, serving 16 students over 4 hours, 4 days, 5 weeks plus Friday field trips to the DIA, Greenfield Village, the Detroit Zoo, Stony Creek Metro Park and the Troy Public Library, staffed by TSD teachers and a para-educator. Transportation was provided at all sites.

**High school summer school**
In-seat enrollment (physical education): Session 1 had 122 students and Session 2 had 86 students. Virtual enrollment: 1601 classes and 1120 students. Math Honors Bridge Program with live instruction at Boulan Park Middle School: 44 students total. COVID Credit Recovery, at no cost to students: 129 students participating, 248 total courses taken. A closing slide is headed Special Education.

**Presentation**
"Summer Professional Learning and Summer School Update," presented at the Troy School District Board of Education meeting on September 19, 2023.

**Objective**
The stated objective under the heading Building Capacity is to provide professional learning opportunities for staff, community, and students throughout OneTroy.

**OneTroy summer learning components**
The summer learning agenda comprised summer curriculum development, an administrative kick-off meeting, a Teaching and Learning Team retreat, a cabinet retreat, literacy and mathematics work, Pre-K literacy and math, Troy Institutes K-12, and new teacher orientation.

**TSD Literacy Project**
Over 80 teachers participated across the grade bands K-2, 3-5, 6-8 and 9-10. The focus was sustaining the workshop method PreK-10 and responsive teaching.

**Preschool Literacy and Math Institute**
Fifty staff members, including teachers and assistants, were present for the Summer Institute. This was the seventh year of summer learning for preschool staff.

**Mathematics Institutes**
Three institutes were held: the Math Recovery Institute, the Bridges Institute, and the Middle School Institute.

**Principal retreats and administrative kick-off**
Sessions covered reflection on the current state and next steps to sustain vision work, review of mission, vision, values and thematic goals, and level-specific meetings for bond engagement addressing furniture, playgrounds, and Smith Design.

**New teacher orientation**
Four days of professional development with each department, a tour of the district, and time with mentor teachers. A separate slide covers staff welcome back August learning.

**Summer program goals for students**
Provide access to all students in need using a flexible delivery model and grant funding sources when possible. District level teams worked with building teams to design for impact at the local level.

**Troy Summer Learning Lab**
A free summer program for students entering grades 6-8, with a focus on deep learning. Students took part in an enrichment program utilizing the Stanford design thinking process to undertake a project of their own choosing. Students started with two weeks of immersion filled with guest speakers and field trips to help them understand and empathize with various ideas and problems, then continued through better defining problems, ideating and prototyping a solution. The program enrolled 112 students from all four district middle schools, and 21 TSD staff served as mentors and teachers.

**Title I summer opportunities**
Morse Summer Nights and Morse Reads: Morse summer nights is a bi-weekly program to keep families engaged with literacy and math concepts throughout the summer, with each summer night carrying a literacy or math focus including access to text or math games to take home. Morse Reads was available at 4 summer nights events throughout the summer and at a new "Morse to You" program in which Morse staff members took a collection of books and projects to one of the local mobile home parks to reach students who could not travel to the school during the summer.

Summer Book Clubs: two sessions for third through fifth grade students reading below grade level, invited to virtual book clubs Tuesdays through Thursdays following the summer school calendar. Students were given 5 different books at their reading level to read together on TEAMS.

Herd of Words Writing and Art Camp: a writing camp allowing rising grade 1-5 students to participate in the writing process both independently and on club meeting days through their writing journals. Students learned about revision through revising their own painting and applying that to further changes in their writing.

Title 1 Summer School: summer school support for students in grades K-4 performing at or below grade level in math, reading or writing. Literacy and math instruction were the foundations of the program, along with engaging projects and media and physical education enrichment classes. Students received a focus in small group instruction and experience with the district's new Bridges math curriculum.

Morse Media Center Summer Reading: the Morse Media Center was open to all Morse students for one hour after each summer school session, providing access to a large number of book titles and support from the Morse Media Specialist.

**Summer programs for multilingual learners**
Morse and Troy Union hosted grades K-7. Morse served 96 students; Troy Union served 72 students. Both ran 3 hours a day, 3 days a week, for 5 weeks, staffed by TSD/EDUStaff certified teachers and assistants. Multilingual students who received Intensive ELD instruction during the 2022-23 school year were invited, and students focused on acquiring English proficiency through content area topics and leveled readers. Transportation was provided.

Boulan hosted grades 8-12, serving 16 students in a program of 4 hours a day, 4 days a week, for 5 weeks, plus field trips on Fridays, staffed by TSD teachers and a para-educator. Multilingual learners going into Beginner or Intermediate ELD English courses were invited, and students selected to take the class for an English elective credit or for no credit. Friday field trips visited the DIA, Greenfield Village, the Detroit Zoo, Stony Creek Metro Park and the Troy Public Library. Transportation was provided.

**High school summer school opportunities**
In-seat enrollment for physical education: Session 1 enrolled 122 students and Session 2 enrolled 86 students. Virtual enrollment totaled 1601 classes and 1120 students. The Math Honors Bridge Program, with live instruction at Boulan Park Middle School, enrolled 44 students total. COVID Credit Recovery, offered at no cost to students, had 129 students participating with 248 total courses taken. The final slide of the deck is headed Special Education.

Barton Malow Builders' Proposal for Construction Services addresses the Troy School District 2022 Bond Program. The cover page carries the date July 8, 2021, while every page footer and the staffing plan are dated July 8, 2022 (the staffing plan header reads Date: 7/8/22). The table of contents lists Section 1 Project Approach Narrative, Section 2 Relevant Firm Experience, Section 3 Project Organizational Chart and Team Resumes, Section 4 Staffing Plan, and Section 5 Utilizing BIM and VDC.

SECTION 1: PROJECT APPROACH NARRATIVE
Barton Malow opens by citing extensive knowledge of school construction and the fact that its team spent over 30 successful years working in the Troy School District, implementing improvements at all district facilities including 12 elementary, 4 middle and 4 high schools, plus a new preschool building, the Early Childhood Center, completed in 2019. The firm commits to involvement in all phases from pre-construction and design through close out, walking each project during design to identify existing conditions and minimize change orders and schedule delays, and meeting with the district's administrative team and building staff before work begins to discuss schedule and phasing.

Design phase: Barton Malow says it takes a leadership role rather than merely assisting, using in-house estimators, architects and engineers to manage the design process. It will establish a design phase schedule tied to bid dates, conduct design team meetings with published minutes, develop a set of Design Standards distributed to all Design Professionals, and perform constructability reviews. The design process is described in three major areas: Schematic Design, Design Development and Construction Documents. The Schematic Design Estimate provides more detail than the original Bond Application and is updated through Design Development, after which Barton Malow develops a very detailed estimate and creates a Cost Control Log documenting value engineering opportunities and possible bid alternates; the log continues to be updated during the Construction Document Phase. Barton Malow's Education group works exclusively with K-12 school districts.

Cost control and value engineering: value engineering is described as a team process evaluating all expenditures relating to construction, maintenance, operation and replacement, balancing performance and quality against initial and life-cycle costs, supported by in-house historical cost data and knowledge of the local market. The firm contrasts its continuous "design to a cost" methodology with traditional end-of-phase estimating.

Minimizing interruptions and safety: the narrative addresses renovating occupied facilities, developing a tentative work plan for administration approval and communicating it to staff, community and contractors, with zero tolerance for anyone failing to work within the plan. A Safety Manager conducts routine in-depth inspections, ensures compliance with Barton Malow safety policies and MIOSHA standards, and participates in MIOSHA inspections. Safety principles listed include zero tolerance for unsafe acts, a best-in-class safety culture with education, mentoring, empowerment and accountability, authority to STOP the job on any worker safety concern, working with subcontractors that share the firm's safety pursuit, and managing every incident to reduce impact on performance.

Bid packaging and technology: bid packages are developed early with the project divided into area and functional phases, tailored to involve local businesses, with long-lead-time items bid first and pre-purchase packages suggested where applicable. Prospective bidders go through a stringent prequalification process. Barton Malow describes itself as the first to market to harness e-bidding technology, livestream bid openings and cloud-based plan rooms, noting it solicited bids nearly every day of the State of Michigan "Stay Home/Stay Safe" executive order. The e-bidding workflow steps listed are bid advertisement, invitation to bid, prequalification, notification and distribution, document distribution, creation of the bid form, addenda, submission of bid security, submission of the bid, bid tabulation and audit trail. Bidder participation over the last 12 months is reported as 32 school districts, 157 unique projects, 68,856 solicitations to bids, 21,732 views, 4,089 bids received, and 5.20 bids per category.

Workforce development: the Barton Malow Boot Camp, created in 2016, is a 6-week paid work experience program for area residents between the ages of 18 and 24. The 120-hour program covers construction industry history and culture, financial literacy, OSHA and soft skills training, apprentice career paths, and on-the-job training in concrete and heavy civil work. Each boot camper is assigned a Barton Malow mentor, a skilled tradesperson on the project site, who spends 2 days per week with participants. Recruiting sources include the Barton Malow workforce database, career fairs, career and technical centers, vocational schools, technical colleges, building trade unions, employment service providers and labor management groups.

Procurement and change management: using the software system Pype, teams create a submittal register as soon as construction documents are issued, issue it with the bid documents, request long lead time information at post bid, and maintain a long lead register reviewed at each job progress meeting. Change management uses a disciplined four-stage approach; change status is tracked as Pending, Approved, or Approximate, and change issues move through four mechanisms: Potential Change Order (PCO), Change Order Request (COR), Prime Contract Change Order (PCCO) and Subcontractor Change Order (SCCO), all entered and tracked in the SAP cost management system, which tracks dollars, quantities, man-hours and schedule. Barton Malow states it places no mark-up on change orders and does not rely on outside agencies to validate change requests. Contractors that fail to comply may receive written notification, notice of contractual default and/or withholding of payment, with a jointly drafted corrective action plan. All final change orders are to be approved, written and billed by subcontractors within 90 days of substantial completion.

Punchlist, closeout and activation: pre-punchlists with required correction dates are generated before the design team's official punchlist. Close-out timelines are set for each bid package, with final close-out typically required within 30 days from completion of all punchlist items; weekly close-out meetings begin at the 90% completion mark. Digital turnover of closeout documents is provided through AutoDesk Build. The Activation Phase covers start-up and testing of systems, training of building engineers and maintenance staff, final completion and occupancy, turnover of keys, manuals, record drawings and maintenance stocks, and securing guarantees, affidavits, releases, bonds and waivers. Final billings include all change orders issued, approved and included no later than 90 days after substantial completion.

PARTIES AND DATE
Fielding International (460 Hilton Road, Ferndale, Michigan 48220; fieldingintl.com; offices listed as Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Rhode Island and Singapore) submitted an Education Design Services proposal dated July 15, 2022 to Ms. Christine DiPalato, Assistant Superintendent, Troy School District, 440 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. SCOPE
The engagement supports Troy School District as it explores a new vision for middle school teaching and learning, auditing staff and student perceptions, designing a new learning ecosystem concept including physical space concepts, and transitioning into a process-consulting phase alongside District leadership.

PHASE 1: PRE-DISCOVERY AND FRAMING

Fielding International submitted a proposal for Education Design Services to the Troy School District. The cover letter is dated July 15, 2022 and addressed to Ms. Christine DiPalato, Assistant Superintendent, Troy School District, 440 Livernois, Troy, MI 48098. Fielding's letterhead reads "Designing schools where learners Thrive," 460 Hilton Road, Ferndale, Michigan 48220 USA, fieldingintl.com, with locations listed as Maryland, Michigan, Minnesota, Rhode Island and Singapore. Interior pages carry the running head "Troy School District Proposal June 20, 2022." The proposal closes with a signature from Michael Posthumus, Education Design Principal (mike.posthumus@fieldingintl.com), and an acceptance block for signature, name/title and date. Fielding states that upon signed acceptance it can begin work immediately.

PURPOSE
The engagement supports Troy School District as it explores a new vision for what middle school teaching and learning might look like now and in the future. Based on previous conversations, Fielding outlines a scope facilitating engagement and planning to form a vision representing a shift in teaching and learning practice priorities better aligned with the District's objectives for strong interdisciplinary programming that also supports student wellness and social-emotional learning. The work begins with auditing staff and student perceptions of the school experience, uses those insights to explore and design ways to transform the school experience with a new learning ecosystem concept including physical space concepts, and finally transitions into a process-consulting phase in which Fielding's educators and designers work alongside District leadership and key staff for detailed planning, implementation and sustaining success. The letter frames the opportunity as creating a flexible and innovative school program and learning environments centered on what is meaningful and relevant to young people, arguing that the existing model of education no longer meets the diverse needs of students.

PHASE 1: PRE-DISCOVERY AND FRAMING
This phase gathers contextual information to understand the current state of Troy School District middle school programs and aspirations for a re-imagined future. It begins with meetings and data collection. The Fielding Team will host one-on-one 30-minute virtual meetings with a selection of school leaders to hear individual aspirations. Ideal interview candidates are the building leaders at the four middle schools in Troy, along with District leaders engaged in the rest of the process. Listed components are a Pre-Discovery kick-off meeting, asynchronous data collection and information gathering, visioning and prioritization workshops, and virtual meetings with focused 1:1 interviews with District leaders. The stated objective is to collect data and observations to complete a Teaching and Learning Audit Discovery Report serving as the foundation for future work. Site visits and proposed activities are scheduled for August and include virtual kick-off and progress/status meetings, data collection through surveys and asynchronous resource gathering, and focus group and individual interviews.

PHASE 2: PROGRAM AND ENVIRONMENT DISCOVERY
The main component is a multi-day immersive site visit by Fielding International team members, during which the team completes structured observations of the middle school experience and conducts informal interviews with students, teachers and staff to capture quantitative and qualitative data on how teaching and learning experiences are delivered, and to identify misalignments between the aspirations of District and school leaders, physical learning environments, and the actual student experience. The team debriefs immediate findings with the District at the end of the visit. Fielding will also introduce school models demonstrating future-ready physical school designs and programmatic approaches to middle years learning; a school site visit from Troy to another school implementing innovative approaches is described as optional and highly recommended.

The Phase Two deliverable is the Teaching, Learning, and Future Facilities Discovery Report, synthesizing information gathered during Program and Environment Discovery, highlighting the core pillars of the future of Troy School District, misalignments between current practice and future aspirations, and priority areas of growth. The report relies on first-hand data including interviews and observations from the site visits and documents middle school learning models existing in other schools or programs. A virtual Discovery Report presentation to a selected "School Design Team" and other desired stakeholders takes place once the report is complete, ending phase two.

Phase 2 components are listed as Discovery kick-off, visioning, multi-day on-site Discovery Visit, and Discovery Report Presentation. Site visits and proposed activities are scheduled for September through October and include leadership kickoff, a visioning workshop, student/staff/leadership focus groups and interviews, middle school program and facility observations, school model exemplar presentations and workshops, and Fielding team data synthesis. Report development is September-October with virtual report delivery in October.

PHASE 3: RE-IMAGINING SCHOOL, A DEEP DIVE
Following Discovery, Fielding facilitates a process helping students, staff and community members re-imagine the learning experience in Troy School District middle school programs. Two components are building a shared understanding of the problems and opportunities facing the District and its students, followed by conceptually re-designing the school experience. The Teaching, Learning, and Future Facilities Discovery Report serves as the foundational document.

Common Understanding consists of workshops leading the School Design Team and potentially an expanded stakeholder group through learning experiences about Students in the 21st Century and post-COVID, reviewing research on the science of adolescent learning, the experiences and aspirations of today's youth, and place-based community needs, using models and case studies of innovative school programs. Design consists of constructive workshops to create a new vision for school, including identifying how mission and culture may need to change, exploring new teaching and learning strategies, empowering students and teachers with agency, using partnerships and networks, and restructuring time, space and technology. Both programs and physical learning environments are addressed.

The Phase Three deliverable is the Learning Ecosystem Concept Design, a narrative describing ideal conditions for learning in a re-imagined Troy School District school, with embedded images and precedent examples of schools already implementing components of the vision.

Phase 3 is structured as 2 Building Common Understanding workshop days, 3 Design Workshop days, and 7 remote planning and reporting sessions. Site visits and proposed activities run October through December. Session 1 covers "Who are the Students of the 21st Century?" (Learn/Reflect Workshop) and Youth Aspirations and Experiences (Design/Produce Workshop). Session 2 covers the Science of Adolescent Learning and Teaching and Learning in the 21st Century. Session 3 covers Establishing the Framework for a New School Mission and Culture and Exploring Alignment between Mission, Culture, Programs, and Physical Space. Session 4 covers Cultivating Student and Staff Agency and Creating the Conditions for Engagement, and Partnerships and Networks to Support a new Mission and Culture. Session 5 covers Re-imagining the Use of Time, Space and Technology and Final Reflections and Summary of the Work. Learning Ecosystem Concept refinement occurs November-December with the report delivered in December.

FUTURE OPPORTUNITIES: PREPARING FOR IMPLEMENTATION AND CHANGE LEADERSHIP
After the design phases, an additional phase supports the District's transition into new teaching and learning models. Fielding would use "Process Consulting," quoting the Society for Process Consulting's description of an iterative form of humble inquiry and guidance in which the consultant works alongside the client to co-create solutions, advancing the client's growth and learning through an authentic discovery process and addressing social, relational, cultural and psychological dynamics of change. Fielding notes that as Troy School District prepares to invest millions in its new facilities, the opportunity to plan for new instructional methodologies is ideal.

Key focus areas listed for Phase 4 are clarifying a future instructional vision, student assessment in the future, restructuring time/space/technology systems, finding coherence and cascading communications about change, building leadership capacity for change, re-imagining the successful middle school team, identifying and supporting early adopters, scaling adoption and improving practice, and sustaining success. Proposed timing is January 2023 through June 2023 and beyond. Winter 2023 covers instructional vision, leadership coherence, cascading communications, student assessment and restructuring systems, with 3-4 workshop days plus remote support, producing described and diagrammed aspirations, a new vision of assessment and operational systems, and formalized internal communication language and plans. Spring 2023 covers building leadership capacity for change, the middle school team, identifying early adopters and planning for professional learning, with 2-3 workshop days plus remote support, producing established norms for an adaptive change mindset with indicators of success, teams beginning pathfinder prototypes, a profile of a successful future middle school team, a detailed strategy for supporting early adopters and change agents, and a drafted professional learning strategy. Summer 2023 covers scaling adoption, improving practice and sustaining success, with 1-2 workshop days plus remote support, producing formalized short-term and long-term educator onboarding methods, a formal continuous improvement and success/failure-sharing strategy, a review of cascading communication and planning for what's next, and finalization of the Teaching, Learning, and Leading for the Future Guidebook.

ADDITIONAL SERVICES: ARCHITECTURAL DESIGN
Fielding states it is also an architecture design firm and can work alongside the District's local architect during Programming, Schematic Design and Design Development to design fully aligned educational facilities. In Michigan, Fielding reports working in this capacity, teamed with a local architect, with Ann Arbor Public Schools and Portage Public Schools. The paragraph introducing this service contains an apparent carryover reference to "the opportunity in front of Holly Area Schools."

FORMAT AND TIMELINE
In addition to face-to-face workshops, select web-based meetings are advised to reduce cost and increase work consistency; remote support often takes the form of bi-weekly team meetings adjusted to the District's needs.

PROFESSIONAL FEES AND EXPENSES
Phase 1 Pre-Discovery covers surveys, data collection, 1:1 interviews, and a start-up and visioning meeting (1-day visit/workshop), with no separate fee figure printed. Phase 2 Discovery is $34,500 and covers a 3-4 day onsite Discovery Visit, interviews, focus groups and development of the Teaching, Learning, and Facilities Discovery Report. Phase 3 Re-Imagining Middle School, A Deep Dive is $54,600 and covers Common Understanding Workshops plus synthesis (one 2-day onsite visit), Design Workshops plus synthesis (one 3-day onsite visit), and remote planning and support with Learning Ecosystem Concept development for facilities and program. Architectural and design services for new or re-imagined facilities and Preparing for Implementation and Change Leadership are listed as future opportunities not included in the proposal. Total cost for Learning Design Services is $89,100. Reimbursable travel expenses are not-to-exceed $20,000, covering airfare, lodging and meals for up to three to four Learning Designers for on-site visits, some traveling from out of state.

TERMS
Invoices will be sent on a monthly basis for a percentage of the work completed by phase, with payment due within 15 days. All travel expenses are reimbursed at cost without markup. Any printing or materials needed for on-site workshops are reimbursed at cost without markup, and may already be on hand at the school (easel paper, markers, sticky notes).
