https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
**Memorandum header**
TO: MJ Policy Service Clients. FROM: MJ School Policy Services. DATE: March 9, 2026. RE: Policy Manual and Administrative Regulations Update - March 2026. The memo transmits substantive updates to all MJ School Policy Services policy and administrative regulations manuals. Proposed revisions are presented by section with a specific update number for ease of reference, along with a narrative providing the basis for the contemplated modification. All updates are numbered individually (i.e., Update 22.01). Additions to policy or administrative regulation language are shown in red; deletions are shown in blue; areas highlighted in yellow require additional information from the district to complete the update. Because each district manual is unique and modified consistent with district priority and prerogative, recommended modifications may already be contained in completed manuals. Questions about how the revisions fit existing manuals go to Policy@MillerJohnson.com, and districts behind on policy updates are urged to contact the office for compliance support.

**Sections with no recommended policy updates**
Introduction - 0000 Series, Bylaws - 1000 Series, and Personnel - 4000 Series each carry the statement that there are no recommended policy updates.

**Update 22.01 - Policy 2003, Education Records (Students - 2000 Series)**
The fiscal year 2026 State School Aid Act includes MCL 388.1764k, which provides additional requirements for school districts and intermediate school districts regarding student surveys. Adoption of the revisions is recommended to ensure compliance with Section 164k. Miller Johnson previously issued guidance titled "New Compliance Requirements Under Section 164k - State School Aid Act (FY 2025-2026)" and "Additional Guidance on Section 164k Compliance - District Surveys & Curriculum Requirements."

The revised Student Surveys language states that, consistent with applicable law, parents may inspect all materials used for any student survey, analysis, or evaluation conducted by the School District in connection with a program funded by the United States Department of Education. Without parental consent, the district will not require a student to participate in such a survey, analysis, or evaluation that reveals or is intended to reveal information concerning the student or the student's parents' political or religious affiliations, beliefs, or practices; mental or psychological problems; sexual behavior or attitudes; illegal, anti-social, self-incriminating, or demeaning behavior; critical appraisals of other individuals with whom the student or the student's parents have close family relationships; legally recognized privileged or analogous relationships such as those with lawyers, physicians, and ministers; or income, other than when required by law to determine eligibility for programs or financial assistance.

New language adds that, in compliance with MCL 388.1764k, the School District will ensure that questions and results of District-wide surveys, state or federally mandated surveys, and surveys distributed to all students in a grade level are made available to the public by being posted on the District's website, and that parents will be notified of these survey questions and results. The District will comply with the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act ("FERPA") before releasing any survey results.

**Update 22.02 - Policy 2004, Extracurricular Activities (Students - 2000 Series)**
This update applies to school districts that are members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association ("MHSAA"). The MHSAA approved an expansion of its personal branding activities ("PBA") / name, image, or likeness ("NIL") rule - Regulation I, Section 11 C - Amateur Status/Awards on January 23, 2026. Effective immediately, a student may earn compensation through their PBA (use of their NIL), such as promoting or endorsing a product or service, regardless of whether the PBA relates to athletics. Because students may now engage in PBA/NIL agreements, the additional policy language is intended to prohibit students from entering agreements that violate Board Policy and/or the Student Code of Conduct and to provide additional protections for the school district.

The Athletics section of the policy states that the Superintendent, in consultation with the Board and selected School District personnel, will develop and administer a robust program of interscholastic athletics, adhering at all times to the principle that participants are students first and athletes second. In addition to MHSAA regulations and limitations, the School District prohibits students from engaging in personal branding activities / name, image, or likeness agreements that violate Board Policy or the Student Code of Conduct, and students may be disciplined under Board Policy and/or the Student Code of Conduct for such violations. PBA/NIL activities shall not occur during school hours or events or on School District property unless prior written approval is provided by the Superintendent.

**Update 22.03 - Policy 2006, Behavior (Students - 2000 Series)**
Governor Whitmer signed House Bill 4141 and Senate Bill 495 on February 10, 2026. Collectively, these amend the Revised School Code, specifically MCL 380.1303a, to require a school district's board of education to adopt a policy prohibiting students from using a wireless communications device during instructional time, effective for the 2026-27 school year. The update revises Miller Johnson's existing policy to comply with MCL 380.1303a and to use language consistent with the statute. Miller Johnson's related guidance is titled "New Law Prohibits Students from Using Wireless Communication Devices - Effective 2026-2027 School Year."

The retitled Wireless Communication Devices section (replacing "Personal Electronic Devices") reserves the district's right to prohibit possession or use of wireless communication devices on district property or at district-related functions. "Wireless communication device" is defined as an electronic device capable of, but not limited to, text messaging, voice communication, entertainment, navigation, accessing the internet, sending and receiving photos and videos, or producing email, replacing the prior definition of a privately owned device used for audio, video, or text communications including cell phones, personal laptops, smartwatches, smart glasses, and other wireless device connections. "Instructional time" means time that any student is assigned to engage in learning and curricular activities by instructional staff. "School grounds" means a building, playing field, or property used for school purposes to impart instruction to students or used for functions and events sponsored by a school. The Superintendent may develop administrative regulations consistent with the policy.

Under the Prohibition of Wireless Communication Devices heading (replacing "Away-for-the-Day Requirements"), and in accordance with MCL 380.1303a, students are prohibited from using wireless communication devices on school grounds unless required by law. The prohibition is enforced by instructional staff through monitoring students during instructional time and the school day. Devices must be turned off and kept out of sight in lockers or cubbies.

Exemptions permitted by law allow students to use a wireless communication device during instructional time and the school day for medically necessary devices; district owned or issued devices under building staff discretion; devices used for instructional purposes with building staff discretion; devices used for special education programming and/or as an accommodation under a Section 504 Plan, Individualized Education Program, or the Americans with Disabilities Act; devices used for lesson-specific academic assignments at building staff discretion; and devices used in emergency situations as described in the School District's Emergency Operations Plan, where applicable per the plan, pursuant to MCL 380.1308b.

Under Recording and Broadcast, students may not use wireless communication devices to broadcast or record audio, images, or video of any student, staff member, or other person in the school or while attending a school-related activity unless the student has received permission from the person or persons to be broadcast or recorded. The prohibition does not apply to curricular or extra-curricular activities for which personal recording is generally permitted, such as athletic events and arts performances.

**Update 22.04 - Policy 3003, Instruction (Curriculum and Instruction - 3000 Series)**
The fiscal year 2026 State School Aid Act includes MCL 388.1764k, which provides additional requirements for school districts and intermediate school districts when an evidence-based curriculum for grades K-5 is not used per MCL 380.1280f. Adoption of the revisions is recommended for Section 164k compliance, with reference again to the Miller Johnson guidance documents "New Compliance Requirements Under Section 164k - State School Aid Act (FY 2025-2026)" and "Additional Guidance on Section 164k Compliance - District Surveys & Curriculum Requirements." The revised policy states that, to the extent feasible, student instruction will be delivered using research-based and peer-reviewed instructional methodologies, and that in compliance with MCL 388.1764k the School District will notify parents if the District uses a curriculum not on the state's evidence-based list per MCL 380.1280f for grades K-5 by September 30, 2026. The Superintendent may develop regulations consistent with the policy.

**Update 22.05 - Policy 5003, Purchasing (Business - 5000 Series)**
This revision corrects a minor spelling/grammatical error. Under State/Federal Grants and Awards, the Superintendent will promulgate legally compliant administrative regulations concerning expenditures of funds received through state/federal grants and awards, and shall establish and maintain effective internal control over financial grants and awards providing reasonable assurance that the program and funds are managed in compliance with applicable statutes (correcting "statuses"), regulations, and the terms and conditions of the awards.

**Update 22.06 - Policy 6013, Facility Dog (Facilities and Operations - 6000 Series)**
The update provides clarity to the definition of a "facility dog," and the policy should be used for school district owned dogs. The revised text defines facility dogs as School District owned dogs trained to work within school facilities and at school events with children with a variety of academic, social, and emotional needs. The Superintendent will promulgate an administrative regulation applicable to the use of Facility Dogs on School District property.

**Update 22.07 - Policy 7001, Goal (School and Community Relations - 7000 Series)**
The update adds a Record Retention section. The School District will retain all public records in accordance with the Michigan Department of Technology, Management & Budget retention schedule for school districts. Unless the District is in receipt of a litigation hold or similar notice, records may be disposed of after the retention period in accordance with the state schedule.

**Update 22.08 - Policy 7008, Advertising (School and Community Relations - 7000 Series)**
The revision provides school districts more flexibility in preparing regulations to consider accepting advertisements generally. No advertising may be distributed, posted, or displayed on or within any District-owned property without the written consent of the Superintendent. The Superintendent shall prepare regulations addressing the circumstances under which the District would consider accepting advertisements, including but not limited to commercial advertisements.

**Update 22.09 - Policy 8003, Website and Digital Content Accessibility (General Policies - 8000 Series)**
The policy title changes from "Web" to "Website and Digital Content Accessibility." The revisions ensure compliance with the WCAG 2.1 Level AA ("WCAG") standard per recently updated requirements of the U.S. Department of Justice, with Miller Johnson guidance titled "New ADA Rules for District Websites & Apps." Under General, the School District is committed to ensuring that its website, online platforms, and mobile applications are accessible for students, parents, employees and members of the public. All pages on the District's website, online platforms, and mobile applications will conform to the W3C WAI's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) 2.1, Level AA conformance, or any updated equivalent standard. The School District will continue to evaluate and test future releases and updates of its website, online platforms, and mobile applications and remains committed to maintaining ongoing compliance and serving the widest possible audience. To support this commitment, the District will conduct periodic accessibility audits of its website, online platforms, and mobile applications.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC issued this draft Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District on October 5, 2021, communicating results of its audit of the district's financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2021 plus informational items on Michigan school finance. The auditors report no disagreements with management, no significant difficulties, and no new accounting policies, and identify the district's share of MPSERS net liabilities, estimated at $308,094,061 for pension and $48,088,931 for OPEB, as the most sensitive estimates. General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000, lifting fund balance to approximately $32,700,000, or 19.88 percent of expenditures.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Document.** Draft "Report to the Board of Education," Troy School District, June 30, 2021, prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC and dated October 5, 2021. Signed by Donna Hanson, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Manager). Organized as Results of the Audit (pages 1-6) and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office for their assistance.

**Audit scope and communications.** The engagement letter is dated June 2, 2021; planning matters were discussed with the board on August 13, 2021. The audit was conducted under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards and Government Auditing Standards, with a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 on internal control over financial reporting and compliance. A federal program audit under 2 CFR Part 200 was also completed, reported separately on October 5, 2021. Management representations are contained in a letter dated October 5, 2021.

**Significant audit findings.** No new accounting policies were adopted and no existing policies changed during 2021. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance; none were recorded in a different period than they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the district's shares of the MPSERS net pension and OPEB liabilities under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75, estimated at $308,094,061 and $48,088,931 respectively as of June 30, 2021, based on Office of Retirement Services data. Disclosures were judged neutral, consistent, and clear. Management corrected all identified immaterial misstatements. There were no disagreements with management and no difficulties in performing the audit.

**State aid background.** The May 2020 Revenue Estimating Conference suggested proration of roughly $685 per pupil; by the August 2020 conference the actual proration for 2019-2020 was $175 per pupil. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at 2019-2020 levels, with a target foundation of $8,529, a minimum of $8,111, and a one-time $65 per pupil payment not folded into the formula. A one-year "super blend" pupil count weighted the 2019-2020 count at 75 percent and the 2020-2021 count at 25 percent. For 2021-2022 the target foundation rises to $8,700 per pupil, with a $171 per pupil increase for districts already at or above target; for hold harmless districts such as Troy the increase is expected as $115 of foundation allowance plus $56 of Section 20m funding. Counts return to 90 percent fall / 10 percent spring weighting.

**Retirement and federal relief figures.**

| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Section 147a1 | $1,070,809 |
| Section 147a2 | $1,838,621 |
| Section 147c1 | $11,658,202 |
| Section 147e | $206,687 |
| Coronavirus Relief Fund available | $4,588,959 |
| ESSER I award | $246,411 |
| ESSER II estimate | $843,258 |
| ESSER III estimate | $1,893,840 |
| ESSER II state equalization payment | $5,036,199 |

The 2020-2021 MPSERS contribution rate ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent, and from 20.96 to 28.21 percent net of state support; total contributions represent about 42 percent of covered payroll with roughly 28 percent borne net by the district. For 2022 the overall rate is expected to rise to 43 percent from 42 percent with the net share near 28 percent. CRF distributions were approximately $362 per pupil; the award was fully expended in fiscal 2021. The ESSER II funding floor was $450 per pupil and the ESSER III floor $1,093 per student, the latter now questioned by the federal government.

**MPSERS plan status.** At September 30, 2020 the plan's net pension liability was approximately $35 billion, up from $33.8 billion at September 30, 2019, an increase of about 3.5 percent. The net OPEB liability was approximately $5.4 billion, down from $7.3 billion, a decrease of about 26 percent, reflecting a health care cost trend rate reduction from 7.5 percent to 7.0 percent and favorable plan experience.

**Fund balance.** General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000 in 2020-2021, increasing General Fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The statewide average at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent of expenditures, equal to about eight weeks of operations; Troy's percentage is 19.88 percent, about 10.3 weeks.

**Forward-looking items.** Recommendations cover grants management risk assessment, budgeting for nonrecurring federal aid with program end dates laddered through 2024, cybersecurity (the "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act" introduced in the House in June 2021 would appropriate $10M yearly for two years), IT assessment, GASB Statement No. 87 on leases effective for the June 30, 2022 statements, SAS No. 134 changing the auditor's report for June 30, 2022, and the GASB financial reporting model exposure draft with phased adoption at June 30, 2025 for districts with revenue over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under. The next Revenue Estimating Conference is set for January 2022.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Plante & Moran, PLLC prepared this draft "Report to the Board of Education" for Troy School District covering the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021. The transmittal letter and each substantive letter within it are dated October 5, 2021. The report is divided into Results of the Audit (pages 1-6) and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The firm extends thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to normal daily activities. The letter is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Manager.

**Responsibility and scope.** As stated in the engagement letter dated June 2, 2021, the auditor's responsibility under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with board oversight are fairly presented in all material respects in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement and does not relieve the board or management of their responsibilities. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on internal control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, under which the firm must communicate matters involving compliance with laws, regulations, contracts and grant agreements, instances of error or fraud, illegal acts applicable to government agencies, and significant deficiencies in internal control; a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 was issued on internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance. The audit followed the planned scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting of August 13, 2021.

**Significant audit findings.** Management is responsible for the selection and use of accounting policies, which are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2021. No transactions were entered into for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions were recognized in a period different from when they occurred. The most sensitive accounting estimates were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75. As of June 30, 2021 those estimates were $308,094,061 for pension and $48,088,931 for OPEB, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures are described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, management corrected all immaterial misstatements identified, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants. A federal program audit required by 2 CFR Part 200 was completed, with results reported separately on October 5, 2021. Management representations are included in a letter dated October 5, 2021. The firm read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and found nothing materially inconsistent with the financial statements. The information is intended solely for the Board of Education and management.

**Informational items - state aid background.** The report frames the period as "A Year Like No Other" and traces the move "From 18 Months of Financial Uncertainty to Projected Stability." Before the pandemic, state resources were stable and predictable. In spring 2020 substantial proration of state aid was feared, prompting two Revenue Estimating Conferences, the scheduled May 2020 conference and an additional August 2020 conference. The May conference suggested proration estimated at $685 per pupil, and many districts adopted final 2020 budget amendments on that basis; by August 2020 the actual proration for the 2019-2020 fiscal year was set at $175 per pupil. Beginning in March 2020 the federal government provided several waves of assistance with evolving spending requirements, though COVID-19 relief funds ultimately allowed more flexibility than traditional federal grants. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at the 2019-2020 level, no prorations were required, and a $65 one-time per pupil payment was provided; the State also supplemented districts that did not reach a minimum per pupil threshold from the Educational Stabilization Fund. For 2021-2022 all schools move to a target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap between base and target, and all districts including hold harmless districts receive at least a $171 per pupil increase, with added funding for special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and the Great Start Readiness Program (GSRP), reflecting School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations.

**2021 funding implications for Troy.** Because of pandemic-related concerns, 2020-2021 foundation levels were maintained at 2019-2020 levels: the target foundation allowance (formerly the basic foundation allowance) was $8,529 and the minimum foundation allowance remained $8,111, with the one-time $65 per pupil payment excluded from the formula and not retained for 2021-2022. For 2020-2021 a one-year "super blend" pupil count combined the 2019-2020 count weighted at 75 percent with the 2020-2021 count weighted at 25 percent, multiplied by the foundation allowance per pupil to determine total foundation funding.

**MPSERS cost support.** Contributions are computed as a percentage of payroll and the required rate continues to increase. The estimated 2020-2021 contribution rate ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent, and the rate net of state funding support paid directly by the employer ranged from 20.96 to 28.21 percent. State support flows through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e of the State Aid Act. Troy received $1,070,809 in 147a1, $1,838,621 in 147a2, $11,658,202 in 147c1, and $206,687 of 147e. Total retirement contributions represent approximately 42 percent of covered payroll recognized as expenditure, with the district responsible for approximately a 28 percent net contribution.

**Coronavirus Relief Fund and other federal funding.** In summer 2020 approximately $362 per pupil was provided to districts by the Michigan Department of Education through summer state aid payments; the total available to Troy was $4,588,959. Because the funding was not approved until July 2020, revenue recognition was deferred to fiscal year 2021, and for the year ended June 30, 2021 the district fully expended the award and recognized the related federal revenue. Two key funding sources are the Education Stabilization Fund (ESF), whose principal programs are the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) Fund and the Governor's Education Emergency Relief (GEER) Fund, and the Coronavirus Relief Fund (CRF), which includes the $362 per pupil passed through by MDE plus amounts from other nonfederal entities. Reimbursement claims could reach back to costs incurred as early as March 2020.

**ESSER awards.** ESSER grants come in three waves: ESSER I, ESSER II (divided between phase 1 and phase 2), and ESSER III. The district's ESSER I award was $246,411; ESSER II and III estimates are $843,258 and $1,893,840 respectively. ESSER I revenue could be recognized in fiscal 2021 to the extent allowable expenditures were incurred. Phase 1 ESSER II revenue could be recognized in fiscal 2021 only if a grant award letter was received by June 30, 2021; many districts did not receive theirs, deferring recognition to fiscal 2022. Phase 2 of ESSER II and ESSER III awards become available in fiscal 2022. ESSER allocations use the Title I model based on economically disadvantaged demographics, so the Legislature and governor established a floor of $450 per pupil for ESSER II with state equalization payments. Based on its ESSER II level, Troy qualified for an equalization payment of $5,036,199, received over the May through August 2021 state aid payments; the district recognized a portion as fiscal 2021 revenue and will recognize the remainder in fiscal 2022. For ESSER III the state set a funding floor of $1,093 per student, but the federal government is now questioning the legality of that state-funded equalization payment.

**2022 funding implications.** The May 2021 Revenue Estimating Conference was optimistic for 2022, 2023, and 2024, projecting the School Aid Fund to close the State's 2021 fiscal year with a fund balance. For 2021-2022 all districts move to the target foundation of $8,700 per pupil; districts already at target receive a $171 per pupil increase from the former target of $8,529, and for hold harmless districts such as Troy the $171 arrives as a $115 per pupil foundation increase plus $56 per pupil of Section 20m funding. Pupil counts revert to the pre-2021 method for 2021-2022, weighted 90 percent fall count and 10 percent spring count. Significant summer 2021 resources supported summer school, credit recovery, and before- and after-school programming through ESSER II plus state aid for innovative summer programming. For 2021-2022 the overall MPSERS contribution rate is expected to increase to 43 percent from 42 percent with the net cost to the district approximating 28 percent.

**Looking forward.** The May 2021 conference projected a 2021 surplus carrying into 2022 with surpluses expected in 2023 and 2024. Factors to monitor include the economic bounce back, the tail-off of federal stimulus over the next two years, the success of returning to in-class instruction, learning loss, enrollment changes, personnel shortages, staffing cost increases, and retirement system cost trends. The next Revenue Estimating Conference will occur in January 2022.

**Grants management and budgeting.** Pandemic programs such as ESSER, GEER, and CRF have increased workload and grants management risk across superintendents and leadership, board members, the business office, staff, information technology, support services, procurement, and facilities. The firm suggests performing a risk assessment of key processes and controls in fiscal 2022. Federal funds carry program end dates laddered through 2024 and are nonrecurring, so recurring uses will require redirecting other revenue or discontinuing programs. Recommended budget practices include multiyear revenue forecasting, monitoring pupil counts, separating recurring contractual payroll costs from variable payroll costs funded by pandemic resources, and budgeting one-time uses of federal and state assistance.

**MPSERS plan net liabilities.** The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2020 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $35 billion, an increase from $33.8 billion at September 30, 2019, about 3.5 percent, driven primarily by less favorable actuarial experience than assumed. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $5.4 billion at September 30, 2020, down from $7.3 billion at September 30, 2019, a decrease of approximately 26 percent, reflecting a reduction in the health care cost trend rate from 7.5 percent to 7.0 percent and favorable experience from lower than projected health benefit costs.

**Fund balance.** During 2020-2021 the district's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000, increasing General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent of expenditures, equal to about an eight-week operating period; the School District's fund balance percentage is 19.88 percent and equals approximately 10.3 weeks of operation. Rising CPI and decisions about spending COVID-19 relief funds are cited as pressures on 2021-2022 fund balance.

**Cybersecurity and IT.** Education remains a top ransomware target. The "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act" was introduced in the House in June 2021 and would appropriate $10M yearly for two years to improve district cybersecurity. The letter warns that weak passwords such as "August2021" are easily guessed, raises questions about data location, PII and FERPA data on file-sharing sites or flash drives, and recommends an external vulnerability assessment. It also recommends an IT assessment covering governance, IT staff and organization, external service providers, service delivery, network and device management, cybersecurity policies, and the technology itself, noting many districts use the results as a two- to three-year action plan.

**Accounting and auditing standards ahead.** GASB Statement No. 87, Leases, is effective for the district's June 30, 2022 financial statements and requires lessees to recognize a lease liability and intangible right-of-use asset and lessors to recognize a lease receivable and deferred inflow, with new disclosures; the district must inventory all lease contracts and embedded leases. SAS No. 134, Auditor Reporting and Amendments, issued by the AICPA Auditing Standards Board in May 2019, takes effect for the June 30, 2022 audited financial statements and moves the opinion to the top of the letter, expands the basis of opinion section, explains materiality, defines reasonable assurance, notes that fraud risk exceeds error risk, enhances going concern reporting, describes auditor responsibilities, and introduces key audit matters. The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013 with an exposure draft, "Financial Reporting Model Improvements," issued in June 2020; the comment period ended in February 2021, Plante & Moran submitted comments, and final standards are targeted by June 2022. Proposed changes include additional MD&A information, a budget-to-actual variance column between original and amended budget, terminology shifts from "revenue" and "expenditures" to "inflows" and "outflows of resources," and replacement of modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" using a 12-month horizon rather than the current 60-day receivable rule. Adoption is phased: districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million adopt for the year ending June 30, 2025, and those under $75 million for the year ending June 30, 2026. A related GASB project, the June 2020 preliminary views on "Revenue and Expense Recognition," could produce a standard during 2025.

**Presentation.** "Facilities Condition & Program Assessment Report," Troy School District, presented to the Board of Education under the agenda item "BOE Shared Copy Program & Facilities Assessment Report." The team included the cabinet, administrators, staff, students, and parents.

**Two areas of focus.** The Facilities Condition Assessment covered interior and exterior infrastructure and sites against code and standards, sorted into categories of 1-3, 4-6, 7-10, 10+, and 15+ years. The Program Assessment identified barriers and deficiencies in buildings and sites that impede delivering education in the most optimum way today and in the future.

**Process.** Kick-off meeting March 2021; facilities toured March through August 2021; status meetings; project worklists developed; items quantified and cost estimates developed; needs categorized and prioritized.

**Fun facts.** Roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, over 50 acres; approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; average building age 48 years; approximately 500 acres of property, roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**System findings and cost ranges.** Roofing, with a typical 20-year lifespan and aging roofs, $10-15 Million. Architectural systems, covering aging doors, flooring, and furnishings such as cabinets, gym equipment, and marker boards, $40-45 Million. Mechanical systems, with a 20-year equipment lifespan, aging boilers, aging classroom unit ventilators, and malfunctioning plumbing fixtures, $45-50 Million. Electrical systems, including LED lighting upgrades with energy rebates and operational savings and replacement of emergency/exit lighting, $30-35 Million, illustrated with existing and new lighting in the Troy High School Media Center. Site work paving, with a 20-year asphalt lifespan, replacing aging parking lots and sidewalks, $20-23 Million. Playgrounds and athletics, assessed on condition, age appropriateness, and safety, $5-7 Million.

**Program assessment.** Program decisions can absorb facilities needs, and the program assessment carries no dollar amount, which comes later in design work. Steps were vision setting and discovery, defining the ideal program, and evaluating existing schools against that ideal. Leaders cited making thinking visible, the 6 C's of learning (collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, character/compassion, citizenship), project-based learning, competency-based learning, social emotional learning, multi-tiered systems of supports, and experiential learning through internships, career pathways, and CTE. Teachers named team collaborative work, one-on-one time, mobile technology, and workshop instruction, and valued good lighting, natural light, and decluttered, flexible space. Among secondary students, 85.7% agree that more connections to real-life experiences should be provided. A workshop with Dr. Tony Wagner explored deep learning, its barriers (money, resources, time; staff and parent readiness; physical structure and furniture; state mandated credits and time requirements), and its ideal space.

Ninety-two-slide presentation titled "Facilities Condition & Program Assessment Report" for Troy School District, brought to the Board of Education meeting of October 5, 2021 under the agenda title "BOE Shared Copy Program & Facilities Assessment Report." The team slide lists cabinet, administrators, staff, students, and parents.

**Two areas of focus.** The Facilities Condition Assessment examined interior and exterior infrastructure and sites, code and standards, using categories of 1-3, 4-6, 7-10, 10+, and 15+. The Program Assessment focused on identifying barriers and deficiencies in the district's school buildings and sites that prevent or impede delivering education in the most optimum way today and in the future.

**Process and agenda.** The condition assessment agenda covered overview, fun facts, facility findings (roofing, architectural, mechanical, electrical, civil, playground/athletics), cost summary, and next steps. The kick-off meeting was held in March 2021, facilities were toured from March through August 2021, status meetings were held, project worklists were developed, items were quantified and cost estimates developed, and needs were categorized and prioritized.

**Fun facts about the district's physical plant.** Roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, described as over 50 acres. Approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures. Over 4,300 doors. Over 2 million square feet of parking lot. 1.7 million square feet of roofing. Average building age of 48 years old. Approximately 500 acres of property, described as roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**Roofing.** Typical roof lifespan is 20 years and the district's roofs are aging. Cost range $10-15 Million.

**Architectural systems.** Aging doors, aging flooring, and aging furnishings including cabinets, gym equipment, and marker boards. Cost range $40-45 Million.

**Mechanical systems.** Mechanical equipment lifespan is 20 years; findings include aging boilers, aging classroom unit ventilators, and malfunctioning plumbing fixtures. Cost range $45-50 Million.

**Electrical systems.** Opportunities include energy rebates and operational savings, upgrading lighting to energy efficient LED, and replacing emergency and exit lighting. Cost range $30-35 Million. Before-and-after images show Troy High School Media Center existing lighting and Troy High Media Center new lighting.

**Site work, paving.** Typical lifespan of asphalt is 20 years; recommendations are to replace aging parking lots and replace sidewalks. Cost range $20-23 Million.

**Site work, playgrounds and athletics.** Assessment completed based on condition, age appropriateness, and safety. Cost range $5-7 Million.

**Cost summary by category.** Roofing Systems $10-15 Million; Architectural Systems $40-45 Million; Mechanical Systems $45-50 Million; Electrical Systems $30-35 Million; Site Work $25-30 Million; Furniture, Kitchen Equipment $23-28 Million; Buses $12 Million; Technology Devices $35 Million; total $220-250 Million.

**Cost summary by priority.** Critical Needs (1-3 years) $45-55 Million; Near Future Needs (4-6 years) $90-100 Million; Future Needs (7-10 years) $85-95 Million; total $220-250 Million.

**Program assessment framing.** The presentation stresses the interplay between facilities needs and program needs, noting that some program decisions may impact and "take care of" facilities needs; the example given is that design of a new instructional space will address the need to update lighting and architectural systems. The program assessment is not accompanied by a dollar amount, which comes in design work moving forward. The sequence is vision setting and discovery, understanding TSD vision and goals and looking to the future of education, defining the ideal program, and evaluating existing schools against the ideal future program of spaces.

**Feedback shared by leaders.** Themes include making thinking visible; the 6 C's of learning - collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, character/compassion, and citizenship; motivating learners to explore information in order to construct new ideas, identify new relationships, and create new models of thinking and behavior; dream and imagination; project based learning leveraging real-world partnerships, scenarios and applications; descriptive grading and alternative assessment; character education; responsive/workshop instruction; social emotional learning; multi-tiered system of supports and the "whole child"; growth mindset; experiential learning through internships, career pathways and CTE; competency based learning with mastery learning and self-paced flexibility; and authentic learning or learning by doing.

**What teachers reported.** Top instructional practices were team collaborative work, one on one with teacher, learning with mobile technology, social emotional learning, independent study, performance based learning, project-based learning, workshop, peer-to-peer, and classroom libraries. Students are most engaged when emotional well-being is prioritized, content extends to students' lives, there is collaboration with peers, opportunities for choice, readily accessible resources, curiosity is piqued, students can see effort paying off, and individualized expectations are visible. Attributes that make a teacher want to be in a space are good lighting, natural light, clean and decluttered, inspiring, active and allowing movement, connection to others, and flexibility to change the space.

**Elementary student responses.** To be successful students said it is important to work well as a team, be creative, and think about hard questions and solve big problems. They learn best working quietly on their own, talking to other students about what they are learning, building projects together, and when they feel happy, and ranked learning with friends, with their teacher, and with their family in that order of importance.

**Secondary student responses.** Interest in going to school is affected by subject matter connecting to interests, fun activities, choosing where and how to work best, opportunities to develop talents, comfortable environments, confidence from succeeding, awareness of expectations, feeling safe to explore ideas without fear of failure, opportunities to work alone, and a flexible class schedule. 85.7% agree that more connections to real-life experiences should be provided to students. Spaces that positively impact learning are social commons, flexible learning studios, partnership space where real life skills can be shared, private space, outdoor spaces, and lab/maker spaces; students are most comfortable with soft comfortable furniture, clean and de-cluttered rooms, access to food and drink throughout the day, and quiet and calm space.

**Dr. Tony Wagner workshop.** Administrators answered five questions. On the most important characteristics of deep learning: inquiry and project based learning; collaboration and feedback; critical thinking with access to resources, tools and technology; foundational feelings of safety and connection to topic; student voice, agency and exhibition; and learning from failure. On activities that lead to deep learning: working collaboratively on a team, encouraging creativity and thinking outside the box, demonstrating, challenging and defending ideas, and spaces and access to research. On current barriers or roadblocks: money, resources and time; preparing staff and parents for change, culture shift and buy in; the physical structure of the building and furniture; state mandated credits and time requirements; and the current system's mindset, tradition and risk tolerance. On the ideal space: flexible and moveable, more natural light, calming colors and tones with students first and safety, a "watering hole" place to collaborate, places for students to showcase work, and space allowing collaboration of students and staff from multiple disciplines. On what success looks like: evidence of student engagement, inspiring future learning, students feeling passionate and finding meaning and purpose, other schools coming to learn from Troy, relationships developing between students and staff, and everyone feeling comfortable sharing ideas.

**Attributes of modern learning environments.** Every school is documented in spreadsheet format with detailed notes for review by the Facilities Review Committee, with a program assessment grade across all buildings and all attributes rated Good, Needs Improvement, or Poor. Attributes assessed include smaller learning communities (systematic organization of spaces sized for a small subset of the school population, adjacency supporting seamless movement and non-traditional schedules, and a menu of spaces encouraging subject-matter cross fertilization); classroom size (space for flexible furniture and student movement, project-based, peer-to-peer and student-centered learning); ability to adapt (spaces easily adapted for current and future programs, with technology and infrastructure supporting fast delivery shifts); collaboration spaces (adjacent to instructional spaces, configured for passive supervision, organized with variety of group size, horizontal surface size and content sharing); connection to the outdoors; entry image (clearly visible and branded secure entry, visible inside and outside, directing visitors to staff/help, consistent brand); traffic separation on site (separate bus and parent drop off, safe traffic flow, dedicated visitor parking, dedicated entrances for academics, athletics and performing arts); appropriate playgrounds (safe and sustainable materials, accessibility, supporting active bodies); teacher collaboration spaces assigned to specific Professional Learning Communities; spaces for physical activities accessible in all weather and supporting social emotional and wellness goals including formal gym class and wellness uses such as meditation and yoga; athletic, recreation and community facilities (safe and in good condition, practice and match/game space, adequate size for players and spectators, equity across genders, easily secured for community use, addressing recreation as well as athletics); spaces for fine and performing arts with practice, gallery and performance space; spaces for community partnerships affording real-life training, accessible to industry professionals and after-hours use, with partnership branding opportunities; universal design; acoustics (surface materials lowering sound reverberation time, reduced background noise, improved speech intelligibility, mechanical systems designed to reduce background noise, and intentional quiet/isolation spaces); environmental control (on demand temperature, ventilation and air quality adjustability, varied lighting solutions with adjustable levels and color temperatures, displayed energy use information); natural light (daylit spaces supporting circadian rhythms, energy reduction through daylighting, views supporting creative thinking); integration of technology (students sharing content from devices, content clearly visible to all learners); and mobile, varied furniture that is easily reconfigured, inclusive of all body sizes and abilities, and encourages movement.

**Guiding principles.** Provide spaces that encourage curiosity, movement and exploration; convenient, direct, safe and welcoming access for students and parents; interior and exterior spaces for gross motor development; organize schools into smaller learning communities supporting belonging, collaboration, inclusion and equity; provide flexible, adaptable and stimulating learning spaces; provide abundant natural light in all instructional spaces; make schools eco-friendly with interaction with the natural environment; provide professional space for teachers and staff to encourage teaming, collaboration, interaction and observation; create a strong, progressive, inviting and innovative visual image promoting the district brand; ensure accessibility for all students and staff through universal design; provide shared collaboration spaces for individual, small group and large groups; create spaces for career exploration and community partnerships supporting real-world experiential learning; design spaces supporting well-being including quiet and sensory spaces; create spaces for interdisciplinary collaboration; provide flexible furnishings to transform existing classrooms into flexible learning studios; improve shared spaces for fine and performing arts, athletics and other performances and competitions for students and the community; assure seamless integration of technology; and transform existing playgrounds into outdoor spaces reinforcing curricular goals and a positive relationship with nature.

**Next steps.** A slide asks "Questions for TMP?" The Facilities Review Committee will have 57 members drawn from community members from all areas of the district plus teachers, administrators, and students. Its first meeting is October 12th, with an update to be given at the BOE Workshop on December 7th.

Final report of the Troy School District Facilities Review Committee (FRC), presented to the Board of Education on May 3, 2022, recommending a $525 million bond program with a 2 mill increase to the current millage rate for the November 8, 2022 ballot.

**Committee charge.** The deck states that the Troy School District's Facilities Review Committee is a decision-making body inclusive of TSD staff and community members representing the diversity of the Troy community, charged with developing a plan for upgrading TSD educational facilities to support flexible, student-centered learning communities that meet the mission and vision of the District, and charged with developing a recommendation at the conclusion of its analysis for the Board of Education's consideration.

**Members.** Gayle Moran, Christian Muellar, Dawn Mulcahy, Brian Nutting, Matthew Olovson, Joe Pettinato, Michelle Phillips, Sarah Phillips, Namita Prasad, David Recker, Tonia Romancheck, Matt Sackrison, Sande Frisen, Sunil Sivaraman, Brian Smiatacz, Beth Soggs, Cornelius Godfrey, Julie Gould, Ahmed Hakim, Elizabeth Hammond, Stephen Hatfield, Alison Hendry, Kimberly Hoyle, Hussein Irani, Kelly Jones, Brian Kelly, Ron Keoleian, Erin Keyser, Ramanathan Krishnamoorthy, Briana Matti, Mark Moebus, Vital Anne, Michelle Barsh, Lauren Bestul, Kerry Brennan, Adam Burns, Renee Burzynski, Chris Centi, Mike Cottone, Scott Courtney, Jonathan Cross, Shaun Dantas, Bob Dowd, Mary Frederick, Tim Fulcher, Roberto Garcia, Michael Giglio, Aparna Sriram, Alyssa Stevens, Ann Sumnar, Swarnalatha Talluri, Debbie Taylor, Lijo Thommana, John Tu, Kelsey Weatherspoon, Alecia West, Nicole Wilson, Fiona Wingblad, Marie Woodman, Hong Ye, Brian Zawislak, Stephanie Zendler.

**Process.** Seven FRC meeting dates and tours are cited. Pre-FRC "Stretch Your Thinking" activities were student and teacher feedback on educational spaces, Cabinet and Board of Education feedback on their vision of education and current state of buildings, and a deep dive with administrative leaders conducted with Dr. Wagner. The path to the recommendation ran Discovery (understand district facilities, program, vision and modern learning), Exploration (examine whether buildings hinder or help the program vision and goals; evaluate and determine the best option), and Recommendation (recommend an option to the Board regarding a future bond program initiative). Discovery inputs listed were TSD Vision & Goals, Program Assessment, Facilities Condition Assessment, Today's Learning Environments, Community Sentiments, Curriculum Vision and District Overview.

**Building inventory.** Elementary buildings: Barnard, 18 acres, 64,192 sq ft, opened 1978, addition 2007; Bemis, 15.2 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1978, 2007; Costello, 23 acres, 52,055 sq ft, 1972, 2007; Hamilton, 15 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1983, 2007; Hill, 12.9 acres, 54,336 sq ft, 1967, additions 71-93-2006; Leonard, 16.1 acres, 59,220 sq ft, 1959, additions 68-94-2006; Martell, 14.2 acres, 52,799 sq ft, 1972, additions 92-2007; Morse, 9.8 acres, 54,636 sq ft, 1956, additions 62-68-94-2006; Schroeder, 10 acres, 61,896 sq ft, 1970, additions 93-2006; Troy Union, 21.8 acres, 66,929 sq ft, 1925, additions 53-70-90-2006; Wass, 21.4 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1978, 2007; Wattles, 19 acres, 59,150 sq ft, 1967, additions 78-2007. Middle schools: Baker, 40 acres, 128,098 sq ft, 2006; Boulan Park, 16 acres, 116,351 sq ft, 1971, 2015; Larson, 32 acres, 116,351 sq ft, 1971, 2015; Smith, 20.1 acres, 100,734 sq ft, 1967, additions 73-82-89-2007. High schools and other: Athens, 50 acres, 398,426 sq ft, 1974, additions 93-99-2006; Troy Learning Center (ITLC), 3 acres, 39,600 sq ft, 2020; THS, 72 acres, 354,210 sq ft, 1992, additions 2005-2015; IA East/TCT shared site with Baker, 91,455 sq ft, 1952, additions 55-67-70-78-80-19; Troy Preschool, 13.6 acres, 68,654 sq ft, 2019; Board Office, 15.5 acres, 12,000 sq ft, 1973, addition 1988; Services Building, shared site with Board, 29,143 sq ft, 2000; Transportation, 3.9 acres, 11,328 sq ft, 1964, 2007; Rankin, 1.5 acres, 24,696 sq ft.

**Fun facts.** Average building age 48 years old; roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, described as over 50 acres; approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; approximately 500 acres of property, roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**Enrollment trend.** 2011-12: 12,312; 2012-13: 12,438; 2013-14: 12,573; 2014-15: 12,553; 2015-16: 12,556; 2016-17: 12,889; 2017-18: 13,080; 2018-19: 13,084; 2019-20: 13,043; 2020-21: 12,730; 2021-22: 12,535. A debt millage rates chart is included as a graphic without extracted values.

**Facilities Condition Assessment.** Categories assessed were roofing, architectural systems, mechanical systems, electrical systems, site work (paving), site work (playgrounds/athletics) and security. Cost summary by priority: Critical Needs (1-3 years) $45-55 Million; Near Future Needs (4-6 years) $90-100 Million; Future Needs (7-10 years) $85-95 Million; TOTAL $220-250 Million. A program assessment graded all buildings against attributes of modern learning environments on a Good / Needs Improvement / Poor scale.

**Bond financing.** Estimated bonding capacity was modeled as a 30-year bond in three series at a 4.00% estimated interest rate. Table_1c: Series 2023 $70,000,000 over 29 yrs., 3 mo. with $48,843,000 estimated total interest cost and $9,450,000 amortized within the first 6 years; Series 2026 $90,000,000 over 30 yrs., 0 mo. with $63,284,000 interest and $9,925,000; Series 2029 $135,000,000 over 30 yrs., 0 mo. with $95,213,000 interest and $13,925,000; total $295,000,000 principal, $207,340,000 interest, first-year millage 1.23, average millage 2.19, total mills all debt 4.10, increase in debt levy 0.00. Table_2c: $110,000,000 / $75,901,000 / $19,925,000; $135,000,000 / $96,061,000 / $14,025,000; $175,000,000 / $121,778,000 / $19,500,000; total $420,000,000 principal, $293,740,000 interest, 2.20 first-year millage, 3.13 average millage, 5.10 total mills, 1.00 increase. Table_3c: $150,000,000 / $100,583,000 / $30,075,000; $175,000,000 / $121,905,000 / $20,175,000; $200,000,000 / $142,299,000 / $20,550,000; total $525,000,000 principal, $364,787,000 interest, 3.19 first-year millage, 3.93 average millage, 6.10 total mills, 2.00 increase. Table_4c: $185,000,000 / $124,042,000 / $38,700,000; $210,000,000 / $146,276,000 / $26,750,000; $230,000,000 / $163,975,000 / $24,375,000; total $625,000,000 principal, $434,293,000 interest, 4.08 first-year millage, 4.68 average millage, 7.00 total mills, 2.90 increase.

**Guiding principles, ranked.** 1 Flexible & Adaptable Learning Spaces; 2 Spaces that Encourage Curiosity & Exploration; 3 Flexible Furniture; 4 Technology; 5 Student Collaboration Space; 6 Smaller Learning Communities; 7 Abundant Natural Light; 8 Interdisciplinary Collaboration; 9 Acoustics - Quiet Spaces/Sensory; 10 Accessibility/Universal Design; 11 Upgrade Performing Arts / Athletic Spaces; 12 Career / Partnerships; 13 Strong Visual Image / Brand Identity; 14 Professional Collaboration Space; 15 Eco-Friendly; 16 Playground Upgrades; 17 Access that is direct, safe & welcoming; 18 Gross Motor Development.

**Conceptual estimates and refinement.** Original conceptual estimates: elementary schools $249,491,086; secondary schools $501,035,611; all school facilities $750,526,697. Revised conceptual estimates: elementary schools $138,184,058; secondary schools $436,249,767; buses, not included in the original estimate, $12,000,000; technology, previously rolled into school estimates, $30,000,000; bond program total $616,433,825 against the original $750,526,697.

**Financial tolerance and survey.** The financial tolerance exercise found the greatest percentage falling at the $525 million mark, with 62% supporting $525M or higher and 38% supporting $420M or lower. A professional survey conducted by EPIC-MRA asked respondents how they would vote on the 2-mill proposal, pressing undecided respondents on whether they would lean YES or NO if the election were held today: 66% Total YES and 27% Total NO, with reported bar values of 52% and 14% on the Yes side, 21% and 6% on the No side, and 7% undecided. Voter progression across proposals showed solid YES of 52%, 58% and 60% and lean YES of 14%, 21% and 24% for the 2-Mill, 1-Mill and 0-Mill proposals, with 66% Total YES, 79% Total YES and 84% Total YES respectively. Feedback analysis noted very consistent thinking across the 2 mill Build and individual selections, one major area of difference being THS academic remodeling, and consensus on allocating renovation dollars to THS without going to the $49M level. The FRC then formed consensus around a new 2 mill Build that included an allocation of $14,790,000 to upgrades at Troy High School.

**Recommendation.** The committee cited over 700 hours of time invested by committee members, 7 Steering Committee meetings, tours of district schools, the EPIC-MRA professional survey, and development and analysis of various ideas, concepts and estimates. Its recommendation: a $525 million bond program; a 2 mill increase to the current millage rate; a proposal on the November 8, 2022 ballot, stated as transforming school facilities to support the future of education and allow Troy School District to continue to provide a World Class Education for ALL.

**Building-level scope.** Every elementary school (Barnard, Bemis, Hamilton, Wass, Costello, Martell, Hill, Leonard, Morse, Schroeder, Troy Union, Wattles) receives infrastructure upgrades per the foundational elements matrix plus accessibility/universal design upgrades to all toilet rooms, new flexible adaptable furniture, playground replacement with new surfaces and accessible equipment, and space (new or remodel) for a 3rd Kindergarten classroom. Morse adds a new art room/general storage addition; Troy Union adds 4 new classrooms to replace removed original structure. Baker Middle School remodels its media center as multi-use space for interdisciplinary collaboration/STEM/robotics. Boulan Park and Larson Middle Schools reconfigure all classrooms and the media center for interdisciplinary collaboration/STEM/robotics with proper sizing, glass walls, and staff and student collaboration spaces. Smith Middle School gets a new 2-story school of 120,000 square feet for 750 students including space for STEM/robotics. Athens High School gets a new 3-level academic wing and major remodeling of remaining academic areas. Troy High School gets upgrades addressing circulation issues, student collaboration enhancements, multi-use space for robotics, fitness and other activities, other identified critical program needs, and expanded plus new music rehearsal spaces. International Academy East and Troy Center for Transition receive toilet room accessibility work and new furniture; Troy Career & College High School receives toilet room accessibility work. District support buildings receive roof replacement, window and exterior door replacement, new ceilings and flooring where needed, toilet partitions and accessories, casework replacement, LED lighting upgrades, replacement of aging mechanical units and plumbing fixtures, exhaust fan replacement, temperature controls, upgraded electrical service and power panels, access control/intrusion detection, asphalt paving replacement and partial concrete walkway replacement.

**Taxpayer impact.** For the $525 million program at a 2 mill increase, by Troy ZIP code: 48083 average home market value $300K, $300 annual and $25 monthly impact; 48084 $353K, $353 and $29; 48085 $392K, $392 and $33; 48098 $470K, $470 and $39.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Second delivery of the Troy School District Facilities Review Committee's report to the Board of Education, dated May 17, 2022, restating the committee's charge, its Facilities Condition Assessment total of $220-250 Million, and conceptual estimates that moved from $750,526,697 to a refined $616,433,825 bond program total. **What it is**
"Presentation to the Board of Education" by the Troy School District Facilities Review Committee, dated May 17, 2022 - the FRC deck brought back to the Board two weeks after its May 3 delivery, with sustainability added to the Facilities Condition Assessment scope and an additional district initiatives slide.

**Committee and process**
The FRC is described as a decision-making body of TSD staff and community members charged with developing a plan for upgrading TSD educational facilities to support flexible, student-centered learning communities and producing a recommendation for the Board. Roughly 62 members are named, among them Gayle Moran, Dawn Mulcahy, Joe Pettinato, Namita Prasad, Matt Sackrison, Cornelius Godfrey, Elizabeth Hammond, Hussein Irani, Ron Keoleian, Ramanathan Krishnamoorthy, Vital Anne, Kerry Brennan, Mike Cottone, Bob Dowd, Roberto Garcia, Aparna Sriram, Swarnalatha Talluri, Lijo Thommana, John Tu, Fiona Wingblad, Hong Ye and Stephanie Zendler. Seven meeting dates and school tours are cited, along with pre-FRC feedback from students, teachers, Cabinet and Board and a deep dive with administrative leaders conducted with Dr. Wagner. The path ran Discovery, Exploration and Recommendation.

**District facts**
Average building age 48 years old; roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, over 50 acres; approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; approximately 500 acres of property, roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area. Athens is the largest building at 398,426 sq ft on 50 acres (opened 1974); THS 354,210 sq ft on 72 acres (1992); Troy Union, opened 1925, is the oldest.

**Enrollment**
2011-12 through 2021-22: 12,312; 12,438; 12,573; 12,553; 12,556; 12,889; 13,080; 13,084; 13,043; 12,730; 12,535.

**Facilities Condition Assessment**
Categories: roofing, architectural systems, mechanical systems, electrical systems, site work (paving), site work (playgrounds/athletics), security and sustainability.

**Estimates and survey**

Revised: elementary $138,184,058, secondary $436,249,767, buses $12,000,000, technology $30,000,000, bond program total $616,433,825. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Facilities Review Committee report delivered to the Troy School District Board of Education on May 17, 2022, a second presentation of the committee's Discovery-Exploration-Recommendation work following the May 3, 2022 delivery. Content is substantially the same deck, with sustainability listed among the Facilities Condition Assessment categories, a Bond Program Estimate slide, and a slide adding district initiatives beyond building work.

**Charge.** The Troy School District's Facilities Review Committee is described as a decision-making body inclusive of TSD staff and community members representing the diversity of the Troy community, charged with developing a plan for upgrading TSD educational facilities to support flexible, student-centered learning communities that meet the mission and vision of the District, and with developing a recommendation at the conclusion of its analysis for the Board of Education's consideration.

**Members.** Gayle Moran, Christian Muellar, Dawn Mulcahy, Brian Nutting, Matthew Olovson, Joe Pettinato, Michelle Phillips, Sarah Phillips, Namita Prasad, David Recker, Tonia Romancheck, Matt Sackrison, Sande Frisen, Sunil Sivaraman, Brian Smiatacz, Beth Soggs, Cornelius Godfrey, Julie Gould, Ahmed Hakim, Elizabeth Hammond, Stephen Hatfield, Alison Hendry, Kimberly Hoyle, Hussein Irani, Kelly Jones, Brian Kelly, Ron Keoleian, Erin Keyser, Ramanathan Krishnamoorthy, Briana Matti, Mark Moebus, Vital Anne, Michelle Barsh, Lauren Bestul, Kerry Brennan, Adam Burns, Renee Burzynski, Chris Centi, Mike Cottone, Scott Courtney, Jonathan Cross, Shaun Dantas, Bob Dowd, Mary Frederick, Tim Fulcher, Roberto Garcia, Michael Giglio, Aparna Sriram, Alyssa Stevens, Ann Sumnar, Swarnalatha Talluri, Debbie Taylor, Lijo Thommana, John Tu, Kelsey Weatherspoon, Alecia West, Nicole Wilson, Fiona Wingblad, Marie Woodman, Hong Ye, Brian Zawislak, Stephanie Zendler.

**Process.** Seven FRC meeting dates and tours are noted. Pre-FRC "Stretch Your Thinking" activities were student and teacher feedback to gain perspective on educational spaces, Cabinet and Board of Education feedback on their vision of education and the current state of buildings, and a deep dive with administrative leaders with Dr. Wagner. Discovery covered TSD vision and goals, program assessment, facilities condition assessment, today's learning environments, community sentiments, curriculum vision and district overview. Exploration examined whether buildings hinder or help the program vision and goals and evaluated the best option to meet the vision. Recommendation delivered an option to the Board regarding a future bond program initiative.

**Building inventory.** Barnard, 18 acres, 64,192 sq ft, opened 1978, addition 2007; Bemis, 15.2 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1978, 2007; Costello, 23 acres, 52,055 sq ft, 1972, 2007; Hamilton, 15 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1983, 2007; Hill, 12.9 acres, 54,336 sq ft, 1967, additions 71-93-2006; Leonard, 16.1 acres, 59,220 sq ft, 1959, additions 68-94-2006; Martell, 14.2 acres, 52,799 sq ft, 1972, additions 92-2007; Morse, 9.8 acres, 54,636 sq ft, 1956, additions 62-68-94-2006; Schroeder, 10 acres, 61,896 sq ft, 1970, additions 93-2006; Troy Union, 21.8 acres, 66,929 sq ft, 1925, additions 53-70-90-2006; Wass, 21.4 acres, 64,192 sq ft, 1978, 2007; Wattles, 19 acres, 59,150 sq ft, 1967, additions 78-2007; Baker, 40 acres, 128,098 sq ft, 2006; Boulan Park, 16 acres, 116,351 sq ft, 1971, 2015; Larson, 32 acres, 116,351 sq ft, 1971, 2015; Smith, 20.1 acres, 100,734 sq ft, 1967, additions 73-82-89-2007; Athens, 50 acres, 398,426 sq ft, 1974, additions 93-99-2006; Troy Learning Center (ITLC), 3 acres, 39,600 sq ft, 2020; THS, 72 acres, 354,210 sq ft, 1992, additions 2005-2015; IA East/TCT on a shared site with Baker, 91,455 sq ft, 1952, additions 55-67-70-78-80-19; Troy Preschool, 13.6 acres, 68,654 sq ft, 2019; Board Office, 15.5 acres, 12,000 sq ft, 1973, addition 1988; Services Building on a shared site with the Board Office, 29,143 sq ft, 2000; Transportation, 3.9 acres, 11,328 sq ft, 1964, 2007; Rankin, 1.5 acres, 24,696 sq ft.

**Fun facts.** Average building age 48 years old; roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, described as over 50 acres; approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; approximately 500 acres of property, roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**Enrollment trend.** 2011-12: 12,312; 2012-13: 12,438; 2013-14: 12,573; 2014-15: 12,553; 2015-16: 12,556; 2016-17: 12,889; 2017-18: 13,080; 2018-19: 13,084; 2019-20: 13,043; 2020-21: 12,730; 2021-22: 12,535. A debt millage rates slide is included as a graphic.

**Facilities Condition Assessment.** Categories assessed: roofing, architectural systems, mechanical systems, electrical systems, site work (paving), site work (playgrounds/athletics), security and sustainability. Cost summary by priority: Critical Needs (1-3 years) $45-55 Million; Near Future Needs (4-6 years) $90-100 Million; Future Needs (7-10 years) $85-95 Million; TOTAL $220-250 Million. The program assessment graded all buildings against attributes of modern learning environments as Good, Needs Improvement or Poor.

**Bond financing scenarios.** Estimated bonding capacity for a 30-year bond, all series priced at a 4.00% estimated interest rate. Table_1c: Series 2023 $70,000,000 over 29 yrs., 3 mo., $48,843,000 estimated total interest cost, $9,450,000 amortized within the first 6 years; Series 2026 $90,000,000 over 30 yrs., 0 mo., $63,284,000, $9,925,000; Series 2029 $135,000,000 over 30 yrs., 0 mo., $95,213,000, $13,925,000; total $295,000,000 and $207,340,000, first-year millage 1.23, average millage 2.19, total mills all debt 4.10, increase in debt levy 0.00. Table_2c: $110,000,000 / $75,901,000 / $19,925,000; $135,000,000 / $96,061,000 / $14,025,000; $175,000,000 / $121,778,000 / $19,500,000; total $420,000,000 and $293,740,000, 2.20 first-year millage, 3.13 average millage, 5.10 total mills, 1.00 increase. Table_3c: $150,000,000 / $100,583,000 / $30,075,000; $175,000,000 / $121,905,000 / $20,175,000; $200,000,000 / $142,299,000 / $20,550,000; total $525,000,000 and $364,787,000, 3.19 first-year millage, 3.93 average millage, 6.10 total mills, 2.00 increase. Table_4c: $185,000,000 / $124,042,000 / $38,700,000; $210,000,000 / $146,276,000 / $26,750,000; $230,000,000 / $163,975,000 / $24,375,000; total $625,000,000 and $434,293,000, 4.08 first-year millage, 4.68 average millage, 7.00 total mills, 2.90 increase.

**Guiding principles, ranked.** 1 Flexible & Adaptable Learning Spaces; 2 Spaces that Encourage Curiosity & Exploration; 3 Flexible Furniture; 4 Technology; 5 Student Collaboration Space; 6 Smaller Learning Communities; 7 Abundant Natural Light; 8 Interdisciplinary Collaboration; 9 Acoustics - Quiet Spaces/Sensory; 10 Accessibility/Universal Design; 11 Upgrade Performing Arts / Athletic Spaces; 12 Career / Partnerships; 13 Strong Visual Image / Brand Identity; 14 Professional Collaboration Space; 15 Eco-Friendly; 16 Playground Upgrades; 17 Access that is direct, safe & welcoming; 18 Gross Motor Development.

**Conceptual estimates and refinement.** Original conceptual estimates: elementary schools $249,491,086; secondary schools $501,035,611; all school facilities $750,526,697. Revised conceptual estimates: elementary schools $138,184,058; secondary schools $436,249,767; buses, not included in the original estimate, $12,000,000; technology, previously rolled into school estimates, $30,000,000; bond program total $616,433,825.

**Financial tolerance and survey.** The financial tolerance exercise found the greatest percentage falling at the $525 million mark, with 62% supporting $525M or higher and 38% supporting $420M or lower. The EPIC-MRA survey asked how respondents would vote on the 2-mill proposal, with undecided respondents pressed on whether they would lean YES in favor of the bond proposal or NO to oppose it if the election were held today; results were 66% Total YES and 27% Total NO, with chart values of 52% and 14% on the Yes side, 21% and 6% on the No side, and 7% undecided. Voter progression showed solid YES of 52%, 58% and 60% and lean YES of 14%, 21% and 24% for the 2-Mill, 1-Mill and 0-Mill proposals, totaling 66% Total YES, 79% Total YES and 84% Total YES. Analysis of feedback recorded very consistent thinking across the 2 mill Build and individual selections, one major area of difference being THS academic remodeling, and consensus on wanting to allocate renovation dollars to THS without going to the $49M level. The FRC then formed consensus around a new 2 mill Build that included an allocation of $14,790,000 to upgrades at Troy High School.

**Recommendation.** Citing over 700 hours of committee time, 7 Steering Committee meetings, tours of district schools, the professional survey conducted by EPIC-MRA, and development and analysis of various ideas, concepts and estimates, the FRC recommended a $525 million bond program, a 2 mill increase to the current millage rate, and a proposal on the November 8, 2022 ballot, stating the program will transform school facilities to support the future of education and allow Troy School District to continue to provide a World Class Education for ALL.

**Building-level scope.** All twelve elementary schools - Barnard, Bemis, Hamilton, Wass, Costello, Martell, Hill, Leonard, Morse, Schroeder, Troy Union and Wattles - receive infrastructure upgrades per the foundational elements matrix plus accessibility and universal design upgrades to all toilet rooms, new flexible adaptable furniture, playground replacement with new surfaces and accessible equipment, and space (new or remodel) for a 3rd Kindergarten classroom. Morse additionally receives a new art room and general storage addition; Troy Union receives 4 new classrooms to replace removed original structure. Baker Middle School remodels its media center into multi-use space for interdisciplinary collaboration, STEM and robotics. Boulan Park and Larson Middle Schools reconfigure all classrooms and the media center for interdisciplinary collaboration, STEM and robotics with proper sizing, glass walls and added staff and student collaboration spaces. Smith Middle School receives a new 2-story school of 120,000 square feet for 750 students including space for STEM and robotics. Athens High School receives a new 3-level academic wing and major remodeling of remaining academic areas. Troy High School receives upgrades addressing circulation issues, student collaboration enhancements, multi-use space for robotics, fitness and other activities, other identified critical program needs, and expanded plus new music rehearsal spaces. International Academy East and Troy Center for Transition receive toilet room accessibility work and new furniture; Troy College and Career High School receives toilet room accessibility work.

**District support buildings and additional initiatives.** Facilities Condition Assessment upgrades for support buildings cover roof replacement, window and exterior door replacement, new ceilings and flooring where needed, toilet partitions and accessories, casework replacement, LED lighting upgrades, replacement of aging mechanical units and plumbing fixtures, exhaust fan replacement, temperature controls, upgraded electrical service and power panels, interior LED lighting, access control and intrusion detection, asphalt paving replacement and partial concrete walkway replacement. Additional district initiatives listed are purchase of buses, special education programming upgrades and technology upgrades.

**Taxpayer impact.** For the $525 million program with a 2 mill increase, by Troy ZIP code: 48083, average home market value $300K, annual impact $300, monthly impact $25; 48084, $353K, $353, $29; 48085, $392K, $392, $33; 48098, $470K, $470, $39. The deck closes by thanking the Board for the opportunity to present the work of the FRC.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the regular Troy Board of Education meeting held May 17, 2022 in the Troy School District Services Building at 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:01 p.m. and adjourned at 9:39 p.m., with Dr. Philippart absent and roughly 70 people in the audience. The Board honored MPAAA award recipients, twenty retiring employees, and a Student Spotlight honoree, and adopted proclamations for National Teacher Appreciation Week and Mental Health Awareness Month. Its most consequential action was Resolution 22-047, authorizing preparation of an Application for Preliminary Qualification of Bonds to the Michigan Department of Treasury for a bond issue of not more than $555,000,000, anticipated for the November 8, 2022 ballot.

**Meeting**
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, May 17, 2022, held in the Troy School District Services Building located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:01 p.m.; the meeting was adjourned at 9:39 p.m. Approximately 70 members of the audience attended. Minutes signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education (GH/jh).

**Attendance**
Present: Schmidt, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Wilson. Absent: Dr. Philippart. Also present: Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Detmer, Keyser, Recker, Fulcher, Canfield, Zendler, Zawislak, and West.

**Recognitions**
- Laura Duzey, Pupil Accounting Coordinator, and Isabella Ball, Data Services Specialist, recipients of the 2022 MPAAA Outstanding Service Award, nominated by Carolyn Claerhout, Manager of Pupil Services for Oakland County.
- Troy School District retirees for the 2021-2022 school year, whose names and service start years were read by Mr. Harris; each received a gift and certificate.
- Student Spotlight: Anoush Rophael, freshman at Athens High School, recognized through the TSD Creative Guild for producing, directing, and editing a video on the annual IA-East Art Show. Thomas Butcher introduced her.

**Actions and Votes**

| No. | Item | Moved / Supported | Vote |
|---|---|---|---|
| 22-041 | National Teacher Appreciation Week resolution, May 1-7, 2022 | Hammond / Gottlieb | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-042 | Mental Health Awareness Month proclamation (Oakland Community Health Network) | Wilson / Anne | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-043 | Consent agenda items A through H | Hauff / Anne | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |
| 22-044 | Two-year administrative contract without tenure to Mrs. Amy Wallace, Principal, Wattles Elementary, beginning 2022-23 | Gottlieb / Hammond | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |

| 22-048 | 2022 Oakland Schools Board election resolution under Public Act 419 of 2004 | Schmidt / Anne | Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart |

**Consent Agenda (22-043)**
Minutes of the April 5, 2022 Board Workshop; minutes of the April 19, 2022 Board Meeting; Treasurer's Report for March 2022; approval of the Oakland Intermediate School District budget; resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2022/2023 school year budget; food service contract renewal; and IA Okma Campus budget approval for the 2022/2023 school year.

**Bond and Facilities Report**
Facilities Review Committee members updated the Board on the upcoming bond proposal. Matt Sackrison described the methodology of the community survey gauging willingness to vote for a bond proposal and potential millage increases; Scott Courtney and Alison Hendry reported FRC feedback and top priorities for additional spending, including which buildings most need improvements.
