https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Official minutes of the regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education held Tuesday, May 17, 2022, in the Troy School District Services Building located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:01 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, and Wilson were present; Dr. Philippart was absent. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Birmingham, DiPilato, Griffor, Harris, Detmer, Keyser, Recker, Fulcher, Canfield, Zendler, Zawislak, and West. There were approximately 70 members of the audience. The meeting was adjourned at 9:39 p.m., and the minutes were respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the typist notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITIONS. The TSD Mission Moment honored Laura Duzey, Pupil Accounting Coordinator, and Isabella Ball, Data Services Specialist, recipients of the 2022 MPAAA Outstanding Service Award. They were nominated by Carolyn Claerhout, Manager of Pupil Services for Oakland County. The citation credited their leadership through the pupil accounting process, their integrity and commitment to the rules, and their internal and external relationship-building, which aided in maximizing student counts and obtaining clean pupil accounting audits.

The Board next recognized Troy School District employees who retired or announced their intention to retire at the end of the 2021-2022 school year. Mr. Harris read each name and length of service: Joyce Brasington (Principal, Wattles Elementary, since 2013); Cheryl Buxton (Teacher, Hamilton Elementary, since 2012); John Fedyk (Workforce Staff, Troy Career Center, since 1998); Tatiana Godlewski (Teacher, Athens, since 2000); Dawn Hayes (Teacher, Athens, since 1995); Kathy Hoppe (Secretary, Troy Learning Center, since 2016); Lois Hurdle (Secretary, Services Building, since 2000); Lynda Keough (Workforce Staff, Troy Career Center, since 2002); Jackie Kochanski (Para-Professional, TSD Preschool, since 2008); Laura Laga (Secretary, Services, since 2014); Jeff McCoy (Teacher, Martell/Morse, since 2000); Jane McKenney (Teacher, Baker Middle School, since 1981); John Morrison (Teacher, Troy High, since 1998); Brad Morton (Teacher, Athens, since 1990); Jane Moss (Teacher, Athens, since 1993); Tammy Polena (Teacher, Schroeder, since 1987); Rick Rinnan (Counselor, Athens, since 2000); Cheryl Schubeck (Workforce Staff, Troy Career Center, since 2007); Rosanne Thomas (Teacher, Barnard/Wattles, since 2004); and Rita Ward (Teacher, Morse, since 1989). Each retiree received congratulations from the Board along with a gift and certificate.

The monthly Student Spotlight recognized Anoush Rophael, a freshman at Athens High School, for work produced through the TSD Creative Guild. She produced, directed, and edited a video focused on the annual IA-East Art Show and the work of seniors over their four years in the art program. Thomas Butcher was invited to speak about Anoush and to share her video; she received praise from the Board and a certificate.

RESOLUTION 22-041, NATIONAL TEACHER APPRECIATION WEEK. Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Gottlieb, reciting that teachers inspire and nurture children, promote democratic equality, develop leaders, encourage critical thinking, and set the bar for excellence, and resolving that the Troy School District supports National Teacher Appreciation Week, May 1-7, 2022, and encourages schools and community to recognize the role of teachers. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

RESOLUTION 22-042, 2022 MENTAL HEALTH AWARENESS MONTH. Introduced in connection with Oakland Community Health Network (OCHN), which with its service provider network hosts initiatives promoting community awareness of mental illness and asked Oakland County school boards to approve a May proclamation. Moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Anne. Recitals noted the COVID-19 pandemic's reminder about integrating mental health into preparedness and public health response plans; disproportionately worse mental health outcomes, increased substance use, and elevated suicidal ideation among younger adults, racial/ethnic minorities, essential workers, and adult caregivers; the World Health Organization statistic that as many as one in six U.S. children ages 6-17 has a treatable mental health disorder such as depression, anxiety problems, or ADHD; Centers for Disease Control and Prevention data that between 2016-2019 approximately 5.8 million children ages 3-17 years were diagnosed with anxiety and 2.7 million were diagnosed with depression; the designation of May 5, 2022 as National Children's Mental Health Awareness Day and May 1 through May 7, 2022 as Children's Mental Health Awareness Week; and OCHN's commitment to being a Zero Suicide organization. The resolution recognized May 2022 as Mental Health Awareness Month. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: none. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION on agenda items: none.

CONSENT AGENDA, 22-043. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne, approving items A through H: minutes of the April 5, 2022 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the April 19, 2022 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report for March 2022; approval of the Oakland Intermediate School District Budget; a resolution to hold a public hearing on the proposed 2022/2023 school year budget; food service contract renewal; and IA Okma Campus budget approval for the 2022/2023 school year. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

PERSONNEL, 22-044. Moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Board issue a two-year administrative contract without tenure in the administrative position to Mrs. Amy Wallace, who will begin duties as Principal, Wattles Elementary, commencing with the 2022-23 school year. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. CURRICULUM: none.

BUSINESS, 22-045, SECONDARY COMPUTER LABS. Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mr. Gottlieb that replacement computers for the secondary labs be awarded as attached in the amount of $476,985.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

BUSINESS, 22-046, STADIUM LIGHTING. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mr. Hauff that the contract for new stadium lighting be awarded to Airport Lighting Employee-Owned LLC in the amount of $652,278.00, approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Funds. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart.

REPORT, FACILITIES REVIEW COMMITTEE BOND UPDATE. Members of the Facilities Review Committee updated the Board on the upcoming bond proposal. Matt Sackrison shared the methodology of the community survey conducted to gauge interest and willingness to vote for a bond proposal and potential millage increases. Scott Courtney and Alison Hendry provided FRC feedback and shared top priorities for additional spending, discussing which buildings were most in need of improvements. Board members asked questions about the FRC surveys, findings, and recommendations, and discussed the upcoming bond proposal, state qualified bonds, the effect on taxpayers, and interest rates.

RESOLUTION 22-047, PRELIMINARY QUALIFICATION OF THE PROPOSED BOND ISSUE. Moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Anne. Recitals stated the School District had considered capital improvement projects described in Exhibit A (the Proposed Projects), considered requesting voter approval for capital improvement bonds, and intended to request preliminary qualification from the Michigan Department of Treasury in order to qualify the bonds under the School Bond Qualification and Loan Program, noting that the Department requires the scope, dollar amount, and number of bond proposals to be determined before reviewing a draft application. The Board authorized administration to work with the District's architect, construction manager, bond counsel, financial advisor, and other professionals in preparing an Application for Preliminary Qualification of Bonds for submission to the Department, and to meet with Department representatives before final Board approval at a future meeting. The total amount of bonds to finance the Proposed Projects shall be not more than five hundred fifty-five million dollars ($555,000,000). The Board anticipated the bonds may be issued in one or more series and expected to submit the proposal to the electors at the Regular School Election to be held November 8, 2022. Conflicting resolutions were rescinded. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart; the resolution was declared adopted. A certification by the Secretary attests the resolution was adopted at a regular meeting held May 17, 2022 in compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION. Mrs. Tracy Owens, Troy resident and parent, addressed ESSER funds, spring tutoring, and the curriculum used to teach reading. Ms. Ashleigh Jennings spoke in support of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion and a safe, inclusive environment. Mr. Ollie Apahidean raised parental rights, concerns about indoctrination, and books available in District media centers. Mrs. Sarah Krieger raised concerns about the content of books in District libraries and read an excerpt. Mr. Jeff Schaeper described a recent meeting with administration. Mrs. Kelly Jones thanked the Board, teachers, staff, and student representatives. Ms. Sarah Primeau, parent of a junior, addressed Mental Health Awareness Month and was informed the resolution had already passed.

STUDENT REPRESENTATIVE REPORTS. Alyssa McLarty (Troy College and Career High School), Yara Mashal (International Academy-East), Hannah DiGiovanni (Athens High School, filling in for Sasha Palmkoeck), and Sarayu Bethamcherla (Troy High School).

OTHER, 22-048, 2022 OAKLAND SCHOOLS BOARD ELECTION. Moved by Mr. Schmidt and supported by Mrs. Anne, reciting Public Act 419 of 2004, which amended election procedures for Intermediate School Districts electing board members at a meeting of constituent district representatives and requires a constituent board to designate its representative and identify the candidate it supports by resolution adopted not earlier than 21 days prior to the election, considered at not less than one public meeting. The Board designated Gary Hauff as its representative and Vital Anne as alternate on the 2022 electoral body for the Oakland Schools Intermediate School District Board of Education; supported candidate Steve Gottlieb for the two positions, each for a term of six years ending June 30, 2028; and directed Gary Hauff to vote for Steve Gottlieb for both candidate positions at least on the first ballot at the June 6, 2022 election. Vote: Yes 6, No 0, Absent Philippart. The attached certification text references a regular meeting held on May 19, 2020.

BOARD COMMENTS. Mrs. Hammond expressed appreciation for teachers. Mr. Gottlieb thanked the student representatives and colleagues for support in the upcoming OISD election ballot. Mrs. Anne thanked teachers and described a professional development session showing job-embedded learning by third grade teachers. Mr. Hauff announced a Preschool Summer Camp at the Troy Learning Center from June 20 through August 12. Dr. Wilson thanked Troy teachers and endorsed the District's professional development. Dr. Machesky thanked the Facilities Review Committee, announced the TFEE Golf Outing on Friday, June 17 at Sanctuary Lake Golf Course with proceeds going back into classrooms, stated the District is not abandoning AP coursework and no changes will be made for the 2022-23 school year, and explained that course reviews broaden opportunities for students. Mr. Schmidt reported participating in APT to Succeed at Larson, discussed improvements in Reading Recovery efforts and improved reading proficiency scores for disadvantaged and special education students, and announced the next Board Workshop for June 14 at 6:00 p.m. in the Administration Building and the regular Board Meeting for June 21 at 7:00 p.m. at the Services Building.

**Document Type**
Resolution Approving Bond Proposition to Be Voted On at the General School Election, Troy School District, County of Oakland, Michigan, for a regular Board of Education meeting held in the School District on the 26th day of July, 2022, at 9:00 a.m. local time. The copy is an unexecuted template: PRESENT, ABSENT, Moved by, Supported by, YES, and NO fields are blank. Signature block is Gary Hauff, Secretary, Board of Education.

**Projects Contemplated**
Remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions to existing school buildings and other facilities; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; and acquiring sites, preparing, developing and improving sites, and the purchase of school buses.

**Resolved Clauses**
1. The School Improvement Bond Proposal attached as Exhibit A is approved and shall be submitted to the electors at the General School Election of November 8, 2022.
2. The Superintendent or his designee is authorized to certify the Proposal to the District's Election Coordinator, the Clerk of the County of Oakland, on or before 4:00 p.m. on August 16, 2022, not later than the twelfth Tuesday before the election.
3. The Superintendent or his designee is authorized to take any and all action required under Michigan Election Law for the November 8, 2022 election.
4. Conflicting resolutions and parts of resolutions are rescinded.

**Legal Framework**
The District is a Michigan general powers school district operating under the Revised School Code; its elections are governed by the Michigan Election Law, Act 116, Public Acts of Michigan, 1954, as amended. The Secretary's certification references the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended.

**Official Ballot: School Improvement Bond Proposition**
Asks whether the Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan, shall borrow not to exceed Five Hundred Fifty-Five Million Dollars ($555,000,000) and issue general obligation unlimited tax bonds in one or more series for: (a) remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities to create a modern learning environment and for health, safety, security and other purposes; (b) erecting, completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions; (c) acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; and (d) acquiring sites, preparing, developing and improving sites, and the purchase of school buses.

|---|---|

| Increase over annual debt millage levied in 2022 | 2 mill increase from 4.10 mills |

School Food Authorities whose weighted average paid lunch price in SY 2021-22 fell below the target weighted average price of $3.31 must either raise their weighted average lunch price or add non-Federal funds to the non-profit school food service account. The guidance also describes the non-Federal source contribution calculation, credit and shortfall carryover, and the data inputs required by the accompanying SY 2022-23 PLE Tool.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Purpose**
Guidance on the calculations School Food Authorities (SFAs) can use to ensure compliance with Paid Lunch Equity (PLE) requirements for School Year (SY) 2022-23. The tool described is for the contiguous States. Dated February 2022.

**SY 2022-23 Paid Lunch Equity Calculation**
For SY 2022-23, SFAs which, on a weighted average, charged less than the target weighted average price for paid lunches in SY 2021-22 must adjust their weighted average lunch price or add non-Federal funds to the non-profit school food service account.

| Target weighted average paid lunch price | Area |
|---|---|
| $3.31 | contiguous States |
| $3.87 | Hawaii, Guam, The U.S. Virgin Islands, and Puerto Rico |
| $5.37 | Alaska |

SFAs must use their unrounded adjusted average paid lunch price requirement from SY 2021-22 when calculating the weighted average lunch price increase for SY 2022-23. The guidance gives an example in which the unrounded SY 2021-22 requirement was $2.98 but the SFA opted to round down to $2.95. If an SFA raised its weighted average paid lunch price above the required amount in SY 2021-22, that excess may be subtracted from the total SY 2022-23 requirement; a shortfall carries the other direction. SFAs must keep sufficient records to document and carry forward the weighted average price calculations.

**Use of Non-Federal Sources**
SFAs that contribute non-Federal sources to the nonprofit school food service account in lieu of raising paid lunch prices determine the total number of paid reimbursable lunches claimed for the previous school year and multiply that by the difference between the SY 2021-22 weighted average paid lunch price requirement and the SY 2021-22 weighted average paid lunch price. Beginning in SY 2013-14, FNS expanded the definition of a non-Federal source. For SY 2022-23, SFAs may continue to count as a non-Federal source: (1) per-meal non-Federal reimbursement for any paid meal, including breakfast and lunch; (2) any funds provided by organizations for any paid meal; and (3) any proportion attributable to paid meals from direct payments made from school district funds to support lunch service.

**Credit for Excess Non-Federal Funds**
If an SFA's SY 2021-22 estimate of the required contribution exceeded the actual level, the excess may be subtracted from the SY 2022-23 requirement; if the estimate was less than required, additional non-Federal funds must be added. The non-Federal Calculator tab applies the same crediting rationale used for paid lunch prices.

**SY 2022-23 PLE Tool**
The first tab contains detailed instructions, which users are advised to print and read first. The Tool calculates the weighted average paid lunch price for SY 2021-22, the required average weighted paid lunch price increase for SY 2022-23, and the required non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23, accounting for credits or shortfalls accrued. A split feature allows SFAs to meet the requirement by both raising prices and contributing non-Federal funds.

**Data Needed**
All SFAs: the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement, or the SY 2010-11 weighted average price, or the most recent unrounded figure; all paid lunch prices for October 2021; and the number of paid lunches served associated with each paid lunch price in October 2021. SFAs contributing non-Federal sources also need the total number of paid lunches served in SY 2021-2022 and the total dollar amount of non-Federal contributions for SY 2011-12, SY 2012-13, SY 2013-14, SY 2014-15, SY 2015-16, SY 2016-17, SY 2017-18, SY 2018-19, SY 2019-2020, SY 2020-2021, and SY 2021-2022. The Tool includes a report SFAs can print and retain for their SY 2023-24 calculations.

Federal guidance document included as item 8A in the July 26, 2022 Troy Board of Education packet, titled in the packet as FS Lunch Prices_1 and dated February 2022. It provides guidance on the calculations School Food Authorities (SFAs) can use in order to ensure they are in compliance with the Paid Lunch Equity requirements for School Year (SY) 2022-23, and states that the tool described is for the contiguous States.

SY 2022-23 PAID LUNCH EQUITY CALCULATIONS. For SY 2022-23, SFAs which, on a weighted average, charged less than the target weighted average price of $3.31 for paid lunches in SY 2021-22 are required to adjust their weighted average lunch price or add non-Federal funds to the non-profit school food service account. The corresponding target weighted average prices for other areas are $3.87 in Hawaii, Guam, The U.S. Virgin Islands, and Puerto Rico, and $5.37 in Alaska. SFAs are reminded that they must use their unrounded adjusted average paid lunch price requirement from SY 2021-22 when calculating the weighted average lunch price increase for SY 2022-23. The guidance offers the example that if the unrounded SY 2021-22 requirement was $2.98 but the SFA opted to round down to $2.95, the calculation of the SY 2022-23 requirement is based on the unrounded figure. If an SFA raised its weighted average paid lunch price above the required amount in SY 2021-22, that excess paid lunch price increase may be subtracted from the total SY 2022-23 paid lunch price increase requirement. SFAs must keep sufficient records to document and carry forward the weighted average price calculations. If an SFA did not raise its weighted average adjusted paid lunch price sufficiently to meet the required amount in SY 2021-22, the shortfall carries forward.

USE OF NON-FEDERAL SOURCES CALCULATION. SFAs that choose to contribute non-Federal sources to the nonprofit school food service account in lieu of raising paid lunch prices must calculate the appropriate amount to contribute. To determine the amount of required revenue in lieu of a paid lunch price increase, the SFA determines the total number of paid reimbursable lunches claimed for the previous school year and multiplies that by the difference between the SY 2021-22 weighted average paid lunch price requirement and the SY 2021-22 weighted average paid lunch price.

SOURCES OF NON-FEDERAL FUNDS. Beginning in SY 2013-14, FNS expanded the definition of a non-Federal source to include all paid meals, in order to help SFAs meet the PLE requirement and to acknowledge continuing support by States and localities to improve access to and participation in the breakfast program; FNS reports having received positive response to this flexibility. Therefore, for SY 2022-23, SFAs may continue to count as a non-Federal source: (1) per-meal non-Federal reimbursement for any paid meal, such as breakfast or lunch; (2) any funds provided by organizations for any paid meal; and (3) any proportion attributable to paid meals from direct payments made from school district funds to support lunch service.

CREDIT FOR EXCESS NON-FEDERAL FUNDS. If an SFA's SY 2021-22 estimate of the required contribution exceeded the actual level, that excess contribution may be subtracted from the total SY 2022-23 contribution requirement. If the SY 2021-22 estimate was less than required, additional funds from non-Federal sources must be added. The non-Federal Calculator tab in the PLE Tool, used to determine the estimated amount of non-Federal source contributions, allows these calculations using the same rationale applied to paid lunch prices, crediting extra funds contributed and accounting for shortfalls when determining the non-Federal funds requirement for the next school year.

SY 2022-23 PLE TOOL. The first tab of the SY 2022-23 PLE Tool includes detailed instructions on how to use the tool and what information is needed to complete the appropriate calculations; each user is recommended to print and read the instructions before attempting the calculations. The attached SY 2022-23 PLE Tool makes the following calculations: the weighted average paid lunch price for SY 2021-22; the required average weighted paid lunch price increase for SY 2022-23; and the required non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23. The Tool takes into account adjustments to paid lunch prices made by the SFA in SY 2021-22 to calculate any credit or shortfall accrued for SY 2022-23, and for SFAs that opted to contribute non-Federal funds it also calculates credits and shortfalls for the SY 2022-23 required non-Federal contribution. The Tool additionally includes a feature that makes calculations for SFAs wishing to split the SY 2022-23 requirement by both raising prices and contributing non-Federal funds, an option described as potentially attractive to SFAs that do not want to raise the weighted average paid lunch price by the entire required amount.

REQUIRED DATA INPUTS. All SFAs need the following data to calculate the Weighted Average Price for SY 2022-23: the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement, or the SY 2010-11 weighted average price, or the most recent unrounded figure; all paid lunch prices for October 2021; and the number of paid lunches served associated with each paid lunch price in October 2021. SFAs that have opted to contribute non-Federal sources also need the total number of paid lunches served in SY 2021-2022 and the total dollar amount of non-Federal contributions for SY 2011-12, SY 2012-13, SY 2013-14, SY 2014-15, SY 2015-16, SY 2016-17, SY 2017-18, SY 2018-19, SY 2019-2020, SY 2020-2021, and SY 2021-2022. SFAs wishing to split the SY 2022-23 requirement by both raising paid lunch prices and contributing non-Federal sources need all of the above information. The PLE Tool also includes a report SFAs can use to track the information needed for their SY 2023-24 calculations, which they can print and keep in their records.

**Document**
School Year (SY) 2022-23 Paid Lunch Equity (PLE) Tool Instructions, dated February 2022, with a blank SFA NAME field. Users are advised they may want to print the instructions and use them while working through the Tool. This version of the PLE Tool applies only to SY 2022-23; a new version will be issued for SY 2023-24.

**Purpose and Authority**
The PLE Tool was created to help School Food Authorities (SFAs) calculate their paid lunch price increase requirement and/or non-Federal source contributions to meet the requirements specified in 7 CFR 210.14(e). If the pricing requirements calculated by the Tool are not met or are exceeded, the Tool also calculates any amounts, including credits or deficits, carried over into the next year. The weighted average prices calculated are the weighted average of all student paid lunch prices charged in the SFA. For more information on amounts carried over, the instructions refer to FNS Policy Memo SP 39-2011 (revised).

**Tips Listed**
1) Have the most recent year PLE tool completed available for reference. 2) Did the SFA have credits carried over from prior years? 3) Is the most recent weighted average paid lunch price above the requirement? 4) Only the tab(s) relevant to the SFA's selected method need to be completed. 5) The $0.10 cap does not mean that every SFA will raise the weighted average paid lunch price or contribute the equivalent in non-Federal funds; depending on where the SFA stands, less than $0.10 may be required or the SFA may choose to contribute more.

**Tab Structure**
The instructions state the SY 2022-23 PLE Tool consists of 8 tabs, with hyperlinks placed throughout for navigation.

| Tab | Content |
|---|---|
| Tab 1 | Instructions |
| Tab 2 | Annual Unrounded Requirement Finder |
| Tab 3 | SY 2022-23 Price Calculator / Price Adjustment Calculator |
| Tab 4 | SY 2022-23 Non-Federal Calculator |
| Tab 5 | SY 2022-23 Split Calculator |
| Tab 6 | SY 2022-23 REPORT |
| Tab 7 | SY 21-22 Price Calculator (optional, as needed) |
| Tab 8 | SY 10-11 Price Calculator (optional, as needed) |
| Tab 9 | PLE Guidance |

Shaded cells designate data entry cells that the SFA must complete for the tool to calculate requirements.

**Data Required**
To calculate the Weighted Average Price for SY 2022-23: the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price; the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price if the SY 2021-22 figure is unknown; all student paid lunch prices for October 2021; and the number of paid lunches served associated with each student paid lunch price in October 2021. SFAs that opted to contribute non-Federal sources also need the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price as needed, the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price if different, the total number of student paid lunches served in SY 2020-21, and the total dollar amount of non-Federal contributions through SY 2021-22.

**Method Walkthroughs**
Weighted average price method: enter the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement in the orange box (using the annual unrounded requirement finder if unknown), then enter October 2021 student paid lunch counts and prices in the Price Calculator; the tool computes amounts needed to meet SY 2022-23 requirements and amounts carried forward to SY 2023-24. An optional Pricing Estimation Calculator lets the SFA vary individual prices until the weighted average reaches the new requirement. Non-Federal source method: enter the unrounded requirement, the current weighted average student paid lunch price, the student paid lunch count for the entire 2020-21 school year, and the amount of non-Federal source funds contributed from SY 2011-12 through SY 2021-22; the tool applies the $0.10 cap if applicable and computes the remaining annual contribution for SY 2022-23, the remaining contribution carried forward to SY 2023-24, and remaining credit carried forward. Split method: combines both, with a New Price Increase entry for the weighted average price the SFA plans to charge in SY 2022-23. Optional tabs 7 and 8 support calculations from previous years.

For more information on amounts carried over, the document refers to FNS Policy Memo SP 39-2011 (revised). This version of the PLE Tool applies only to SY 2022-23; a new version of the PLE Tool will be issued for SY 2023-24.

TAB STRUCTURE. The instructions state that the SY 2022-23 PLE Tool consists of 8 tabs, with hyperlinks placed throughout the tool to navigate between them, and that only the tabs for the selected method have to be completed. The tabs identified are Tab 1: Instructions; Tab 2: Annual Unrounded Requirement Finder; Tab 3: SY 2022-23 Price Calculator, also referenced as the SY 2022-23 Price Adjustment Calculator; Tab 4: SY 2022-23 Non-Federal Calculator; Tab 5: SY 2022-23 Split Calculator; Tab 6: SY 2022-23 REPORT; Tab 7: SY 21-22 Price Calculator; Tab 8: SY 10-11 Price Calculator; and Tab 9: PLE Guidance. The SY 21-22 and SY 10-11 Price Calculator tabs are for use as needed. Shaded cells designate data entry cells, and the SFA must enter the applicable data in those cells for the tool to calculate requirements. Only the tabs for the method used to meet the requirement, raising prices, contributing non-Federal sources, or the split calculator, should be completed.

DATA NEEDED. SFAs need the following data to calculate the Weighted Average Price for SY 2022-23: (1) the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price; (2) the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price, if the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price is unknown; (3) all student paid lunch prices for October 2021; and (4) the number of paid lunches served associated with each student paid lunch price in October 2021. SFAs that opted to contribute non-Federal sources for SY 2022-23 need: (1) the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price, as needed; (2) the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price, if different from the SY 2010-11 Weighted Average Price; (3) the total number of student paid lunches served in SY 2020-21; and (4) the total dollar amount of non-Federal contributions through SY 2021-22.

WEIGHTED AVERAGE PAID LUNCH PRICE CALCULATION. Step 1 directs the user to enter the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement in the orange box, using the annual unrounded requirement finder if that requirement is not known; this figure sets the pricing requirements throughout the Tool and helps determine amounts carried forward, and was calculated through the SY 2021-22 PLE Tool. After calculating the SY 2022-23 weighted average price requirement for student paid lunches, the user clicks the link to the SY 2022-23 Price Calculator. In Step 2, the box at the top of the tab displays the SY 2022-23 Weighted Average Price Requirement; to calculate the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price, the SFA enters the student paid lunch count for October 2021 associated with each paid meal price in the Monthly # of Paid Lunches column, and enters each student paid lunch price in the SFA, including all schools such as elementary, middle, and high, for October 2021 in the Paid Lunch Price column. Using the SY 2021-22 weighted average price, the tool calculates amounts necessary to meet the SY 2022-23 weighted average price requirements and any amounts carried forward to SY 2023-24. A report is generated for use in the SY 2022-23 PLE tool displaying the SY 2022-23 requirements and any amount carried forward as determined on the SY 2022-23 Price Calculator, and the user selects the SY 2022-23 method used to ensure sufficient funds are provided for paid lunches.

OPTIONAL STEP 3, PRICING ESTIMATION CALCULATOR. After calculating the SY 2022-23 average student paid lunch price requirement, the PLE tool can be used to determine how the SFA wants to distribute the price increase within the SFA to reach the new average paid lunch price. The SFA enters the student paid lunch count for October 2021 associated with each student paid meal price in the Monthly # of Paid Lunches column, then changes individual student paid lunch prices until the average student paid lunch price reaches the new average requirement, which appears in the Weighted Average Price box. SFAs have flexibility to raise individual student prices using many different price combinations so that the weighted average student price equals the new SY 2022-23 required level.

NON-FEDERAL SOURCE CONTRIBUTION CALCULATION. Step 1 again requires entry of the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement in the orange box, with the annual unrounded requirement finder available if unknown; this figure was calculated through the SY 2021-22 PLE Tool. After calculating the SY 2022-23 weighted average price requirement for paid lunches, the user goes to the SY 2022-23 Non-Federal Source Calculator tab. In Step 2, the box at the top of the tab displays the SY 2021-22 Weighted Average Price Requirement. The user enters the current weighted average student paid lunch price, which may be the same as the SY 2021-22 weighted average price determined on the Unrounded Requirement Finder tab if the SFA did not raise the weighted average price in SY 2021-2022; the most current average weighted price can be determined on the SY 2021-2022 Price Calculator tab. The user then enters the student paid lunch count for the entire 2020-21 School Year in the orange Annual # of Paid Lunches box in the Non-Federal Source Contribution Calculator for SY 2022-23, and enters the amount of non-Federal source funds contributed for SY 2011-12 through SY 2021-22 in the orange box labeled as such. The Tool calculates the annual non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23 and applies the $0.10 cent cap if applicable. Based on the actual amount contributed for SY 2021-22, the tool calculates the remaining annual non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23, the remaining annual non-Federal source contribution carried forward to SY 2023-24, and the remaining credit carried forward to SY 2023-24.

SPLIT CALCULATOR. This tab is for SFAs wishing to split their requirement by both raising prices and contributing non-Federal sources. Step 1 enters the SY 2021-22 unrounded price requirement; Step 2 displays the SY 2022-23 Weighted Average Price Requirement and requires entry of October 2021 student paid lunch counts and each student paid lunch price across all schools; Step 3 requires entry of the weighted average price the SFA plans to charge for student paid lunches in SY 2022-23 in the New Price Increase field; and Step 4 requires entry of the student paid lunch count for the entire 2020-2021 School Year in the orange Annual # of Paid Lunches box and the actual amount of the non-Federal source contribution in the orange box labeled Amount of Non-Federal Source Funds Contributed from SY 2011-12 through SY 2021-22. The tool then calculates the remaining annual non-Federal source contribution for SY 2022-23, the remaining annual contribution carried forward to SY 2023-24, and the remaining credit carried forward to SY 2023-24. SFAs may use optional tabs 7 and 8 to make calculations from previous years.

**Instrument and parties**
First Amendment to the Amended and Restated Pupil Transportation and Transportation Fleet Maintenance Services Contract, entered into as of July 1, 2025 (the Effective Date), attached to and made part of the Contract dated July 1, 2022. Parties: TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, a Michigan general powers school district, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098; and FIRST STUDENT, INC., a Delaware corporation, 191 Rosa Parks Street, Suite 800, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202. Agenda item 3.b, June 3, 2025 meeting. Document control stamp 282059785.v1.

**Renewal Term**
Under Section 2.2, the School District exercises its option to extend, with the Parties agreeing to modify Section 2.2 and extend for two (2) years, commencing July 1, 2025 and expiring June 30, 2027. Thereafter the District may extend by up to one (1) additional year on a year-to-year basis, subject to written approval in its sole and absolute discretion (the Extension Term). Extension Term rates are to be mutually agreed under Section 10.3. The Contractor is stated to have no expectation of a contract beyond the Renewal Term.

**Other amended terms**
Exhibit B is replaced in its entirety. Sections 19.1 and 19.2 (Notices) are amended: notices to the District go to the Superintendent, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098, copy to Jeremy S. Motz, Esq., Clark Hill PLC, 220 Park Street, Suite 200, Birmingham, Michigan 48009; notices to the Contractor go to First Student, Inc., Attn: Area General Manager, 120 Hart Avenue, Troy, Michigan 48098, copy to FirstGroup American, Attn: General Counsel, 191 Rosa Parks Street, 8th Floor, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202. A Change In Law clause terminates the District's obligations if federal or state law makes payment of the Rates illegal, impracticable or impossible. Further modification requires a writing signed by both Parties; the Contract is ratified and reaffirmed except as modified, with the First Amendment controlling in a conflict; execution may be in counterparts.

**Exhibit B charges and rates (Transportation & Bus Maintenance Services)**

| Pricing parameter | # of Routes | 2025-2026 | 2026-2027 |
|---|---|---|---|
| General Education Route Daily Route Charge | 33 | $306.78 | $334.39 |
| Special Needs Route Daily Route Charge - In District | 17 | $454.93 | $495.87 |
| Special Needs Route Daily Route Charge - Out of District | 7 | $454.93 | $495.87 |
| Mid-Day Runs & Shuttles (hourly, if not attached to Route) | 24 | $78.33 | $85.38 |
| Special Needs Route Daily Route Charge - Summer | 20 | $379.63 | $413.80 |
| Extra-Curricular/Athletic Trips (per hour) | Varies | $69.91 | $76.20 |
| Transportation Aides (per hour) | | $33.63 | $36.66 |

Footnotes state the charges include all costs and expenses for maintenance services for the buses; the Special Needs Daily Route Charge includes Out-District and Wing Lake Routes; the General Education Daily Route Charge also includes Summer General Education Routes; and extra-curricular/athletic trips carry a 1-hour minimum charge. White Fleet maintenance labor rates (parts at cost) are left to be mutually agreed before services are performed.

**Pricing assumptions**
Daily Route Charges assume an average Daily Route Time of 6.0 hours per day per Route, measured gate to gate from the District's Transportation Facility. Field, athletic and extra-curricular trips are invoiced hourly in quarter-hour increments. Pricing assumes 175 days per academic year of regular route service, with a 175-day Academic School Year Minimum; one free dry run per Route is provided before school year start-up. Snow days are billed at 80% of the Daily Route Charge when driver pay is documented, otherwise 40%; intermittent closures at 40%; extended closures beyond ten consecutive school days at 70% or 25% depending on driver employment status. The District supplies fuel. A route-volume change of 10% or greater is deemed material and triggers good-faith renegotiation.

The First Amendment to the Amended and Restated Pupil Transportation and Transportation Fleet Maintenance Services Contract is entered into as of July 1, 2025, designated the Effective Date, and is attached to and made a part of the Amended and Restated Pupil Transportation and Transportation Fleet Maintenance Services Contract dated July 1, 2022. The Parties are TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, described as a Michigan general powers school district with an address of 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098, and FIRST STUDENT, INC., a Delaware corporation with an address of 191 Rosa Parks Street, Suite 800, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202. All capitalized terms carry the meanings set forth in the Contract unless expressly noted. The recital states that the Parties desire to exercise a Renewal Term and to amend the Contract Rates and other terms and conditions. The item appears on the Troy Board of Education agenda as 3.b for the June 3, 2025 meeting. Each page of the instrument carries the document control stamp 282059785.v1, and the signature block provides unexecuted By / Its / Date lines for TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT and FIRST STUDENT, INC.

Section 1, Renewal Term of Contract, recites that pursuant to Section 2.2 of the Contract the School District desires to exercise its option to extend, provided that the Parties agree to modify Section 2.2 and extend the Contract for two (2) years, commencing July 1, 2025 and expiring on June 30, 2027, defined as the Renewal Term. Thereafter the School District has the option to extend by up to one (1) additional year on a year-to-year basis, subject to the written approval of the School District in its sole and absolute discretion, defined as the Extension Term. Rates for any Extension Term are to be mutually agreed in accordance with Section 10.3 of the Contract. Nothing requires the School District to exercise the option, and the Contractor is stated to have no expectation of a contract beyond the Renewal Term or any exercised Extension Term.

Section 2, Rates, provides that as of the Effective Date the Rates set forth in Exhibit B are updated and Exhibit B of the Contract is replaced in its entirety with the Exhibit B attached to the First Amendment. Section 3, Notices, amends Sections 19.1 and 19.2 in their entirety while leaving the remainder of Section 19 unchanged. Under amended Section 19.1, required notices to the School District go to the Superintendent, Troy School District, 4400 Livernois Road, Troy, Michigan 48098, with a copy to Jeremy S. Motz, Esq., Clark Hill PLC, 220 Park Street, Suite 200, Birmingham, Michigan 48009. Under amended Section 19.2, required notices to the Contractor go to First Student, Inc., Attn: Area General Manager, 120 Hart Avenue, Troy, Michigan 48098, with a copy to FirstGroup American, Attn: General Counsel, 191 Rosa Parks Street, 8th Floor, Cincinnati, Ohio 45202.

Section 4, Change In Law, provides that if any federal or state law, rule, regulation or ordinance is enacted, modified or otherwise changed that would make the School District's payment of the Rates and fees illegal, impracticable or impossible to pay, the School District's obligations under the First Amendment and the Contract cease and are not in effect. Section 5 limits further modification to a written agreement signed by both Parties. Section 6 states in capitals that the Contract is ratified and reaffirmed and continues in full force and effect except as modified, and that in the event of a conflict the First Amendment controls. Section 7 permits execution in one or more counterparts, each an original and all together constituting one document.

Exhibit B, captioned Contractor's Pricing, opens with pricing assumptions and conditions. Daily Route Charges are billed per Route per day; a Route includes the AM tier runs, Mid-Day or Shuttle runs if any, and PM tier runs operated by the same bus as part of the same Route package, and a Mid-Day or Shuttle run built into an AM/PM package is included in the daily Route charge while one not incorporated into a package is charged at the applicable listed rate. Daily Route Charges are based on an average daily Route time of 6.0 hours of service per day per Route, the Daily Route Time, calculated gate to gate from the School District's Transportation Facility. All Field Trips, Athletic Trips and Extra-Curricular Trips are calculated and invoiced on an hourly basis or portion thereof in quarter-hour increments.

The Contractor's pricing and fixed costs assume the School District operates school and requires regular route home-to-school transportation for 175 days per academic year for general education routing. The Contractor will conduct one (1) dry run for each Route in advance of school year start-up without charge. A 175-day Academic School Year Minimum applies to regularly scheduled Routes, with the academic year running from the first day of school in September until the last day of school in June and excluding summer transportation. The School District is not charged for Routes on days school is not in session or when Other Transportation Services are not operated, provided cancellation follows Section 10.1, subject to stated exceptions. For snow days, the School District is charged 80% of the Daily Route Charge for each Route not operated provided the Contractor demonstrates that all bus drivers are paid at their normal rate for their normally scheduled route; if the Contractor fails to pay or document such payment, the charge drops to the 40% rate. For intermittent closures, where the School District operates less than 180 per academic school year requiring Transportation Services because of power outages or similar intermittent events, the charge is 40% of the Daily Route Charge for each Route not operated less than 175 days.

Extended closures are defined as a period extending beyond ten (10) consecutive school days. Where the District replaces in-person instruction with hybrid or remote learning, it agrees to pay 70% of the then-current cost per Route per day for each Route not operated, provided that a qualified and trained bus driver is assigned and in active employment status receiving at least the driver's daily minimum pay rate; that all other Contractor staff positions, namely the Site Manager, Dispatcher and Router (the Management Personnel) and one (1) Mechanic (the Maintenance Personnel), remain in active employment status at full pay; that all wages are paid at prevailing or regular rates rather than a discounted hourly wage; and that the Contractor performs all other Transportation and Maintenance Services within contract parameters. If the Driver is not in active employment status receiving full pay, the rate is 25% of the then-current cost per Route per day. The School District may elect to operate under the 25% provision at its option during an extended closure. As a condition of payment, no later than five (5) days after each weekly or bi-weekly payroll cycle the Contractor must make available for inspection all books, records and data related to wages paid to personnel assigned to the School District; if verification shows terms were not met or that personnel are no longer employed, laid off or furloughed, charges are adjusted and the Contractor must reimburse overpayments. If the District operates under the 70% provision and also runs a food delivery program, athletic or extra-curricular routes or other auxiliary transportation, the Contractor uses staff from its to/from school or extra trips service team without additional fee unless services exceed contemplated parameters.

The Contractor's rates assume the School District provides the necessary fuel, and the Contractor is liable for all costs and expenses associated with misuse of that fuel. If changes to District operations cause a material increase or decrease in the volume of Routes, the Parties will convene and negotiate in good faith changes to Route Rates and Charges, with material defined as a change of equal to or greater than 10%. Adjustments to charges for any Extension Term follow Section 10.3.

The Charges and Rates schedule for Transportation & Bus Maintenance Services lists, by pricing parameter, number of routes and rate for 2025-2026 and 2026-2027: General Education Route Daily Route Charge, based upon 6.0 Daily Route Time, 33 routes at $306.78 and $334.39; Special Needs Education Route Daily Route Charge - In District, 17 routes at $454.93 and $495.87; Special Needs Education Route Daily Route Charge - Out of District, 7 routes at $454.93 and $495.87; Mid-Day Runs & Shuttles, hourly charge per run if not attached to a Route, 24 at $78.33 and $85.38; Special Needs Education Route Daily Route Charge - Summer, 20 routes at $379.63 and $413.80; and Extra-Curricular/Athletic Trips, charge per hour, quantity Varies, at $69.91 and $76.20. Exhibit B, captioned Contractor's Pricing, opens with pricing assumptions and conditions. Daily Route Charges are billed per Route per day; a Route includes the AM tier runs, Mid-Day or Shuttle runs if any, and PM tier runs operated by the same bus as part of the same Route package, and a Mid-Day or Shuttle run built into an AM/PM package is included in the daily Route charge while one not incorporated into a package is charged at the applicable listed rate. Daily Route Charges are based on an average daily Route time of 6.0 hours of service per day per Route, the Daily Route Time, calculated gate to gate from the School District's Transportation Facility. All Field Trips, Athletic Trips and Extra-Curricular Trips are calculated and invoiced on an hourly basis or portion thereof in quarter-hour increments.

The Contractor's pricing and fixed costs assume the School District operates school and requires regular route home-to-school transportation for 175 days per academic year for general education routing. The Contractor will conduct one (1) dry run for each Route in advance of school year start-up without charge. A 175-day Academic School Year Minimum applies to regularly scheduled Routes, with the academic year running from the first day of school in September until the last day of school in June and excluding summer transportation. The School District is not charged for Routes on days school is not in session or when Other Transportation Services are not operated, provided cancellation follows Section 10.1, subject to stated exceptions. For snow days, the School District is charged 80% of the Daily Route Charge for each Route not operated provided the Contractor demonstrates that all bus drivers are paid at their normal rate for their normally scheduled route; if the Contractor fails to pay or document such payment, the charge drops to the 40% rate. For intermittent closures, where the School District operates less than 180 per academic school year requiring Transportation Services because of power outages or similar intermittent events, the charge is 40% of the Daily Route Charge for each Route not operated less than 175 days.

Extended closures are defined as a period extending beyond ten (10) consecutive school days. Where the District replaces in-person instruction with hybrid or remote learning, it agrees to pay 70% of the then-current cost per Route per day for each Route not operated, provided that a qualified and trained bus driver is assigned and in active employment status receiving at least the driver's daily minimum pay rate; that all other Contractor staff positions, namely the Site Manager, Dispatcher and Router (the Management Personnel) and one (1) Mechanic (the Maintenance Personnel), remain in active employment status at full pay; that all wages are paid at prevailing or regular rates rather than a discounted hourly wage; and that the Contractor performs all other Transportation and Maintenance Services within contract parameters. If the Driver is not in active employment status receiving full pay, the rate is 25% of the then-current cost per Route per day. The School District may elect to operate under the 25% provision at its option during an extended closure. As a condition of payment, no later than five (5) days after each weekly or bi-weekly payroll cycle the Contractor must make available for inspection all books, records and data related to wages paid to personnel assigned to the School District; if verification shows terms were not met or that personnel are no longer employed, laid off or furloughed, charges are adjusted and the Contractor must reimburse overpayments. If the District operates under the 70% provision and also runs a food delivery program, athletic or extra-curricular routes or other auxiliary transportation, the Contractor uses staff from its to/from school or extra trips service team without additional fee unless services exceed contemplated parameters.

The Contractor's rates assume the School District provides the necessary fuel, and the Contractor is liable for all costs and expenses associated with misuse of that fuel. If changes to District operations cause a material increase or decrease in the volume of Routes, the Parties will convene and negotiate in good faith changes to Route Rates and Charges, with material defined as a change of equal to or greater than 10%. Adjustments to charges for any Extension Term follow Section 10.3.

**Form and association**
Michigan High School Athletic Association membership resolution for 2025-26, presented as item 6E on the June 17, 2025 Troy Board of Education agenda. The MHSAA is located at 1661 Ramblewood Drive, East Lansing, MI 48823, telephone (517) 332-5046. It is described as a voluntary, nonprofit corporation of public, private and parochial junior high/middle and senior high schools whose boards of education or governing bodies have applied for and received membership on behalf of their secondary schools. Completed forms are to be saved and sent to camala@mhsaa.com as an attachment, with one signed copy returned and one retained.

**Terms of membership**
The association sponsors statewide tournaments and makes eligibility rules for participation. Boards that wish to host or participate must join and agree to abide by and enforce MHSAA rules, regulations and qualifications on eligibility, game rules and tournament policies, procedures and schedules. Participation in MHSAA postseason tournaments is conditioned on high schools adhering to at least the minimum standards of Regulation I and the maximum limitations of Regulation II in all MHSAA tournament sports. MHSAA tournaments are the collective property of the association rather than of any individual member school, and the association reserves rights over publication information, exclusive arrangements for recognition and exposure, restrictive policies against exploitation and commercialization, proprietary interests, and the use of images or transmissions identifying officials, spectators, students, personnel and marks. Resolutions that are modified or supplemented with letters imposing additional conditions are rejected.

**Resolution language**
The resolution covers the year August 1, 2025 through July 31, 2026 and enrolls the named schools as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc. and to participate in its approved interschool athletic activities. The board delegates supervision and control of those activities to the Superintendent or designee, accepts the association's Constitution and By-Laws, and adopts the rules, regulations and interpretations in the current Handbook as minimum standards and as the governing code, agreeing to primary enforcement. The authorization is effective from August 1, 2025 until July 31, 2026 and may not be revoked during that period. A Record of Adoption block provides for the day and month in 2025, the governing body name, board secretary or designee signature, address, city and zip, and contact e-mail; all are blank.

**Eligibility rules for listed schools**
Under the MHSAA Constitution, high schools, junior high/middle schools and comparable schools may join provided the building has enrollment and onsite attendance of at least 15 students, whether grades 6 through 8 or 9, 7 through 8 or 9, or 9 or 10 through 12, and provided nonpublic schools qualify for federal income tax exemption as not-for-profit organizations. Schools may join at the 6th-grade level to reach the 15-student minimum whether or not 6th-graders participate. Districts are not required to hold junior high/middle school membership or to sponsor 6th-grade athletics. If a listed junior high/middle school sponsors a 6th-grade team in any sport or lets a 6th-grader play with 7th and 8th graders, all of Regulations III and IV apply to all 6th-graders in all sports involving 6th-graders on that school's teams; if no 6th-graders participate in a sport, MHSAA rules do not apply in that sport.

**Completed entry**
The school listing pages are largely blank templates for up to 15 high schools and multiple junior high/middle schools. The single filled entry is line 4 under member junior high/middle schools: SMITH MIDDLE SCHOOL, grade configuration 6-8, anticipated 2025-26 7th and 8th grade enrollment of 419, anticipated 2025-26 6th-grade enrollment of 184, with Yes marked for 6th-graders participating in at least one sport with 7th and 8th graders and grade levels for membership marked 6, 7 and 8.

The association sponsors statewide tournaments and makes eligibility rules with respect to participation in MHSAA-sponsored tournaments in the various sports. Each board of education or governing body that wishes to host or participate in such meets and tournaments must join the MHSAA and agree to abide by and enforce MHSAA rules, regulations and qualifications concerning eligibility, game rules, and tournament policies, procedures and schedules. It is stated as a condition for participation in any MHSAA postseason tournaments that high schools adhere to at least the minimum standards of Regulation I and the maximum limitations of Regulation II in all MHSAA tournament sports.

The form asserts that MHSAA tournaments are the collective property of the MHSAA and not of any individual member school, and that the association reserves the right to promote and advance the membership's interests through publication information; exclusive arrangements to create recognition and exposure for school-sponsored activities; restrictive policies prohibiting exploitation and commercialization of MHSAA-sponsored tournaments; appropriate proprietary interests; and the use of images or transmissions identifying contest officials, spectators, and member schools' students, personnel and marks. To obtain membership the board of education or governing body must adopt the resolution for its junior high/middle and senior high schools; the resolution must be formally ratified and properly signed, with one signed copy returned to the MHSAA for its files and one copy retained. Resolutions that are modified in any way or supplemented with letters placing additional conditions on MHSAA membership or tournament participation are to be rejected. The form directs the user twice to save the document and send it to camala@mhsaa.com as an attachment.

The membership resolution itself is captioned for the year August 1, 2025 through July 31, 2026. It provides blanks for the schools under the direction of the board, the city or township, and the county, all within the State of Michigan, and states that such schools are hereby (A) enrolled as members of the Michigan High School Athletic Association, Inc., a nonprofit association, and (B) further enrolled to participate in the approved interschool athletic activities sponsored by that association. The board of education or governing body delegates to the Superintendent or designee the responsibility for the supervision and control of those activities, accepts the Constitution and By-Laws of the association, and adopts as its own the rules, regulations and interpretations, as minimum standards, published in the current Handbook as the governing code under which the schools shall conduct their program of interscholastic athletics, agreeing to primary enforcement of those rules, regulations, interpretations and qualifications. Schools that host or participate in association meets and tournaments must follow and enforce all tournament policies, procedures and schedules. The authorization is effective from August 1, 2025 and remains effective until July 31, 2026, during which period it may not be revoked. A note specifies that junior high/middle and senior high schools of the school system to be listed as MHSAA members and to receive MHSAA mailings during 2025-26 must be listed on the back of the form.

The Record of Adoption block states that the resolution was adopted by the board of education or governing body of named schools on a blank day of a blank month, 2025, and is so recorded in the minutes of that board's meeting. Signature lines are provided for the governing body name, board secretary signature or designee with a checkbox to indicate a designee, address, city and zip code, and contact e-mail. As presented, these lines are unfilled.

The reverse side, headed Schools Which Are To Be MHSAA Members During 2025-26, sets out eligibility conditions from the MHSAA Constitution. All high schools, junior high/middle schools, or other Michigan schools doing a corresponding grade of work may become members provided that the school building has enrollment and onsite attendance of at least 15 students, whether for grades 6 through 8 or 9, grades 7 through 8 or 9, or grades 9 or 10 through 12; and, if a nonpublic school, that the school qualifies for federal income tax exemption as a not-for-profit organization. To reach the 15-student minimum for middle school membership, schools may join the MHSAA at the 6th-grade level whether or not 6th-grade students participate in athletics. Paragraph A states that the section does not require school districts to become member schools at the junior high/middle school level and does not require districts to sponsor any interscholastic athletics for 6th-grade students. Paragraph B states that if a district's MHSAA Membership Resolution lists a junior high/middle school as a member school, and if that school sponsors a 6th-grade team in any sport or permits a 6th-grade student to participate with 7th- and/or 8th-grade students in any sport, then all of Regulations III and IV apply to all 6th-graders in all sports involving 6th-graders on teams sponsored by that school; if the school does not allow any 6th-graders to participate in a sport, MHSAA rules do not apply in that sport.

The listing pages provide numbered blanks for up to fifteen member high schools and separate blocks for member junior high/middle schools covering 6th, 7th and 8th-grade buildings, each block asking for the name of the member school, the configuration of grades in the building with examples K-6, 6-8, 7-8 and 7-9, anticipated 2025-26 7th and 8th-grade enrollment, anticipated 2025-26 6th-grade enrollment, grade levels for membership among 6, 7 and 8, and a yes/no indication of whether 6th-graders will participate in at least one sport with 7th and 8th graders, with a line for the building housing 6th-graders if not the same building. Instructions direct that junior high/middle schools be listed separately from high schools even where all grades are housed in the same building, and that additional schools be listed on a separate sheet if necessary.

Only one school entry is completed in the document as presented. Under member junior high/middle schools, line 4 names SMITH MIDDLE SCHOOL, with the configuration of grades in the building given as 6-8, the anticipated 2025-26 7th and 8th-grade enrollment given as 419, and the anticipated 2025-26 6th-grade enrollment given as 184. The Yes box is marked X for 6th-graders participating in at least one sport with 7th and 8th graders, with the line for a separate building housing 6th-graders left blank, and grade levels for membership are marked X for 6, X for 7 and X for 8.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education organizational and regular meeting held January 18, 2022 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. The Board re-elected Karl Schmidt president, Dr. Wilson vice president, and Gary Hauff secretary, each through December 31, 2022, and adopted the annual housekeeping resolutions on treasurer, depositories, legal counsel, meeting schedule, and committee assignments, all by 7-0 votes. On the business side the Board awarded site work for the retention pond project to Simone Construction Services for $416,176.50 from the Building and Site Sinking Fund. The meeting adjourned at 8:22 p.m.

Meeting and Attendance
Board meeting minutes for January 18, 2022, held at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. Present in addition to Mr. Schmidt were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, and Wilson; also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators DiPilato, Godfrey, and West. Approximately 14 members of the audience attended. Mr. Schmidt explained that the evening's meeting is where the Board elects officers, appoints committee members for the upcoming year, and approves or authorizes items considered on an annual basis, with the regular meeting following the organizational portion.

Organizational Actions (all votes 7-0)
| Item | Action |
|---|---|
| 22-001 | Mr. Schmidt to serve as acting chairperson until election of a president (moved Philippart, supported Wilson) |
| - | Judy Holmes appointed temporary secretary |
| 22-002 | Mr. Schmidt elected president until December 31, 2022; roll call 7-0 |
| 22-003 | Dr. Wilson elected vice president until December 31, 2022; roll call 7-0 |
| 22-004 | Mr. Hauff elected secretary until December 31, 2022; roll call 7-0 |
| 22-005 | Rick L. West, Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, appointed Treasurer for January through December 2022 |
| 22-006 | Resolution on Fund Depositories and Investments adopted for January through December 2022 |
| 22-007 | Legal counsel designations continued for calendar year 2022 |
| 22-008 | Superintendent continued as Deputy Secretary of the Board for 2022 |
| 22-009 | Judy Holmes designated to post notices of meetings for 2022 |
| 22-010 | 2022 calendar-year meeting schedule adopted |
| 22-011 | Board Committee Memberships for 2022 adopted |

Depositories and Legal Counsel
Depository institutions named: Bank of America, Citizens Bank, JP Morgan Chase Bank, Comerica Bank, Huntington Bank, Fifth Third Bank, Flagstar Bancorp, MILAF (Michigan Liquid Asset Fund Plus, managed by PFM Asset Management, Inc. through Fifth Third Bank), and PNC Bank. Funds may be invested according to Board Policy 5000.06, and the Treasurer may combine money from more than one fund under subsection (1)(h) of Section 380.1223 of the Revised School Code. Designated legal counsel: Clark Hill, PLC; Collins & Blaha, P.C.; Miller Johnson; Thrun Law Firm, P.C.; and Miller Canfield.

Recognition
Seniors Lucia Lee (Athens) and Heejin Shyn (Troy High) were honored for Japanese speech contest awards, along with teacher Mina Mori. January was recognized as School Board Appreciation Month, tied to the district's World Class for ALL - Project 26 strategic plan.

Consent Agenda (22-012)
Approved items A, B and C: minutes of the December 7, 2021 Board Workshop; minutes of the December 14, 2021 Board Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for November 2021. Vote 7-0. Student representatives Alyssa McLarty (Troy College and Career High School), Yara Mashal (International Academy-East), Sasha Palmkoeck (Athens High School), and Sarayu Bethamcherla (Troy High School) reported on school events.

22-013 awarded the bid for flooring replacement work, approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund and/or Building Site and Sinking Fund (7-0). 22-014 awarded the bid for site work projects to Simone Construction Services in the amount of $416,176.50, approved as an expenditure of the Building and Site Sinking Fund (7-0).

Six residents spoke, most on the student mask mandate, the "Test to Stay" program, and diversity instruction. Moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Board adopt the Board Committee Memberships for the 2022 school year as attached; Yes 7, No 0.

Recognition - TSD Mission Moment, Japanese Program. The Board recognized two seniors, Lucia Lee from Athens and Heejin Shyn from Troy High, for recent awards in Japanese speech contests. Heejin won the Silver Award in the J.LIVE Talk Japanese Speech Contest hosted by George Washington University in November 2021, one of only three high school students in the nation selected to participate. Lucia Lee took first place in the Michigan Japanese Speech Contest the previous February and was selected by the government of Japan as one of the American High School Ambassadors invited to visit Japan under the Kakehashi Project - The Bridge to Tomorrow Program, spending 10-14 days in Japan the following spring, all expenses paid. Their teacher, Mina Mori, was recognized for advocacy and dedication in expanding the Japanese program in both high schools. Board Recognition Month. Each January the Troy School District honors and celebrates the trustees of its Board of Education. Personnel and Curriculum. No items recorded.

Business - Flooring Replacement and Polishing Project (22-013). Moved by Mrs. Hammond and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for flooring replacement work be awarded as stated and that the amount be approved as an expenditure of the Capital Projects Fund and/or Building Site and Sinking Fund. Moved by Mr. Gottlieb and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the bid for site work projects be awarded to Simone Construction Services in the amount of $416,176.50 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the Building and Site Sinking Fund. Yes 7, No 0.

Public communication (non-agenda items). Mr. B. J. Lennon, Troy resident and parent of students in the district, addressed the Board regarding his opposition to the mask mandate in place for students. Mrs. Kacy Bailey, Troy resident and parent, thanked the Board and district for ending the quarantine for close contacts with the "Test to Stay" program and also spoke about her opposition to the student mask mandate. Mr. Ollie Apahidean, Troy resident and parent, read an article written by a Troy resident 10 years earlier about how the Troy Board of Education was at that time. Mr. John Tyson, Troy resident, addressed the Board about the type of diversity being taught in the Troy School District. Mrs. Sarah Krieger, Troy resident and parent of one student in the district, addressed the Board about her opposition to the mask mandate and said she had pulled two of her three students from the district. Mrs. Kelly Jones, Troy resident and parent, expressed gratitude for the recent MLK Day presentation and the district's initiative on diversity, equity, and inclusion and thanked the Board for the work being done for the children.

Board comments. Dr. Philippart thanked Mr. Schmidt, Dr. Wilson, and Mr. Hauff for continuing to serve as officers. Upcoming meetings and adjournment. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: An email chain forwarded to the Troy Board of Education packet concerning the IDEA Full Funding Act. The K-12 Alliance of Michigan, through Oakland Schools, asked member districts to pass board resolutions supporting the IDEA Full Funding Act of 2021 (HR 5984) ahead of a March 10 trip to Washington, D.C., noting that Congress committed in 1975 to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost of special education but that the federal investment is today less than 14 percent. Superintendent Richard Machesky forwarded the alert to Board President Karl Schmidt on February 7, 2022, recommending the item be discussed Thursday and placed on the February agenda; Schmidt replied "okiedokie."

Chain of Correspondence
A three-message email thread. The top message is from Karl Schmidt (Troy Board of Education President) to Richard Machesky, copying Judy Holmes, sent Monday, February 7, 2022 at 4:36:01 PM, reading simply "okiedokie." It responds to a forward from Superintendent Richard M. Machesky, Ed.D. (rmachesky2@troy.k12.mi.us, office phone 248-823-4003), sent Monday, February 7, 2022 at 12:28 PM, which stated: "I would also recommend we discuss this on Thursday and prepare to have it on our February agenda." The underlying alert came from the OCSA listserv (ocsa-request@lists.oakland.k12.mi.us) on behalf of Nicole Christian, sent Thursday, February 3, 2022 at 4:57 PM to the OCSA ListServ, copying OSCabinet, David Randels, and Lisa Hansknecht, and forwarded on behalf of David Randels of Oakland Schools.

The Ask
K-12 Alliance members will meet with members of Congress in Washington, D.C. in March to push for full funding of the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), and the alert seeks evidence of broad Michigan support. Districts are asked to work with their school boards to pass resolutions in support of the IDEA Full Funding Act; a sample school board resolution (Sample School Board Resolution.docx) was provided, with the request that boards pass it or a similar resolution at their next meeting if at all possible.

Funding Background
When Congress enacted IDEA in 1975 to ensure all students with disabilities have access to quality public education, it committed to fund up to 40 percent of the additional cost schools would face to provide those services. Today the federal investment in IDEA is less than 14 percent. The IDEA Full Funding Act of 2021 (HR 5984) would require yearly increases to funding for IDEA programs so that the federal government reaches an annual appropriation of 40% of the cost of special education services within the next 10 years.

Logistics
Passed resolutions are to be shared with Katie Whitman-Herzer by email at katie@k12michigan.org. The Alliance will compile the passed board resolutions and bring them to Washington on March 10th to share with members of Congress. Signatories are Robert McCann, Executive Director, and Katie Whitman-Herzer, Administrative Director, The K-12 Alliance of Michigan, P.O. Box 16085, Lansing, Michigan 48901, United States.

Attached Media Clips
The newsletter closes with links to Michigan education coverage: Betsy DeVos backing Michigan petitions for a voucher-like school choice program; Whitmer's proposal to cut taxes and boost schools with Michigan GOP agreement; a Michigan bill to let college students lead classes to curb the teacher shortage; a new Oxford High shooting lawsuit seeking to limit government immunity protection for public schools; Whitmer's call for schools to return to in-person learning; Whitmer and lawmakers exploring ways to ensure in-person classes amid the pandemic; polling on using COVID-19 windfall funds for tutoring and mental health first; Democrats pushing to allow local boards to meet virtually again; districts running out of snow days; and nonprofit and national money pouring into voter ID, public health, and school initiatives. A standard Oakland Schools caution notes the email originated outside the organization.

Substance of the appeal. Addressed to "K-12 Alliance Members," the alert states that in March, members from the K-12 Alliance will be meeting with members of Congress in Washington, DC to push for full funding for the federal Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA), and that the Alliance needs help demonstrating the broad support behind this effort in Michigan. What happens now?" (bridgemi.com, talent-education); and "Nonprofit, national money pour into voter ID, public health, school initiatives" (detroitnews.com, politics, February 2, 2022).
