https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.verbose:
Official minutes of a Board Meeting of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, dated November 17, 2020, held remotely via Zoom Webinar. A public notice was posted to allow community members to participate remotely. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present via Zoom videoconference were Board members Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Wilson, all connecting remotely from locations in Troy, Michigan. Also present were Superintendent Machesky; administrators Birmingham, Carrier, Griffor, DiPilato, Roncone, Haezebrouck, House, Pagel and West; two Student Board Reps; and approximately 48 additional members of the audience. The minutes were submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, with the notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITION. The TSD Mission Moment honored the Michigan Council of Teachers of English (MCTE) Diversity, Inclusion, Justice & Equity (DIJE) Grant Award to Troy High School English teachers. The MCTE DIJE subcommittee awarded Jodie Duda, Erin Fischer-Ballew, Annie Gallagher, Christina Rick and Valerie Valentino of Troy High School a DIJE professional development grant. The grant's goal is to support Michigan English teachers across the state as they engage in professional development they design that privileges diversity, inclusion, justice, and equity work. The five teachers created a program of reading and learning supporting their commitment to "disrupting stock stories, stereotypes, and westernized narratives." Their selected texts are "Black Appetite. White Food: Issues of Race, Voice and Justice Within and Beyond the Classroom" by Jamila Lyiscott; "We Got This.: Equity, Access, and the Quest to Be Who Our Students Need Us to Be" by Cornelius Miner; "The Anti-Racist Teacher: Reading Instruction Workbook" by Lorena German; "Educating Activist Allies: Social Justice Pedagogy with the Suburban and Urban Elite" by Katy Swalwell; and "Linguistic Justice: Black Language, Literacy, Identity, and Pedagogy" by April Baker-Bell. Their intention is to use the concepts and practice from the readings to plan learning for students to build community and engage in rich activist lives.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION. Andrew Rodman, Troy resident and parent of two students who attend Martell Elementary School, addressed the Board about the decision to move elementary students back to remote learning and when they plan to return to in-seat instruction.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA (Resolution 20-084). It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mrs. Hammond that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B and C on the consent agenda: minutes of the October 6, 2020 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the October 20, 2020 Board of Education Meeting; and the Treasurer's Report for September 2020. On roll call vote, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff and Philippart all voted Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

PERSONNEL and CURRICULUM sections contained no items.

BUSINESS - Building Signage (Resolution 20-085). It was moved by Mrs. Anne and supported by Dr. Philippart that the bid for signage for the refurbishment of the school messaging sign at Athens High School and new messaging signs at the Troy Preschool and Troy Learning Center be awarded to Johnson Sign Company in the amount of $92,000 (inclusive of 6% contingency), and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund and/or the Sinking Fund. On roll call vote, Wilson, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart and Schmidt all voted Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

BUSINESS - Bus Purchase (Resolution 20-086). It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mrs. Anne that the bid for school buses be awarded to Hoekstra Transportation in the amount of $1,687,276.00 and that this amount be approved as an expenditure of the 2019 Capital Projects Fund. There was discussion about the end of life cycle for buses and how much money the District could sell them for, and about looking into grants for electric buses; however, Mr. West explained that electric buses would be cost-prohibitive at this time. On roll call vote, Anne, Gottlieb, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt and Wilson all voted Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

Public Communication on non-agenda items: None.

OTHER - Extended Learning Plan. Dr. Machesky shared an update on the District's extended learning plan and provided PowerPoint slides showing the most recent numbers in COVID cases and how much they had been climbing in Michigan and in Oakland County. Ms. Birmingham, Mrs. Griffor and Mrs. DiPilato also shared updates from their respective areas, followed by further discussion among Board members.

Reconfirmation of COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan (Resolution 20-087). The minutes recite that Governor Whitmer's Executive Order 2020-142 provides a structure to support all schools in Michigan as they plan for a return of Pre-K through Post High School education in the fall, and that under this order Michigan school districts must adopt a COVID-19 Preparedness and Response Plan laying out how they will cope with the disease across the various phases of the Michigan Safe Start Plan. Each district must submit a reconfirmation plan to its Board of Education for approval on a monthly basis, and once approved must post its Preparedness Plan on the district website home page for public access. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Dr. Philippart that the Troy Board of Education approve the District's Reconfirmation of the COVID-19 Preparedness & Response Plan. On roll call vote, Gottlieb Yes, Hammond No, Hauff Yes, Philippart Yes, Schmidt Yes, Wilson Yes, Anne Yes. Yes: 6, No: 1.

Open Meetings Act Resolution (Resolution 20-088). It was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Mr. Hauff. The whereas clauses state that Michigan Senate Bill 1108 of 2020 amended the State's Open Meetings Act to restrict the reasons a member of a public body may attend a public meeting remotely beginning January 1, 2021; that advancing technology enabled school districts across the State to meet remotely during the COVID-19 pandemic, develop and implement plans to educate students safely and effectively, and ensure safe and effective public participation; that the restrictions in Senate Bill 1108 allow remote attendance after December 31, 2021 only for absence due to military duty; that threats to public health and other disasters will not vanish on December 31, 2020, and that contagious diseases, flooding, tornadoes, acts of terrorism or other causes occurring after that date could make it unsafe or impossible for public bodies to meet in person or for some members to attend in person; that not allowing an immune-compromised member of a public body to participate remotely would be a clear violation of the Reasonable Accommodation clause of the Federal Americans with Disabilities Act; and that decisions about situations meriting remote attendance are best determined by the local body and the community it represents rather than the State Legislature. The resolved clauses urge the Legislature ideally to amend Senate Bill 1108, Sec. 3a(b) to include a provision requiring local public bodies to set their own policies regarding remote meeting participation based on the needs and priorities of their own local communities rather than dictating universal policy without regard to local control; urge the Legislature at a minimum to amend Sec. 3a(b) to extend indefinitely its provisions allowing remote attendance to accommodate absence due to a medical condition or a statewide or local state of emergency or state of disaster, in addition to military service, and to add accommodations for family emergencies and work obligations; and direct the Board Secretary to transmit copies of the resolution within five business days of adoption to Senator Mallory McMorrow, Representative Padma Kuppa, Oakland Schools Intermediate School District, and the Michigan Association of School Boards. On roll call vote, Hammond, Hauff, Philippart, Schmidt, Wilson, Anne and Gottlieb all voted Yes. Yes: 7, No: 0.

BOARD COMMENTS. Mrs. Hammond spoke about events during the last Board meeting, said it was unfairly presented, and stated she will continue to advocate for what she believes in. Dr. Wilson thanked teachers and administrators for their hard work. Dr. Philippart announced that the TFEE is holding a pandemic-safe fundraiser offering a raffle for $1,000 worth of gift cards, with tickets available at $5 each. Mr. Gottlieb thanked TSD staff and fellow board members. Mr. Hauff thanked veterans for their sacrifice and service, thanked the Central Office staff and teachers, and said oneTROY is the greatest school district in Michigan. Mrs. Anne thanked everyone for their work during difficult times.

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES. Pranay Gupta, student representative from International Academy - East, reported on students learning virtually at his school. Nathania Nartey, student representative from Athens High School, reported on happenings now that students are 100% virtual. Sejal Patel, student representative from Troy High School, and Carleton Thomas, student representative from Troy College & Career High School, were not in attendance.

Dr. Machesky thanked the Board for its continued efforts and support of the LIVE program, congratulated Bemis Elementary School on being recognized as a National Blue Ribbon School for the second time, and wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving. Mr. Schmidt wished everyone a Happy Thanksgiving and announced the next Board Workshop for December 1 at 6:00 p.m. via Zoom.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting was adjourned at 8:45 p.m.

Of that total, the portion for projects and associated issuance costs may not exceed $193,000,000; if net present value savings on the refunding fall below 3.00% of the principal of the Refunded Bonds, the district may issue only the $193,000,000 project portion. **Instrument**
Resolution Authorizing 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), Troy School District, County of Oakland, State of Michigan. Recited as adopted at a regular meeting of the Board of Education held in the School District on November 18, 2025, at 7:00 p.m. local time, with Present/Absent, mover, supporter, AYES and NAYS lines left blank. | Parameter | Limit |
|---|---|

Title and setting: TROY SCHOOL DISTRICT, COUNTY OF OAKLAND, State of MICHIGAN, RESOLUTION AUTHORIZING 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (UNLIMITED TAX GENERAL OBLIGATION). The resolution recites a regular meeting of the Board of Education held in the School District on November 18, 2025, at 7:00 p.m., local time. The PRESENT and ABSENT member lines, the names of the offering and supporting members, and the AYES and NAYS lines are blank in this draft. RESOLUTION DECLARED ADOPTED is followed by signature blocks for Emina Alic, Secretary, Board of Education, including a certification that the foregoing is a true and complete copy of a resolution adopted at a regular meeting held on November 18, 2025, conducted with public notice given in full compliance with the Open Meetings Act, Act 267, Public Acts of 1976, as amended. The document bears the reference number 44944687.

Recitals. At the General School Election held November 8, 2022, the qualified electors approved issuance of bonds, in one or more series, in an amount not to exceed $555,000,000 (the 2022 Bond Proposal), for remodeling, equipping, re-equipping, furnishing and re-furnishing school buildings, athletic fields, playgrounds and other facilities; erecting and completing, equipping and furnishing a replacement middle school and classroom additions and other additions to existing school buildings and other facilities; acquiring and installing instructional technology infrastructure and equipment; and acquiring Sites, preparing, developing and improving Sites, and the purchase of school buses (the Projects). Under Section 6, Article IX and Section 16, Article IX of the Michigan Constitution of 1963, the tax levies for those bonds are without limitation as to rate or amount. The School District previously issued its 2023 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated March 7, 2023, in the original principal amount of $171,370,000, as the first series under the 2022 Bond Proposal. Due to prevailing market conditions at sale, the 2023 Bonds were issued with net original issue premium of $18,629,212.85, which is counted against the $555,000,000 authorization. The Board desires to authorize a second series in an aggregate principal amount of not to exceed $193,000,000. Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, permits refunding of funded indebtedness. The School District previously issued its 2016 School Building and Site Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), dated December 28, 2016 (the Prior Bonds), and the Board determines it is in the best interest of the district to currently refund all or a portion of the Prior Bonds maturing May 1, 2027 through May 1, 2032, inclusive (the Refunded Bonds). Because the source of payment is the same and to reduce issuance and administration cost, the Board combines the new money and refunding issues into a single series in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000, while maintaining a separate capital projects fund for the Projects. If market interest rates rise so that refunding becomes noneconomic or inefficient, the Board retains the option of issuing only not to exceed $193,000,000 for the Projects. The district will sell the bonds by negotiated sale, and authorizes the Superintendent and the Assistant Superintendent, Business Services, either acting individually (the Authorized Officer), to accept a purchase offer, negotiate, approve and execute a bond purchase agreement, and approve other terms and documents. The district must be granted qualified status under Act 34 or receive prior approval from the Michigan Department of Treasury.

Issuance of Bonds. The Bonds are designated 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation), issuable in one or more series with appropriate name, designation or suffix changes, in an aggregate principal amount not to exceed $220,000,000 or such lesser amount as determined by the Authorized Officer, to finance a portion of the Projects, refund the Refunded Bonds, and pay costs of issuance. The portion issued for the Projects and associated issuance costs shall not exceed $193,000,000, with the balance used to refund the Refunded Bonds. If the Authorized Officer, on advice of the Municipal Advisor, determines that net present value savings from refinancing the Refunded Bonds is not at least 3.00% of the principal of the Refunded Bonds, the district may issue not to exceed $193,000,000 for Projects and issuance costs only, in which case the bonds are designated "2026 School Building and Site Bonds" and conforming changes are made to Exhibit A, the Debt Retirement Fund name and purpose, and the application of proceeds.

Bond Details. Bonds are registered as to principal and interest, in denominations of $5,000 or integral multiples, dated as of the date of delivery or another date set by the Authorized Officer, and numbered as determined by the Transfer Agent. Maturities fall on May 1 and/or November 1 in years and amounts set at sale, with final maturity not later than thirty (30) years from the date of issue. Interest rates are set upon negotiated sale, not exceeding a true interest cost of 5.50% per annum, payable semiannually on May 1 and November 1. The underwriter's discount shall not exceed 0.75% of the principal amount. Principal is payable at a bank or trust company selected by the Authorized Officer as registrar and transfer agent; interest is payable by check drawn on the Transfer Agent mailed to the registered owner of record as of the fifteenth day of the month prior to each payment date, subject to future change to conform to market practice. The Bonds may be issued in book-entry-only form through The Depository Trust Company in New York, New York, as serial or term bonds or both, subject to optional or mandatory redemption at times, manner and prices determined by the Authorized Officer. Official notice of redemption by the Transfer Agent must state at minimum the original issue date, maturity dates, interest rates, CUSIP numbers if any, certificate numbers and called amounts, redemption date, redemption price, the place of surrender, and that interest ceases to accrue after the redemption date.

Execution. The Bonds shall be substantially in the form of Exhibit A, signed by manual or facsimile signatures of the President and Secretary of the Board, and are not valid until authenticated by the Transfer Agent, which delivers them to the purchaser per instructions from the Treasurer of the Board upon payment.

Funds. Unless a Common Debt Retirement Fund is established, the Treasurer opens a special depositary account designated 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Debt Retirement Fund, receiving all tax proceeds levied for principal, interest and redemption price, plus any accrued interest received on delivery. A Capital Projects Fund designated the 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Projects Fund receives amounts specified by the Authorized Officer from net sale proceeds and net original issue premium, used solely for Project costs and, as necessary, rebate of arbitrage earnings to the United States Department of Treasury under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended. Issuance costs go to a separate 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds Cost of Issuance Fund, with remaining moneys allocated between the Capital Projects Fund and the Debt Retirement Fund on the advice of Bond Counsel. Moneys remaining after Project completion may be used first for any purpose permitted by the 2022 Bond Proposal and second for any other purpose permitted by law. Net original issue premium related to the new money portion is counted against the 2022 Bond Proposal authorization. An Escrow Fund, funded from the balance of Bond proceeds plus any moneys transferred from the Prior Bonds' debt retirement funds and other available funds, is held as cash or invested in direct obligations of, or obligations unconditionally guaranteed by, the United States of America, held by an Escrow Agent under an Escrow Agreement that irrevocably directs a call for redemption of the specified Prior Bonds, with investments sufficient without reinvestment to pay principal and interest on the Refunded Bonds.

Unlimited Tax. Commencing with the fiscal year beginning July 1, 2026, the district must levy a tax annually sufficient to pay principal and interest when due, without limitation as to rate or amount.

Sale and professionals. Having weighed competitive versus negotiated sale under Act 34 and on the advice of the Municipal Advisor, the Board determines a negotiated sale gives greater flexibility in structuring maturities and timing. Huntington Securities, Inc. is appointed senior managing underwriter; the Authorized Officer may appoint co-managing underwriters if recommended by the Municipal Advisor, and may execute the bond purchase agreement without further Board approval subject to the parameters: true interest cost not exceeding 5.50% per annum, net present value savings not less than 3.00% of the projected debt service on the Refunded Bonds absent refunding based on Treasury guidelines, and underwriter's discount not exceeding 0.75% of principal. The Authorized Officer may execute a sale order evidencing final terms. The law firm of Miller, Canfield, Paddock and Stone, P.L.C. is appointed Bond Counsel, with its periodic representation in unrelated matters of Huntington Securities, Inc. and other potential parties expressly approved. PFM Financial Advisors LLC is appointed Municipal Advisor. The Authorized Officer may apply for bond ratings and purchase municipal bond insurance if deemed appropriate; the President of the Board and the Authorized Officer may each approve preliminary and final official statements and execute the final Official Statement and any amendments.

Disclosure, tax and reimbursement. The district covenants under Rule 15c2-12 to provide the information in Exhibit B. It covenants to maintain the exclusion of interest from adjusted gross income for federal income tax purposes under the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended. Reimbursement declarations under Treas. Reg. § 1.150-2 state the district expects to reimburse itself from debt proceeds for Project expenditures paid subsequent to sixty (60) days prior to the resolution date; the maximum principal amount of debt expected to be issued for the Projects, including issuance costs, is $193,000,000; the reimbursement allocation will occur not later than 18 months after the later of payment or placement in service or abandonment, and in no event more than three (3) years after the original expenditure; expenditures are capital expenditures as defined in Treas. Reg. § 1.1.150-1(b); and no proceeds will be used in a manner described in Treas. Reg. § 1.150-2(h), including creating replacement proceeds within Treas. Reg. § 1.148-1 within one year of the reimbursement allocation. The Authorized Officer may adjust final bond details under Section 315(1)(d) of Act 34, may apply to Treasury for prior approval or file a qualifying statement, may request waivers including rating waivers, and may file a Security Report. Officers may submit a request for interim approval and other actions for qualification under the School Bond Qualification, Approval, and Loan Act, Act 92, Public Acts of Michigan, 2005; the Authorized Officer may approve the Application for Final Qualification in substantially the form of Exhibit C and sign loan agreements, and the Secretary of the Board is directed to execute and submit the completed Application. All conflicting resolutions are rescinded.

Exhibit A, Bond Form. United States of America, State of Michigan, County of Oakland, Troy School District, 2026 School Building and Site and Refunding Bonds (Unlimited Tax General Obligation). Registered Owner: Cede & Co. Interest is computed on the basis of a 360-day year consisting of twelve 30-day months. The bonds are issued under Act 451, Public Acts of Michigan, 1976, as amended, and Act 34, Public Acts of Michigan, 2001, as amended, pursuant to the resolution adopted November 18, 2025, as the second series authorized by the November 8, 2022 election and to refund a portion of an outstanding issue. The full faith and credit of the School District is irrevocably pledged. Transfer agent designation may be changed on notice mailed not less than 60 days prior to an interest payment date. Notice of redemption is given at least 30 days and not more than 60 days prior to the redemption date; bonds are called in multiples of $5,000, and denominations greater than $5,000 are treated as the number of bonds obtained by dividing by $5,000. The Transfer Agent need not register a transfer or exchange during the period beginning 15 days before mailing of a redemption notice and ending at the close of business on the day of mailing. The bond form includes blanks for Interest Rate, Maturity Date, Date of Original Issue, and CUSIP, a Certificate of Authentication with Date of Authentication in 2026, and signature blocks for the President and Secretary.

Exhibit B, Form of Continuing Disclosure Undertaking. Definitions cover Audited Financial Statements (annual audited statements prepared by independent certified public accountants as required by Act 2, Public Acts of Michigan, 1968, as amended), Bondholders, EMMA (the MSRB's Electronic Municipal Market Access system), Financial Obligation, MSRB, Rule, and SEC. The district agrees to provide to the MSRB through EMMA, on or before the last day of the 6th month after the end of its fiscal year, commencing with the fiscal year ending June 30, 2026, annual financial information and operating data similar to Official Statement tables covering: Enrollment - Historical Enrollment; State Aid Payments; Property Valuations - History of Valuations; Major Taxpayers; School District Tax Rates (per $1,000 of Valuation); Tax Levies and Collections; Retirement Plan - Contribution to MPSERS; Debt Statement - Direct Debt; School Loan Revolving Fund (SLRF) Program; and General Fund Budget Summary, current year only, in Appendix C. Audited Financial Statements are filed when available, with unaudited statements filed by the deadline if necessary. Notice of failure to disclose must be timely. Sixteen listed events must be reported within ten business days, including principal and interest payment delinquencies; non-payment related defaults, if material; unscheduled draws on debt service reserves or credit enhancements reflecting financial difficulties; substitution or failure of credit or liquidity providers; adverse tax opinions, IRS proposed or final determinations of taxability, Notices of Proposed Issue (IRS Form 5701-TEB); modifications to holder rights, if material; bond calls, if material, and tender offers; defeasances; release, substitution, or sale of property securing repayment, if material; rating changes; bankruptcy, insolvency, receivership or similar event; consummation of a merger, consolidation, acquisition or sale of substantially all assets, if material; appointment of a successor or additional trustee or trustee name change, if material; incurrence of a material Financial Obligation or agreement to covenants, events of default, remedies, priority rights or similar terms affecting security holders, if material; and default, event of acceleration, termination event, or modification of terms under a Financial Obligation reflecting financial difficulties. Materiality is determined under federal securities laws. Reporting terminates when the district is no longer an obligated person, including upon legal defeasance. The undertaking benefits Bondholders and is enforceable only by specific enforcement, with noncompliance not constituting a default on the Bonds. Amendment provisions track SEC interpretations, including comparison of financial statements if accounting principles change, with notice sent to the MSRB through EMMA. **Purpose**

SOLICITATION AND OUTREACH. RFP 9929 was announced publicly on Tuesday, August 3, 2021, with a newspaper announcement included in the packet, and posted on www.troy.k12.mi.us. RFP TERMS. Troy Schools accepted firm, sealed proposals to establish a five-year building lease beginning November 1, 2021, extending over a five-year period ending October 31, 2026, annually renewed, containing conditions for termination of the lease without penalty costs or fees should federal funds or other applicable funding sources become unavailable. Proposals and two copies marked "RFP 9929 MI Works Professional Office Space Lease" were due no later than Wednesday, 1:00 p.m., August 18, 2021 at the Purchasing Department, Troy School District, 1140 Rankin, Troy, Michigan 48083, where bids would be publicly opened and read aloud. Pre-proposal questions were due no later than noon, Wednesday, August 11, 2021, in writing only, faxed to 248.823.4077 or emailed as a Word document to PurchasingOffice@troy.k12.mi.us. The timeline listed RFP Released Tuesday, August 3, 2021; Pre-proposal Questions Due Wednesday, August 11, 2021 @ Noon; Proposals Due Wednesday, August 18, 2021 @ 1:00 PM; Board Award September 2021. Proposals remain firm for a minimum period of 180 days following opening. Section 1.26 states the intent to award at the September 2021 Board of Education meeting, with the contract in the form of a purchase order.

RFP CONDITIONS. Vendors must provide both a sworn and notarized familial disclosure covering any familial relationship between the owner or key employee of the vendor and any member of the Troy Schools Board of Education or the Troy Schools Superintendent, and a completed, sworn and notarized Iran Economic Sanctions affidavit under Michigan Public Act No. 517 of 2012; a false certification carries a civil penalty of not more than $250,000.00 or two (2) times the amount of the contract, whichever is greater, plus investigation costs and reasonable attorney fees, and three (3) years of ineligibility to bid. Section 1.21 requires satisfactory Workers' Compensation coverage and General Liability and Property Damage Insurance of at least $1,000,000.00 per occurrence and $1,000,000.00 in Aggregate, plus automobile insurance of at least $1,000,000.00. Section 1.23 requires certification of non-debarment and registration on www.sam.gov. Section 1.20 permits Troy School District to end the Agreement term upon thirty (30) days written prior notice under a superseding regulatory order. The proposal form requires that the bid not be withdrawn until after forty-five (45) days after receipt of bids, and that the undersigned execute a contract if notified of acceptance within thirty days. Other clauses cover FOIA exposure, survival, incorporation by reference, non-waiver, nondiscrimination, tax-exempt status except for enhancements or additions to real property, standard forms and contracts, and a non-collusion covenant.

SCOPE AND SPECIFICATIONS. Scoring on a 100 point scale used three factors: (a) Location and proximity to client population, 50 points, considering boundaries within the City of Troy, public transportation access and public parking access; (b) Cost Reasonableness, 25 points, reviewing lease changes, annual updates, lease extensions and increases in local government assessments and insurance; (c) Lease requirements, 25 points, covering updates to the property, maintenance responsibilities, upkeep and repair, indemnification, subrogation and related liabilities. Specifications required no less than 7,000 square feet and no more than 8,000 square feet; free public parking including at least one handicapped space; public transportation access within walking distance; at least 4 bathrooms for staff and customers; a kitchen facility with running water; and accessibility to internet, wireless and telephone technology systems. Additional proposal contents included building specifications, a cost proposal with a 2 year cost history of pass-throughs, a proposed schedule of work, and readiness of facility. The proposal form provides blanks for total square feet and lease cost for 2021-22 through 2025-26, plus five references and an exceptions section.

LEASE COSTS SUBMITTED. L Mason Capitani proposed $104,916.00 for 2021-22 on 7,494 square feet at $14.00 per square foot; $106,789.50 for 2022-23 at $14.25; $110,536.00 for 2023-24 at $14.75; $112,410.00 for 2024-25 at $15.00; and $114,283.50 for 2025-26 at $15.25. Friedman Real Estate proposed $105,000.00 - $150,000.00 for 2021-22 on 7,000 - 10,000 square feet at $15.00; $107,100.00 - $153,000.00 for 2022-23 at $15.30; $109,270.00 - $156,100.00 for 2023-24 at $15.61; $111,440.00 - $159,200.00 for 2024-25 at $15.92; and $113,680.00 - $162,400.00 for 2025-26 at $16.24, with a first year of $15.00/sq ft and rates reflecting a 2% annual increase; amortized leasing costs are listed as TBD. All bid amounts are 'plus' electric and include daily janitorial services; L Mason Capitani costs include maintenance (CAM) costs while Friedman's are additional.

SCORING OF BIDS. Location/Proximity to client Population (50 pts): L Mason Capitani 45, Friedman 40. L Mason Capitani was credited with close proximity to a bus stop and two expressways (696 & I-75) and closeness to the Troy/Clawson/Madison Heights population served; Friedman with close proximity to a bus stop and one expressway (I-75) and closeness to the Troy/Rochester Hills population served. Cost Reasonableness (25 pts): L Mason Capitani 25, with an overall rate per square foot of $14 - $15/square ft including maintenance costs described as below market rates and no cost for moving expenses, buildouts or technology; Friedman 20, with a rate of $15 - $16.24/square ft in line with market rates but higher than current costs, maintenance additional, buildout included, and additional expenses for moving and technology. Lease Requirements (25 pts): both 25, each meeting requirements including space, parking, kitchen and bathrooms and permitting lease termination with notice for financial reasons. Total Points (100 pts): L Mason Capitani 95, Friedman 85. Bids were reviewed and scored by a committee of Todd Hensley, Purchasing Supervisor – Troy School District; Denise Van Hee, Director – Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy; and Cheryl Schubeck, Program Coordinator – Oakland County Michigan Works! Troy, with final scores reflecting the average of all three scores in each category; all three scored L Mason Capitani 45/25/25 and Friedman Real Estate 40/20/25. The district determined that L Mason Capitani received the highest evaluation score and is the most reasonable and cost-effective option at this time, with a proposed rate per square foot below current market rates, adding that it would be very costly to move.

FRIEDMAN PROPOSAL DETAIL. The Friedman Integrated Real Estate Solutions lease proposal, dated Aug 18, 2021 and presented by Robert Gagniuk, Real Estate Specialist, Client Solutions (robert.gagniuk@freg.com, 248.848.4093, ECODE 737, cc Anya Eliassen), covers North Troy Corporate Park, 5505 Corporate Drive, Troy, MI 48084, addressed to Denise. https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Twenty-slide Troy School District presentation titled "2026 TSD Blueprint – World Class for All," presented September 21, 2021, organizing the district's strategic plan around four color-coded pillars: Green (Early Childhood to Career), Red (Equity and Well-Being), Blue (Deep Learning), and Gold (Building Capacity). The stated mission is "Ensuring learning for all," centering the ONETROY community, with each pillar carrying an overview, objectives and key results. Named targets include applying for 16-32 additional GSRP slots from the State of Michigan in 2021-22 and opening an additional 2-3 PreK classrooms serving 40-60 students.
https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.page:
**Format**
Twenty-slide PowerPoint, "2026 TSD Blueprint – World Class for All" (Project 2026 Blueprint), on the Troy School District Board of Education agenda for September 21, 2021. Slides 1-3 cover title, Introduction, and Key Themes and Next Steps; slide 19 is a Summary.

**Mission and Vision (Re)Fresh – slide 4**
Troy School District mission: "Ensuring learning for all. Centers ONETROY community." Four framing statements: Early Childhood to Career – expands on research with access through career; Equity and Well-Being – ensures safety, belonging, and connection; Deep Learning – ensures learning for all throughout the system; Building Capacity – expands to include students, staff, and community as learners.

**Core values and accountability – slides 5-6**
World Class for All pillars are described as carefully aligned to core values of Collaboration, Deep Learning, and Focus. The accountability plan holds the team accountable to Objectives and Key Results.

**Green Pillar – Early Childhood to Career (slides 7-9)**
Objectives: continue investing in high-quality early childhood education, including advocating for universal preschool for all three- and four-year-olds and access for all; expand college and career pathways for middle and high school students through high-quality career and technical education that expands access to computer science, connects underrepresented students to in-demand careers in high-growth sectors, and builds partnerships with higher education institutions and employers for work-based learning, credentials and college credit.
Key results: apply for 16-32 additional GSRP slots from the State of Michigan in the 2021-22 school year; open an additional 2-3 PreK classrooms (40-60 students) in 2021-22; schedule two meetings and/or site visits with local legislators regarding free preschool for all; building leaders participate in Career Readiness meetings and report back to administrative and building teams twice during 2021-22; the Green Pillar Team researches the Portrait of a Graduate framework during two Career Readiness meetings and develops a Portrait of a Graduate survey by the close of the 2021-22 school year.

**Red Pillar – Equity and Well-Being (slides 10-12)**
Overview: safely reopen schools and support students, particularly those disproportionately impacted by the pandemic; fund additional investments supporting the whole child, including community schools providing wraparound services such as afterschool programs and hiring more counselors, social workers and school psychologists; assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities in all school communities.
Key results: increase social work and counseling support in all buildings; review and monitor student data; emphasize adult learning in well-being and equity; create a common understanding of a system of support at all levels.

**Blue Pillar – Deep Learning (slides 13-15)**
Objectives: create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice; improve technology access for students and families with quality training; pursue global best practices in all content areas; assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities.
Key results: monitor instructional data at least 3 times per year; expand job-embedded coaching; leverage technology for all students in all buildings.

**Gold Pillar – Building Capacity (slides 16-18)**
Objectives: improve educator preparation, strengthen pipelines for underrepresented educators, and support current educators; continue job-embedded professional learning for all staff; provide professional learning for staff, community and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community.
Key results: expand hiring networks; expand job-embedded coaching; implement a Delayed Start Model of 90 minutes to ensure collaboration through professional learning, with emphasis on advancing strategic planning priorities; ensure all staff are trained in all departments.

CORE VALUES AND ACCOUNTABILITY PLAN. RED PILLAR – EQUITY AND WELL-BEING. Slide 10 introduces the section. Slide 12 lists key results: increase Social Work and Counseling support in all buildings; review and monitor student data; emphasis on adult learning in areas of well-being and equity; and create common understanding of a system of support at all levels.

BLUE PILLAR – DEEP LEARNING. Slide 13 introduces the section. Slide 14 sets the objectives: create and sustain systems of support at all levels that deepen learning and empower student voice, with access to deep learning described as imperative for all children; improve technology access for students and families while providing quality training to leverage use of technology to deepen learning; continue to pursue the global best practices of all content areas; and assess the need and take action for upgraded facilities to meet the demands of a world class learning environment in all school communities. Slide 15 lists key results: monitor instructional data at least 3 times per year; expand job-embedded coaching; and leverage technology for all students in all buildings.

GOLD PILLAR – BUILDING CAPACITY. Slide 16 introduces the section. Slide 17, headed "Building Capacity of Students, Staff, and Families," sets the objectives: improving educator preparation, strengthening pipelines for underrepresented educators, and supporting current educators; continue to provide job-embedded professional learning experiences for all staff; and provide professional learning opportunities for staff, community, and students with the goal of co-designing impactful experiences to better the OneTroy community. Slide 18 lists key results: expand hiring networks; expand job-embedded coaching; implement a Delayed Start Model to ensure collaboration through professional learning – 90 Minutes, with emphasis on ensuring learning for all staff on advancing strategic planning priorities, citing the Red pillar as an example; and ensure that all staff are trained in all departments.

The deck contains no dollar figures, votes, contract parties or policy numbers; it is a strategic planning framework document.

Agenda item 8.B. for the Troy School District Board of Education meeting of October 19, 2021 is the annual "Report to the Board of Education" for the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021, prepared by the District's independent auditors, Plante & Moran, PLLC. The transmittal letter and all component letters are dated October 5, 2021. The report is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Manager. The firm records its thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to staff's normal daily activities. The document is organized in two parts: Results of the Audit at pages 1-4 and Informational Items at pages 5-15.

RESULTS OF THE AUDIT. Plante & Moran audited the financial statements of Troy School District as of and for the year ended June 30, 2021 and issued its report thereon dated October 5, 2021. The engagement letter is dated June 2, 2021; internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures. The audit was also conducted under Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, with a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 covering internal control over financial reporting and compliance testing. Scope and timing followed the planning meeting of August 13, 2021.

Significant audit findings: significant accounting policies are described in Note 2. No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2021. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance or consensus, and none were recognized in a period different from when they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75; the District's estimates as of June 30, 2021 were $308,094,061 for the pension plan and $48,088,931 for the OPEB plan, based on data from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures are described as neutral, consistent, and clear. There were no significant difficulties with management, no disagreements, and no consultations with other independent accountants; management corrected all immaterial misstatements and signed a representation letter dated October 5, 2021. A 2 CFR Part 200 audit of federal programs was completed, with the compliance report dated October 5, 2021. The auditors read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and noted nothing materially inconsistent.

STATE AID FUNDING BACKGROUND. Spring 2020 predictions of negative impacts to the School Aid Fund led to two Revenue Estimating Conferences, the scheduled one in May 2020 and an additional conference in August 2020. The May conference suggested proration estimated at $685 per pupil, and many districts adopted a final 2020 budget amendment reflecting it; by August 2020 the result was a proration of $175 per pupil for the 2019-2020 fiscal year. Federal assistance began in March 2020 and arrived in waves through 2020 and 2021. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at the 2019-2020 level, no prorations were required, and a $65 one-time per pupil payment was provided; the State also funded districts that fell below a minimum per pupil threshold from the new Educational Stabilization Fund federal program. For 2021-2022, all schools reach the target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap between base and target foundations, with all schools including hold harmless districts receiving at least a $171 per pupil increase, plus progress on School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations covering special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and Great Start Readiness (GSRP).

2021 FUNDING IMPLICATIONS FOR THE DISTRICT. The 2020-2021 target foundation allowance (formerly the basic foundation allowance) was $8,529 and the minimum foundation allowance remained $8,111; the District received a one-time per pupil payment of $65 that was not added to the foundation formula and not retained for 2021-2022. A one-year "super blend" pupil count combined the 2019-2020 count weighted at 75 percent with the 2020-2021 count weighted at 25 percent.

MPSERS COST SUPPORT. Contributions are computed as a percentage of payroll and the required rate continues to increase. The estimated contribution rate for 2020-2021 ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent, with the rate net of state funding support, paid directly by the employer, ranging from 20.96 to 28.21 percent. State support flows through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e of the State Aid Act. The District received $1,070,809 in 147a1, $1,838,621 in 147a2, $11,658,202 in 147c1, and $206,687 of 147e. The total cost of retirement contributions in 2020-2021 represents approximately 42 percent of covered payroll recognized as expenditure, with the District responsible for approximately a 28 percent contribution net of state support.

CORONAVIRUS RELIEF FUND. In summer 2020, approximately $362 per pupil was provided to districts by the Michigan Department of Education through summer state aid payments; the total available to Troy School District was $4,588,959. Because the funding was not approved until July 2020, revenue recognition was deferred to fiscal year 2021, and for the year ended June 30, 2021 the District fully expended the award and recognized the related federal revenue.

PANDEMIC-RELATED FEDERAL FUNDING AND ESSER. Key sources are the Education Stabilization Fund (ESF), whose principal programs are the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) Fund and the Governor's Education Emergency Relief (GEER) Fund, and the Coronavirus Relief Fund. Reimbursement claims could reach back to March 2020. ESSER grants come in three waves: ESSER I, ESSER II (phases 1 and 2), and ESSER III. The District's ESSER I award was $246,411, with ESSER II and ESSER III estimates of $843,258 and $1,893,840. Many districts did not receive phase 1 ESSER II award letters by June 30, 2021, deferring that revenue to fiscal 2022; phase 2 of ESSER II and ESSER III awards become available in fiscal year 2022. ESSER allocations follow the Title I model using economically disadvantaged demographics, so the Legislature and governor set a per pupil floor of $450 for ESSER II; based on its ESSER II level, the District qualified for an equalization payment of $5,036,199 received over the May through August 2021 state aid payments, recognized partly as fiscal 2021 revenue with the remainder in fiscal 2022.

2022 FUNDING IMPLICATIONS. The May 2021 Revenue Estimating Conference was optimistic for 2022, 2023, and 2024. Districts not at the target level in 2021 move to the new $8,700 per pupil target; those already at or above the former $8,529 target receive the $171 per pupil increase. For hold harmless districts such as Troy, the $171 increase is expected in two pieces: $115 per pupil of foundation allowance and $56 per pupil of Section 20m funding. The State set an ESSER III funding floor of $1,093 per student, but the federal government has begun questioning its legality. Pupil membership returns to the pre-fiscal year 2021 method for 2021-2022, weighted 90 percent fall and 10 percent spring. Resources went to summer 2021 programming, credit recovery, and before- and after-school programming through ESSER II plus state appropriations. For 2021-2022 the overall MPSERS contribution rate is expected to increase to 43 percent from 42 percent, with net cost to the District approximating 28 percent.

LOOKING FORWARD TO 2023 AND BEYOND. 2021 carries a projected surplus into 2022, with surpluses expected for 2023 and 2024. Monitoring factors include the economic "bounce back," tapering federal stimulus, the return to in-class instruction, learning loss, enrollment changes, personnel shortages, staffing costs, and retirement system cost trends. The next Revenue Estimating Conference will occur in January 2022.

GRANTS MANAGEMENT AND BUDGETING. The report catalogs increased grants management burden across leadership, board members, the business office, staff, procurement, information technology, support services, and facilities, and recommends a fiscal 2022 risk assessment of key processes and controls. Budget guidance covers multiyear revenue forecasting, monitoring pupil counts, separating recurring contractual payroll from variable pandemic-funded payroll, and budgeting one-time uses of assistance. Federal grant program end dates are laddered through 2024.

MPSERS PLAN STATUS. The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2020 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $35 billion, an increase from $33.8 billion at September 30, 2019, an increase of approximately 3.5 percent, driven largely by less than favorable actuarial experience. At September 30, 2020 the retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $5.4 billion, a decrease from $7.3 billion at September 30, 2019, a decrease of approximately 26 percent, reflecting a reduction in the health care cost trend rate from 7.5 percent to 7.0 percent and favorable plan experience from lower than projected health benefit costs.

FUND BALANCE. During the 2020-2021 school year the District's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000, increasing General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent of expenditures, roughly equal to average operating costs for an 8-week period. The District's fund balance percentage is 19.88 percent, equal to approximately 10.3 weeks of operation. The report cautions that Consumer Price Index growth and decisions on spending COVID-19 relief funds will pressure fund balance in 2021-2022.

CYBERSECURITY AND IT. Education remains a top ransomware target. The "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act," introduced in the House in June 2021, would appropriate $10 million yearly for two years for a school cybersecurity program. The auditors note weak passwords such as "August2021," raise questions about PII and FERPA-covered data on file-sharing sites, flash drives, and personal email, and offer an external vulnerability assessment plus a broader IT assessment covering governance, IT staffing, external service providers, service delivery, network and device management, and cybersecurity policies.

ACCOUNTING AND AUDITING CHANGES. GASB Statement No. 87 (Leases) is effective for the District's June 30, 2022 financial statements, requiring lessees to recognize a lease liability and intangible right-of-use asset and lessors a lease receivable and deferred inflow of resources, with an inventory of lease and embedded-lease contracts needed. SAS No. 134, "Auditor Reporting and Amendments, including Amendments Addressing Disclosures in the Audit of Financial Statements," issued by the AICPA Auditing Standards Board in May 2019, takes effect for the June 30, 2022 audited financial statements, moving the opinion to the top of the letter, expanding the basis of opinion section, explaining materiality and reasonable assurance, enhancing going concern reporting, and introducing key audit matters. The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013; an exposure draft titled "Financial Reporting Model Improvements" was issued in June 2020 with a comment period ending February 2021 on which Plante & Moran commented, and the GASB goal is final standards by June 2022. Proposed changes include more MD&A information, a budget-to-actual column showing variances between original and amended budget, renaming "revenue" as "inflows of resources" and "expenditures" as "outflows of resources," and replacing modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" covering amounts converted to or paid in cash within 12 months of year end, versus today's 60-day receivable rule. Phased adoption would apply at June 30, 2025 for districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under $75 million. A related GASB preliminary views document, "Revenue and Expense Recognition," was released in June 2020, with a standard anticipated during 2025.

https://media.karpowitsch.org/troysd-boa.paragraph: Presented to the Troy School District Board of Education as agenda item 3C on April 21, 2026, the draft Athletic Handbook for Students, revised Spring 2026, sets out eligibility, conduct, and discipline rules for all district student-athletes under MHSAA regulations and the district Student Code of Conduct. It runs 27 numbered pages across fifteen sections covering enrollment and age limits, FinalForms registration, academic eligibility, awards, amateur status, attendance, the TROY CAP PACT, transportation, substance-use discipline, Name-Image-Likeness activity, and appeals. **Document**
Athletic Handbook for Students, Troy School District, Revised Spring 2026. Board of Education draft, agenda item 3C, meeting of April 21, 2026. Fifteen sections, paginated -1- through -27-. Policies marked with an asterisk are Troy School District policies that also align with MHSAA regulations.

**Section I - Eligibility**
Students must be enrolled by the Monday of the fourth week of the semester in which they compete and must reside in and attend the school they represent; students at TCCHS and IA East compete at their home school by residency. High school participants must be under nineteen (19); a nineteenth birthday on or after September 1 preserves eligibility for the balance of the year. Seventh and eighth graders must be under fourteen (14) and fifteen (15) respectively. All registration runs through FinalForms, including the CAP PACT Agreement, Application to Participate, Pay to Participate Agreement (paid before the first competition), Athletics Transportation Agreement, Concussion Awareness form, and MHSAA Acknowledgement of Risk; paper submissions are no longer accepted. Physicals must be completed by an M.D., D.O., physician assistant, or nurse practitioner and dated on or after April 15 of the previous school year. MHSAA limits competition to four (4) seasons per sport in grades 9-12 and four (4) first and four (4) second semesters of eligibility; grades 7-8 are unlimited.

**Academic Standards**
| Setting | Standard |
|---|---|
| District baseline | Passing credit in a minimum of five (5) classes the previous semester |
| Troy College and Career High School | Pass 7 of 8 classes over the previous two semesters |
| Intersect and Inspire High School | Pass 5 of 6 classes over the previous two semesters |
| International Academy | Pass 7 of 8 classes the previous semester |
| Middle school | Pass 5 of 6 classes the previous quarter |

Eligibility is reviewed at the end of each marking period (every 10 weeks); ineligibility runs no less than one full calendar week, Monday through Sunday. Deficiencies from a prior semester carry a minimum sixty (60) scheduled school days of ineligibility. New transfers get one transitional semester at the MHSAA minimum of four (4) passing classes.

**Sections II-XIII**
Awards may not exceed a fair market value of twenty-five dollars ($25.00); violations bring at least one semester of ineligibility. Amateur status bars pay for play, paid officiating, and professional contracts across sixteen listed MHSAA sports, with reinstatement possible only after one full school year. Outside competition in the same sport during the season costs a minimum of two (2) contests at middle school and three (3) at high school. Full-day school attendance is required to participate. Attendance expectations are tiered across middle school, freshman, junior varsity, and varsity, with religious and cultural observances automatically excused. Section VII contains the TROY CAP PACT (Coach-Athlete-Parent) and a grievance ladder: informal contact allowing the coach two (2) school days, Level 1 written complaint answered within five (5) school days, Level 2 to the building Athletic Coordinator answered within seven (7) school days, Level 3 with the building principal and District Athletic Director. Transportation violations cost the next contest, then possible removal. Section XII permits Name, Image, and Likeness activity, called Personal Branding Activity by MHSAA, only outside school time and without school marks, collectives, or booster involvement.

**Substance and Discipline**
High school substance violations are cumulative across a career: first tobacco/nicotine violation is 1 contest or 1 week, not to exceed 10% of the regular season; first alcohol/drug or second tobacco violation is 2 contests or 2 weeks, not to exceed 20%; the next step is removal for the season and ineligibility for the first 50% of the next season; then a 365-day suspension; then permanent loss of eligibility. Middle school violators are removed from the team immediately. The Section XIV framework grades misconduct as Level I (0%, coach-managed), Level II (10-20% of contests), Level III (20-40%), and Level IV (removal, 50-100% of the season). Appeals go in writing to the building principal or athletic coordinator within five (5) school days, with a meeting in two (2) school days and a written decision in two (2) school days; further appeal goes to the district Director of Athletics within two (2) school days. MHSAA eligibility and transfer appeals are separate and final at the state level.

The Troy School District Athletic Handbook for Students, revised Spring 2026, was submitted to the Board of Education as draft agenda item 3C for the meeting of April 21, 2026. The handbook spans fifteen sections over 27 numbered pages and integrates Michigan High School Athletic Association (MHSAA) rules as adopted by the district with district-specific interscholastic policies. It operates under the umbrella of the Troy School District Student Code of Conduct, is in effect throughout the entire year including all seasons of practice and competition, and marks with an asterisk those policies that align with MHSAA regulations. A student-athlete ruled academically ineligible for contests or scrimmages may still practice provided they are not under school suspension, though inability to compete may affect award eligibility under team-specific requirements set by the coach.

Section I, Rules of Eligibility for Participation, requires enrollment by the Monday of the fourth week of the semester of competition, residence within the boundaries of the school attended, and enrollment in the school for which the student competes. Students attending TCCHS and IA East must participate in athletics at their home school based on residency. Under paragraph B, high school students in grades nine through twelve must be under nineteen (19) years of age, with a nineteenth birthday on or after September 1 of the current school year preserving eligibility for the balance of the year; seventh and eighth graders must be under fourteen (14) and fifteen (15) years of age respectively, with the same September 1 rule. Paragraph C requires a parent/guardian and student FinalForms account, the district designated digital platform for athletic clearance, including complete parent and student accounts, all electronic forms and agreements, a current physical form dated after April 15 of the previous school year, and a completed health history and medical profile. Families must read and acknowledge the Athletic Handbook for Student-Athletes, the CAP PACT Agreement form, the Application to Participate form, the Pay to Participate Agreement (paid before the first competition), the Athletics Transportation Agreement form, the Concussion Awareness form, and the MHSAA Acknowledgement of Risk form. Records are stored in FinalForms and accessible to coaches, athletic trainers, the building athletic coordinator, and the district athletic director; paper submissions are no longer accepted.

Paragraph D requires an athletics physical examination by a physician (M.D. or D.O.), physician assistant, or nurse practitioner, dated on or after April 15 of the previous school year, submitted electronically on the MHSAA physical form. Paragraph E limits students to four (4) seasons of interscholastic competition in a specific sport in grades 9 through 12, distributed as no more than four first semesters and four second semesters, with no more than one season per sport per school year even where a sport such as bowling or tennis is offered twice; fall sideline cheer does not count as a competition season against winter competitive cheer. Grades 7 and 8 are not limited in seasons. Paragraph F caps eligibility at four (4) first semesters and four (4) second semesters in grades 9 through 12, with enrollment by the Monday of the fourth week or participation in one or more contests constituting a full semester; high school semesters must be consecutive.

Paragraph G sets academic eligibility. The MHSAA and district baseline requires passing grades (credit) in a minimum of five (5) classes in the previous semester. Troy College and Career High School students must pass at least seven (7) of eight (8) classes over the previous two semesters; Intersect and Inspire High School students at least five (5) of six (6) over the previous two semesters; International Academy students seven (7) of eight (8) in the previous semester; middle school students five (5) of six (6) in the previous quarter. Eligibility is formally reviewed at the end of each marking period (every 10 weeks). A student failing a quarterly grade check becomes ineligible for competition and may regain eligibility through a weekly academic progress report, with ineligibility lasting no less than one full calendar week (Monday through Sunday), a rule that also applies to the MHSAA 60-Day Rule. Deficiencies tied to the previous semester carry a minimum of sixty (60) scheduled school days of ineligibility in the current semester. Transfer students new to the district receive one transitional semester during which they must meet the MHSAA minimum of passing four (4) classes. Middle school student-athletes in grades 7-8 must pass at least five of six classes each marking period, with weekly progress monitoring for those who fall below.

Section II, Awards, permits symbolic or merchandise awards not exceeding a fair market value of twenty-five dollars ($25.00), plus banquets, luncheons and dinners, non-competitive trips, and spectator admission to non-Troy School District events accepted in kind. Cash, merchandise certificates, negotiable financial documents, and memberships, privileges, services, athletic equipment, apparel or jewelry above the $25 limit are prohibited, as is acceptance of an award on a student-athlete's behalf by a parent, relative or friend before high school graduation. Violation brings ineligibility for at least one semester from the date of the violation; a violation after the fourth Monday of a semester costs the remainder of that semester and the entire next semester.

Section III, Maintaining Amateur Status, bars accepting money or valuable consideration for athletic participation (separate from permissible Name, Image and Likeness activity), receiving compensation for officiating interscholastic contests, and signing a contract or agreement to play or try out with a professional team. The rule applies to MHSAA-sponsored baseball, basketball, cross country, football, golf, gymnastics, soccer, softball, skiing, tennis, track and field, volleyball, wrestling, ice hockey, competitive cheer, and swimming and diving. Instructional fees or pay for coaching youth or recreational sports may be allowed if unconnected to interscholastic athletics. Violators are ineligible and may not apply to the MHSAA for reinstatement until one full school year has passed.

Section IV, Outside of School Athletic Competition, prohibits non-school club, AAU, travel or rec competition in the same sport during the season once a student has practiced, tried out, scrimmaged or competed for a school team. Middle school violators are ineligible for a minimum of the next two (2) contests or dates of competition, high school for a minimum of the next three (3), with ineligibility extending up to the remainder of the season. The Limited Team Membership provision sets a minimum of the next three (3) days of competition and a maximum of the remainder of the season. Students may not participate in all-star contests in an MHSAA-sponsored sport during the school year. These rules reflect Section 12(A) - Limited Team Membership of the MHSAA handbook.

Section V requires a student to be in school for the full instructional day to participate that day. Excused absences include illness with documentation, medical or dental appointments with verification, court appearances, religious observances, bereavement or family emergencies, and pre-approved college visits or academic travel, with extenuating circumstances approved by the building principal or designee. Unexcused absences, including skipping class, oversleeping, leaving campus without permission, and failure to document, render a student ineligible that day, and participation anyway is a Code of Conduct violation. Section VI addresses attendance at practices and contests, listing excused categories including religious holidays and cultural observances, which the district states will be automatically excused without penalty when the coach is notified in advance. Unexcused absences may bring reduced playing time, loss of leadership roles, and team consequences. Level-based expectations are stated separately for middle school (grades 7-8), freshman level (primarily 9th grade), junior varsity (JV/JVA), and varsity, each repeating that school-day attendance is required and that cultural and religious observances are honored.

Section VII sets season expectations by level with distinct philosophies: middle school focuses on skill development and playing time for all when possible; the freshman/JV B level introduces merit-based playing time and a shift from equal play to earned play; junior varsity/JVA (9th-11th grades) prepares athletes for varsity demands; varsity represents competitive excellence with playing time earned. The section contains the TROY CAP PACT (Coach-Athlete-Parent PACT), which all student-athletes, parents and coaches must review and sign before each season through FinalForms, enumerating the coach's expectations of parents (nine items), parents' expectations of the coach (six items), the coach's expectations of the athlete (fourteen items), the athlete's expectations of the coach (ten items), and the athlete's expectations of parents (six items). A complaint/grievance policy follows: the athlete first speaks with the coach; informally the parent then contacts the coach and allows two (2) school days for a response and possible face-to-face meeting; Level 1 is a written concern to the coach with a written reply within five (5) school days; Level 2 is a written disagreement to the building Athletic Coordinator within five (5) school days with the Level 1 response attached, an independent investigation, and a written reply within seven (7) school days; Level 3 is a meeting with the Building Principal and District Athletic Director. Complaints alleging a potential criminal act or immoral behavior by a coach begin at Level 2.

Section VIII requires travel with the team on district-provided transportation, whether school-owned, chartered or otherwise approved. Students may leave a contest site with a parent, legal guardian, or adult family member only with prior written permission through FinalForms and advance coach approval. Where district transportation is not used, the coach must document departure with a signed sign-out form or approved sign-off list. A first violation makes the student ineligible for the next scheduled contest while still practicing; a second may bring removal from the team for the season. Section IX makes student-athletes financially responsible for uniforms and equipment lost, abused, damaged through negligence, or not returned, suspending future season participation and withholding awards, letters and recognitions until resolved.

Section X prohibits use, possession, sale or distribution of tobacco and nicotine products including vaping devices, alcohol, marijuana, non-prescribed controlled substances, look-alike substances, banned performance-enhancing drugs or supplements as defined by the NCAA and Michigan Department of Health, prescription medication not prescribed to the student, and misuse of over-the-counter medication, at all times on and off school grounds year-round. Middle school violators are immediately removed from the team, with reinstatement considered only after a meeting with the student, parent/guardian and building administrator. High school consequences are cumulative from the first day of participation as a freshman: a first tobacco/nicotine violation brings a minimum 1 contest or 1 week suspension, whichever is greater, not to exceed 10% of the regular season, an optional educational workshop at family cost, and possible parent conference; a first alcohol/drug violation or second tobacco violation brings a minimum 2 contests or 2 weeks, not to exceed 20% of the regular season, a mandatory parent meeting with coach and building administrator, and a required substance education or intervention program at family cost, with missed games carrying over to the next season; a second alcohol/drug or third tobacco violation brings immediate removal for the current season and, if less than 50% of the season remains, ineligibility for the first 50% of the next season plus a professional assessment from a Michigan Department of Health-approved provider at family cost; a third alcohol/drug or fourth tobacco violation brings suspension from all athletic participation for 365 days from the date of the confirmed violation; a fourth alcohol/drug or fifth tobacco violation brings permanent loss of athletic eligibility in the Troy School District. In-season violations apply immediately; out-of-season violations are enforced at the start of the next season of participation, even in the next school year.

Section XI makes summer and off-season camps, clinics and conditioning strictly voluntary, and per MHSAA regulations prohibits requiring off-season participation as a condition of making a team, earning a roster spot, receiving playing time, or level placement. Section XII permits Name, Image, and Likeness activity, termed Personal Branding Activities by the MHSAA, only when independent of school teams, not tied to athletic performance or team success, outside school time and away from school facilities and events, and compliant with MHSAA rules. Prohibited are use of school names, logos, uniforms, mascots or facilities, implying school, district or MHSAA endorsement, pay-for-play, agreements arranged by coaches, school personnel or booster organizations, collectives or group NIL agreements, and promotion of products violating school policy. Agreements must be reported per MHSAA requirements before participation; the district, coaches and staff provide no legal, tax or contract guidance; NIL may not be used to influence enrollment, transfer or team placement.

Section XIII allows sport-specific supplemental rules developed by coaches and approved by the building athletic coordinator and building principal or designee, with athlete-specific plans or behavior contracts approved by the building athletic coordinator or Director of Athletics; all supplemental rules must be written and distributed at the start of the season. A student suspended from school is ineligible for practices and contests during the suspension; an academically ineligible student may practice at the coach's discretion; a student dismissed for the season forfeits team awards and varsity letters.

Section XIV establishes the Student-Athlete Handbook Disciplinary Framework, aligned with MHSAA and National Federation of State High School Associations (NFHS) standards, with the district Code of Conduct taking precedence in any conflict. Level I minor violations (tardiness, dress code, non-directed inappropriate language, failure to follow team procedures) draw warnings, parent communication, temporary reduction in playing time, team consequences, and restorative conversation. Level II moderate violations (repeated Level I, disrespect, minor unsportsmanlike conduct, social media misuse) draw suspension from contests (1-3 or a defined percentage), parent conference, behavioral contract, and removal from leadership roles. Level III major violations (insubordination, ejection per MHSAA/NFHS rules, bullying, harassment or hazing, substance use, academic dishonesty) draw multi-contest suspension aligned with MHSAA minimums, temporary removal from team activities, mandatory parent conference, educational interventions, and probation. Level IV severe violations (fighting, hazing, theft, vandalism, criminal behavior, distribution of controlled substances, serious harassment or threats) draw immediate suspension, removal for the remainder of the season or longer, referral to school or legal authorities, and loss of awards, honors and leadership roles. Parent/guardian notification is required for Levels II-IV. The accompanying percentage-based suspension framework sets Level I at 0% (coach-managed), Level II at 10-20% of contests (typically 1 contest), Level III at 20-40% of contests and must meet or exceed MHSAA minimums, and Level IV at removal covering 50-100% of the season. The Athletic Director has final authority on athletic eligibility decisions; athletic suspensions may carry from one season to the next, including into the subsequent school year.

The final section, headed Section XIV but listed in the table of contents as Section XV, sets appeal procedures for violations of Sections V-XII. An appeal must be initiated in writing to the building principal and/or building athletic coordinator within five (5) school days of the date the discipline was communicated; a meeting including the student and coach, and possibly the parent/guardian, is convened within two (2) school days; a written decision upholding, modifying or revoking the action issues within two (2) school days. Further appeal goes in writing to the district Director of Athletics within two (2) school days of the building-level decision. Appeals concerning eligibility, transfer rules, or MHSAA regulation violations are submitted through the school athletic coordinator or district director of athletics to the MHSAA, follow a separate process, and are final and binding at the state level.
